articles.text: On Thursday, September 22 Piedmont’s League of Women Voters held an online forum for candidates for City Council in the November 8 General Election. Moderator Nancy Beninati posed questions to the candidates and a recording is available on the League’s Youtube Channel: Youtube.com/ watch?v=8wVGNA_B_AU/ Five of the six candidates were in attendance for the forum; Bridget Harris did not attend, but Beninati read a prepared statement by Harris. Betsy Andersen, Nancy Bostrom, Jennifer Long, Tom Ramsey, and Jeanne Solnordal answered seven questions posed in advance by Piedmont residents. Questions were selected by LWV members to eliminate duplicate inquires. Each candidate delivered a two-minute opening statement and following each question had 90 seconds to provide an answer. The forum ended with each candidate allowed to provide a one-minute closing statement. articles.text: Let’s elect proven local leaders Editor: In our small and very engaged community, we benefit most from leaders who are good listeners, who do their research, and who work well with others. As we’ve all experienced, so often the most difficult issues are ones that weren’t expected: for example, the impact of COVID on our schools, and the State-imposed requirement to plan for more housing in Piedmont. We need level-headed leaders who respond well to unexpected challenges by listening to all community members, who keep an open mind and seriously consider differing opinions, who study the options and consider all ramifications, and who work respectfully with staff and stakeholders in support of community goals. I wholeheartedly endorse Betsy Andersen and Jen Long for City Council. Betsy and Jen are both experienced attorneys who are also excellent listeners, clear thinkers, and thoughtful policy makers. As they have proven by their service on our City Council, Betsy and Jen ask good questions, meet with residents to navigate challenges, and look for creative opportunities to strengthen our community. My third vote for City Council will go to Tom Ramsey, an architect whose long service to our Planning Commission demonstrates his ability to listen carefully and make thoughtful well-reasoned decisions. While I was still on the Board of Education, I had the pleasure of working with Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson. They both served as Parent Club Presidents during the pandemic, and they clearly are committed to the impressive in their own right, and they will be outstanding representatives for the community on our School Board. We are fortunate to have so many talented community members step up to volunteer their time on behalf of our city and schools. Please join me in voting for these proven leaders in the upcoming election! –Sarah Pearson Piedmont Board of Education, 2012-2020 460 Boulevard Way, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org

articles.text: Editor: I am grateful to the candidates who have stepped up to lead our community forward. To me the choices on November 8 for City Council are clear: Betsy Smegal Andersen, Jen Long and Tom Ramsey. I have had the pleasure of working closely with Betsy since her appointment to City Council in 2017. Betsy brings a deep understanding of the essence of what is great about living in Piedmont and a vision for how we will continue to thrive in the future. She has prioritized infrastructure investments with a keen focus on prudent fiscal management to make the most of taxpayers resources. The council unanimously appointed Jen Long to the Piedmont City Council, from among a pool of qualified and talented community volunteers. articles.text: I subscribed to PREC’s newsletter when I was editor of the Piedmont Post because I understand the positive traction this group has in the community. PREC was formed during my tenure at the Post and I greatly value the good work this group does in the community. I’ve since left the Piedmont Post to pursue other journalistic endeavors. I’d like to add my unsolicited two cents, introduced with verbatim quotes from PREC’s newsletter dated September 22: “The PREC steering committee must correct the record: we did not create the website, nor do we have control over its content.” 1 – Please understand that letters to the editor are not factchecked by journalists and editors (especially if they do not name an elected official or office) in the same way a news story is. This is true in all publications, from Piedmont Post to the NY Times. Although NYT v Sullivan honed in on publishers’ liability with advertising, I would argue the same situation applies here. In this quote you are asking for leniency from those who read your published content, took it as fact, and still perceived it negatively; and yet, you ask a publication to review a published sample with to-the-line fact-checking. If the Post were to say, “we did not create the [letter to the editor], nor do we have control over its content,” would that be acceptable to you? My answer is no – of course you should review anything you publish. “We call upon the Post to follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous content” 2 – I believe that your call for the Post to “follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous contact” is self-serving at best. There is no clarification or expansion on what is considered “erroneous content” published – how does this help your readers? – there should be some supporting arguments since that is a fairly pointed statement. Think of letters to the editor as an open forum. In my opinion, the right thing to do would be to contact the publisher and ask for that person’s contact information to have an informed and educated dialogue. The decision you made was to attack the press – and, history will tell you better than I where that leads. “If the Post had contacted us, PREC would have been happy to clarify” 3 – I have worked with Piedmont Post since PREC’s inception. Only a handful of times did anyone at PREC send me a press release. I received this newsletter after my departure and was stunned. The newsletter is authored by seven individuals and should offer a contact for reporters to follow-up. In this case, someone who did not author the article is assumed to have written the article, which would be used as a quote. I had a great rapport with many organizations in Piedmont, but PREC never reached out to me or the Post for publicity, whereas the others took initiative. My point being – help us help you but fostering a relationship with press. The Post, Mercury, EBX, many would love to hear and publish what you’re doing. As a layperson and not press, I strongly ask you to hear all dialogue as you approach issues that the community holds at heart. I promise you it won’t all be nice, as is the nature of community dialogue. This newsletter felt pointed and angry, both at a local publication and a resident. This made me sad as a journalist knowing the relationship I had with PREC was minimal. I felt as though I should have done more to promote and highlight the good work you do, and yet, slamming a local publication seems antithetical to your mission of transparency. Quite literally, journalism is the only profession protected by the constitution. We take our jobs seriously – which is why now, even after leaving, I was personally offended by this newsletter. I truly hope all has been amended and that a fluid relationship between PREC and the Post can be fostered. I understand that a very productive meeting took place in the Post’s office last Friday at the invitation of the Post. I believe we are all hoping it Will benefit all community leaders, members, and stakeholders in the long run.
articles.title: In response to recent assertions by PREC

articles.text: Editor: In its September 21, 2022, issue, the Piedmont Post published a letter from Tu Ngoc Nguyen asserting that the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) created a website, PiedmontVotes.com, that “smears” several candidates in the upcoming election. The PREC steering committee must correct the record: We did not create the PiedmontVotes.com website, nor do we have control over its content. We shared the site’s link in our newsletter because it was the only resource we found that had collected public information about all candidates. If anyone is upset by the site’s content, please note that: 1) The website is a compilation of candidates’ public statements and other publicly available information. 2) Concerns should be sent through the website itself to the site’s creator. In addition, counter to the claim in Nguyen’s letter that PREC is anti-Asian, we point out that the PREC steering committee supports an Asian American candidate, three of our steering committee members are Asian American, and we organized the only anti-Asian hate solidarity event in our city to speak out against Asian hate. Facts do matter. Let’s keep the focus of the upcoming elections on the most important issues that will help our schools and city move forward in creating a great community for all. –The PREC Steering Committee: Amy Whalen Griffith Deb Leland Diana Lee Fairuz Abdullah Irene Cheng Sarah Karlinsky Susy Struble prec-steering@googlegroups.com

Let’s keep the focus of the upcoming elections on the most important issues that will help our schools and city move forward in creating a great community for all. –The PREC Steering Committee: Amy Whalen Griffith Deb Leland Diana Lee Fairuz Abdullah Irene Cheng Sarah Karlinsky Susy Struble prec-steering@googlegroups.com Accusations in print seen as baseless Editor: Prior to reading the letter to the editor from Tu Ngoc Nguyen in the Post (September 21), I was only vaguely aware of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign and completely unaware of the website, piedmontvotes.com. I was unable to find any candidate endorsements by PREC on their website, but I did go to the piedmontvotes.com site to review the smear campaign against Shirley Hooi that had so upset the writer. I cannot see how posting public letters from Ms. Hooi to the Piedmont Post and a public statement about an Exedra article, without comment one way or the other, can be characterized as a “smear campaign”. What I read on the Piedmont Votes site are Ms. Hooi’s own words accompanied by a single letter from another citizen correcting Ms. Hooi’s representation of critical race theory and challenging the notion that it is being taught, or contemplating being taught, to young children in our public schools. This is a “smear”? Further, to imply through rhetorical questions that PREC and what was posted on the Piedmont Votes site contributes to the climate of Asian hate – indeed “encourages attacks” – is, well, beyond any objective reading of the contents, to put it as politely as I can. In my view, such baseless accusations diminish the tragic reality of the actual threats and attacks faced by persons of Asian descent in our society today, and the shameful history of discrimination, threats, and attacks visited upon Asians in America (about which I learned nothing when I was in public school). I read Ms. Hooi’s letters to the editor when they were first published. I thought it unfortunate to see the contentious – and, in my opinion, false – narratives promoted in those letters enter into the public discourse in our small town. The writer is “embarrassed” and laments that there is “divisive national politicking” in Piedmont. I sympathize and agree; and that is why I won’t be voting for Shirley Hooi. –Bill Brizendine Anonymous websites do not serve our kids Editor: As a candidate for school board in November, I’m responding to a letter in last week’s Piedmont Post that pointed to an anonymous website sharing the past letters and editorials of candidates like myself. The website draws from publicly available information online; however, it fails to name the owner or group behind the site. I want to state clearly that I am unequivocally opposed to any website that hides behind anonymity, while degrading civil discourse in our community. It’s extremely disheartening to see anonymous outreach and communication become a staple of political discussion in our town. Last year, we saw an anonymous online survey posted by a group called Piedmonters for Fair Education, which asked the school community to report on Piedmont teachers who discussed diversity in a way that offended the group’s politics. This tactic is reprehensible. It is reminiscent of authoritarian governments that break down the bonds between citizens by asking neighbors to spy on each other. I call on my fellow candidates running for office to condemn the use of anonymous political websites that attempt to stifle candid discussion or intimidate community members. I also want to correct an error in last week’s letter stating that there is a “lone Asian running for school board.” I am the daughter of immigrants from India, who came to the United States with extremely limited resources to attend school and improve the opportunities available to them. Knowing the tenacity and resilience needed to pursue that dream, and knowing what they have overcome to build a life in the Bay Area, I am extremely proud of who they are and what they have accomplished. Like many children of immigrants, I have deep appreciation for my heritage and strive to instill the same sense of pride in my children. I would like to stress that I am my own candidate. While I value endorsements and support from individuals and groups that are aligned with me in the priorities I see for the school district, one of my campaign promises is to increase dialogue and transparency among community members so that all stakeholder voices are heard. I encourage voters to attend the League of Women Voters’ Candidate Forum on Thursday Sept. 29 at 7 pm, where you will have a chance to hear directly from all three candidates and learn about our platforms and priorities. Our children deserve more than voting for the loudest person in the room shouting half-truths. As an active volunteer for Piedmont School District and the City of Piedmont, I have had the privilege of meeting many members of our community so I feel like I know this community. I trust this community. I truly believe we are capable of having the important and necessary conversations that ultimately serve our kids. In this quote you are asking for leniency from those who read your published content, took it as fact, and still perceived it negatively; and yet, you ask a publication to review a published sample with to-the-line fact-checking. If the Post were to say, “we did not create the [letter to the editor], nor do we have control over its content,” would that be acceptable to you? My answer is no – of course you should review anything you publish. “We call upon the Post to follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous content” 2 – I believe that your call for the Post to “follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous contact” is self-serving at best. There is no clarification or expansion on what is considered “erroneous content” published – how does this help your readers? – there should be some supporting arguments since that is a fairly pointed statement. Think of letters to the editor as an open forum. In my opinion, the right thing to do would be to contact the publisher and ask for that person’s contact information to have an informed and educated dialogue. The decision you made was to attack the press – and, history will tell you better than I where that leads. “If the Post had contacted us, PREC would have been happy to clarify” 3 – I have worked with Piedmont Post since PREC’s inception. Only a handful of times did anyone at PREC send me a press release. I received this newsletter after my departure and was stunned. The newsletter is authored by seven individuals and should offer a contact for reporters to follow-up. In this case, someone who did not author the article is assumed to have written the article, which would be used as a quote. I had a great rapport with many organizations in Piedmont, but PREC never reached out to me or the Post for publicity, whereas the others took initiative. My point being – help us help you but fostering a relationship with press. The Post, Mercury, EBX, many would love to hear and publish what you’re doing. As a layperson and not press, I strongly ask you to hear all dialogue as you approach issues that the community holds at heart. I promise you it won’t all be nice, as is the nature of community dialogue. This newsletter felt pointed and angry, both at a local publication and a resident. This made me sad as a journalist knowing the relationship I had with PREC was minimal. I felt as though I should have done more to promote and highlight the good work you do, and yet, slamming a local publication seems antithetical to your mission of transparency. Quite literally, journalism is the only profession protected by the constitution. We take our jobs seriously – which is why now, even after leaving, I was personally offended by this newsletter. I truly hope all has been amended and that a fluid relationship between PREC and the Post can be fostered. I understand that a very productive meeting took place in the Post’s office last Friday at the invitation of the Post. I believe we are all hoping it Will benefit all community leaders, members, and stakeholders in the long run. articles.text: This year’s Piedmont Artisanal Brewing Contest will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday evening, October 7. The Piedmont Center for the Arts will host one of its most popular events of the year the first weekend of October. On Friday, October 7, the 10th Annual Piedmont Beer Festival will take over the Center for the Arts for a celebration of Artisanal brewers and their finest home brews. In addition to sampling the best of local home brewers, guests are invited to have a legitimate German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center, with freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. Food is provided by Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery. A panel of Piedmont celebrity judges will award prizes to home brewers for Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, Best IPA, and Best in Show. This year’s celebrity judges are Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson. Brewers already registered include Piedmont brewers Matt Gerhardt, Carter Dunlap, Trevor Fleshman, Zachary Jones, Ed Sweeney and Case Gardner. In addition, a 2021 winner, Kyle Blomseth, a member of the Bay Area Mashers, has also signed up. He won last year’s Specialty Beer Category with a Belgian Style Ale. To enter home brews, contact Center for the Arts board member Carter Dunlap at carter@dunlapclan.net. Include your name, phone & e-mail address and the type of beer you will bring. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue.

articles.text: from the City of Piedmont The City of Piedmont is currently updating the Housing Element of the City’s General Plan , which outlines the policies and programs that will guide g rowth and development in within Piedmont over the next 8 yea rs. Community involvement is essential to shaping this docu ment. To that end, the City of Piedmont is sharing t hese facts about the Housing Element that every resident should know. Lea rn more about the Housing Element update process at P P i i e e d d m m o o n n t t i i s s H H o o m m e e . .o o r r g g . FACT: Adopting an updated Housing Element IS NOT OPTIONAL. The State of California requires all cities to update their Housing Element every 8 years to accommodate their assigned Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA). The updated Housing Element must receive certification from the FACT: Putting the draft Housing Element to the voters as a ballot initiative would diminish—not enhance—local control. Voting on the Housing Element would not eliminate any requirement for Piedmont to comply with State law. Failure to adopt an updated Housing Element by the State mandated deadline could result in harsh and costly fines and could limit Piedmont’s authority over future local land use decisions. FACT: The City Charter does not require a vote on the type of zoning changes proposed in the draft Housing Element. Piedmont’s City Charter (Sec 9.01) gives the City Council authority over the General Plan, which includes the Housing Element. Adding uses or changing densities to existing zones does not require voter approval. FACT: The Housing Element does not require Piedmont to build 587 units of new housing. The Housing Element only plans for the CAPACITY for development of new housing. It does not require the actual development or construction of those housing units. FACT: The City government itself would not build housing. Any development being planned in the Housing Element would be carried out by individual property owners and private developers. FACT: Affordable housing is less than half of the City’s allocation. Piedmont’s allocation includes 257 affordable (low and very low income) units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units, for a total of 587. FACT: The City cannot reduce its RHNA allocation or otherwise get out of updating its Housing Element. Piedmont submitted seven letters to the Association of Bay Area Governments (ABAG) articulating concerns about the 6th cycle housing allocations. Due in part to these actions, our mandate is 50% less than many comparable cities. The period for appeals is over. If the City had appealed to ABAG, we would have risked increasing our numbers. All appeals to ABAG were rejected except for one that involved an incorrect jurisdictional boundary. FACT: The Draft Housing Element DOES NOT include “high-density” apartment buildings throughout Piedmont. The current draft does not propose allowing apartment buildings in single-family areas, which comprise about 86% of land in Piedmont. The draft proposes increasing allowed density only in existing commercial/mixed use areas, public facilities, and multifamily zones, as well as for houses of worship building on their own property. Visit PiedmontIsHome.org to learn more, share comments, and stay informed about Piedmont’s Housing Element update. Questions? Contact us at piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: FACTS ABOUT PIEDMONT’S HOUSING ELEMENT

articles.text: Wildwood moms Xenia Meyer (left), Anne Wheeler, Amelie Kappes, Beach Elementary. “We wanted to make sure families who weren’t within walking distance of the park also had the chance to join the fun,” says Giving Campaign co-chair Katie Sharafi. As in past years, Mulberry’s Market donated the popsicles. The day ended with a reception for new incoming parents at the Community Hall courtyard. This year’s campaign chairs are Dana Murray, Julia Ruthven and Katie Sharafi, supported by the Piedmont Education Foundation staff and a dedicated group of volunteers. Over a marathon few months this team will put up banners at the schools, conduct community outreach, write personal letters, and make hundreds of phone calls. “We start planning the next Giving Campaign as soon as the current one ends,” said PEF executive director Heather Frank, “The messaging, outreach, events, and materials represent months of work from the office team and dozens of volunteers.” A nearly unprecedented California budget surplus has provided a one-time infusion of additional funds for the coming school year, allowing the Giving Campaign to reduce the requested per-child donation from prior years. This year, the team asks that families donate $1,980 representing the funding gap for each student. “Even when the state has a surplus, there’s still an enormous funding gap that needs to be filled by the community,” says Sharafi. The requested amount will help cover the difference between what the district receives from other funding sources and the cost of providing the quality of education that students receive in Piedmont. “We are asking for less per student but working to have increased participation rates this year,” said Sharafi. “We want everyone to participate and hope families will give a gift that is Wildwood students Isabelle Wheeler (left), Margot Miller, James DiPiazza, Nina Meyer, Liana Shahid, and Piper Lang. meaningful to them.” Last year’s record-breaking Giving Campaign raised $3.7 million for Piedmont schools. “Parents and community members dug deep, but overall participation was still down from preCOVID levels,” said Frank, “We want everyone to understand that participation matters. A donation of any amount makes a real difference for our schools.” The funds from the Giving Campaign will help keep Piedmont class sizes small and fund a broad array of student needs, from wellness to classroom aides to libraries and the arts. “I’ve always seen our family contribution to the Giving Campaign as an investment, not a gift,” says Sharafi. “You really do see the return on that investment in the caliber of the teachers and staff.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to make a donation, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org. Beach School students: Mila Small (left) and Brianna Ackerman.

articles.text: Family Sanity, a non-profit parent support group for families with older children and young adults dealing with mental illness is hosting a special event on Monday, October 3, at 7 p.m. on Autism. The meeting will be available on Zoom. Do you have an older teen or a young adult with Autism? Are you wondering what their options are after high school? Is having them live at home getting more and more difficult? Do you want to know about special programs or schools for them? Are you wondering if there are services provided by the state that you should explore? The meeting will cover all this and more with a group of parents who have been down these roads. It can be a constant challenge keeping on top of what is available for those with ASD, and this special Family Sanity meeting is designed to help you. One of the participants will be Piedmont resident and Oakland therapist Liz Fitzgerald, who holds an MFT and is well-versed in counseling families with autistic children. Monthly meetings are held on the third Tuesday of each month at 7 pm via zoom. The organization was founded nine years ago by former Piedmont resident Lisa Scimens. Register now on the website: www.familysanity.org. Space will be limited to 12 parents.
articles.title: Family Sanity hosts event on Autism on October 3

articles.text: For people ready to jump back into worldwide travel, Piedmont Adult School is offering a class titled “Travel Planning: Where Do You Want To Go? Make It Happen!”. articles.text: What is launching onboard Artemis 1? Aside from exciting new technology, there are also special items like 245 Silver Snoopy pins, a Moon rock from Apollo 11 and a USB with essays from the Artemis essay contest. One of the essays launching with Artemis 1 was written and submitted by teen Galaxy Explorer, Sowmya. In her essay, titled Yin for the Win, the high school student considers what it would be like to lead a lunar expedition, including who she would bring and what she would leave behind. She imagines an all-woman crew exploring and collecting samples on the South Pole. Two years after submitting her essay, she is finally watching her ideas launch with Artemis 1. “I feel honored that the words I wrote are on a USB on Artemis I,” said Sowmya, “To think, something I wrote is aboard the most powerful rocket ever made and will go to the Moon and back!” Fifty years after the Apollo missions, NASA is preparing to send the first woman and person of color to the Moon by 2025. While Sowmya has read about and learned about past space missions, the Artemis program will be the first time she will witness astronauts stepping foot on the lunar surface. “It’s electrifying to think of the discoveries Artemis will make and the possibilities it and seismometers to discover lunar properties. The third crew member is an Experimental Astrobotanist. She investigates the ideal growing conditions for lunar farming. She is hardworking and surpasses expectations. Finally, we have a Systems Engineer. She is jovial and a strong communicator. I have handpicked this crew based on their expertise, backing-up abilities, and character traits for optimal teamwork. We are prepared to face solar winds and meteorites using precautionary sensors and alarms. Still, to prepare future astronauts, we would leave immersion technology - XR. This captures the sights and sensations of the moon as well as magnetic and radiation data to emulate the South Pole. This also enables common people to experience our wonderful Moon. Chabot Space and Science Center, is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. Following the guidance from the CDC and local medical officials all in-person public programs and gatherings at the Center have been postponed or cancelled until further notice. But you can check us out at https://chabotspace.org/ events/events-listing/ Teenager Sowmya wrote an essay that will be launched with Artemis 1. will open for space travel of the future,” said Sowmya, “My hopes for future space travel include affordable civilian travel. I dream of seeing our beautiful planet, the little blue marble, from above.” Yin for the Win Of the 12 people who have landed on the moon, we would be the first all-women crew to set foot there. We represent the Yin population. The mission goal is to map and chart the South Pole’s resources. As the lead Lunar Researcher and Mission Commander, I ensure the South Pole is completely explored. I always think clearly and critically. Along with a Lunar Geologist, we explore the South Pole regolith. The geologist is instinctive and reacts well under pressure. As she records field data, I collect samples and use tools such as magnetometers

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Part 3 in a series In advance of the November 8 Municipal Election, six candidates have filed papers for three available seats on the Piedmont City Council. They were asked to answer the following two questions, which were sent to them on Thursday, September 22. This marks week 3 of the Post’s election coverage. Next week the focus will return to the school board candidates. Beginning with the October 12 edition, the Post’s weekly coverage will include questions and answers from both City Council and School Board candidates until the election on November 8. Week 3 QUESTIONS 1. What do you consider as the City’s most pressing problems? How do you plan to address them? 2. If elected, how do you plan to make yourself available to residents? ment. As a current Councilmember, my contact information is available on the City’s website. My email and phone number are also published in the Piedmont Post each week. If residents have any questions for me about the election, please reach out to me via my campaign website Betsyforpiedmont.us. and decide on options by a vote is not only necessary but legally required. directly tied to my strong desire to engage the community beyond the limited confines of City Council meetings. 2. Availability This year I transitioned from partner to “of counsel” at my law firm which allows me to devote more time to civic and non-profit service. My years of legal and tax experience has prepared me to better serve the city of Piedmont. For decades I have reviewed and responded to daily emails and calls with clients who expect a prompt response. I will extend that same diligence and respect to the residents of Piedmont. Resident communication is of paramount importance to finding solutions. To that end, I intend to dialogue with individuals in the community through email, phone, social media channels, and with monthly “office hours” in a hybrid setting. Finally, I expect to use door knocking when necessary to educate residents and solicit their participation on important issues. There should be no surprises. NANCY BOSTROM 1. Most pressing problem Safety is the #1 issue. People say they live here for the schools, but it’s really the safety. When there is safety the mosques, synagogues and churches, scouts, schools, libraries, choirs, can do their jobs. I ran before and wanted cameras at every Piedmont entrance. I didn’t win, but you did. After the election, cameras were installed. I suggest using armored cars for our Police. I suggest we arm our teachers and provide 160 hours of training like the police. 2. Availability I am going to be handing out plans and ideas for ADU’s which I think are the answer to a lot of our concerns. You can find me at most Piedmont functions, and at the coffee hour at Piedmont Community Church. You can phone me at 203 998-1776 and email me at winstonmalloryboston@gmail.com. BETSY ANDERSEN Incumbent 1. Most pressing problem In the short term, the most pressing issue is to complete the 6th cycle state-mandated Housing Element plan. Every California city is required to have a state-certified Housing Element plan that is updated every eight years. As a City Councilmember, I think the most important thing I can do is to be transparent about this process, listen to all ideas and concerns, and make information available. Please visit the City of Piedmont housing website Piedmontishome.org where you can find answers to FAQs, legal analyses, links to meetings and informational videos, and much more. Over the next four years, we need to focus on our aging civic buildings. Our Police and Fire Departments operate out of spaces that are between 70 to 110 years old. We are currently in the process of renovating the 911 Dispatch Center. If re-elected, I will continue to support efforts to bring our city buildings up to current standards. 2. Availability I welcome all opportunities to talk and meet with residents. I love participating in community events, and I am always happy to attend meetings with local civic and school organizations. While Councilmembers are unpaid volunteers and do not have office space at City Hall, I am happy to schedule meetings in the City Hall conference room or (weather permitting) outside in one of our beautiful parks. Piedmont is a great place to live because our residents are engaged – volunteering their time and talents – at every level of our local governBRIDGET HARRIS 1. Most pressing problem At this time I believe the City’s most pressing problem is the divisiveness of the Housing Element. I believe the discord originates from both the communication and the process. There is no need for rancor; we need to join together for a solution. Having been made aware of the Housing Element late in the development, I understand the need for more effective disclosure and inclusion by the residents of Piedmont. Increasing the population by approximately 10% and housing units by 15% is a substantial change for our small city. Broad public participation and true engagement by an election process will help unify the city and increase the likelihood of a fair and successful outcome. Delaying submission of a Housing Element Plan until all of Piedmont has the chance to understand the consequences JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. Most pressing problem Our most pressing issue is hiring a strong leader to fill the vacancy that will be left when our current City Administrator, Sara Lillevand, retires in April 2023. This crucial leadership role oversees essential city services including fire and police; infrastructure and planning; and parks and recreation. The City Administrator also provides oversight of budget development and spending. As our city works to comply with a state housing mandate, the City Administrator serves as an ambassador and advocate for Piedmont’s interests. We need to make sure Piedmont hires someone who invites constituent input, listens and learns, and puts forth solid recommendations for the Council to act upon. As a City Council member, I will work to ensure that we hire a strong leader who will successfully advance important projects like the new pool construction and the state-mandated housing plan. 2. Availability Connecting with Piedmont residents is one of my favorite things to do as a City Council member. As a current member of Council I am regularly invited to meet with organizations and individuals. Community events such as the recent “Cops, Coffee, and Cars” are opportunities for me to speak to residents, deepen my understanding of community perspectives, and hear new ideas. When elected, I am looking to be even more accessible by creating “office hours,” which will be a scheduled day and time when I am available to talk with community members. My reason for expanding my availability is JEANNE SOLNORDAL 1. Most pressing problem Housing Element – Cycle 6, is the most pressing problem facing our community. Finding space for 587 units is extremely challenging. Unfortunately, the city did not appeal the allocation, therefore we have lost our right to join any future lawsuits that may be filed against the state. The city agreed to the 587 units without protest. This was fiscally irresponsible, as taxpaying residents will bear the cost of the civic services needed by the new residents. So where do we put them? City center, Moraga Canyon/ Blair Park are unfeasible as traffic, parking and children/ pedestrian safety are an issue. Accessory dwelling units will offset our requirement, but their numbers are minimal and will not eliminate the need for a large build. The only sites I see we could consider are multi-story units on Grand Avenue or at Zion Lutheran Church. Both sites would require owner participation and a rezoning vote. 2. Availability I am already available to residents. As president of a local organization, I am always reaching out. As a city council member representing the community, it is important to always keep an open-door policy. My home is always open, and my email and phone number are in many directories. I am always available for a conversation, regardless of subject, now and in the future. Some of the softest voices in Piedmont are our seniors. I will make a concerted effort to get to know every senior personally. I will check in on them on a regular basis to ensure their needs and concerns are being addressed. I will advocate for senior services just as we advocate for our youth. Please reach out at votesolnordal@gmail.com or 510-368-8880. TOM RAMSEY 1. Most pressing problem For several budget cycles, our City Administrator, our Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee and City staff have listed critical infrastructure as Piedmont’s most pressing problem. I agree. It’s past time to make needed upgrades to Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and facilities. Our critical facilities need to be made safe, so our first responders can keep us safe. I also agree that our financial stewardship includes an obligation to plan for the substantial repair / replacement of our facilities. The facility upgrade process will take time, robust public engagement, careful consideration of the phasing of work, and a commitment to seamlessly deliver excellent public services during the work. I’ve spent 30 years working as an architect tackling this type of work for commercial clients. I’ll put that experience to work for Piedmont. 2. Availability The best part of this campaign has been getting to meet new people and reconnecting with neighbors. If elected, I’ll expand connecting with residents by: • Encouraging participation because public engagement improves our decision-making process. Our town is home to an impressive depth of expertise. This collective wealth of experience is a great resource and I’ll leverage that resource as much as possible. • Transparent communication. I believe that transparency is a best practice to promote accountability. I’ll always make myself available via email, a chat at a public event or better yet, a conversation over coffee at Mulberry’s. And as I’ve done for the past 7 years through my service on the Planning Commission, I’ll listen first, ask questions, read every letter, and work together to make decisions with Piedmont’s best interest front and center.

The event attracted car fanatics near and far including John Day who drove from San Jose with his Corvette after hearing of the event that morning. “My favorite car was ‘63 spilt window black on black. It’s a Corvette, there is only one car, the Chevy Corvette. It is not a car, it is a cult,” he said. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers was all smiles after the event. “Community – that’s what it’s all about; bringing the community together,” he said.

The decision came after the team suffered more injuries in last Friday’s loss to St. Mary’s. The team has experienced six season-ending injuries after beginning the season with a roster of only 20 players. The Junior Varsity team has suffered three season-ending injuries, and De Anza decided its JV team will not travel from Richmond to Piedmont for Friday’s game. “We’ve had to forfeit the varsity football game this week. articles.text: In a strong week for Piedmont’s tennis team, the Highlanders defeated North Coast Section rival Lick Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco on Tuesday, September 20, and followed up two days later with a mighty 6-1 victory at Castro Valley on Thursday. The victory over Lick came against a Div. 2 North Coast Section opponent, which will help Piedmont earn a higher seeding in the NCS tournament at the end of the season.. “This was a very satisfying win over Lick Wilmerding,” said coach Jim Landes. “It shows we are in a good position to compete well in the NCS championships at the end of the season. But we must keep working to improve,” After the 6-1 win over Castro Valley Piedmont remained undefeated against WACC opponents, They earlier had beaten Bishop O’Dowd in a tournament in Fresno, and San Leandro and Arroyo in league matches. The tournament victory over O’Dowd means Piedmont has technically played just three league matches. The Highlanders are challenging to be the top team in its league, with Berkeley and Alameda likely being the other two contenders. 4-3 win over Lick Wilmerding Piedmont won all of its matches in straight sets against Lick, splitting the four singles matches and winning two of three doubles matches. At singles, No. 1 starter Tanya Kononova made quick work of her opponent in an easy 6-1, 6-1 victory. At No. 2, Anne Jumper lost 6-1, 6-1. Carolina Romanczuk at No. 3 won in straight sets 6-3, 6-1, and at No. 4, Annika Gilliland lost 6-1, 6-2. “Tanya trounced her opponent while Anne probably played their real No. 1 starter. Anne’s opponent ran down most of Anne’s shots making it difficult to hit winners,” said Landes. In doubles, Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini paired together for the first time but lost at No. Photo by Todd Marshburn Tanya Kononova at No. 1 singles won 6-1, 6-1 against Lick Wilmerding and 6-3, 6-0 versus Castro Valley. 1 by scores of 6-4, 6-3. At No. 2, Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio won 6-3, 6-3. The freshmen combination of Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 3. “Mara and Michaela lost in two close sets. They definitely had their chances; I expect this team to improve a lot in the next few weeks as they sharpen their volleys. Cecilia and Emma and Arianna and Kate both won in straight sets, playing aggressively but with good control. It was great to see,” said Landes. 6-1 win over Castro Valley Piedmont swept the doubles matches and only lost one singles match against Castro Valley. They won all of their matches in straight sets. At singles, Kononova won easily at No. 1 in straight sets, 6-3, 6-0. At No. 2, Anne Jumper won 6-2, 6-3. Emma Eisemon, who usually plays doubles, appeared at the No. 3 spot but lost in three sets, 6-0, 5-7, 10-4. Romanczuk won at No. 4, 6-2, 6-2. At doubles, LaForte and Bini paired at No. 1 to win 6-0, 6-2. At No. 2 was Anne Jumper and Kortum, winning 6-0, 6-4. DeFazio and Abigail Call won 6-0, 6-4 at No. 3. Tuesday vs. College Prep Piedmont hosted NCS opponents College Prep yesterday, Tuesday, September 27. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-3 overall, 3-0 league) hosts Alameda at the Corey Reich Tennis Center today, Wednesday, September 28 at 4:00 p.m., in a key league match. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Junior Varsity girls’ tennis team is currently 3-4 to start its season. They defeated San Leandro on August 28 to start their schedule, lost to Miramonte on August 30, and lost to Campolindo on September 7. The squad also played four tournament matches at James Logan on September 17, beating Heritage and Irvington but losing to Campolindo and Mission HS. Here’s a rundown of their season so far. 10-6 win over San Leandro Piedmont opened its season with a 10-6 win over San Leandro in a format that Included 10 doubles matches and six singles. At singles, Ishaia Goldberg-Berman won at the No. 1 spot 4-0. At No. 2, Sophie LaForte lost 4-1. At No. 3, Alina Shahid also lost 4-1. Maddy Tran won at No. 4 narrowly, 4-3. At No. 5, Lila Rosen won 4-0. Playing No. 6 was Olivia Jackson, losing 4-2. In doubles, LaForte and Shahid paired at No. 1, losing 4-1. At No. 2, Tran and Luisa Cole won 4-1. At No. 3 was Rosen and Inara Mehta won 4-0. Jordan Kim and Samantha Hyun paired at No. 4, winning 4-0. Ruby Guzdar and Sabrina Carling won 4-3 at No. 5. At No. 6 was Jackson and Amelia Addington winning 4-0. Hallie Burden and Peyton Watson played at No. 7, winning 4-0. At No. 8 was Lily Colbert and Dahlia Osman losing 4-3. Jameson Sanford and Charlotte Silver lost 4-2 at No. 9. Sparrow Lieu and Nuala Price lost 4-2 at No. 10. 11-3 loss to Miramonte Against upper-division Miramonte PHS suffered an 11-3 loss. Laforte won Piedmonts only match at singles, winning 6-4 at No. 3. Goldberg-Berman lost 6-2 at No. 1. At No. 2, Tran lost 6-1. Shahid lost 6-4 at No. 4, Cole lost 6-3 at No. 5, and Rosen lost 6-4 at No. 6. In doubles, Burden and Watson won 6-5 at No. 5, while Colbert and Osman won their set 6-2 at No. 6. Losses include: Mehta and Guzdar at No. 1, 6-3, Kim and Hyun at No. 2, 6-4, Macy Puckett and Carling 6-4 at No. 3, Jackson and Addington narrowly 7-6 at No. 6, Sanford and Silver 4-0 at No. 5, and Lieu and Price 4-2 at No. 7. 13-0 loss to Campolindo The JV team got shut out 13-0 by a strong Campolindo team on September 7. Singles matches include: Tran falling 8-3 at No. 1, LaForte 8-4 at No. 2, Shahid 8-0 at No. 3, Rosen 8-5 at No. 4, Mehta 8-4 at No. 5, and Burden narrowly 9-7 at No. 6. Doubles matches include: Kim and Hyun losing 8-3 at No. 1, Guzdar and Jane Hempeck 8-4 at No. 2, Sanford and Watson 8-6 at No. 3, Jackson and Carling 8-3 at No. 4, Osman and Colbert 8-4 at No. 5, Silver and Addington 8-2 at No. 6, and Price and Lieu 8-0 at No. 6. At No. 2, Kim won a close set, 7-6. Sanford won 6-4 at No. 3, while Osman won 6-1 at No. 4. In doubles, Tran and Golderberg-Berman won 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. At No. 2, Hyun and Burden won 6-2. At No. 3, Price and Silver lost 6-2. PHS continued its winning ways against Irvington with a 4-3 victory. In singles, Goldberg-Berman won 6-4 at the No. 1 spot. Mehta lost 6-3 at No. 2. Rosen won her set 6-4 at No. 3, while Colbert narrowly lost 7-6 at No. 4. In doubles, Tran and Shahid won their set at No. 1 easily, 6-1. At No. 2 was Sanford and Addington winning a close set, 7-5. Price and Silver lost at No. 3, 6-1. Niko Kalamas is a freshman at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: Piedmont’s cross country teams ran away with victories at the first league meet of the season at Hayward High on Wednesday, September 21. The boys’ team won with 39 points, and the girls won with 58 points, PHS junior Xander Schulte-Sasse led his team by placing 2nd in a field of 84 runners, and freshman Skylar Best led the girls’ team with a 2nd place overall finish out of 59 runners. “Everyone is coming to practice, working hard with real effort, and it is paying off,” said Piedmont coach Jeanine Holmlund. “Consistency matters. Piedmont scored against six Shoreline teams in our first WACC League meet, so our record now stands at 6-0,” It marked the second appearance for the cross country team and first official look at the complete team for both the boys and girls. Boys results Schulte-Sasse led the way for the boys with a time of 15:27.57 on the three-mile course. His time was a personal record by 36 seconds. He’s begun to install himself as the squad’s top runner after placing 21st of 222 at the Lowell Invitational, and clocking 15:33 at a scrimmage meet on August 27. Behind Schulte-Sasse was senior Parker Long finishing fourth with a time of 15:52.1, also a personal record by 24 seconds. In seventh was senior Christian Taylor, crossing the line in 16:10.89, while junior Julien Lee was right behind in eighth with a time of 16:16.81. Rounding out the top five times was sophomore and first-year varsity runner Evan Byun in 18th, clocking a 17:05.26. Girls results Best led the girls with a time of 19:32.24, claiming 2nd overall. She’s been an eye-catching freshman on the team by placing 12th of 204 runners at the Lowell Invitational Frosh/Soph event earlier this month, and fourth out of 74 runners at a scrimmage meet on August 27 at Hayward’s threemile course. Right behind Best was junior Jamie Schwarz in third with a time of 20:30.93, and junior Josie Oesterer in fifth in 19:51.50. Next in for PHS was freshman Cora Chun in 19th, clocking a 20:56.30, while another freshman, Elia Kwong, rounded out the top five placing 31st in 21:52.34. NEXT UP Piedmont looks ahead to hosting the Be The G.O.A.T. (Greatest Of All Time) Invitational at the Pinole Multi-Use Trails outside Hercules on Saturday, October 1 at 9:00 a.m. It marks the second time PHS will host the event. Xander Schulte-Sasse was Piedmont’s top runner in second with a time of 15:27.57, which marked a personal record for the junior athlete. Christian Taylor placed seventh with a time of 16:10.89.

articles.text: Highlanders beat Berkeley 14-3 earlier in week Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team’s undefeated streak was interrupted at the Napa Valley College tournament last weekend, Playing on Friday and Saturday, September 23-24, they lost a 10-9 barn-burner to Ripon in Friday’s first round in overtime, but rebounded by defeating league opponent Berkeley 9-4 later in the day. On Saturday, PHS lost to Amador Valley 13-6 and then pulled out a dramatic 11-10 victory in overtime over Foothill. The team was without a key player, Peter Krumins, for the tournament. In a separate game, the Highlanders dominated Berkeley 14-3 on Wednesday, September 21 at the Yellowjackets’ home gym, “We played well. We were without Peter Krumins, so the other boys had to step up. Declan Linnane and George Stein played lights out; solid defensively and offensively. Finn Burke played well. His two-meter play improved throughout the tournament,” said assistant coach John Savage. Savage also had high praise for a group of sophomores and juniors who made their presence felt at the tourney. “Lots of sophomores stepped up; Hayden Jahn, Charlie Wright, Photos by Nancy Brahm Declan Linnane scored four goals and had two steals in an overtime win over Foothill at the Napa Valley College tournament. Yotem Kariv, Ori Aloush – all saw time this weekend. Our team is young, carried by juniors. Declan and George were great, but Quincy Scherman, Daniel Banin, Evan Dickason all had goals and improved defensively,” said Savage. 11-10 overtime win over Foothill In the first quarter, Foothill jumped out to a 2-0 lead, but Hayden Jahn scored a minute later and Daniel Banin tied the game with 22 seconds left. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team, hanging on by a thread, suffered its fourth straight loss on Friday, September 23 at Witter Field, falling to St. Mary’s 49-15. With a depleted roster and additional players now out with injuries, it was an uphill fight for survival. The Highlanders struggled to find their mojo in the first half but actually outscored the Panthers 15-14 in the second half. “I feel good that we scored two touchdowns in the second half; I can find some solace in that we won 15-14 in the second half. All week, we talked about being able to get the first punch, and we just couldn’t get that done all night,” said coach Jordan Seiden. The game saw former Piedmont head coach John Trotman’s return to Witter Field, now as head coach at St. Mary’s. His team has a 4-0 record. The Panthers ended the first quarter leading 14-0 and went into halftime up 35-0. Piedmont scored one touchdown in the third quarter and closed the game with a touchdown and a two-point conversion in the final minute. “We had a lot of opportunities; it was more of us just defeating ourselves. We couldn’t block a soul in the first half and had no continuity in getting anything going. I love our passion and how hard we play despite our numbers,” said Seiden. Although Piedmont took a beating with a sophomore-laden varsity roster, the second half showed some bright spots. The Highlanders’ execution noticeably improved, including the recovery of an onside kick at the start of the second half. “It was encouraging that we didn’t just pack it in and call it a night [when we were] down 35-0. It’s hard to come back after that. I wanted to get the momentum going and catch them sleeping with a quick kick. We just wanted to create some momentum and walk out with our head high feeling good about something,” said Seiden. In the second half, Piedmont recovered a fumble, and quarterback Markos Lagios completed a 37-yard pass to Matteo Costa, setting up Costa’s touchdown on a six-yard reception. Lagios also had an impressive run to convert a fourth down, had a 30- yard pass to Sam Shelby, and a 13-yard TD throw to Shelby. NEXT UP Piedmont’s homecoming game against De Anza this Friday has been canceled. The current status of the future of the team is unclear given low roster numbers in addition to extensive injuries. articles.text: Due to popularity Circus Bella has added six more free showings of its newest show, Flip Flop Fly, from October 15-23. This series of performances, featuring some of the dazzling circus talent from the Bay Area, will delight audiences of all ages in a family event for all ages. Flip Flop Fly is directed by Circus Bella co-founder and director Abigail Munn. The performances will celebrate the circus’s 13th year. The 60-minute show is circus arts at its most exuberant, exploring human curiosity and sky-high imagination. Circus Bella is a diverse and talented troupe of acrobats, aerialists, jugglers, and clowns - performing to the live music of Rob Reich and the six piece Circus Bella All-Star Band. Guests are invited to bring picnic blankets and small folding chairs to all locations. A preshow performance by the Stars of Prescott Circus Theatre will also be held. To learn more visit: Circusbella.org/flipflopfly or call 415- 480-4239. ®

articles.text: Final performance is Sunday, October 2 Shotgun Players’ Man of God, written by playwright Anna Ouyang and directed by Michelle Talgarow, ends this Sunday, October 2. Tickets are available online for shows on Thursday through Sunday, September 29-October 2. Man of God is inspired by a real-life incident at a Christian mission in Southeast Asia. The comedy, described by the playwright as a “feminist thriller,” follows four students Mimi (Lauren Andrei Garcia), Samantha (Alexandra Lee), (Joyce Domanico-Huh), and KyungHwa (Sharon Shao) while on a church mission to Bangkok. The girls, visiting from Southern California, discover a hidden camera in their hotel room that they conclude was placed by the church pastor. “I wrote the play in part to examine my own desire for and participation in the concept of the ‘revenge fantasy’ narrative that our culture is so fond of and the way that narrative can fail survivors of sexual abuse who are unable to enact those fantasies in reality,” said Ouyang. Man of God runs 90 minutes without an intermission at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The play will be available to stream online beginning October 5. articles.text: Aaron Sorkin’s play adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird is currently in production at the Golden Gate Theatre with performances through October 9. Sorkin’s adaption of Harper Lee’s famous 1960 novel opened on Broadway in 2018 and has been the highest-grossing American Play since its debut. Set in Alabama in 1934, Lee’s novel is widely considered an American classic and an enduring story of racial injustice. The cast includes Richard Thomas as Atticus Finch, Melanie Moore as Scout Finch, Jacqueline Williams as Calpurnia, Justin Mark as Jem Finch, Yaegel T. Welch as Tom Robinson, Steven Lee Johnson as Dill Harris and Mary Badham as Mrs. Dubose. They are joined by Joey Collins as Bob Ewell, Richard Poe as Judge Taylor, Luke Smith as Horace Gilmer, Arianna Gayle Stucki as Mayella Ewell, David Christopher Wells as Sheriff Heck Tate. Golden Gate Theatre is at 1 Taylor Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available at www. broadwaysf.com. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse celebrates its 20th season with the debut of Indecent on September 22. The show will run through November 5. Paula Vogel’s play is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as traitorous libel. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago. Being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present it.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The principal cast members include Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. The production is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features klezmer music. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years, and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English explained. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/get-tickets/ to purchase tickets. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Malka Wallick (left) and Rivka Borek in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Indecent, a play by Paula Vogel.
articles.title: Indecent at SF Playhouse through November 5

articles.text: Photo by Kevin Berne Anna Ishida (left) and Rajesh Bose in Aurora Theatre Company’s current production of This Much I Know. Aurora Theatre Company’s current production of This Much I Know will end on Sunday, October 2. Jonathan Spector’s play weaves together the story of Stalin’s daughter who defected to America through protagonist Natalya (Anna Ishida) as she works through a horrible calamity. Natalya is considering divorce and a move to her homeland Russia. She believes her grandmother’s connections to Stalin might help, and the story begins a deep-dive into her family history as her husband Lukesh (Rajesh Bose) tries to persuade her to return. The play is directed by Aurora Artistic Director Josh Costello. Aurora Theatre Company is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley. To purchase tickets call box office 510-843-4822 or purchase online at www.auroratheatre.org.
articles.title: This Much I Know ends on Sunday at Aurora Theater

articles.text: The San Francisco-based dance company, Smuin Ballet, will perform its “Dance Series One” at Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek and Cowell Theater at San Francisco’s Fort Mason now through October 8. articles.text: Last Wednesday, a scant few hours after the Post reported on protests by unpaid ushers, Berkeley Rep abruptly reversed direction and cancelled its policy requiring the ushers to show up an extra half hour earlier for performances. The Front of House (FOH) Director, who instituted the policy that caused the protests, liberalized the prior policy by allowing ushers to arrive 15 minutes later than in the past. An email from Berkeley Rep dated 11:32 a.m. on September 21 stated: “We are going to shut down the combined FOH/BO ‘Team’ experience. It seems that ushers in general do not want to so [sic] this. I will start working on a seperate [sic] usher group that will work events, giftshop etc. with the FOH Team. Ushers in this group can come 15-30 minutes befor [sic] the lobby opens. Sign in - get you [sic] badge and go to your assigned door. This goes into effect today.” While the timing of the email might seem a bit coincidental, it’s reasonable to assume that someone higher up at Berkeley Rep was notified about the article and decided it was time to de-escalate the situation. The email must have resulted in a number of questions, because a few hours later, the FOH Director sent out a second, all bold email to cut off the discussion: “Hello Ushers, please just focus on ushering. Let us get through Goddess and Ripple. The other program is not happening yet. I have to build it [sic] I have no other information for you at this time. As soon as I get a clearer picture of what the ‘event ushers’ will be, I will reach out. This will be next season if it is approved.” While this appears to have put the matter to rest for the remainder of the current season, the status quo has not been totally restored. At least one usher who questioned the new policy and asked to be removed until the old policy was restored has not yet been reinstated. That person has emailed the FOH Director multiple times since Wednesday and has left a voicemail, all without a response. The Post will continue to follow the situation as it unfolds. Wily Hoag is the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs Reporter.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep backtracks after Piedmont Post report

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum featuring exbibit by Carlos Villa

When choosing musical entertainment, I suggest going to small venues. A musical friend invited us to attend a concert recently in the Community Hall at the Lafayette Library, the home base of Pamela Freund’s Gold Coast Chamber Players. The concert was presented by the Lamorinda Arts Council and Ensemble ARI …a group that is new to me. One of the major benefits of small auditoriums is that you sit close to the performers so your experience is more personal. In addition, the musicians simply try harder. The program offered a considerable variety of music from the most contemporary-avant-garde to the classics. The musicians played their hearts’ out. After the concert, there was a very lovely reception with excellent food. The larger organizations simply don’t treat you so beautifully. It reminded me of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: In the Heights plays until October 16 Berkeley Playhouse is currently performing Lin Manuel Miranda’s musical, In the Heights. Directed by Melissa Martinez, it will be at Berkeley Playhouse through October 16, In the Heights is the second musical theater production developed by Miranda. His first production, Hamilton, told the story of Alexander Hamilton and federalism with a modern tune. This production draws on similar musical themes but tells the story of growing up in the Washington Heights neighborhood of New York City. The Berkeley Playhouse offers a season pass for avid theater fans or single show passes. The theater is located at 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. For tickets or season passes visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org or call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351. Tickets purchased at the door are cash only.

McDonald, exploring the relationships between human structures and their natural surroundings. Entry to the show is free. Saturday and Sunday, October 1-2 and 8-9, 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Sunday, October 2, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Select musicians from Berkeley Symphony will open their 2022-23 season with a Chamber concert entitled Fall Colors that will include music from several different eras — from Tchaikovsky to modern times. The program will include 7 Dances for Flute, Clarinet & Cello by Brian Raphael Nabors; Five Folksongs in Counterpoint for String Quartet by Florence Price, and Tchaikovsky’s String Quartet No. 1. Get your tickets in advance from the Berkeley Symphony website or by calling (510) 841-2800. Food tickets are $10 at the door, and a souvenir beer glass for $15 will admit you to unlimited tastes of the various brews. Sunday, October 9, 3:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert paying tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which or more than 50 have become American standards. This concert is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing PCA’s magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets are $20 at the door, or online at https://bpt.me/5316993. Enjoy wine & appetizers while mingling with Left Coast friends old & new, while musicians Nikki Einfeld, soprano, and Eric Zivian, piano, perform selections by Stephen Sondheim, Florence Price & Kurt Weill. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Opus 132, String Quartet in A minor, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. In this and other late works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. articles.text: Charlie Callas and Sean Marshall (as the voice of Elliot the Dragon) in Pete’s Dragon. Review by Chris Honoré Pete’s Dragon is a movie aimed squarely at the 10-year-old demographic and never wavers, avoiding inside jokes or frenetic, over-the-top chase scenes that might appeal to the accompanying adults. Here’s the wonderful assumption that the filmmakers build on: kids believe in magic. They don’t have to push very hard to get the pre-tween crowd to suspend their disbelief and buy into a sweet premise involving a young boy (not exactly a feral child but not far from Mowgli, either). His only friend, Elliot, happens to be a 24-foot tall, furry green dragon. Yep. And when he sneezes you have to reach for a towel. But first things first: A young boy, Pete (Oakes Fegley), only five, is on a vacation adventure with his mom and dad in the Pacific Northwest. He’s in the backseat of their station wagon, reading an illustrated story titled, Elliot Gets Lost. Suddenly his father swerves to miss a deer and rolls the car. Pete is thrown clear, uninjured. His parents are killed. Panicked, alone, surrounded by strange sounds, he runs into the forest where he is surrounded by wolves. Unexpectedly, he is saved by Elliot, the dragon, who takes the boy under his wing, so-tospeak, and nurtures and cares for him (seeming half parent and half pet), helping him build an elaborate tree house. Six years pass. Pete seems to have thrived, and he and Elliot have now formed a deep and abiding bond. One day, a group of loggers, who have penetrated deep into the forest, appear and Pete is captivated by these men in their trucks and large bulldozers, signaling the encroachment of a civilization of which he is complete unaware. And now begins the juxtaposition of two realities – Pete’s natural world, and a world that is filled with cars and hospitals and people, such as forest ranger Grace (Bryce Dallas Howard) who watches over Pete as he struggles to cope. For decades, in this small northern logging town, called Millhaven, there has existed the legend of a dragon that lived deep in the woods, sighted rarely. No matter the witness, such sightings have always been immediately discounted as fantasy or perhaps simply wind in the high trees. One such purveyor of the Millhaven dragon legend is a wizened woodcarver (Robert Redford), who, like Pete, believes that if we look hard enough magic will reveal itself to us. His daughter, Grace, is a lifelong skeptic. What happens next will be embraced by the youngsters without question, as is the relationship between Elliot and Pete. There’s magic in this world if we are only open to letting it into our lives, amazing things are possible. Magic can transform our lives. The way it has transformed Pete’s. What is wonderful about this film is that Pete also discovers that there is magic in being enfolded in the collective arms of a family and that the two are not mutually exclusive. Kids love this stuff. Pete’s Dragon. Directed by Don Chaffey. Voiced by Helen Reddy, Mickey Rooney, Red Buttons. 2 hrs., 14 min. Rated PG. Released in 1977 as a fusion of animation and reallife. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+.
articles.title: Pete’s Dragon a sweet story of a boy and a touch of magic

articles.text: swaps his aloha shirt for western Just when you thought computer-generated imagery (CGI) had peaked, the folks at Industrial Light and Magic (ILM), under the direction of Gore Verbinksi (Pirates of the Caribbean), create Rango, an animated feature film that is a showstopper. It’s a marvel, done brilliantly in 2D, no less, with attention to detail that is unlike anything created thus far. The essential story is classic, a familiar Western trope. It begins with a thespian lizard in his terrarium (a small pool, a palm tree, and a plastic fish), riding in the back of a car. The family is driving across the Mojave Desert when they hit a bump in the road and the terrarium and lizard are bounced out, landing in the road, while the car continues out of sight. And so the lizard – a chameleon of sorts, blue-skinned, bugeyed, wearing an aloha shirt – stands on the side of the road as the sizzling sun leaches moisture out of everything. Parched, he makes his way across the desert to a town called Dirt, inhabited by an array of critters – rodents, lizards, Gila monsters – all desperate for water. Dirt, according to the mayor (Ned Beatty), is having a small drought. The remaining water, so precious, is in a bank vault. Our aloha lizard walks into a saloon where, when challenged, creates a persona and a story that is so authentic that he is quickly viewed as a savior and as the next sheriff. The stranger calls himself Rango (Johnny Depp) and soon duds. Unbeknownst to the townsfolk, Rango is a tenderfoot, a true dude, about to go up against the meanest, gnarliest, most conniving set of desert critters imaginable, all in on something nefarious. And all the dude is packing is his faux story (he killed a mess of outlaws with one shot, he says) and a rusty six-gun with only one bullet in the chamber. Wearing his tin star, his spurs jingling, Rango has to ride hard, shoot straight, and eventually face down hombres like Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) and Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy), all while trying not to flinch. His life is further complicated when he meets Beans (Isla Fisher), a sweet little thing, also a lizard, who is fighting with the shifty, underhanded, no’count Mayor (Ned Beatty) over selling her pappy’s ranch. Close your eyes and you can hear a spaghetti-western soundtrack. Keep the faith, buckaroos, and you will meet the Spirit of the West, a leathery, tough-as-nails cowboy ridin’ his golf cart across some pretty mean territory, a lean question mark of a man who gives Rango some darned good advice. Are ya feeling lucky? Well, are ya? This is a great movie. But the writing is so adult, the jokes and vocabulary at times so dang highfalutin, that a lot of what is said will sail right over the heads of the peanut gallery. But no worries. There’s enough adventure packed into Rango for both audiences. Which is a good thing. Rango. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Animated. Voiced by Johnny Depp, Bill Nighy, Alfred Molina. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO Max. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 John K. articles.text: Part 53 I was so impressed to read of the Safer and Cleaner School Commute event (Walk and Roll) in last week’s Piedmont Post. Maybe you read it. Piedmont High senior Skye Yeh, as part of her Girl Scout Gold Award program, came up with a plan to mitigate the crowded “unsafe” dropoff and pick-up situation in front of Wildwood School. Simple as can be, the event, with the cooperation of the school and police authorities, encouraged students to walk, scooter or bike to school from home. With 78% of students participating, the one-day event was nothing but a complete success! What a simple solution to a growing national trend/problem. I had a chance to talk with Skye recently, and as part of her program she astutely listed the benefits of getting to school without a car. Healthy exercise is high on the list: not only does it benefit the body, but as she put it, in the morning “it gets your brain going too.” That is a fact backed up by numerous scientific studies, such as Dr. John Ratey at Harvard Medical School who writes that morning exercise substantially improves learning in schools. The other obvious benefit is the pollution reduction of fewer cars on the road. Even with electric cars and their highly reduced carbon footprint, there is still environmental impact from the energy production to charge batteries, the manufacturing processes, and the end of useful life treatment of recycling. Safety and congestion is another issue. Sitting in a line of cars waiting is at best frustrating for everyone; the more cars on the road, especially in a small drop-off area, the less safe is the auto-pedestrian mix, especially with children involved. Sketches by Will Adams Skye also suggests that walking, scootering and biking is both friendly and fun, not only with classmates but with the community through which students pass on their way to school. While automobile travel is a part of the human DNA in our era, there are clearly downsides. Solutions to the inherent problems involve mitigating the exclusivity of car transportation – providing alternative ways of getting places. Certainly not everyone can walk or bike everywhere, but as Skye Yeh has recently shown us, most of us can walk at least some of the time to some places. Even eliminating a small proportion of auto trips reduces congestion, pollution, the need for so many parking spaces, and at the same time can enhance, rather than compromise our destinations. Congratulations to Wildwood School and the Piedmont Police for their support, and to Skye Yeh for thinking out of the box: “I hope that kids and parents will remember their experience and try to continue walking and scootering instead of driving,” she said. Not incidentally, data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration shows students are about 70 times more likely to get to school safely when taking a bus instead of traveling by car. Will Adams writes a biweekly column in the Piedmont Post. He is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: Oakland Zoo is excited to host its annual “Healthy Living Festival,” presented by the United Seniors of Oakland and Alameda County.
