pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 28, 2022 Features your Alternative transportation to schools By Will Adams Part 53 I was so impressed to read of the Safer and Cleaner School Commute event (Walk and Roll) in last week’s Piedmont Post. Maybe you read it. Piedmont High senior Skye Yeh, as part of her Girl Scout Gold Award program, came up with a plan to mitigate the crowded “unsafe” dropoff and pick-up situation in front of Wildwood School. Simple as can be, the event, with the cooperation of the school and police authorities, encouraged students to walk, scooter or bike to school from home. With 78% of students participating, the one-day event was nothing but a complete success! What a simple solution to a growing national trend/problem. I had a chance to talk with Skye recently, and as part of her program she astutely listed the benefits of getting to school without a car. Healthy exercise is high on the list: not only does it benefit the body, but as she put it, in the morning “it gets your brain going too.” That is a fact backed up by numerous scientific studies, such as Dr. John Ratey at Harvard Medical School who writes that morning exercise substantially improves learning in schools. Oakland Zoo to host annual Healthy Living Festival for seniors this Thursday Oakland Zoo is excited to host its annual “Healthy Living Festival,” presented by the United Seniors of Oakland and Alameda County. This year’s event will take place on Thursday, September 29, from 9:00 a.m.to 2:00 p.m. The festival promotes health and wellness for aging adults, and includes admission to the zoo, free food, music, fun and more. A free lunch will be given to all pre-registered participants. “We are honored to be once again asked to host this year’s event, and we’re grateful to do our part to help ensure the health of our senior community. We are here to support all ages, both as a resource and as a long-standing destination dedicated to animals, nature, and education,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Healthy Living Festival is a free event for seniors 55+ living in Alameda County to promote health and wellness. In previous years, this annual event drew an average of more than 2,000 participants. “For many, getting vaccinated, tested, and staying social in a safe way has been a challenge. Oakland Zoo continues to be our gracious and flexible partner, and I am excited that this year’s Healthy Living Festival is a safely organized drive-through, offering all three necessities to those who need them the most”, said Alameda County Supervisor Nate Miley. As the Zoo currently celebrates its Centennial year, it will continue to expand its outreach in the community. For more information, visit: Oaklandzoo.org/programs-andevents/healthy-living-festival The other obvious benefit is the pollution reduction of fewer cars on the road. Even with electric cars and their highly reduced carbon footprint, there is still environmental impact from the energy production to charge batteries, the manufacturing processes, and the end of useful life treatment of recycling. Safety and congestion is another issue. Sitting in a line of cars waiting is at best frustrating for everyone; the more cars on the road, especially in a small drop-off area, the less safe is the auto-pedestrian mix, especially with children involved. Sketches by Will Adams Skye also suggests that walking, scootering and biking is both friendly and fun, not only with classmates but with the community through which students pass on their way to school. While automobile travel is a part of the human DNA in our era, there are clearly downsides. Solutions to the inherent problems involve mitigating the exclusivity of car transportation – providing alternative ways of getting places. Certainly not everyone can walk or bike everywhere, but as Skye Yeh has recently shown us, most of us can walk at least some of the time to some places. Even eliminating a small proportion of auto trips reduces congestion, pollution, the need for so many parking spaces, and at the same time can enhance, rather than compromise our destinations. Congratulations to Wildwood School and the Piedmont Police for their support, and to Skye Yeh for thinking out of the box: “I hope that kids and parents will remember their experience and try to continue walking and scootering instead of driving,” she said. Not incidentally, data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration shows students are about 70 times more likely to get to school safely when taking a bus instead of traveling by car. pages.text: Wednesday, September 28, 2022 23 What should Alzheimer’s caregivers know? If you have a family member who has been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, or is starting to show symptoms, you will face some real challenges. Navigating the Alzheimer’s experience involves a long journey, and there’s no easy answer for how you can cope with your emotions. But you can at least address some of the financial issues involved to help give yourself a greater sense of control. Here are some moves to consider: • Plan for care costs and identify insurance coverage. The list of Alzheimer’s-related medical expenses is long and includes ongoing medical treatment, medical equipment, home safety modifications, prescription drugs and personal care supplies. As a caregiver, you’ll want to know the extent of your loved one’s health insurance: Medicare, supplemental policies, veteran’s benefits if applicable, and so on. One big question is how much coverage they might have for adult day care services, in-home care services and full-time residential care services, and other long-term care options. Long-term care is one of the largest health care costs not covered by Medicare, so you’ll want to determine if your loved one has a long-term care policy or another insurance policy with a long-term care rider. • Identify assets and debts. You’ll need to know your family member’s financial position, both what they own – bank accounts, investments, property, etc. – and what they owe, such as credit card debt, a mortgage, lines of credit, and so on. This knowledge will be essential if you’re granted power of attorney to take over your loved one’s finances. • Look for tax breaks available to caregivers. If you’re a caregiver, you may have to pay for some care costs out of pocket. Consequently, you could receive some tax credits and deductions. These benefits vary by state, so you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor to determine your eligibility. • Ensure necessary legal documents are in place. As a caregiver, you may need to ensure some legal documents are in place, such as a durable power of attorney for finances, which lets you make financial decisions for your loved one with Alzheimer’s, and a durable power of attorney for health care, which lets you make health care and medical decisions on their behalf. articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Tom Ramsey as a candidate for Piedmont’s City Council. I have had the privilege of working with Tom for several years as a volunteer with the Rebuilding Together Oakland program. Tom’s experience as an architect was invaluable in the successful completion of numerous RTO projects. As a seven-year member of the Piedmont Planning Commission, Tom has devoted his inexhaustible talents to this city. He is dedicated and passionate about our city and its future. His ability to listen, analyze and discuss the issues would make him an excellent addition to our City Council as the city navigates our housing challenges, civic improvements and day-to-day issues. I urge my fellow Piedmonters to support his election to the City Council. –Colin Wong
articles.title: Tom Ramsey – tireless volunteer with abundant talent

articles.text: Editor: Over the last five years, I’ve had the privilege of knowing Ruchi Medhekar and working together with her as co-room parents and during her time as VP and President of Beach Parents Organization. Based on those experiences, I enthusiastically endorse her for school board. Beyond Beach, Ruchi has been very active with district-wide initiatives and in the greater Piedmont community. Her experiences serving on PUSD’s TriSchool Site Council, the LCAP committee, Budget Advisory Committee as well as being on the board of the Piedmont Education Foundation have provided opportunities for her to learn about district operations, build consensus among different stakeholders, and develop a strong understanding of our community’s challenges and opportunities. Along with her peers in the Piedmont Recreation Commission, earlier this week she voted for the creation of a subcommittee to explore how Schoolmates can best serve the needs of families. However, the impact Ruchi has made in Piedmont extends well beyond her official resume. For example, because of her dedication to academic excellence and her desire to build an inspiring environment where students and teachers thrive, she has proactively elevated experts’ voices (for example in literacy) to explore how we can best serve our students in the district. Ruchi takes the time to educate herself, ask thoughtful questions, and truly listen before coming to a conclusion. Once informed, Ruchi’s passionate and collaborative approach puts people at ease
articles.title: Ruchi is invested in our collective success

articles.text: Editor: I met Jen Long almost a decade ago when our boys played basketball together. Jen was very invested in her kids’ lives. We had many lovely conversations on the sidelines of baseball and basketball games about our families. She is grounded, practical and witty, and appreciates the opinions and perspectives of others. I believe her ideals and vision for the future of our city – fiscal responsibility, robust public discourse and prioritizing public safety – align with mine. As a resident on Oakland Avenue, safe streets are a top priority for me and I am glad to know that public safety is high on her list. I know she would be a valuable city council member. I look forward to casting my vote for Jen Long for Piedmont City Council on November 8. –Amy McKenzie
articles.title: Values of Jennifer Long consistent with city

Candidates were notified that the forum would be recorded on video for posterity and accountability. “One candidate was uncomfortable with video recording, fearing it could create a gotcha situation in the future,” noted Titan. “Another candidate hired a campaign manager in early September who expressed discomfort with the PEEP forum in its entirety. On September 20 candidate Shirley Hooi agreed to fill out the PEEP questions but canceled her attendance at the forum the next day. Titan then emailed everyone who had signed up for the forum to notify them that the three candidates had withdrawn and would not be attending. “Because it appears that two candidates were highly distrustful of the PEEP questions, our organization is making the questions available to readers of the Piedmont Post to let them make their own judgment,” said Titan. Multiple choice answers include options of what the current board behavior has been, what past candidates did, as well as some choices coming up. LET US VOTE BRIDGET HARRIS for CITY COUNCIL Donations can be sent to Bridget Harris Piedmont City Council at 6114 La Salle Avenue, #300, Oakland, CA 94611 PRIORITIES for PIEDMONT A friend recently said to me “the Housing Element was not an issue until it became an issue.” This is so true. I believe most Piedmont residents were not aware or focused on the Housing Element until the City Council presented a draft plan and that plan included downtown Piedmont, the Highland grassy strip, the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, and the Piedmont Center for the Arts. At that point the Housing Element became an issue for many; objections were raised. The latest plan pushes most of the units to Grand Avenue and Moraga Avenue. Grand Avenue is an appropriate location for multi-family units in that it is an area that is considered “walkable oriented development”. Park Boulevard is also an appropriate location. Both Grand and Park provide residents walkable options to grocery stores, hardware stores and other services as well as accessible transportation. The Piedmont Center for the Arts (801 Magnolia) and the Moraga Avenue locations, such as Blair Park, are not suitable locations for several reasons. 1 There has been little, or no analysis of the impact multi-family units will have on traffic, water, students, and safety. 2 Moraga Avenue is already very congested at certain times of the day; adding more cars will make it worse for both Oakland and Piedmont residents. 3 Both locations are in Zone B which is park and public lands. Multi-family units are only allowed in Zone C. Multifamily units are not allowed in Zone B. The Proposed change to the zones requires a vote. Section 9.02 of Piedmont’s City Charter states "The Council may classify and reclassify the zones established, but …no existing zones shall be reclassified without submitting the question to a vote at a general or special election." The city’s zoning ordinance, codified in Section 17.02.010 of Piedmont’s Municipal Code states “…the prohibition not to reduce, enlarge, or reclassify a zone without a vote is understood to mean the city may not change zone boundaries, or change (reclassify) a property from one zone to another.” Piedmont has Five Zones: A- Single Family Residential B- Public land C- Multi-family Residential D- Commercial and Mixed Use, and E- Estate Residential. Presently Zone B does not allow for Multi-family Residential, which is only allowed in Zone C. Likewise Zone B does not allow for Mixed-use commercial/residential development which is currently only allowed in Zone D. The current City Council position is that NO vote is required for the Council to allow Multi-family Residential and Mixed-Use/Commercial in Zone B. Recently the City defended its position that a vote is not needed. The City stated that “The adoption of a Draft Housing Element does not enact any modifications to the Zoning Ordinance. The Draft Housing Element includes policies and programs that call for revisions to the Zoning Ordinance that allow for ….” multi-family units. More…flip side www.bridgetforpiedmont.com

BRIDGET HARRIS for CITY COUNCIL PRIORITIES for PIEDMONT The City goes on to say that after the Housing Element is approved by the state, then the City will implement modifications to the Zoning Ordinance. There is no provision for a vote; instead, the City takes us through four administrative steps to validate the proposed changes to Zone B. 1. 2. 3. 4. The City states that revisions to the Zoning Ordinance require “several public meetings”. The revisions will be posted for public comment. The Planning Commission will make final recommendations to the City Council. The City Council twice reads the revisions to the City Code , then the revisions become law. (See https://www.piedmontishome.org/faqs) If that were true, there is no reason the City Council could not make the same changes to Zone A which is single family residences. The City plans to push forward its agenda to rezone areas, even though our charter and our municipal code clearly state that any changes, any reclassifications, and any enlargements require approval by Piedmont voters. The City further states “The Charter does not require a vote if the City changes uses or density within a zone.” Changing the density of 801 Magnolia and Blair Park to allow 100+ multi-family units is a re-zone no matter what language is used. Revising the City Code as proposed is just a euphemism for re-zoning and violates both the spirit and the letter of the City Charter. If I am elected, I will strive to make sure any re-zone, revision, change in classification, or increase in density in Piedmont is brought to a vote of all the voters in Piedmont, not just the City Council. Safety and Infrastructure. The Piedmont community greatly values its police and fire departments, yet both operate in outdated and unsafe facilities. In 2020 the City Council discussed deficiencies in the buildings and noncompliance with the state’s Essential Services Act. At that time the Council considered improving the facilities with funding by issuance of public safety bonds. For various reasons, including the pandemic and the focus on the pool, the project did not move forward. Modernizing Piedmont’s public infrastructure is vital to our future. Our community came together for the Aquatic Center, approving a bond measure, and we can repeat that success to rebuild our City Hall and public safety buildings. I will clearly explain the issues and the need for renovations and then provide detailed options and costs before asking for increases in fees, taxes, or approval of any bond measure. I am a tax attorney, working with clients in many different industries. I have been involved for many years on various finance committees. The community deserves excellent public safety services, and we must insure those services by capital investment in City Hall and the police and fire department infrastructure. I am certain our City can find the ways and means to complete the renovations needed to improve Piedmont's infrastructure – but we need community involvement in this process. We need to vote. www.bridgetforpiedmont.com Donations can be sent to Bridget Harris Piedmont City Council at 6114 La Salle Avenue, #300, Oakland, CA 94611

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town this Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and is organized by Officer Tyler Petit. Last year’s Car Show had vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 91 vehicles have signed up for this year’s show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, and a 1987 Ferrari Testarossa. The car show includes free coffee and donuts. In addition, a taco truck will be on hand to feed the masses, and Piedmont teens will sell baked goods. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want their cars to be in the show need to register by tomorrow, September 22, on the Eventbrite website: Eventbrite.com/e/coffee-cars-cops-car-show-tickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue near Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov. Last year’s Piedmont Car Show featured a row of gleaming exotic sports cars in front of the Exedra at Piedmont Park.

articles.text: Dr. Elise Marks, President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers, encouraged members of the Piedmont School Board at their September 14 meeting to provide a raise for all teachers in part due to a spiraling economy and cost of living. Prior to the meeting, teachers gathered with signs outside of City Hall in a rally urging a pay raise. teachers have taken their message to the streets by coordinating rallies and signs in the mornings during a time when students are dropped off at school. APT is requesting a 7.5% salary increase, plus a one-time bonus pay of $4,000 per full-time member. Inflation and a shortage of teachers drive their requests. Speech by: Dr. Elise Marks, APT President It’s all over the news: the national teacher shortage. Too many classrooms have no teachers. Young people aren’t entering teacher training programs. Mid-career teachers are quitting, often mid-year. Exhausted veteran teachers are retiring early. It’s not just about low wages, but low wages are enough to drive the decision for many. Teacher wages in the US have been flat since 1996, and currently, compared to other professionals with equivalent education, teachers earn 23.5% less–the worst that “wage gap” has ever been. Inflation is pushing teachers over the brink–after a high of 9.1% earlier in the year, inflation was still at 8.3% for August. Prices on most commonly bought groceries are up 30%. This is an emergency. As you know, the problem is especially acute in the Bay Area, where the cost of living is so high the Milpitas school district is asking families to rent rooms out to teachers–like it’s Kansas in 1882, trying to house the schoolmarms, who, of course, were not permitted to have families of their own. This is not a sustainable model for the profession. A generation or so ago, the profession was sustainable. Teachers have never expected to live in luxury, but they were solidly middle class. A teacher could afford a modest home, a modest car. They could afford to have kids, and send those kids to college. Their health insurance was paid in full and they could look forward to a modest but secure retirement. No more. You’ve heard the stories of Piedmont teachers living in uninsulated, mice-infested garages. –Dr. Elise Marks President, Association of Piedmont Teachers Teachers have been wearing their red Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) shirts every Tuesday this year for awareness of the need for raises. On a number of occasions this year and last,

The Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town this Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and is organized by Officer Tyler Petit. Last year’s Car Show had vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 91 vehicles have signed up for this year’s show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, and a 1987 Ferrari Testarossa. The car show includes free coffee and donuts. In addition, a taco truck will be on hand to feed the masses, and Piedmont teens will sell baked goods. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want their cars to be in the show need to register by tomorrow, September 22, on the Eventbrite website: Eventbrite.com/e/coffee-cars-cops-car-show-tickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue near Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov. Last year’s Piedmont Car Show featured a row of gleaming exotic sports cars in front of the Exedra at Piedmont Park. The need for the position comes in part from the demands See Echa Schneider on page 32 Teachers Union President Elise Marks’ speech compels school board for raises Dr. Elise Marks, President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers, encouraged members of the Piedmont School Board at their September 14 meeting to provide a raise for all teachers in part due to a spiraling economy and cost of living. Prior to the meeting, teachers gathered with signs outside of City Hall in a rally urging a pay raise. teachers have taken their message to the streets by coordinating rallies and signs in the mornings during a time when students are dropped off at school. APT is requesting a 7.5% salary increase, plus a one-time bonus pay of $4,000 per full-time member. Inflation and a shortage of teachers drive their requests. Speech by: Dr. Elise Marks, APT President It’s all over the news: the national teacher shortage. Too many classrooms have no teachers. Young people aren’t entering teacher training programs. Mid-career teachers are quitting, often mid-year. Exhausted veteran teachers are retiring early. It’s not just about low wages, but low wages are enough to drive the decision for many. Teacher wages in the US have been flat since 1996, and currently, compared to other professionals with equivalent education, teachers earn 23.5% less–the worst that “wage gap” has ever been. Inflation is pushing teachers over the brink–after a high of 9.1% earlier in the year, inflation was still at 8.3% for August. Prices on most commonly bought groceries are up 30%. This is an emergency. As you know, the problem is especially acute in the Bay Area, where the cost of living is so high the Milpitas school district is asking families to rent rooms out to teachers–like it’s Kansas in 1882, trying to house the schoolmarms, who, of course, were not permitted to have families of their own. This is not a sustainable model for the profession. A generation or so ago, the profession was sustainable. Teachers have never expected to live in luxury, but they were solidly middle class. A teacher could afford a modest home, a modest car. They could afford to have kids, and send those kids to college. Their health insurance was paid in full and they could look forward to a modest but secure retirement. No more. You’ve heard the stories of Piedmont teachers living in uninsulated, mice-infested garages. articles.text: Voting website piedmontvotes.com seen as selective Editor: On September 15 a kind neighbor shared a post with me from the private Piedmont Families Facebook group with a group called Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and with a link to a PREC newsletter. In that newsletter, it stated that “PREC as an organization is not making formal endorsements in this election cycle....however, as individual members of the steering committee....we are supporting the following candidates”. It goes on to list Medhekar, Thomasson, Andersen, Long and Ramsey. Within the newsletter, there was a link to a voting website, piedmontvotes.com. Expecting a nonpartisan voting website, I was met with a smear campaign against each of the candidates which PREC did not recommend voting for. This website was clearly created by PREC and was blatantly promotional. My neighbor has yet to hear any of the PREC endorsed candidates or their supporters speak out against chosen a community that would bring itself down to these standards. The PREC website states that they are an organization that “strives to build a thriving community.” I hardly think so. PREC appears to have brought divisive national politicking to the small town of Piedmont. I am new here and this is no way to treat your neighbors who are willing to sacrifice their personal time to run for office. I am especially disturbed that the lone Asian running for school board received the brunt of the attacks. In a climate of Asian hate is this acceptable behavior? Is PREC encouraging Asian attacks against the school board candidate? After seeing this campaign, I will not be voting for any of PREC’s recommended candidates. I will be voting for candidates that stand up for what they believe in rather than candidates that PREC “places” on the City Council and School Board. – Tu Ngoc Nguyen Piedmont resident For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. The first section (1-11) of complaint and grief is represented by words like “They set fire to your sanctuary, burned it to the ground” (7a). It is followed by a second section (12-17) of gratitude and confidence represented by words like “Yet God has been my king from ancient days” (12a). A lost sheep would have been an occasion for both fear and grief. A caring shepherd would not take such a loss easily or lightly. Jesus then speaks of the joy that comes when the lost is found and the terrified lamb is carried home. When the lost is found there is gratitude. One reason this parable continues to speak, even to those of us unfamiliar with sheep and shepherds, is that most us are well acquainted with loss and grief. We are also well acquainted with the gratitude that comes with restoration, recovery and remembering. Grief and gratitude travel together. They intersect. The prayer, the hope, of the great religious traditions, and my personal faith as well, is that at their point of intersection grace is born and that is grace which will lead us home. With that in mind, consider that the City will soon have to face up to the State’s mandate to bring Essential Services Buildings or ESB (police, fire and city offices) up to State code requirements. For comparison, consider that the Pool project is heading toward a $22-23M price tag while the ESB project costs, as compiled by the City Staff in April 2020, was estimated to be between $80 to 100M – and that was with very preliminary plans and scope. articles.text: I saw a lawn sign today that read, “Let Us Vote.” This is a fantastic slogan. What upstanding American citizen would oppose voting? But when applied to the issue of housing planning, this approach is deeply flawed. City Council candidates Bridget Harris and Jeanne Solnordal are calling for a citywide vote on the City’s housing plan, even though the City Attorney has stated repeatedly that the proposed zoning changes don’t require a citywide ballot. These candidates claim fiscal responsibility and smart planning. In fact, holding an unnecessary citywide vote would be expensive, counterproductive, and against the City’s interests. To demonstrate this, let’s walk through how such a vote would play out: • First, the City would have to cover the cost of the ballot measure. Unlike the cost of building housing, which is borne by private developers, this would be a public expense of tens of thousands of dollars borne exclusively by Piedmont’s taxpayers. • An election could not be held before the City’s looming deadline to submit its housing plan to the State for approval, so the City would miss the State certification deadline, subjecting Piedmont to a host of penalties. The first penalty is that the City would have one year instead of three years to implement zoning code changes to facilitate housing development, making it extremely difficult for the City to create rational and well-designed zoning requirements that best respond to the community’s needs. pages.text: Wednesday, September 21, 2022 3 City needs to take Project Management seriously By Donald Chandler, AIA While cost overruns on public projects are sadly nothing new, the Pool project’s overrun before construction bids have been received and after scope reductions have been made is hard to fathom and extremely disappointing. With that in mind, consider that the City will soon have to face up to the State’s mandate to bring Essential Services Buildings or ESB (police, fire and city offices) up to State code requirements. For comparison, consider that the Pool project is heading toward a $22-23M price tag while the ESB project costs, as compiled by the City Staff in April 2020, was estimated to be between $80 to 100M – and that was with very preliminary plans and scope. Without vastly better methods of cost control for the ESB projects, overruns of the scale of the pool project could easily cause a financial crisis for our small town. A little background. In the lead up to Measure UU, the Pool project was represented as a $15 million project with a $4.5M Contingency added to cover latent conditions, change orders, scope changes, etc. That resulted in the $19.5M Measure UU Bond. The $4.5M Contingency was prudent and warranted given the status of the plans at the time. Now plans have been fully developed (and modified once to reduce the cost) and yet residents are still being asked to fund an additional $2.6M to complete the project. There is also a separate special funding plan seeking $500K to install Heat Pumps to make the project all-electric. So, the project is currently about $3M over budget. If we add the original $4.5M Contingency to the current $3M overage, we have exceeded the original estimate $15M estimate by a whopping $7.5M or 50%. That is quite a miss and underscores my main message: Piedmont must adopt a more rigorous and professional Project Management model. What is that model? It is one where the design team, the project management team and the estimating team all have equal weight and input into the project from the very early stages. The team needs to avoid iterative design exercises - where a design is completed and then estimated and then often redesigned and estimated again. The design and estimating processes must go forward simultaneously. This management model is not new. It is a model used by most major corporations or entities which have significant building programs. But these are top-down decisions. The Owner, in our case the City Council, must lead and require this model of Project Management if the City hopes to avoid replicating the Pool experience in the future. Regarding the Pool project, it is up to the City Council to establish any accountability for how the Pool project got to where it is. I maintain that the issue is poor project management and definitely not hyperinflation as claimed by some. (Hyperinflation is defined as monthly inflation of 50% or more, and we are not experiencing that.) No, our problem and our issue to resolve is our current method of Project Management. It is not serving us well. We should not and cannot continue to exceed our budgets and then go hat-inhand to our residents to bail out our projects. How Piedmont manages the Pool project moving forward and the ESB projects in the very near future will depend largely on the will of the City Council and City Staff to chart a different path. OPINION 2 campaigns mislead voters on housing Issues By Deborah Leland I saw a lawn sign today that read, “Let Us Vote.” This is a fantastic slogan. What upstanding American citizen would oppose voting? But when applied to the issue of housing planning, this approach is deeply flawed. City Council candidates Bridget Harris and Jeanne Solnordal are calling for a citywide vote on the City’s housing plan, even though the City Attorney has stated repeatedly that the proposed zoning changes don’t require a citywide ballot. These candidates claim fiscal responsibility and smart planning. In fact, holding an unnecessary citywide vote would be expensive, counterproductive, and against the City’s interests. To demonstrate this, let’s walk through how such a vote would play out: • First, the City would have to cover the cost of the ballot measure. Unlike the cost of building housing, which is borne by private developers, this would be a public expense of tens of thousands of dollars borne exclusively by Piedmont’s taxpayers. • An election could not be held before the City’s looming deadline to submit its housing plan to the State for approval, so the City would miss the State certification deadline, subjecting Piedmont to a host of penalties. The first penalty is that the City would have one year instead of three years to implement zoning code changes to facilitate housing development, making it extremely difficult for the City to create rational and well-designed zoning requirements that best respond to the community’s needs. Failure to meet that deadline would lead to escalating penalties, including loss of local control over land use and, potentially, fines. • If a ballot measure is held and the electorate approves the City’s current proposal to allow for additional multifamily housing in certain areas of the City, then we’d be right back where we are today, but at significant cost and detriment to the City, as described above. • If a ballot measure is held and the electorate does not approve the City’s plan to allow additional multifamily housing, then the City will be back at square one in creating a new housing plan to meet State law, while penalties pile up. And, most importantly, if constrained to accommodating multifamily housing in only the limited locations where it is currently allowed, the scale and density of new development that would have to be allowed along Highland Ave. and Grand Ave. would be much greater than what is currently proposed. How is that prudent planning? The promotion of such an untenable proposition by these two City Council candidates is irresponsible and short-sighted, and hardly a model of wise leadership. I urge Piedmonters to confront this reality, and not be fooled by a catchy slogan and an appeal to voter rights. Subscribe!Don’t miss an issue of the paper of Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Part two in a series much more likely to apply, and stay, in Piedmont administration and teaching positions. Three candidates are running for two open seats on the Piedmont School Board in the November 8 election. The Piedmont Post will provide extensive coverage on candidates for School Board and for City Council. The Post’s first month of campaign coverage will alternate weekly between City Council and School Board. This week, all School Board candidates were asked to answer the two questions shown below. Due to space limitations, candidates were asked to contain their answers to 150 words per question. QUESTIONS 1. If elected, how would you utilize the ample amount of parent involvement in Piedmont to benefit the schools? 2. PUSD was tasked with finding three new principals and an interim superintendent last summer. What needs to be done to attract and retain top administrators in the district? RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement Our parent community is an incredible resource and one of the reasons I love living in Piedmont. COVID has provided countless examples of how parents have had to pivot and problem-solve to support their kids’ learning and our schools. I firmly believe that the parent community is an underutilized asset in key ways, which has been frustrating for many of us. We have a remarkable level of expertise which PUSD has leveraged in the past (one example is the Curriculum Forum Committee, which has been inactive since 2014). In other exceptional school districts, there are opportunities for parents to collaborate with their schools to achieve the best decision for students, and we should be open to learning from those models. It is less about parents “getting their way” and more about the integrity of the process, and how (and when) to get buy-in for important decisions. ideas, innovation, and leadership are encouraged, prized, and rewarded. The school board sets the strategy for the district, but it is the superintendent’s role to bring this vision to life. Having a clear and focused direction at the top will help ensure that talent is retained at all levels. SHIRLEY HOOI 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement I applaud the dedication that Piedmont parents have in their volunteer roles across all three school levels and the extraordinary fundraising efforts benefitting the schools. In terms of how to utilize additional parent volunteer time towards the schools, I propose that parents consider utilizing their time to help students directly in strengthening academic outcomes. I envision middle and high school parents stepping into the elementary schools to help the younger students overcome math or reading struggles in order to help create an early love of learning. LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement In my roles as Havens Parent Club President, on the Superintendent Advisory Committee, and in numerous volunteer roles, I’ve experienced firsthand PUSD’s parents’ willingness to give generously of their time, money, and talents, including raising millions of dollars annually for PEF. I value this involvement as one of PUSD’s greatest resources. Yet, many parents voice frustration that they aren’t engaged with the district in meaningful ways. There is not a systematic way for parents to have a seat at the table when decisions regarding new courses, curriculum or hiring occur. I will form district sub-committees that have formal application processes, terms, and responsibilities. They will be subject to the Brown Act so will conduct business in public like the board is required to do. They will ensure stakeholder feedback and buy-in throughout the process. I will also work to increase transparency around administrator hiring processes. 2. Retaining Administrators This year the school board will have the important job of hiring a new superintendent and this person will drive the culture and practices that are critical to attracting and retaining excellent principals. As I know from my experience in building out high-performing teams, a number of important factors play a role in cultivating strong leadership. We must ensure that salaries are in line with the cost of living for all of our district’s employees. We need to cultivate transparency, respect, trust, and open communication. Those foundational elements can move the district to a culture of professionalism where new 2. Retaining Administrators Attracting and retaining qualified teachers and administrators is critical for the success of a school district. With the growing shortage of teachers and administrators nationwide, it is essential that PUSD offers a competitive compensation package and supportive workplace for principals and a superintendent. In retaining principals, it is important for PUSD to provide a rewarding vertical career pathway within PUSD. As for retaining a superintendent, I believe the first step is to hire a superintendent that can achieve PUSD’s set goals. It is not a superintendent’s job to set a district’s goals but rather systematically achieve those goals set by the school board. If the school board lays the road to success for the superintendent, I believe success is a determining factor of retention. 2. Retaining Administrators PUSD should conduct exit surveys of all educators, both administrators and teachers, who depart the district. They must be done in a way that educators feel comfortable responding forthrightly. Responses should be shared with the board and superintendent so we can quickly identify and address concerns, and remedy issues. We also need to have robust conversations with all stakeholders to determine our community priorities. What are our goals for our students when they graduate from our schools? Our collective values as they relate to education? When we can articulate these goals, we can hire administrators who support them, and in turn can support our administrators in achieving our collective objectives. Clear direction from the board on goals and objectives, and allocating funds accordingly, is critical. Administrators who feel supported and empowered to work collaboratively with stakeholders are

The first notice of a cancellation came at 7:32 p.m. on Friday evening in a message from Jazz Festival coordinator Greg Slatoff notifying the bands scheduled to play that the music portion of the festival had been canceled. The city historically sets up a large stage in the Main Park with a sound system and a piano for the performers. “It is with the greatest disappointment that I must tell you the Jazz Festival has been canceled due to the impeding rain. Issues related to the erection of the stage and maintenance of sound/ electronic systems in wet weather were the factors that prompted the City’s decision,” his message read. The City followed with its own message at 9:53 p.m. “After much deliberation and hoping for a change in the impending storm’s arrival, the City of Piedmont has made the difficult decision to cancel all outdoor activities for Sunday’s Harvest Festival. The weather forecast predicts significant rain and wind gusts starting early Sunday morning and through the early afternoon.” The City has not indicated why alternate sites were not used for some of the festival’s components, to include Scarecrow Alley, Farmer’s Market, Kids’ Carnival and art show. No mention has been made of the availability of the high school gym or its auditorium, the three elementary school auditoriums, or the Staff Photos A rain gauge, with artificially collected water, in the foreground of Piedmont Park. Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church. The Harvest Festival Committee met late Friday afternoon to discuss the possibility of hosting the event given the impending storm, which was projected to bring half an inch of rain on Sunday. The actual amount of rain was considerably less than the half inch projected. “Staff considered possible alternatives for the Jazz Festival, however moving indoors was not feasible,” said Recreation Department Director Chelle Putzer. The Harvest Festival, which normally attracts 800-1000 attendees, requires the service of dozens of vendors, musicians, students, artists, staff, and volunteers. Three days before the event, on Thursday, September 15, the Piedmont Education Foundation, which helps with the kid’s carnival and scarecrows, sent out a newsletter saying the event would continue “rain or shine.” The optimistic sentiment was not enough, however. articles.text: Last summer, a cohort of Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer high school students worked at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley as part of a larger partnership between NASA Ames and Chabot Space & Science Center. As full-time interns they were placed in departments for project work and close mentorship by NASA staff. Students were paired with scientists and staff based on their interests and For 3-year Galaxy Explorer Sage Mosley, the passion for space began at a young age. She began exploring the cosmos with a Planet Project at age nine, continuing on to Space Camp during middle school for two summers at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Alabama, and continuing her internship at Chabot Space & Science Center, which she started as a freshman at Piedmont High School. –Sage Mosley, Chabot Galaxy Explorer and NASA Aeromechanics Intern Piedmont High School senior Sage Mosley is in her fourth year as an intern at Chabot Space & Science “In 3rd grade, I told my parents I wanted to work for NASA,” said Mosley, “Eight years later, I was reading my offer letter to intern at Ames Research Center. I started jumping up and down, and I immediately ran to share the news. My family and friends were beyond proud.” Now as a high school senior, Mosley plans to study Aerospace A photo of the eight Galaxy Explorer interns from Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland. Engineering in college, with the ultimate goal is of becoming a NASA astronaut. “The most exciting thing about the internship is meeting people with the same passions. While I was nervous to be the youngest in the room on my first day, I was welcomed into a super friendly environment at Ames. Through my example, I hope to encourage others my age to follow their dreams and keep going until they succeed.” Mosley was one of eight Galaxy Explorers interning at NASA Ames last summer. The interns learned directly from mentors in the field, working on projects in supercomputing, data analytics, rotorcraft aeromechanics, lunar missions, public engagement, computer science and STEM engagement. Sage Mosley with a prototype space vehicle.

articles.text: You’ve heard teachers talk about how they have to take second jobs at night and on weekends to pay their bills, and how they’re maxing out their credit cards to survive. You’ve heard young teachers tell you how they cannot afford to have children of their own. In the 23 years I have worked in Piedmont, teacher wages have consistently fallen below inflation, and not just because our salary increases haven’t kept pace. Health insurance is another huge piece of the problem. As of 2008, our health insurance in Piedmont was fully paid by the district. In the economic downturn of that year, to help the district maintain all its programs, teachers agreed to take on paying part of our own premiums. The district promised that as the economic picture improved, we’d try to restore some of those benefits. It hasn’t gone that way. As of January– with the cost of Kaiser climbing yet again–I personally will be paying the equivalent of 10% of my take-home pay every month for health insurance. That’s an effective 10% pay cut right there over what I earned just a few years ago. Some local districts–like Oakland and Lafayette–have returned to paying full health benefits for their teachers. Others have significantly raised the caps for the amount of the premium they cover. The maximum health benefit for a Piedmont teacher is $19,800, as it has been for several years. So just under $20,000. San Ramon, which has about the same maximum salary we have, covers $26,493. Acalanes, $27,000. Moraga, $26,700. Albany, $25,169. Martinez, a notoriously low-paying district, covers $27,000; $7,000 a year more than Piedmont. And our maximum salaries are falling behind. As I said last time, one teacher we lost during the summer had four local offers each more than $30,000 a year over what Piedmont pays. How can we hold on to our teachers when our salaries and benefits can’t compete with districts all around us? I’m hearing that Piedmont teachers are getting cold-called.– in September, when the school year has already started – by other desperate local districts looking to poach them right now from Piedmont, offering hiring bonuses of $6000 to $10,000, not to mention higher overall benefits and pay. Almost daily, teachers pull me aside or email me asking, “Do you think we’ll settle soon? Will we get what we’re asking for? I need to decide whether to start sending out my resumé.” In negotiations, APT is asking for a 7.5% salary increase, plus some one-time bonus money – $4,000 per full-time member – to help us recover from the hard hit of inflation. It is estimated to be costing the average Bay Area household an extra $4,400 in 2022. We need [a raise] to make a dent in some of those maxed out credit cards. pages.text: Wednesday, September 21, 2022 7 Dr. Marks’ Speech Continued from page 1 You’ve heard teachers talk about how they have to take second jobs at night and on weekends to pay their bills, and how they’re maxing out their credit cards to survive. You’ve heard young teachers tell you how they cannot afford to have children of their own. In the 23 years I have worked in Piedmont, teacher wages have consistently fallen below inflation, and not just because our salary increases haven’t kept pace. Health insurance is another huge piece of the problem. As of 2008, our health insurance in Piedmont was fully paid by the district. In the economic downturn of that year, to help the district maintain all its programs, teachers agreed to take on paying part of our own premiums. The district promised that as the economic picture improved, we’d try to restore some of those benefits. It hasn’t gone that way. As of January– with the cost of Kaiser climbing yet again–I personally will be paying the equivalent of 10% of my take-home pay every month for health insurance. That’s an effective 10% pay cut right there over what I earned just a few years ago. Some local districts–like Oakland and Lafayette–have returned to paying full health benefits for their teachers. Others have significantly raised the caps for the amount of the premium they cover. The maximum health benefit for a Piedmont teacher is $19,800, as it has been for several years. So just under $20,000. San Ramon, which has about the same maximum salary we have, covers $26,493. Acalanes, $27,000. Moraga, $26,700. Albany, $25,169. Martinez, a notoriously low-paying district, covers $27,000; $7,000 a year more than Piedmont. And our maximum salaries are falling behind. As I said last time, one teacher we lost during the summer had four local offers each more than $30,000 a year over what Piedmont pays. How can we hold on to our teachers when our salaries and benefits can’t compete with districts all around us? I’m hearing that Piedmont teachers are getting cold-called.– in September, when the school year has already started – by other desperate local districts looking to poach them right now from Piedmont, offering hiring bonuses of $6000 to $10,000, not to mention higher overall benefits and pay. Almost daily, teachers pull me aside or email me asking, “Do you think we’ll settle soon? Will we get what we’re asking for? I need to decide whether to start sending out my resumé.” In negotiations, APT is asking for a 7.5% salary increase, plus some one-time bonus money – $4,000 per full-time member – to help us recover from the hard hit of inflation. It is estimated to be costing the average Bay Area household an extra $4,400 in 2022. We need [a raise] to make a dent in some of those maxed out credit cards. This ask is relatively modest, given rampant inflation. Most other local teacher unions are asking for increases of between 10-12%. L.A. Unified is asking for 20%, and frankly, that’s the kind of number needed to actually make this profession sustainable. Remember: given where inflation is this year, 7.5% will still be an effective pay cut for Piedmont teachers. Piedmont Unified can afford to give us what we’re asking. Not only does the district have about 3.5 million dollars more than we thought when the budget was approved in June (when APT was offered an average 5% salary increase), it seems clear that with the numbers of veteran teachers we’ve had retiring or resigning, and who are being replaced with much newer teachers, payroll expenses have been dropping dramatically. I’ve been arguing for several years that this savings was coming, as we have a very large number of teachers currently at the highest [level] on our salary schedule, most of whom are planning to retire soon – this year, next year, in another year or two beyond that. Few are planning to stay for another five years. That wave of retirements has been looming for years and is about to break. And indeed, last year when we negotiated a 2.5% raise, we were told at the bargaining table that the district could not afford the raise. We were told, based on typical numbers from years past, that the percentage increase would cost the district about $527,000. Lo and behold, just as I’ve been predicting, with the larger-than-usual number of veteran teachers who left by the end of last year – either retiring or resigning – that 2.5% percentage increase for APT salaries turned out not to cost $527,000 once the Unaudited Actuals were calculated this month. As you see in the budget presentation tonight, the actual cost has turned out to be…$78,000. I want to make sure everyone hears that. Not $527,000, but $78,000 – difference of almost $450,000 in the district’s financial favor. That savings will keep happening. Because veteran teachers will keep leaving in higher numbers each year. The district office hasn’t even had the chance yet to calculate the impact of the record 18 teachers who left the district this past spring. The rate will be faster or slower depending on what Piedmont does with salary right now, but the net effect will be the same: the district will have more and more money left over with which they can raise teacher pay, and hopefully retain the teachers they still have. And meanwhile the cost of living in the Bay Area will surely continue to increase. Members of the School Board, I know you have a solemn duty to watch over the budget, and I know there are many worthy things that need funding. But you have to hear us when we say that budgets are value statements. You have to hear us when we say that we cannot keep on with business as usual, with staff getting raises only when there’s “a little left over” at the end of the budget year. You have to take a very, very hard look at district priorities. How can there be schools when there is no staff, when there are no teachers? I keep telling you we are in a crisis. The 7.5% cost of living increase and the one-time money we’re asking for isn’t even a solution; it’s not enough to make being a teacher in Piedmont a truly sustainable proposition. 7.5% is just a life preserver. Your teachers and all of your staff are drowning, and we are asking you to throw us a life preserver. If you don’t, more of us will soon be lost. articles.text: Two weeks ago, my 6-yearold daughter was all set to do a fun art project. She was going to make an animal pet rock. In front of her was a pile of small rocks to select from, acrylic paints, googly eyes and some bit of fake fur. She was super excited and we started thinking about what kind of animal she would make. All of a sudden, her entire mood changed. Her eyes filled with tears and she curled into a little ball and she looked up at me and said, “Mommy, I’m just so scared it won’t be perfect.” My heart breaks. We talk it through with some really challenging questions: • Why do we make art? • What does “perfect” look like? • Why do you want “perfect”? • If your fear was a creature, what would it look like? • Can we make friends with your fear? Eventually, she came around to a lesson that she had learned in kindergarten: “Perfect doesn’t exist.” She took a deep breath, chose a rock and spent the next hour making a perfectly imperfect Hummingbird pet rock. She was smiling and happy during the process and proud of the outcome which she gave to her grandma as a present. But this whole episode really made me reflect on the power that the concept of “perfect” holds over so many of us. Kids and Why do we make art? adults alike, we can completely knock out entire categories of activities for fear that we won’t do it perfectly. But the creative process is just that, a process. In the end, the outcome is only the sum total of a number of tiny steps. So, how can we ask ourselves for perfection? We can’t control every single tiny step we take. And the joy of the experience of creating is in finding the fun and flow in each of those steps. What creative act would you try if you had no fear of failing? What would your kids want to explore if there was no expectation to be “good” at it? The act of creation is an act of courage because it is putting our own inner self out in the world in some capacity. Most of us didn’t have a kindergarten teacher who taught us that there is no such thing as perfect, so we need to teach ourselves and our kids that it’s ok to be scared and it’s ok to try and it’s ok to just see what happens. When it comes to creativity, it’s not about the destination, it’s about appreciating and enjoying the journey. .Nina Meehan is the CEO and Founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre, currently performing “Elephant and Piggie: We are in a Play.” For tickets see www.bactheatre.org.
articles.title: The fear of not being perfect

articles.text: A rafting trip is one of the most iconic Scout outings. In addition to being thrilling, it also offers a unique experience and is so much fun. The Scouts weren’t the only ones screaming and laughing; the adult advisors had their share of fun too. After a three-hour drive to Lotus, a tiny town in El Dorado County, the Scouts piled out of the cars into an unbearable heat. After lunch we got our helmets, life jackets and paddles and headed to the American River where we received important safety lessons. We were all baking in the heat, so we were glad to get our feet wet as we waded into the water and climbed into the rafts. After about 10 minutes on the water, we hit the first rapid – not a huge one, but a slightly calmer class II rapid called Swimmers Rapid. Some of us jumped out of the raft and enjoyed a quick dip in the river. This was followed by a string of class II and a few class III rapids. Our guide was wonderful, pointing out the unique rocks and the names given to them, such as Rabbit Rock and Crocodile Rock. I think that “screaming right turn” was one of my favorites. It looked harmless, but there was a reason it was called a “screaming” right turn, believe me. After about an hour and a half of rafting, something worthy of documentation happened – a Scout was tossed out of the boat. He quickly resurfaced and was pulled back into the raft, but became the talk of the trip (which is why I’m including it here. There would be consequences if I didn’t.) At about the same time we stopped for a snack and turned a raft upside down by standing on it with a rope and toppling backwards. What was the purpose? To create a water slide! The line of Scouts wanting to take turns on the slide quickly formed and stretched forever. It was so much fun to plunge into the water endlessly and cool off from the earlier heat. After the break I had more sand and water in my shoes than ever and was soaked. There were more class III rapids for the second part of the trip and several people claimed they were tossed upside down. After an epic race to the end of the run at Folsom Lake, 10 miles downstream from where we started, we climbed into the bus with a cold drink and returned to the Mother Lode campground, a mere 18 minutes away. With every step we left behind sopping footprints that almost immediately evaporated in the dry heat. After washing our gear we found our campsite and set up. Most of the Scouts chose to sleep under the stars, but a friend and I wanted some protection from the elements, so we grabbed a tent – only to discover it had no poles. Luckily Scoutmaster Cantrill was kind enough to lend us his tent, an example of one of the points of the Scout Law– kindness. That made my day. articles.text: The City of Piedmont began its scheduled street sweeping on September 19, and will continue for the next six months. Street sweeping will be conducted on the day after green waste, recycling, and trash are picked up for homes, and will be on a threeweek cycle alternating between odd- and even-numbered sides of the street, followed by a week with no sweeping. The street sweeping schedule is printed very week in the Piedmont Post. Residents are also made aware of the schedule in advance so that they can relocate their cars and move the green waste, recycling, and trashcans to create free and clear access up to the curb. Since Piedmont relies on residents to move their vehicles, knowledge of the sweeping dates is essential. To help promote resident cooperate and knowledge, the City Council approved linking the street sweeping schedule to the regular green waste, recycle, and trash pickup days. week’s schedule. For questions regarding the updated street sweeping schedule, contact the Public Works Department at (510) 420-3050.
articles.title: Fall street sweeping begins

pages.text: Wednesday, September 21, 2022 9 Fall street sweeping begins The City of Piedmont began its scheduled street sweeping on September 19, and will continue for the next six months. Street sweeping will be conducted on the day after green waste, recycling, and trash are picked up for homes, and will be on a threeweek cycle alternating between odd- and even-numbered sides of the street, followed by a week with no sweeping. The street sweeping schedule is printed very week in the Piedmont Post. Residents are also made aware of the schedule in advance so that they can relocate their cars and move the green waste, recycling, and trashcans to create free and clear access up to the curb. Since Piedmont relies on residents to move their vehicles, knowledge of the sweeping dates is essential. To help promote resident cooperate and knowledge, the City Council approved linking the street sweeping schedule to the regular green waste, recycle, and trash pickup days. See below for the current’s week’s schedule. For questions regarding the updated street sweeping schedule, contact the Public Works Department at (510) 420-3050. articles.text: Girl Scout project by Wildwood alum benefits everyone On September 1, an estimated 200 students at Wildwood Elementary School took action and walked, scootered and biked to school. The event was the idea of Piedmont High senior Skye Yeh, a Wildwood alum, as part of her Girl Scout Gold Award. During the summer she and some helpers built three new scooter racks which now reside in the school courtyard. The idea came after seeing the over-crowded drop off and pick ups in front of the school. Too many cars have created unsafe situations for the students. After talking with Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer, and a safety officer at Piedmont Police, Skye decided she wanted to get more cars off the streets. A list of reasons for students to participate in the Walk and Roll event was compiled and shared with students, teachers and parents; along with some safety rules. The school had almost 78% of students walk, scooter, bike and even one who roller skated to school. The classes ranged from a 95% participation to a 61% participation. The street in front of the school was noticeably emptier that morning. The teachers were thankful for the scooter racks and for the event and hope for a continued habit of choosReasons to walk or scoot to school • It’s Fun. Walking and scootering are more fun than sitting in a car. • It’s Healthy. Exercise is good for your body. • It’s a great way to start the day. Exercise gets your brain going, too. • It’s planet friendly. Fewer cars means less pollution. • It’s friendly. Walking with neighbors makes new friends • It’s safer. Fewer cars make safer streets. Safety rules when walking to school • Stay on sidewalks • Use crosswalks • Walk with friends and neighbors • Look both ways before crossing a street and wait for cars to stop • Be aware of your surroundings, especially near driveways • Listen to crossing guards and police officers Safety rules when riding a scooter to school • Wear a properly fitting helmet • Adjust your scooter to a proper and safe height • Be mindful of pedestrians and alert them you are near • Follow all walking rules • Ride on the sidewalk, not in the street • Use the new racks at school to store your scooter and helmet • Remember to take your helmet and scooter home at the end of the day Skye Yeh and Nikila Rao building a rack. Skye Yeh and Carol Cramer stand by the newly installed racks. Skye attaching hardware. ing self-propelled transportation over cars. ”I’m so proud of all the students who biked or scootered to school or found a way to walk The new scooter rack being used. instead of being driven,” said Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer. Skye commented that she hopes students and parents learned something or felt empowered to make a difference in their future choices that affect their safety, health and the health of the environment. Walkers Nora and Julio Montes with Izzy and Greg Wheeler. The unusually empty drop off area during event. Sarah scootering to school. The overflowing bike racks at Wildwood school.

articles.text: Due to the threat of rain on Sunday, September 18, the city of Piedmont made the decision at 9:53 p.m. on Friday, September 16, to cancel nearly the entire multi-faceted annual event scheduled for Sunday in Piedmont Park from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The lone survivor was the Edible Food Contest, a mainstay of the Festival since its first year. With 127 entries of homemade jams, jellies, breads, and pickles, the contest turned the Community Center into a large array of produce and baked goods displaying the bounty of Piedmont cooks and gardeners, Founded in 1998 by Bill Drumm and former mayor Susan Hill, the Festival itself is a sixring circus, with a jazz festival, Kids’ Carnival, Farmers Market, art exhibit, and Scarecrow Alley – a large collection of life-sized scarecrows made primarily by school kids. And the Edible Food Contest. Categories of foods in recent years have included curds, pies, pesto, and cookies, and a prize for the biggest zucchini and most unusual vegetable. The Vitter family shares a laugh with Greg Slatoff (right). Staff photo Staff photo Katia, Anastasia, and Sasha Lindgardt, winners of growing the largest zucchini. Staff photo The Vitter family had relatives visiting from Vienna during the Harvest Festival.

articles.text: In a one-sided affair, Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team dominated San Leandro, 21-3, at the Pirates’ home pool on Tuesday, September 13. Piedmont remains undefeated with a 5-0 record. The Highlanders finished the night with 12 different players scoring, led by Declan Linnane, Finn Burke, and Hayden Jahn each with. A hat trick (3 goals). Notably, Jahn was just called up from the junior varsity team. Piedmont led 8-3 by the end of the first quarter and 14-3 at halftime. The Highlanders extended the gap to 16-3 in the third quarter and closed off with five more goals in the final period. In the first quarter, Peter Krumins scored the opening goal after barely one minute. San Leandro quickly tied after 17 seconds, but Finn Burke scored just 12 seconds later to put the Highlanders ahead 2-1, a lead they never relinquished. Burke scored once more with 5:02 left in the first just eight seconds after drawing a man-advantage, 3-1, followed by three quick goals by Linnane, Farris Saffouri, and Daniel Banin in the next minute to make it 6-2 with 3:31 left. San Leandro made it 6-3 with 3:03 left in the quarter but Evan Dickason and George Stein answered with goals at 1:29 and 1:01 for a Piedmont 8-3 lead.. Piedmont added six unanswered goals in the second quarter. It took just 18 seconds for PHS to score in the second quarter when Linnane sent one in. Krumins then made it 10-3 after 30 seconds. A minute later, Charlie Wright netted one and just 20 seconds later Jahn made it 12-3. With 2:10 left in the second, Linnane made it 13-3 and Evan Dickason sent one in with just four Photos by Nancy Brahm Declan Linnane scored three goals, and had an assist and three steals against San Leandro. ticks left. In the third, the Highlanders added two goals from Jahn with 5:33 and 4:28 left in the quarter. The. Highlanders scored five more times in the last period. Leo Hurwitz scored 50 seconds into the quarter and then Burke put in another goal 40 seconds later. With 2:26 remaining, Ori Aloush scored two goals, and Hurwitz scored the final goal with 15 seconds left on the clock. Final stats: Linnane scored three goals, one assist, and three steals. articles.text: Staff Photos Anne Jumper won at No. 1 singles in straight sets over Bentley, 6-1, 6-0. Cecilia DeFazio paired with Emma Eisemon at No. 1 doubles for a decisive 6-2, 6-2 win. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team had a cakewalk with Bentley on Tuesday, September 13. Playing at home, the Highlanders rolled to a 6-1 victory, including three matches that were shutous. “We had a solid day with several shutout double-bagel (6-0, 6-0) wins. We won all of our matches in straight sets,” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Playing No. 1 singles, Anne Jumper won handily, 6-1, 6-0. Carolina Romanczuk pitched a shutout No. 2, 6-0, 6-0, as did Ellie Broscow at No. 3. The only loss on the day was at No. 2 singles with Annika Gilliland falling 6-3, 6-0. It marked Jumper’s fourth win of the season and Romanczuk’s fifth. The match was Broscow’s first appearance in the singles lineup after playing two doubles matches earlier this season. In doubles, Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio paired at the No. 1 spot for another easy win, 6-2, 6-2. Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum combined for a 6-0, 6-1 win at No. 2 doubles, and Asha Byers and Abigail Call recorded another double-bagel at No. 3, winning 6-0, 6-0. Freshmen Kate Jumper and Kortum, are making a solid start on the varsity roster, marking their second win as a pair. Emma Eisemon and DeFazio, a strong pairing in 2021, have moved into the No. 1 doubles role. They have won twice as a tandem, and have appeared in the top slot in several big matches. “They may be our top doubles team,” said Landes. “We could move around some singles players, but they were great last season,” The Highlanders look ahead to league opponents Castro Valley tomorrow, September 22 at the Trojans’ home courts. It will be Piedmont’[s fourth match in the Western Alameda County Conference, where it is undefeated at 3-0. Piedmont currently looks like the best team in the WACC after defeating last year’s champions, Bishop O’Dowd, 5-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on September 10. articles.text: With a scheduled early-season Senior Night on Tuesday, September 13, Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team ran roughshod over San Leandro at Pirates’ home pool, 14-3. A ceremony honored the team’s five seniors: Rosie Feldman, Odessa Dando, Annika Nilsson, Macie Gard, and Molly Ashton. Coach Sarah Mooney had high praise for each of them. “Rosie has been a major contributor for many years, same with Odessa these last four years, while Annika has been the backbone of our defense. Macie’s growth has allowed her to understand every position in the pool. Molly’s mental toughness and fighter mentality is huge asset that inspires the team,” said coach Mooney. PHS led 5-0 by the end of the first quarter and 10-1 by halftime. Piedmont started the fourth quarter leading 13-3 and scored once more in the fourth for the 14-3 final. It took only 10 seconds for Piedmont to score its first goal. Dando won the opening sprint, leading to Katerina Melian scoring on a shot from distance. Dando made it 2-0 at the 5:30 mark in close distance on a breakaway opportunity. Thirty seconds later, PHS Macie Gard (left) is honored by coach Sarah Mooney in a postgame ceremony for seniors. Kate Meyjes had two goals for Piedmont against San Leandro. Photos by Nancy Brahm Piedmont honored their five seniors on the roster during Senior Night on Tuesday, September 13. Pictured are: Rosie Feldman (left), Molly Ashton, Odessa Dando, and Annika Nilsson. (Not pictured, Macie Gard.) drew an exclusion to gain a man-advantage, leading to Ashton scoring after 12 seconds of time on the penalty, making it 3-0. Ashton scored once more with 4:14 left in the quarter after an assist by Dando, while Gard made it 5-0 with 2:09 remaining on a long pass from Feldman. In the five-goal second quarter, Kate Meyjes scored after two minutes when Alicia Bernales sent in a pass in front of the net. With 3:46 left in the half, Meyjes scored again after recovering a loose ball for a 7-0 lead. With 1:56 on the clock, Sonja ten Grotenhuis scored on an assist by goalie Friedie Schickedanz – a nice gift on ten Grotenhuis’ birthday. Anne Reardon made it 9-0 for Piedmont after Sage Gilbert sent an assist with 40 seconds left. The Pirates scored with 22 seconds left to make it 9-1 but Sydney Olson scored for PHS with 12 seconds remaining on a ten Grotenhuis assist, for a 10-1lead. Piedmont scored three times in the third period and allowed the Pirates two goals with substitutions in the water, San Leandro scored after two minutes, but Vivian Burke answered a minute later, making it 11-2. With 3:33 left, Melian sent a pass to Bernales in close distance for the goal, 12-2. Olson scored with 1:30 left in the third after rebounding her own penalty shot off the crossbar. The Pirates added a goal with 1:15 left in the quarter. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont killed an early penalty opportunity for San. Leandro in the first minute of action with the help of Gard, now playing as goalie. The Highlanders scored the only goal in the fourth when Feldman netted one with 3:37 left in the game. Final stats: Meyjes, Ashton, and Olson also scored twice. Feldman, Melian, ten Grotenhuis, Bernales, and Dando each scored once and had an assist. Gard, Burke, and Reardon had individual goals. Schickedanz and Gilbert had assists. Tuesday vs. Marin Academy The Highlanders were scheduled to play Marin Academy in San Rafael yesterday, Tuesday, September 21. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3 overall, 1-1 league) heads to Berkeley today, Wednesday, September 21 for a 5:45 p.m. match.
