articles.text: Piedmont’s football team suffered a 56-35 loss to Pierce in Arbuckle on Friday, September 16. It was the team’s third straight loss. The Highlanders fought evenly with the Bears in the first half and went into halftime down by one touchdown, 28-21, but Pierce ate away at the Purple and White defense with continuous running plays to charge ahead in the second half on Piedmont’s tired legs with a roster of only 17 players. “We were going back-andforth in the first half and just couldn’t get any stops in the second half. We shot ourselves in the foot a couple of times, but we put up some good points and played hard,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “The battle with attrition is always going to be an issue for us. Our core group is great, but it’s a lot to ask them to play all four quarter both ways. Pretty much every single player starts both ways. We ask a lot of them and they’ve been great about it.” The Bears rushed for over 500 yards and only attempted a few passes, accumulating 32 first downs on the night with successive long drives, including four of five fourth-down conversions. “We did pretty good on third downs, but they converted multiple fourth downs,” said Seiden. “They just ran the ball, but we did well stopping the inside run but lost discipline on a lot of outside runs,” said Seiden. Piedmont started the game off with a bang on a trick play when running back Jack Nelson took a sweep and tossed the ball to receiver Sam Shelby running a reverse. Shelby, who is the backup quarterback, pulled up to pass and hit DominIc Alexander wide open downfield for a 62-yard touchdown. Pierce responded on its next series with a touchdown drive to make it 7-7. But the Highlanders were able to regain the lead on a 60-yard pass reception by Shelby. On the play, quarterback Markos Lagios connected with Shelby on an eight-yard buttonhook. The receiver then shook off two defenders and raced down the sideline, making another two defenders whiff on tackles as he sped to the end zone. Pierce scored the next two touchdowns with its Wing-T offense, churning out rushing yards on long drives to go ahead Photos by Mike McConathy Dominic Alexander scored twice against Pierce on pass receptions of 62 and 25 yard receptions. Matteo Costa scored on an 86-yard kickoff return against Pierce. Sam Shelby had a 62-yard touchdown pass on a trick play and also turned multiple defenders inside-out on a 60-yard touchdown reception. 21-14 in the early portion of the second quarter. But Piedmont answered with an 86-yard kickoff return for a touchdown by Matteo Costa to tie the game once more at 21-21 Pierce added one more touchdown before the half for a 28-21 lead, and Piedmont struggled to find productivity in the second half. “I firmly appreciate the effort they give for all four quarters. To ask them to play as much as they do, I have nothing but the utmost love for these players. But it can’t be an excuse for the mental mistakes we make,” said Seiden. The Bears scored two more unanswered touchdowns in the third quarter to make it 42-21, but Nelson scored on another kickoff return making it 42-28. Alexandre scored Piedmont’s last touchdown on a 25-yard catch in the fourth quarter. PHS had 221 passing yards, with Shelby’s 62-yard strike and Lagios passing for two touchdowns, and an interception. Official stats were not provided. The Highlanders look ahead to Friday’s game against St. Mary’s at Witter Field against former PHS head coach John Trotman. The Panthers are 3-0 this season, but have played against three winless teams. “We need to come out and play our game. We have played three really good teams who have winning records and we played them all tough. Del Norte and Seaside are two strong teams who we played really tough, we just need to keep working,” said Seiden. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-3) hosts St. Mary’s on Friday, September 23 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Makenna Thiel, the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021. and 2019 as a sophomore, is currently on the University of California tennis team in Berkeley as a second-year student. Cal is the defending Pac-12 Champion, Thiel powered through a busy summer competing at the professional level on the International Tennis Federation circuit and recently played in the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Women’s $60,000 Challenger on Monday, September 19. “For Makenna, coming out in these professional tournaments, I think she competes hard and competes well. This summer, she was able to compete a lot. We work on a lot of stuff put it into match play is the next piece,” said Cal head coach Amanda Augustus. The Berkeley Tennis Club’s Women’s Challenger often hosts several of the world’s top-100 players. For instance, Sophia Kenin won the 2018 BTC Women’s Challenger and later won the 2020 Australian Open. Thiel lost in the first round of qualifying this past weekend to No. 16 seeded Alana Smith of North Carolina State by scores of 6-2, 6-3. Smith, 22, is a graduate student and earned an honorable mention for All-ACC in 2021 and 2019, to go along with All-American doubles selections in 2021, 2020, and 2019. Smith is a tall player with a powerful serve. She recorded nine aces in Monday’s match. “This was my first hard court match in a bit over a month. It’s a big stage on center court at my former home club,” noted Thiel. “She had a really good serve and I knew I had to stay on her and focus a bit more on my service games. I think my first-serve percentage, especially in the first set, could’ve been better. I now know what I need to work on,” she added. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, September 21, 2022 Football team loses 56-35 to Pierce By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s football team suffered a 56-35 loss to Pierce in Arbuckle on Friday, September 16. It was the team’s third straight loss. The Highlanders fought evenly with the Bears in the first half and went into halftime down by one touchdown, 28-21, but Pierce ate away at the Purple and White defense with continuous running plays to charge ahead in the second half on Piedmont’s tired legs with a roster of only 17 players. “We were going back-andforth in the first half and just couldn’t get any stops in the second half. We shot ourselves in the foot a couple of times, but we put up some good points and played hard,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “The battle with attrition is always going to be an issue for us. Our core group is great, but it’s a lot to ask them to play all four quarter both ways. Pretty much every single player starts both ways. We ask a lot of them and they’ve been great about it.” The Bears rushed for over 500 yards and only attempted a few passes, accumulating 32 first downs on the night with successive long drives, including four of five fourth-down conversions. “We did pretty good on third downs, but they converted multiple fourth downs,” said Seiden. “They just ran the ball, but we did well stopping the inside run but lost discipline on a lot of outside runs,” said Seiden. Piedmont started the game off with a bang on a trick play when running back Jack Nelson took a sweep and tossed the ball to receiver Sam Shelby running a reverse. Shelby, who is the backup quarterback, pulled up to pass and hit DominIc Alexander wide open downfield for a 62-yard touchdown. Pierce responded on its next series with a touchdown drive to make it 7-7. But the Highlanders were able to regain the lead on a 60-yard pass reception by Shelby. On the play, quarterback Markos Lagios connected with Shelby on an eight-yard buttonhook. The receiver then shook off two defenders and raced down the sideline, making another two defenders whiff on tackles as he sped to the end zone. Pierce scored the next two touchdowns with its Wing-T offense, churning out rushing yards on long drives to go ahead Photos by Mike McConathy Dominic Alexander scored twice against Pierce on pass receptions of 62 and 25 yard receptions. Matteo Costa scored on an 86-yard kickoff return against Pierce. Sam Shelby had a 62-yard touchdown pass on a trick play and also turned multiple defenders inside-out on a 60-yard touchdown reception. 21-14 in the early portion of the second quarter. But Piedmont answered with an 86-yard kickoff return for a touchdown by Matteo Costa to tie the game once more at 21-21 Pierce added one more touchdown before the half for a 28-21 lead, and Piedmont struggled to find productivity in the second half. “I firmly appreciate the effort they give for all four quarters. To ask them to play as much as they do, I have nothing but the utmost love for these players. But it can’t be an excuse for the mental mistakes we make,” said Seiden. The Bears scored two more unanswered touchdowns in the third quarter to make it 42-21, but Nelson scored on another kickoff return making it 42-28. Alexandre scored Piedmont’s last touchdown on a 25-yard catch in the fourth quarter. PHS had 221 passing yards, with Shelby’s 62-yard strike and Lagios passing for two touchdowns, and an interception. Official stats were not provided. The Highlanders look ahead to Friday’s game against St. Mary’s at Witter Field against former PHS head coach John Trotman. The Panthers are 3-0 this season, but have played against three winless teams. “We need to come out and play our game. We have played three really good teams who have winning records and we played them all tough. Del Norte and Seaside are two strong teams who we played really tough, we just need to keep working,” said Seiden. articles.text: The Mosquito Fire roaring through Tahoe and El Dorado National Forests is now up to 76,290 acres since last week, but containment has increased to 47 percent after being at 25 percent at this time last week. It has destroyed 78 structures At 76,290 acres, it is the largest wildfire in California this year. “This increase in containment can be attributed to the hard work of firefighters who have been working around the clock to strengthen and secure containment lines in and around the communities,” wrote Cal Fire. Recent rainfall has helped efforts, allowing firefighters to create a perimeter in recent days. However, officials are expecting dry conditions to return by the end of this week. “Widespread, abundant rain over the fire area continues to reduce fire behavior, but warm, dry weather will return at the end of the week. Fire activity has slowed down, but the firefighters have not. While the rain presents a different set of challenges to the fire-suppression effort, crews continue to work, taking advantage of the lull in fire activity to secure the fire perimeter and increase containment before warm, dry weather returns,” wrote Inciweb, an official government database for wildfires. Cal Fire announced that the Photo courtesy of 2News.com Firefighting efforts have helped contain the Mosquito Fire at 47 percent as of Tuesday night. rain could provide some added complications, including potential flash floods due to the loose gravel created by the recent fires. “Thus far, the total accumulation for this storm has ranged from 1 to 2.25 inches of rain over the fire. Isolated thunderstorms moved from south to north across the fire area this afternoon. A Flash Flood Watch remains in effect for the fire area until midnight for potential ash and debris flows due to the presence of these thunderstorms,” said Cal Fire. Inciweb points out that the fire is primarily burning brush and dry timber, with large logs and duff under thick vegetation continuing smoldering conditions, which they consider to be “minimal” risk. “The fire is burning primarily in brush, and timber. The record-dry vegetation has responded to recent days and nights of high relative humidity and precipitation. However, very dry large logs and trees and the vegetation and duff under thick tree canopies all continues to smolder. Fire behavior Tuesday was minimal, consisting primarily of smoldering. From 0.75 to 2 inches of rain soaked all areas of the fire, greatly diminishing fire behavior,” said Inciweb. Inciweb adds that the current outlook for the near future includes constructing direct and indirect fire lines as conditions allow, to improve existing containment lines, and to assess needs for suppression repair. Although rain in the area is expected to subside by Wednesday, the 24-hour outlook is that fire growth will continue to be “minimal.” “Showers will begin to taper off Wednesday. A transition to a warmer, drier period will gradually start to build. Fire growth will be minimal,” per Inciweb.
articles.title: FIRE SEASON Mosquito Fire now 76,290 acres with 47 percent containment

articles.text: Photos by Cory Weaver Baritone Gerald Finley in the world premiere of John Adams’ Antony and Cleopatra at San Francisco Opera. widely cited as the leading American composer alive today. World Premiere The world premiere of John Adams’ Antony and Cleopatra opened September 10 at the War Memorial Opera House, celebrating San Francisco Opera’s 100th year. The opera is in English with supertitles; nine scenes, two acts, just over three hours. Repeat performances continue to October 5. For info: (415) 864-3330, or go online: www.artsSF.com. Berkeley composer John Adams has made a welcome attempt to bring under control the unwieldy “Antony and Cleopatra” story out of Shakespeare. Evolving from there, past composer Samuel Barber’s grand 1966 Met failure, to Adams’ world premiere, it has been boiled down from some 40 scenes and two dozen solo voices (ouch!) to Adams’ sleek, late-model version in three hours, two acts. It debuted September 10 to mark the 100th year of the San Francisco Opera. If you were waiting for gooey Pucciniesque scenes of the two lovers, this was not your opera. Instead of affairs, Adams focused on affairs of state, plus ensuing conflicts, in a historian’s more formal way. This Antony and Cleopatra is a chess match turned civil war between the ancient Romans Caesar (Augustus) and Antony, with the alluring queen Cleopatra running all over the chess board and resetting all the clocks with impunity. The punchy, highly rhythmic score festooned with electric outbursts of brass and percussion was all Adams, making no concession to popular expectations (nor any semblance of the silver screen’s Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton pairing). His music is at its best conveying scenes of high tension, which the opera provides in abundance. If there was more than the normal quota of opera-house dissonance, how else to portray the would-be hero sonically walking away from two wives, moving in with a minority woman from North Africa, and taking up arms in a power struggle? Historical severity was there on all counts. And Eun Sun Kim’s orchestra was aboard to make it all happen. Antony hops in and out of so many bedrooms and marriages, with yet more disasters in real combat, you wonder how ancient Rome ever survived anything. Well, civil wars are as good a way as any to start or to bring down the greatest dynasties (here, pitched battles leading to the victorious Caesar becoming the first emperor of the Roman Empire). The cast turned out much better than expected, given the cancelation of the original Cleopatra, Julia Bullock, due to pregnancy. Lyric soprano Amina Edris stepped in smartly with a sterling high range and the look of an Egyptian queen – at least, as close as you might get with this 1930s setting of 2,000-year-old history. We could certainly have done well without those 1930s perms, or films of early Ford touring cars, right, Caesar? In the early going, the Antony of baritone Gerald Finley was the night’s apex, getting strong support from tenor Paul Appleby (Caesar) as the opponent, an emperor outfitted in plain modern business suit that deserved at least a few epaulets. Stage Director Elkhanah Pulitzer and the various designers made it work with minimal tools like sliding panels and a couch or bed, all allowing for rapid scene changes. Working with a dramaturg but no credited librettist, Adams leaned on cherry-picking scenes and texts out of Shakespeare, plus adding snippets from Plutarch and Virgil. A complete overview will appear subsequently, as I could not remain to the final curtain. Earlier on, the visual highlight was playing out Antony’s disastrous naval battle at Actium, bolstered by the ballast of the robust chorus on stage – a much-needed glimpse of large-scale operadrama in a work with scarcely any show-piece soliloquies or ensembles. Acoustical Tip If you are attending, the best sonics in the whole Opera House (and lowest prices) are in the nose-bleed section of the top balcony, in Row L. An acoustic-horn effect up there magnifies the sound breathtakingly while enabling patrons to hear the pit orchestra in all its glory. Cognoscenti head up there, dressing lightly, sometimes taking binoculars. About John Adams Previous operas by Berkeleyite Adams, 75, involving historical figures and events, included Nixon in China, The Death of Klinghoffer, Dr. Atomic and The Girls of the Golden West. He is Lyric soprano Amina Edris sings the lead role as Cleopatra in John Adams’ new opera, Antony and Cleopatra.
articles.title: SF Opera premieres John Adams’ new opera, Cleopatra and Antony

Lyric soprano Amina Edris stepped in smartly with a sterling high range and the look of an Egyptian queen – at least, as close as you might get with this 1930s setting of 2,000-year-old history. We could certainly have done well without those 1930s perms, or films of early Ford touring cars, right, Caesar? In the early going, the Antony of baritone Gerald Finley was the night’s apex, getting strong support from tenor Paul Appleby (Caesar) as the opponent, an emperor outfitted in plain modern business suit that deserved at least a few epaulets. Stage Director Elkhanah Pulitzer and the various designers made it work with minimal tools like sliding panels and a couch or bed, all allowing for rapid scene changes. Working with a dramaturg but no credited librettist, Adams leaned on cherry-picking scenes and texts out of Shakespeare, plus adding snippets from Plutarch and Virgil. A complete overview will appear subsequently, as I could not remain to the final curtain. Earlier on, the visual highlight was playing out Antony’s disastrous naval battle at Actium, bolstered by the ballast of the robust chorus on stage – a much-needed glimpse of large-scale operadrama in a work with scarcely any show-piece soliloquies or ensembles. Acoustical Tip If you are attending, the best sonics in the whole Opera House (and lowest prices) are in the nose-bleed section of the top balcony, in Row L. An acoustic-horn effect up there magnifies the sound breathtakingly while enabling patrons to hear the pit orchestra in all its glory. Cognoscenti head up there, dressing lightly, sometimes taking binoculars. About John Adams Previous operas by Berkeleyite Adams, 75, involving historical figures and events, included Nixon in China, The Death of Klinghoffer, Dr. Atomic and The Girls of the Golden West. articles.text: Due to popularity Circus Bella has added six more free showings of its newest show, Flip Flop Fly, from October 15-23. This series of performances, featuring some of the dazzling circus talent from the Bay Area, will delight audiences of all ages in a family event for all ages. Flip Flop Fly is directed by Circus Bella co-founder and director Abigail Munn. The performances will celebrate the circus’s 13th year. The 60-minute show is circus arts at its most exuberant, exploring human curiosity and sky-high imagination. Circus Bella is a diverse and talented troupe of acrobats, aerialists, jugglers, and clowns - performing to the live music of Rob Reich and the six piece Circus Bella All-Star Band. Guests are invited to bring picnic blankets and small folding chairs to all locations. A preshow performance by the Stars of Prescott Circus Theatre will also be held. To learn more visit: Circusbella.org/flipflopfly or call 415- 480-4239.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is in its final week of performing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. Cast members of Berkeley Rep’s production of Goddess. Photo by Calvin Ngu
articles.title: Final week for Berkeley Rep’s Goddess

articles.text: It’s hard to imagine a more charming town than Half Moon Bay. The citizens made the decision to preserve their history… and they were successful. In some ways, time seems to stand still in Half Moon Bay. The town is like a large chunk of amber – preserved as it once was. When you go there, you are immediately in a different world. If you take Highway 92 to the end, you arrive in the camping area at the beach where there are lots of convenient facilities. It is hard to find a reasonably priced hotel room, but I did. Some of the places are luxurious in the extreme. The main street is not long, but that’s where most of the shops are. We started our eating adventure at the Flying Fish Inn. I had eaten there before and enjoyed it. The Flying Fish Inn can boast that it has the sixth best fish and chips in the entire United States. When I was a youngster, I went to the Redondo Beach pier and had fish and chips with a cornmeal batter. The Flying Fish Inn makes it the usual English way. Our large plate of fish was tender and flavorful, the French fries were blistered to a light crispness, and the tangy thousand Island dressing was fantastic. We also got the pan-seared striped bass which was also good. Breakfast places abound, and you can just walk down the street and select any one. All feature excellent breakfast pastries. The coffee was unimpressive, but the breakfast portions are big. For lunch we drove north to Sam’s famous Chowder House. The place was crowded, but we had no problem finding seats at the bar. Peter, the bartender, greeted us in a friendly manner and we ordered the famous clam chowder. It was good, but I thought it lacked a real clam flavor. The variety of restaurants in half Moon Bay is impressive. There is a restaurant for every taste, including Himalayan. Trattoria e Mare is an upscale Italian-themed restaurant. Everything here is plated beautifully and served elegantly. We began with a roasted beet and strawberry salad. Then we had a good, old Italian standby… a pan-roasted whole Bronzino fish. The roasted potatoes came with a spicy aoli. I felt that the potatoes would be improved with a few shavings of rock salt. Everywhere you go service is gracious and sincere. The servers are very accommodating, and when I told them that it was my birthday, they brought out a beautiful dessert with the words “Happy Birthday” emblazoned on the plate. Music is important in the lives of the Half Moon Bay citizens. They have lively jazz clubs, and they have resumed a concert series in the beautiful library. They also know that an orchestra legitimizes a city. Did you know that Half Moon Bay has a fine symphony orchestra – the Coastside Symphony. I remember hearing them play a concert a few years ago, and I was impressed by their enthusiasm. It is things like this that make music truly inspiring. Enjoying dinner at the Flying Fish Inn in Half Moon Bay.
articles.title: Half Moon Bay – the whole story

articles.text: In an “only in Berkeley” situation playing out at Berkeley Rep, unpaid ushers have staged two protests and have threatened to unionize over working conditions and management’s refusal to engage in any dialogue. The ushers – many of whom have been donating their time for years – are an important part of the Rep’s infrastructure. They arrive hours before each performance, check tickets, show people to their seats, answer questions, clean up after the show, and – in the past – distributed and collected programs. In exchange, they get to see the show for free. If there are seats available, the ushers can sit down during the performance; otherwise, they must watch the show on monitors in the lobby. Things were going smoothly before COVID hit. For an 8PM curtain, ushers would arrive at 6:30, have their usual ten-minute briefing, and then would have until 7:00 to eat their dinner and/or buy food from the concession stand at a discount. At 7:00 the doors to the lobby would open, and patrons could come inside. At 7:30 the theatre doors would open, and people could start taking their seats. COVID, of course, brought things to a screeching halt. When plays resumed and ushers returned, two changes were implemented: Ushers (and patrons) were no longer able to eat or drink anything in the lobby, and the concession discount inexplicably disappeared. Although understandable, the former forced ushers to go outside to eat or drink, regardless of the weather. Recently, two more policy changes were announced that pushed things to the brink. First, ushers were given less flexibility in scheduling, so that if they did not usher at least once at every play, they would be dropped. Second, and more importantly, ushers were now required to show up half an hour earlier. As a result, ushers would have 50 minutes of dead time after the evening briefing before people were even allowed into the lobby. Not surprisingly, the ushers were not happy, and asked the Front of Houses (“FOHs”, the paid employees who oversee the theatre operations at each performance) about the rationale. The FOHs told them that they agreed it was not necessary, but that it was “above their pay grade” and that they could not do anything about it. A few ushers then emailed the Front of House Director, who oversees the FOHs and who instituted the policy. She replied that Berkeley Rep was “evolving” and that if ushers couldn’t meet the time commitment, they were free to drop out. When ushers continued to email her for more explanation, she responded, “This is the last time that I will address this. Volunteering is a choice. You make the choice to come here. If you choose to come here we have rules and protocols. It’s your choice.” Ushers were understandably unhappy with both the tone and content of the FOH Director’s email and responded with their own missives. The following are quotes from emails sent by ushers obtained by this reporter: • I feel disrespected by this approach. • This situation does not demonstrate that I and my peers are valued or that our concerns about a 33% increase in preshow call time are receiving appropriate attention. • The fact that there is this much discontent should be a sign that perhaps something needs to be addressed from the management side. • Making us come earlier to hang out can be seen as not respecting our time. • We are not petulant children. Finally, things reached a breaking point. On a recent weekend, ushers showed up on time on both Saturday night and Sunday night but refused to enter the lobby for the briefing. They told the FOH that “they were protesting the start time”, “they were rebelling”, and “they were going to unionize”. Berkeley Rep is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, which means it pays no income tax (with a few possible exceptions). Unfortunately for the ushers, it means that they cannot unionize, since California courts have ruled that volunteers for nonprofits are not employees. But it also means that its Tax Returns (excluding donor information, which is confidential) are publicly available. To its credit, Berkeley Rep provides a direct link on its website that takes you to the Federal 990, the nonprofit version of a tax return (https://www.berkeleyrep.org/media/ktpjyzem/ fy2021-990publicdisclosure.pdf). It lost well over $3 million in the year ending August 31, 2000, but then made $1.7 million in the next 12 months as donations and grants soared to offset dramatically reduced ticket sales. However, it doesn’t seem to have a problem paying salaries. According to its most recent filing, both the Artistic Director and the Managing Director earned over $280,000, and the nine highest paid salaries (including the outgoing Artistic Director) totaled $1.8 million. Not too shabby. Part of the reason that they can show such a profit and pay such salaries is because of the unpaid ushers. Using an average of ten ushers per show per night working a minimum of 4¾ hours at Berkeley’s minimum wage of $16.99 per hour, and assuming normal payroll taxes and benefits, it appears that having unpaid ushers reduces expenses by about $1,000 per performance. Since Berkeley Rep puts on over 250 performance each season, using unpaid ushers saves around a quarter of a million dollars per year (less any revenue from ushers’ purchasing tickets to any shows they might want to see). At present the situation seems to have devolved into a stalemate between an autocratic FOH Director and a group of dedicated volunteers. There is no indication that management has any idea of what is unfolding, so don’t expect any changes in the short term. However, don’t leave your seats as this Berkeleyesque drama unfolds. The Post will be there when the curtain rises on the next act, ready to keep you informed of any developments. Wiley Hoag is the Consumer Affairs reporter for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep ushers, unpaid, stage protests

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum featuring exbibit by Carlos Villa

It lost well over $3 million in the year ending August 31, 2000, but then made $1.7 million in the next 12 months as donations and grants soared to offset dramatically reduced ticket sales. However, it doesn’t seem to have a problem paying salaries. According to its most recent filing, both the Artistic Director and the Managing Director earned over $280,000, and the nine highest paid salaries (including the outgoing Artistic Director) totaled $1.8 million. Not too shabby. Part of the reason that they can show such a profit and pay such salaries is because of the unpaid ushers. Using an average of ten ushers per show per night working a minimum of 4¾ hours at Berkeley’s minimum wage of $16.99 per hour, and assuming normal payroll taxes and benefits, it appears that having unpaid ushers reduces expenses by about $1,000 per performance. Since Berkeley Rep puts on over 250 performance each season, using unpaid ushers saves around a quarter of a million dollars per year (less any revenue from ushers’ purchasing tickets to any shows they might want to see). At present the situation seems to have devolved into a stalemate between an autocratic FOH Director and a group of dedicated volunteers. There is no indication that management has any idea of what is unfolding, so don’t expect any changes in the short term. However, don’t leave your seats as this Berkeleyesque drama unfolds. The Post will be there when the curtain rises on the next act, ready to keep you informed of any developments. Wiley Hoag is the Consumer Affairs reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: In the Heights plays until October 16 Berkeley Playhouse is currently performing Lin Manuel Miranda’s musical, In the Heights. Directed by Melissa Martinez, it will be at Berkeley Playhouse through October 16, In the Heights is the second musical theater production developed by Miranda. His first production, Hamilton, told the story of Alexander Hamilton and federalism with a modern tune. This production draws on similar musical themes but tells the story of growing up in the Washington Heights neighborhood of New York City. The Berkeley Playhouse offers a season pass for avid theater fans or single show passes. The theater is located at 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. For tickets or season passes visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org or call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351. Tickets purchased at the door are cash only. Cristina Hernandez (Nina Rosario) and Jordan Covington (Benny) embrace in the romantic climax of the show.

articles.text: Daisy Edgar-Jones’s Kya stars in Where the Crawdads Sing. Where the Crawdads Sing is a Southern gothic story based on the 2018 best-selling novel by Della Owens. As of this writing, it has sold more than 12 million copies worldwide and has developed a passionate fan base. It was inevitable that it would find its way to the screen. Set in the small North Carolina town of Barley Cove, the story spans some 20 years, from the 1950s to the 1970s. The film, which doesn’t quite follow the narrative plot of the book, opens with a young woman, Kya Clark (Daisy Edgar-Jones), also called “the Marsh Girl,” on trial for murder. She is charged with killing Chase Andrews (Taylor John-Smith), a popular young man from a wealthy and prominent family. Her defense counsel is a retired attorney, Tom Milton (David Strathairn), who has known Kya since she was a child and is committed to her innocence. The tale is told in a series of flashbacks, beginning with Kya as a young girl living on the edge of a stretching marsh with her mother, siblings, and abusive, drunken father. Her mother one day simply walks away, soon to be followed by her brother and sisters. Kya finds herself left with her father. But before long he vanishes as well. Barely a tween, she finds herself alone, living in the shack, struggling to survive, while relying on her knowledge of the marsh, her innate intelligence, and resourcefulness. And so, Kya develops into a fiercely independent young woman who wanders the marsh in her father’s old boat and sells mussels to a local store owner in exchange for needed supplies. She did go to school – for one day – but was laughed at by the children when she stood before them barefooted and uncombed. Years later she is taught to read by a local boy, Tate Walker (Taylor John-Smith), who has known Kya since they were children (they are now in their teens). Once she discovers books, a new and astonishing world opens up to her, and she begins to read about the marsh animals. She soon sketches them in her notebooks, demonstrating an extraordinary descriptive talent. Where the Crawdads Sing gradually develops into two love stories involving Tate and Chase (it’s Chase that Kya is accused of killing). But the essence of the film is the solitude of the marsh and the small shack where Kya has lived alone, shunned by the judgmental townspeople. Time and place, as well as the splendor of the marsh, become as central to this story as are its characters. Those who loved the book will embrace the film. Others may find it less intense than it might have been, especially the trial. But as a whole, it is engaging and at times irresistible. Where the Crawdads Sing. Directed by Olivia Newman. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Taylor John-Smith, Harris Dickinson. 2 hrs., 5 min. PG-13. Appearing in theaters and streaming on Prime/ VUDU.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Pedro Almodovar has won two Oscars, six BAFTAs (British), nine Goyas (Spanish), honorary doctorates from Harvard and Oxford, and has been working for 40 years at the craft of filmmaking. His chosen medium has allowed him to repeatedly examine the kaleidoscopic richness of the human condition. In his most recent film, Pain and Glory, he has created a spare narrative, never stark, never confused by vanity, but one that is close-to-the-bone subtle and nuanced, offered written and directed by Almodovar, who is now in his 70s. The lead character, Salvador Mallo, is a world-famous writer and filmmaker named Salvador Mallo, superbly portrayed by Antonio Banderas who is a ringer for Almodovar, down to the clothes he wears, his graying beard and spiky hair. The setting, almost exclusively, is Mallo’s Madrid apartment (recreated from Almodovar’s own apartment, with his personal art one the walls). Mallo is a man who is aging badly and feels betrayed by his body. And to be clear about the vagaries of that betrayal, at the outset of the film, using animation, Mallo, in voice over, lists the afflictions that plague him: sciatica, depression, tinnitus, migraines, insomnia, a fused back, a throat that abruptly closes causing uncontrollable coughing, all buffered by alcohol and meds. Professionally he refuses to write because physically he cannot direct what he might create. He wonders if he will ever work again, a voiced lament to a longago collaborator, actor Alberto Crespo (Asier Etxeandia), a man he has not seen for some 30 years, and with whom he smokes heroin for the first time – anything to relieve the pain. When he falls into a heroin-induced reverie and dreams about his childhood and his mother, Jacinta (Penelope Cruz). He remembers an apartment-like cave they lived in when the family left their village. He remembers this underground home being filled with his mother’s love. In truth, Pain and Glory is a kind of reverie, often dream-like, when Mallo, lives hermit-like and is visited or rescued by loyal women who satellite his life while caring for him. In is a series of revelations, often steeped in regret, his story now a soft lament. But the audience must keep in mind that this film is told by an unreliable narrator (Mallo/ Almodovar) and is framed by a spectrum of startling primary colors that belie Mallo’s condition and viewpoint. Deep reds enter almost every scene, often coordinated with his shirts and the window coverings; rainbows of colors are everywhere, in his flashbacks and in his daily life, a seeming contradiction. In an unexpected way, the exposition is uplifting, for Mallo still refuses to yield. He even writes as if that very act is one of self-deception, yet the words are his own. Pain and Glory is a quiet meditation on aging and the physical betrayal that accompanies that experience. For Mallo, his physical pain is a reminder of a reality from which he can find no exit. He acknowledges that he is in the autumn of his life, heading toward winter. His dreams – his mother, of her washing clothes by a river, singing with the other village women – are of spring. And even now his thoughts sway like long stalks of grass, bending back and forth, only slowing righting themselves. This is his life, wistfully told, tenderly offered, a nexus of pain and glory while he hopes that still there is work ahead. A fact that is demonstrated so eloquently in this film. Pain and Glory. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. In Spanish with subtitles. Starring Antonio Banderas, Penelope Cruz and Asier Etxeandia. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime.

articles.text: As students have returned to class and are in the thick of new academic conquests, adults can keep pace by reading some of the newest literary releases. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of inspired recommendations by picking six paperback and 25 new releases called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received reviews from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support independent book stores. spark of a life is granted lush, compassionate detail in The Marriage Portrait. The frills and deceits of medieval court society come alive as our dear protagonist fights to survive them. An outstanding read.” —Celina Muñoz, Brick & Mortar Books, Redmond, WA Daisy Darker Books, Thriller “Daisy Darker headed in a direction I didn’t expect, and I was torn between re-reading all I just read or going forward to see what was next. A dark and twisty tale — from the moment we arrive at Seaglass with the waves pounding until the very end.” —Nona Camuel, CoffeeTree Books, Morehead, KY The Fortunes of Jaded Women Books, Fiction “A story about the pushes and pulls of first-generation Americans, of grandmothers, mothers, sisters, and daughters. There is love, accomplishment, community, and it’s laugh out loud funny. Give yourself the gift of reading this book.” —Holly Hendricks, Sunriver Books & Music, Sunriver, OR Solito Memoir “Man, what a brave and brilliant memoir. It’s hard to imagine what Javiercito endured in his quest to be reunited with his parents, not to mention the mental and physical journey north to La USA. I’ll be putting this in readers’ hands for a long time. Essential.” —Javier Ramirez, Exile in Bookville, Chicago, IL One Hundred Saturdays: Stella Levi and the Search for a Lost World man Illus.), Avid Reader Press/ Simon & Schuster, Biography “Saturday after Saturday, Stella Levi’s story forms the lively, tragic tale that is One Hundred Saturdays. This is the best book I’ve read all year, and with Maira Kalman’s brilliant illustrations it may be the best book of the decade.” —Angie Tally, The Country Bookshop, Southern Pines, NC The Lost Girls of Willowbrook Kensington, Historical Fiction “Based on the horrible truth of the Willowbrook State School, Wiseman tells a powerful story of sisters and the true strength of family. An emotional ride that speaks to real historic events and the cruelty in institutions like Willowbrook.” —Mia D’Alessandro, Thunder Road Books, Spring Lake, NJ Other Birds Martin’s Press, Fiction “It has been over a week since I finished Other Birds and I am still enchanted. A beautiful story with an eclectic bunch of characters in a dreamy southern town with a touch of mystery, love, and loss.” —Elisa McIntosh, The Bookstore Plus Music & Art, Lake Placid, NY A Taste of Gold and Iron dotcom, Fantasy “A sizzling romance that had me on the edge of my seat. Kadou and Evemer are compelling and their world is full of delightful intrigue. Themes of fealty, forgiveness, and the true value of things make this an unforgettable adventure.” —Katie Elms, Bookbug, Kalamazoo, MI Fox Creek: Cork O’Connor Mystery Series #19 Atria Books, Mystery “Fox Creek continues the saga of Cork O’Connor who is now a licensed private investigator. Krueger’s concern for the Native people of Northern Minnesota is very evident in this tense and dramatic mystery with many unexpected twists.” —Carolyn Statler, Three Sisters Books & Gifts, Shelbyville, IN Nona the Ninth: The Locked Tomb Series #3 Science Fiction “Every book in this series somehow surpasses the last in writing, plot, character development, and sheer off-the-wall entertainment. Without spoilers, I’ll just say that you are going to love Nona as much as Nona loves you and Noodle.” —Brooke Williams, Bookends & Beginnings, Evanston, IL Didn’t Nobody Give a Shit What Happened to Carlotta Brown and Company, Fiction “Carlotta, a trans woman, is released home to Brooklyn after 22 years in a male prison. As she adjusts to life outside, she faces one injustice after another. Through so many inequities, Carlotta maintains her optimism, humor, and hope.” —Mary Kay Burnett, Buttonwood Books and Toys, Cohasset, MA People Person Gallery/Scout Press, Fiction “Meet the Penningtons: Five siblings from four mothers, raised in London with no support from their father and with vastly different backgrounds. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 21, 2022 Features The Wine Corner The Wines of Georgia invent in a modern world; you could only inherit them through the mists of time, maybe as far back as human records go.” Historians note that Georgia could be seen to be the crucible from which the great majority of Europe’s wine grape varieties emerged. Winemaking evidence has been found in Georgia dating back into the sixth millennium B.C. How did they make wine? Georgians would hollow out a tree trunk, fill it with grapes, tread them, and then tip the juice, skins, pips and even stems into a big beeswax-lined clay jar called a kvevri. They would then seal it and leave the juice to ferment, for six months to a year before cracking it open and drinking it. What is amazing is that this is still the way they make wine in Georgia. For the first time in my life, I had the opportunity to sample some of the wines of Georgia and was absolutely delighted to experience these vibrant, exciting and totally new flavors. In terms of accessing these wines, K&L Wines has a small selection of Georgian wines, or you can contact Marion Helluy at mhelluy@ colangelopr.com for information on availability. Large clay urns called Kvevri are used to ferment and age the wines. articles.text: One of my favorite types of design projects is when we are able to do a remodel that completely transforms an existing house. In some situations, the transformational change can be triggered simply by a client’s desire for change and improvement to the existing house. The extent of change can be the need to move basic functions from one part of the house to another, like the kitchen, or the bathroom or laundry. It could be driven by the desire to create a larger gathering space by combining rooms, doing a major expansion to add bedrooms and bathrooms, or enlarging the kitchen and eating areas. Sometimes a client will provide an outline of all the changes they wish, allowing us to see an opportunity to improve the overall character of the house, along with providing for the functional needs of the client. In other words, sometimes the remodeling request is so extensive we can see an opportunity to completely transform the existing character and function of the house all at once. How we approach this depends on the existing house. Does the existing house have a character and level of design worth keeping and enhancing, or is there little design character worthy of preserving? Either way, I always see this as an opportunity to make things better. If the desire is there and the budget is sufficient for the scope of work needed, we can really make quite a transformation. Many homes built today were done from stock plans in plan books. The homes were not designed to suit site-specific considerations nor were they custom designed for a specific user in mind. Also, many homes are older and no longer suited to today’s lifestyles. In the past, the public areas of the home were designed to have small, private, compartmented, separate rooms whereas today, people prefer having larger gathering spaces that are multipurpose and take advantage of available natural light, views, and a connection to the outdoors. The transformation of a house can also extend to the exterior. We think of the house as an integration of the interior and exterior. Exterior finish materials and trim can also bring about significant changes to the character of a house. Changing windows for energy efficiency reasons can produce opportunities to enhance the character. Even adjusting the window configuration to improve the interior layout of a space, and capture views and natural light, can add to the transformation. Edward Kaplan AIA, NCARB, is principal of Kaplan Architects, based in Oakland and San Francisco since 1985. Kaplan Architects believes that excellent design solutions emerge through a thoughtful iteration of ideas, challenging preconceptions, and rethinking the solutions we develop. We strive for the results of our work to be functional, timeless, and beautiful. We create spaces with our clients’ needs and desires foremost in mind, and we strive to create spaces that are warm and inviting. For information contact info@kaplanarchitects.com. Photo by Ed Kaplan Before: This mid-1970’s house needed to be reorganized and updated. The kitchen and dining spaces were too small and needed to open to the main living space. The windows needed to be expanded to capitalize on the expansive views. Photo by Mitch Shenker After: This whole house project transformation was accomplished in four phases starting with an expanded great room space with a yard addition along the entire rear of the house, and opening the remodeled kitchen to the dining space and living area.
articles.title: Transforming an existing house

articles.text: Dear Abby: I heard there was an app that translates cat meows into plain English? Is this true or is this horse poop? Do you think there’s one for dogs? Howling woof. –Tank the Lab, Hank the Cat and Momma Anne Dear Tank, Hank and Momma Anne, There are several apps that proclaim to translate cat talk into English. I am somewhat skeptical yet always optimistic. MeowTalk Translator is a mobile app that says it can decode basic cat’s meows into basic English. Apparently, cats use different types of melodies when they are trying to communicate (and I believe dogs do, too.) MeowTalk uses machine-learning algorithms to decode them. In 2021, MeowTalk researchers reported that the app could distinguish nine different meow intents with 90% accuracy. I did find others. There’s one called: Human-to Cat Translator. another titled Cat Translate: Talk to Kitty, one other My Talking Pet: Dog and Cat Translator, and one called: Dog Translator, What My Dog is Saying. The prices on these vary and some reviews advise you pay for a premium version and avoid the ads. I am not sure if any of these work. The one thing they allow you to do is to easily store your cat’s meows so that when they run out of their nine lives, you can still listen to those recordings and remember those funny days. As for dogs, there are a few interesting apps that translate and offer whistle techniques and games: Human to Dog Translator and DogSpeak look promising, and a start-up, Zoolingua, is working on an A.I. powered woof translator that analyzes canine vocalizations and even dog body language. The urge to talk to animals is centuries old and it makes sense that data can be used to help give animals another voice. But I can’t help wonder if we will always want to hear what they have to say. Woof-bah (canine for thank you). –Abby Please address all questions, concerns and fun activities about any animal to Abby at Melandogs@gmail.com. Reticent dawn erases the Harvest Moon glow, Shining into your room; Into an empty closet. The echo of your footsteps; And your laughter. Your smile, That brightened my every day, Linger in fading shadows, Of our last night. Autumn; Queen of Thieves; Commands her chilling winds; Pluck our treasured blossoms! One by one. Wisk them away! To distant ivy halls; While a million magic memories, Melt in the morning mist. But to rise again with the sunshine, Of that distant day, When you shall return, With a new light in your eyes.
articles.title: An app to know what your cat is really saying

Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets An app to know what your cat is really saying By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: I heard there was an app that translates cat meows into plain English? Is this true or is this horse poop? Do you think there’s one for dogs? Howling woof. –Tank the Lab, Hank the Cat and Momma Anne Dear Tank, Hank and Momma Anne, There are several apps that proclaim to translate cat talk into English. I am somewhat skeptical yet always optimistic. MeowTalk Translator is a mobile app that says it can decode basic cat’s meows into basic English. Apparently, cats use different types of melodies when they are trying to communicate (and I believe dogs do, too.) MeowTalk uses machine-learning algorithms to decode them. In 2021, MeowTalk researchers reported that the app could distinguish nine different meow intents with 90% accuracy. I did find others. There’s one called: Human-to Cat Translator. another titled Cat Translate: Talk to Kitty, one other My Talking Pet: Dog and Cat Translator, and one called: Dog Translator, What My Dog is Saying. The prices on these vary and some reviews advise you pay for a premium version and avoid the ads. I am not sure if any of these work. The one thing they allow you to do is to easily store your cat’s meows so that when they run out of their nine lives, you can still listen to those recordings and remember those funny days. As for dogs, there are a few interesting apps that translate and offer whistle techniques and games: Human to Dog Translator and DogSpeak look promising, and a start-up, Zoolingua, is working on an A.I. powered woof translator that analyzes canine vocalizations and even dog body language. The urge to talk to animals is centuries old and it makes sense that data can be used to help give animals another voice. But I can’t help wonder if we will always want to hear what they have to say. Woof-bah (canine for thank you). –Abby Please address all questions, concerns and fun activities about any animal to Abby at Melandogs@gmail.com. Equinox By Rich Saykally Reticent dawn erases the Harvest Moon glow, Shining into your room; Into an empty closet. The echo of your footsteps; And your laughter. Your smile, That brightened my every day, Linger in fading shadows, Of our last night. Autumn; Queen of Thieves; Commands her chilling winds; Pluck our treasured blossoms! One by one. Wisk them away! To distant ivy halls; While a million magic memories, Melt in the morning mist. But to rise again with the sunshine, Of that distant day, When you shall return, With a new light in your eyes. articles.text: Oakland Zoo is excited to host its annual “Healthy Living Festival,” presented by the United Seniors of Oakland and Alameda County. This year’s event will take place on Thursday, September 29, from 9:00 a.m.to 2:00 p.m. The festival promotes health and wellness for aging adults, and includes free food, music, fun and more. A free lunch will be given to all pre-registered participants. The last day to register is this Friday, September 23. “We are honored to be once again asked to host this year’s event, and we’re grateful to do our part to help ensure the health of our senior community. We are here to support all ages, both as a resource and as a long-standing destination dedicated to animals, nature, and education,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Healthy Living Festival is a free event for seniors 55+ living in Alameda County to promote health and wellness. In previous years, this annual event drew an average of more than 2,000 participants. “For many, getting vaccinated, tested, and staying social in a safe way has been a challenge. Oakland Zoo continues to be our gracious and flexible partner, and I am excited that this year’s Healthy Living Festival is a safely organized drive-through, offering all three necessities to those who need them the most”, said Alameda County Supervisor Nate Miley. As the Zoo currently celebrates its Centennial year, it will continue to expand its outreach in the community. For more information, visit: Oaklandzoo.org/programs-andevents/healthy-living-festival Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf dances with guests at Oakland Zoo’s Healthy Living Festival last year.

articles.text: A strong turnout of 37 showed up for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays on September 14. An extra incentive planned was a visit to the beautiful garden of Christina Schneck on Estates Drive. Christina gave the group a tour a couple of years earlier. The group started off taking a familiar route up Highland to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. The group continued up Hampton Road to its intersection with St. James Drive. They went down to La Salle Avenue where two white columns mark this entrance to what was the St. James Woods development, a large real estate project about a hundred years ago. It was noted that all the sidewalks throughout the development have a four tile per section inlay pattern. This original design has been continued to this day when sidewalks are repaired. They continued on past Corpus Christi Church to Park Way and then up Estates Drive where Christina was outside waiting for the group. She shared the history of the garden she has created. It started about 35 years ago when she began the transformation of a traditional grass front yard to the impressive garden it is today. It starts with the car strip at the street curb with a quilt-like artwork of different succulents and other plants. The front yard is equally impressive, and composed of larger plants and trees, some of which are 30 years old. Christina then led the group to her backyard where more of her gardening creation was on display. Tall redwoods provide shade for her forest of plants. There is also a large urn that is a fountain in the middle of yard that attracts fantail pigeons, hummingbirds, blue jays, crows, and others. The fountain provides water and also safety for the birds. Additionally, the garden includes a number of metal sculptures by local sculptor Mark Bulwinkle, who works in cut steel. It was fun to see what Christina’s years of hard work have created. The walkers thanked Christina for her hospitality and then made their way back via Sandringham Place, Cambrian, and St. James. It was a long walk, more than 3-1/2 miles, but seeing the natural beauty that Christina has created made it well worthwhile. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: October 5, 1940 – September 1, 2022 PIEDMONT, CA – Jim McCrea, 81, resident of Piedmont, formerly of Cuba City, WI, passed away peacefully in Oakland on September 1, 2022, following a nearly yearlong battle with cancer. Born October 5, 1940 in Cuba City, WI to Guerdon “Butch” and Sylvia (Lacke) McCrea. Survived by his life partner of 50 years, Gregory L. Jurin, who he married in 2015; his sister, Barbara (Ron) McDermott, of Dubuque, IA; nephews, Brad (Brittney) McDermott of Glenview, IL and their children, Lucy, Tate, and Mae; Scott (Catie) McDermott of Atlanta, GA and their children, Jack and Finn; and niece, Sara (Mark) Kasemeier of Dubuque, IA and their children, Charlie and Beau. He was preceded in death by his parents and sister Karen McCrea. Jim graduated from Cuba City High School (1958) and Marquette University, Milwaukee (1962) to enlist in the US Air Force as a Captain. Jim continued to serve in the Air Force 8 years then moved to the San Francisco Bay Area and spent the majority of his career in Human Resources within a wide variety of businesses, primarily banking, retiring in 2003. During his military and professional careers, Jim developed a love of travel, and was fortunate to travel extensively during his retirement years. He was the appointed organizer of family reunions, and he enjoyed returnJames Philip McCrea ing to Cuba City for many high school reunions. Jim was such a wonderful man of lively faith and someone passionate about social, political, and environmental justice. He died on the World Day of Prayer for the Care of Creation. Family and friends are respectfully invited to attend his Vigil Friday, September 23rd 7pm and funeral liturgy and reception 10am, Saturday September 24th both at Corpus Christi Church, 322 Saint James Drive, Piedmont, CA. For those in Wisconsin, private services October 10th in Cuba City. Internment at a later date at St. Rose Cemetery, Cuba City. Remembrances may be made in Jim’s name to the Dominican Sisters of Sinsinawa, at their Motherhouse, 585 Co Rd Z, Sinsinawa, WI 53824, or charity of your choice. articles.text: The First Monday Reading Group met outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on September 12 and had a lively discussion of Magpie Murders, a 2016 mystery novel by English writer Anthony Horowitz and the first novel in his Susan Ryeland series. The book has been translated into multiple languages and has been adapted into a sixpart PBS Masterpiece Theatre drama series that will be aired in the U.S. and the UK in October. The story is about the murder of a mystery author and utilizes an unusual story-within-a story format. Susan Ryeland is the editor of mystery author Alan Conway, who is known for his novels about detective Atticus Pünd, described as a difficult person. Fans are eagerly awaiting Conway’s latest novel, rumored to be the last in the series, but when Ryeland reads the manuscript she realizes it is unfinished. Soon after she hears that Conway has died. To find the book’s final chapters Susan begins her own investigation. She learns that Conway’s novel may have been based on true events, which might have led to his murder. The group’s response to the book was largely positive. Many readers enjoyed Horowitz’s creativity, especially his use of the story-within-a story and murder-within-a murder structure. There are two books here, but the author blended them together so that they support and reinforce one another. The book was praised for its interesting characters. Readers felt a connection to Susan Ryeland and her personal challenges and empathized in her quest to find the missing chapters and solve the murders of Pünd and Conway. Horowitz has a lot going on for the reader to consider. It is a mystery with many characters, and it seems everyone has a solid reason to be Conway’s killer. The reader is challenged with what turns out to be an impossible task of figuring it all out and solving the crimes before Horowitz reveals the answers. It was noted that reading novels keeps minds’ sharp, and this type of mystery with all its clues and possibilities was good mental exercise for the group. However, there was some criticism as well. This book is not written in a simple Agatha Christie who-done-it on-the-train structure. For some members of the group, the story was too complex and confusing. The book’s two stories and 560 pages were a lot to manage. There were many names and events to keep track of, and it was impossible to know what was relevant for solving the crimes. The story-within-a story structure also made the storyline difficult for some to follow. The conclusion with Conway’s killer revealed was not believable for some readers, although it was accepted that suspending some level of disbelief is required in this type of fiction. It was also agreed that mysteries like this one are usually for entertainment and “guilty pleasure,” and for most readers Magpie Murders delivered on this. Horowitz wove all the evidence together at the book’s conclusion to solve the causes of the two deaths, and also provided a somewhat happy ending for Susan Ryeland. He also did that for most readers, who almost universally are going to watch the PBS mini-series in October. Ut was noted that among those participating in the discussion was Piedmont resident Bob Hall who has written a number of Ben Franklin mysteries under his full name, Robert Lee Hall. His works include: Exit Sherlock Holmes, The Great Detectives Final Days, Murder at San Simeon, and Benjamin Franklin Takes the Case. He has been the principal theater reviewer for the Piedmont Post for more than 20 years. The readers had previously selected Joel Richard Paul’s non-fiction Unlikely Allies, the true story of how three men used espionage, betrayal, and sexual deception to help win the American Revolution, for October. After some discussion, the readers picked Klara and the Sun by Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro for November. This is an intriguing novel about how artificial intelligence might play a role in our futures. The group discussed a number of non-fiction possibilities for December, but decided to hold off on a selection until their meeting on October 3, at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling 510-420-3070. Participating in the First Monday Reading Group discussion on September 12 were Jerry Gragg, Carol Long, Phil Witte, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Peggy Rourke, Sarah Johnson, Lois Price, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Martin Levy, Ken Young, Robert and Madeline Hall, and Dick Carter, in addition to first-time participants Dale Benveniste and Sarah Moldenhauser-Salazar.

articles.text: To experience the magic of Broadway musicals from the comfort of your own home, residents can now enroll in a class online through Piedmont Adult School titled “The Musicals of Rodgers and Hammerstein.” From familiar shows like South Pacific and The King and I, to less well-known ones like Allegro and Pipe Dream, this class will explore 11 musicals created by the famous team of Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein. The class will meet twice, on October 13 and 20, and registration is now open. The class will feature video clips of song and dance numbers from the shows and live commentary by the instructor about the background content and creative process behind their creation. Instructor Ken Ross has extensive experience in musical theater as a director, performer, teacher and long-time theater attendee. For 20 years he was head of the theater department at Las Positas Instructor Ken Ross has performed featured roles in seven musicals at Woodminster Summer Musicals and currently serves on the Woodminster Theater Advisory Board. College in Livermore, and in earlier years he was theater instructor and director of plays and musicals at Bishop O’Dowd High School and the Athenian School in Danville. The Musicals of Rodgers and Hammerstein October 13, 20 (2 sessions) Thursdays, 7:00-9:00 p.m. $54 Online Instructor: Ken Ross

articles.text: Remembering James Motlow Chance meetings happen for a reason. On a cool December day last year, my sister and I with two friends had the great fortune of visiting Locke, CA. It’s not exactly a well-known town. For a reunion weekend with friends, one might have wondered why we picked the Sacramento Delta, given all the other exciting attractions in the San Francisco Bay Area. Pulling up to Locke, I had the distinct sense that I had stepped back in time. Wood frame buildings looked like they had been untouched for decades. There was a leaning theater façade, houses which sat on foundations of cinder blocks, and a gambling house museum that harkened to a way of life that I could only imagine. The town was literally made up of four streets. My sister had visited once before and was fascinated with the history of this once all-Chinese town. She had booked us a private tour and was thrilled to find that our tour guide was none other than James Motlow, a Locke resident, photographer and co-author of the book, Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town. It is a poignant photographic oral memoir that tells the history and legacy of Locke and its Chinese community. Readers of this article will be interested in knowing that Motlow was also a former Piedmont resident from 1992 to 2009. Spending two hours with James was like getting a rare opportunity to meet the people of Locke themselves. We learned how he befriended Jone Ho Leong, who at first was skeptical of this “outsider.” We began to understand the quiet ways of life for so many of the Chinese families who lived there. As younger generations grew up and left, few returned to Locke. James’ earnestness and his great love for the community of Locke were impossible to forget. We corresponded for months afterwards, about his dreams for a film about the history and stories of Locke, about the release of recent films covering Chinese American history – Far East, Deep South and The Six – and about plans to bring friends, colleagues, and fellow Piedmonters to visit Locke. We joined the Locke Foundation and purchased a tile for Locke Memorial Park to commemorate our weekend visit, with a special thank you note to James. Sadly, I received news that James passed away unexpectedly in August. My sister and I attended the memorial service in the gardens of Locke where nearly 150 family, friends, and colleagues gathered. Listening to their testimonials, we began to understand even more the impact of his life and work – and why he had made such an indelible impression in our one chance meeting. Friends Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town by James Motlow spoke of his commitment to history as well as the love and joy he infused into his art. James had seen the “magic of Locke.” Beyond the faded past and the failing buildings, he understood the deep legacy of the town – and he became part of the history of Locke. So if you are ever in the Sacramento area, make time to visit Locke. Stop by the Visitor Center and pick up a copy of Bitter Melon or one of James’ signed prints. And if you want a tour by James himself, play this video created by the University of the Pacific https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=13ZpNaJK0jo. Step back in time and immerse yourself in a community that once was – and still is. Support the legacy of Locke and the memory of James Motlow by donating to the Locke Foundation at: http://www.locke-foundation.org Leslie Wang (left), Tina Wang, Joan Lo, and Eliza Lo Chin with author and former Piedmont resident James Motlow. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, September 21, 2022 Former Piedmonter finds his roots in Locke Remembering James Motlow By Eliza Lo Chin Chance meetings happen for a reason. On a cool December day last year, my sister and I with two friends had the great fortune of visiting Locke, CA. It’s not exactly a well-known town. For a reunion weekend with friends, one might have wondered why we picked the Sacramento Delta, given all the other exciting attractions in the San Francisco Bay Area. Pulling up to Locke, I had the distinct sense that I had stepped back in time. Wood frame buildings looked like they had been untouched for decades. There was a leaning theater façade, houses which sat on foundations of cinder blocks, and a gambling house museum that harkened to a way of life that I could only imagine. The town was literally made up of four streets. My sister had visited once before and was fascinated with the history of this once all-Chinese town. She had booked us a private tour and was thrilled to find that our tour guide was none other than James Motlow, a Locke resident, photographer and co-author of the book, Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town. It is a poignant photographic oral memoir that tells the history and legacy of Locke and its Chinese community. Readers of this article will be interested in knowing that Motlow was also a former Piedmont resident from 1992 to 2009. Spending two hours with James was like getting a rare opportunity to meet the people of Locke themselves. We learned how he befriended Jone Ho Leong, who at first was skeptical of this “outsider.” We began to understand the quiet ways of life for so many of the Chinese families who lived there. As younger generations grew up and left, few returned to Locke. James’ earnestness and his great love for the community of Locke were impossible to forget. We corresponded for months afterwards, about his dreams for a film about the history and stories of Locke, about the release of recent films covering Chinese American history – Far East, Deep South and The Six – and about plans to bring friends, colleagues, and fellow Piedmonters to visit Locke. We joined the Locke Foundation and purchased a tile for Locke Memorial Park to commemorate our weekend visit, with a special thank you note to James. Sadly, I received news that James passed away unexpectedly in August. My sister and I attended the memorial service in the gardens of Locke where nearly 150 family, friends, and colleagues gathered. Listening to their testimonials, we began to understand even more the impact of his life and work – and why he had made such an indelible impression in our one chance meeting. Friends Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town by James Motlow spoke of his commitment to history as well as the love and joy he infused into his art. James had seen the “magic of Locke.” Beyond the faded past and the failing buildings, he understood the deep legacy of the town – and he became part of the history of Locke. So if you are ever in the Sacramento area, make time to visit Locke. Stop by the Visitor Center and pick up a copy of Bitter Melon or one of James’ signed prints. And if you want a tour by James himself, play this video created by the University of the Pacific https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=13ZpNaJK0jo. Step back in time and immerse yourself in a community that once was – and still is. Support the legacy of Locke and the memory of James Motlow by donating to the Locke Foundation at: http://www.locke-foundation.org Leslie Wang (left), Tina Wang, Joan Lo, and Eliza Lo Chin with author and former Piedmont resident James Motlow. You know he’s a stickler for a clean house, orange juice with no pulp, and the thermostat at 67°. We’ll know that, too. articles.text: On their latest outing the Piedmont Seniors visited a quirky new museum in San Rafael on Thursday, July 21. The Museum of International Propaganda was founded seven years ago by Tom and Lilka Areton. The husband and wife team visited over 80 countries in their travels, with an eye towards collecting vintage propaganda wherever they went. Mr. Areton is from the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic where there was only one political party, the Communist party. Mr. Areton told the Piedmont group that the “only election you had was that you could vote on Friday or Saturday!” The Aretons are very careful not to include current political issues in their displays, such as Biden, or Trump. Instead, their focus is on the political propaganda of the 20th century, which includes propaganda from Italy, North Korea, Iran. Nazi Germany, China, and Cuba, along with a myriad of books from the private collection of the Aretons. Prior to Covid, they hosted weekly movie screenings dedicated to different aspects of propaganda, complete with wine from their private vineyard. The Piedmont Seniors saw a pincushion of Adolph Hitler and a tall gold ashtray with a swastika on its base, which someone anonymously left at the museum’s door. The museum also has a painting of Lenin that hangs above the reception desk, which the Aretons discovered at a flea market in an abandoned soccer stadium in Warsaw. The best part of the visit was Mr. Areton’s infectious enthusiasm about his collection. He told the group that for propaganda purposes, it was commonplace to show small children on posters to give dictators a gentler appearance and mislead the public. The Areton’s goal is to make the public aware of how we can be influenced by propaganda, how to recognize propaganda, and then make independent decisions about how to think. There is no admission fee at the museum, but the Aretons gratefully accept donations. The museum is located at 1000 Fifth Street in San Rafael. The Areton’s “real job” is organizing a large student exchange program through Cultural Homestay International. The museum has limited hours Thursday through Saturday in the afternoons, or by special appointment. The Piedmont Seniors then enjoyed a nice luncheon in downPiedmont Seniors: (front) Janet Epstein (left), Penny Robb, Sue Getreuer, Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska; (back) Jim Ayotte, Gregory Jurin, Susan McCreary, Museum curator Tom Areton, and Cheryl Stanton. town San Rafael at “Bogies, Too,” which displays various pictures of Humphrey Bogart in his numerous films. After lunch the Piedmont Seniors front of Mission Arcángel in San Rafael. A poster at the Museum of International Propaganda shows Joseph Stalin in his glorified military uniform holding a baby (symbolizing the future) to show his humanity. group visited “Art Works Downtown”, a variety of art galleries conveniently located next to the restaurant. These galleries are run by independent local artists and include beautiful jewelry, paintings, and crafts. The last stop of the day was a visit to Mission Arcángel, a focal point in San Rafael. It was founded as a hospital to treat sick Native Americans in 1817. The mission served as Alta California’s first sanitarium, therefore was called the “Angel of Bodily Healing.” It received full mission status in 1822 from the Roman Catholic Church. Unfortunately, the hospital and much of the property no longer exists, but services in the two chapels take place every week.
