articles.text: It’s one thing to ask for a little help with daily activities in the home, but getting 24-hour care can be intimidating at first. Around-the-clock care can be needed for the following reasons: • Post-surgery recovery • Support of hospice and palliative care • Chronic conditions such as dementia that may include symptoms such as wandering • Increased fall risk A trained caregiver can help with bathing assistance, grooming, meal preparation, toileting, medication reminders, transportation to medical appointments, and more when 24-hour care is needed. Whatever the need, there are benefits to receiving 24-hour care in the home for yourself or a loved, either temporarily or for an extended period of time: 1. Family caregivers can get much-needed rest when there is a professional caregiver as part of the team. This is called Respite Care, and it allows friends and family to take care of themselves when a loved needs overnight care as well as daytime assistance. As the saying goes, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” and a caregiver cannot truly be helpful if they are not getting good sleep and exercise to recharge. 2. When someone becomes more confined to their home due to age or illness, a companion caregiver can lift their spirits. Loneliness does not need to be added to illness and people can truly benefit from a kind smile and friendly conversation. There can be give and take in a care partnership, where someone who is in need of care can still feel valued and share their experiences and knowledge with their caregiver. 3. Call it peace of mind, being reassured, having a safety plan, whatever you prefer, but it comes down to the fact that a compassionate and trained caregiver can provider more security. Illness and age can create vulnerability and someone who is in a weaker condition may need the eyes, ears, and extra set of hands for improved well-being. A falls risk assessment in the home can help to determine how simple changes can be made to make the environment safer for everyone involved in care. 4. When someone is transitioning from a hospital to home or from a rehabilitation center to home, it can be reassuring to have a caregiver who is with them through all of it. This caregiver can observe any changes and share concerns with the family to communicate to the health care provider. 5. Something as simple as making sure medications are taken at the correct times and doses can be the difference between a trajectory of getting better or being readmitted to the hospital. A caregiver can stay on top of medication reminders as well as meal preparation to encourage noticeable improvements. 6. Not all forms of care can come to the home so that’s why it’s beneficial to have a reliable caregiver who can provide transportation to and from medical appointments, whether to a physical therapist or the primary care provider. In order to fully heal, follow-up appointments and adherence to prescribed therapies are critical. If any of these needs ring true, 24-hour care might benefit you and your family. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com.

articles.text: It’s no secret that when a new baby joins a family, every member’s role shifts a bit. Or a lot. Depending on the family structure and its history of interaction, the transformation of your role as Parent to that of Grandparent may suit you to a T, or may be a rather difficult adjustment. With communication and compromise, finding the right balance is possible. The clock starts ticking as soon as you learn that your adult child or their partner is pregnant. During this time, the young parents-to-be are going through a whirlwind of preparations for themselves; they wonder if their baby will be healthy, how they will manage work issues, housing, childcare, and wonder if they will succeed at being parents. For the expectant grandparents, a different set of questions may arise, mainly because Grandparenthood is a role that is awarded through a life event happening to their child, and its timing is out of the grandparents’ control. A grandparent-to-be may wonder: • Do I live close enough to the young family to be involved regularly? • If so, will the parents want my involvement, and if so how much? • Am I physically fit enough for childcare? For a newborn? A busy toddler? • Do I have time in my personal life to devote to the young family’s day-to-day life, and do I have the desire? • What kind of grandparent have I imagined myself to be? • Does my vision sync with the vision and expectation that the parents have for me? What if they want more or less input from me? • How will I react if my vision of the grandparent role differs from the parents’? It can be hard to predict what a young family may need once a baby is born. It may be that the parents are well-prepared and invite you to participate at any level that you desire. For a first baby, the parents may simply be exhausted from lack of sleep and any help you can provide will be welcome. If the baby is the second or third child, all the issues get more complicated, and the parents may desire your help more and more. Finding balance as a grandparent is at least two-fold: discovering what feels right for you, and learning what will suit your adult children’s expectations. You’ll want to find a comfortable role for yourself, one that is compatible with the vision you have always had for what you’ll be like as a grandparent. Take a look at your life and your future, and think about how you may be able to incorporate your growing grandchildren into that life, while continuing to find personal satisfaction in other areas of life that you enjoy. Your adult children may have their own hopes and dreams for what kind of grandparents they will have in their life. They may remember their own grandparents and want something that is the same – or very different. They may need lots of help with childcare and finances, or they may want absolutely no input. Like all the other important issues that arise in your family, this new journey to grandparenthood will benefit from communication. The best time to talk things through with your adult children is before the baby is born, even though there is still so much unknown. Talk honestly about how you think you will thrive best as a new grandparent. Let the young adults know what level of involvement you are hoping for, so that they are neither overwhelmed with your input nor disappointed in your remoteness. In any growing family, each member may have their own set of expectations and capabilities as their role changes. Uniting the two generations’ vision of shared family life is the goal. For grandparents, finding the right balance as you approach this important stage of life is a team effort. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com
articles.title: Finding the right balance as a grandparent

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. pages.text: Wednesday, September 21, 2022 29 6 ways 24-hour care is beneficial By Benjamin Bloom It’s one thing to ask for a little help with daily activities in the home, but getting 24-hour care can be intimidating at first. Around-the-clock care can be needed for the following reasons: • Post-surgery recovery • Support of hospice and palliative care • Chronic conditions such as dementia that may include symptoms such as wandering • Increased fall risk A trained caregiver can help with bathing assistance, grooming, meal preparation, toileting, medication reminders, transportation to medical appointments, and more when 24-hour care is needed. Whatever the need, there are benefits to receiving 24-hour care in the home for yourself or a loved, either temporarily or for an extended period of time: 1. Family caregivers can get much-needed rest when there is a professional caregiver as part of the team. This is called Respite Care, and it allows friends and family to take care of themselves when a loved needs overnight care as well as daytime assistance. As the saying goes, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” and a caregiver cannot truly be helpful if they are not getting good sleep and exercise to recharge. 2. When someone becomes more confined to their home due to age or illness, a companion caregiver can lift their spirits. Loneliness does not need to be added to illness and people can truly benefit from a kind smile and friendly conversation. There can be give and take in a care partnership, where someone who is in need of care can still feel valued and share their experiences and knowledge with their caregiver. 3. Call it peace of mind, being reassured, having a safety plan, whatever you prefer, but it comes down to the fact that a compassionate and trained caregiver can provider more security. Illness and age can create vulnerability and someone who is in a weaker condition may need the eyes, ears, and extra set of hands for improved well-being. A falls risk assessment in the home can help to determine how simple changes can be made to make the environment safer for everyone involved in care. 4. When someone is transitioning from a hospital to home or from a rehabilitation center to home, it can be reassuring to have a caregiver who is with them through all of it. This caregiver can observe any changes and share concerns with the family to communicate to the health care provider. 5. Something as simple as making sure medications are taken at the correct times and doses can be the difference between a trajectory of getting better or being readmitted to the hospital. A caregiver can stay on top of medication reminders as well as meal preparation to encourage noticeable improvements. 6. Not all forms of care can come to the home so that’s why it’s beneficial to have a reliable caregiver who can provide transportation to and from medical appointments, whether to a physical therapist or the primary care provider. In order to fully heal, follow-up appointments and adherence to prescribed therapies are critical. If any of these needs ring true, 24-hour care might benefit you and your family. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. Including computer password in a Will? By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Finding the right balance as a grandparent By Cynthia Kane It’s no secret that when a new baby joins a family, every member’s role shifts a bit. Or a lot. Depending on the family structure and its history of interaction, the transformation of your role as Parent to that of Grandparent may suit you to a T, or may be a rather difficult adjustment. With communication and compromise, finding the right balance is possible. The clock starts ticking as soon as you learn that your adult child or their partner is pregnant. During this time, the young parents-to-be are going through a whirlwind of preparations for themselves; they wonder if their baby will be healthy, how they will manage work issues, housing, childcare, and wonder if they will succeed at being parents. For the expectant grandparents, a different set of questions may arise, mainly because Grandparenthood is a role that is awarded through a life event happening to their child, and its timing is out of the grandparents’ control. A grandparent-to-be may wonder: • Do I live close enough to the young family to be involved regularly? • If so, will the parents want my involvement, and if so how much? • Am I physically fit enough for childcare? For a newborn? A busy toddler? • Do I have time in my personal life to devote to the young family’s day-to-day life, and do I have the desire? • What kind of grandparent have I imagined myself to be? • Does my vision sync with the vision and expectation that the parents have for me? What if they want more or less input from me? • How will I react if my vision of the grandparent role differs from the parents’? It can be hard to predict what a young family may need once a baby is born. It may be that the parents are well-prepared and invite you to participate at any level that you desire. For a first baby, the parents may simply be exhausted from lack of sleep and any help you can provide will be welcome. If the baby is the second or third child, all the issues get more complicated, and the parents may desire your help more and more. Finding balance as a grandparent is at least two-fold: discovering what feels right for you, and learning what will suit your adult children’s expectations. You’ll want to find a comfortable role for yourself, one that is compatible with the vision you have always had for what you’ll be like as a grandparent. Take a look at your life and your future, and think about how you may be able to incorporate your growing grandchildren into that life, while continuing to find personal satisfaction in other areas of life that you enjoy. Your adult children may have their own hopes and dreams for what kind of grandparents they will have in their life. They may remember their own grandparents and want something that is the same – or very different. They may need lots of help with childcare and finances, or they may want absolutely no input. Like all the other important issues that arise in your family, this new journey to grandparenthood will benefit from communication. The best time to talk things through with your adult children is before the baby is born, even though there is still so much unknown. Talk honestly about how you think you will thrive best as a new grandparent. Let the young adults know what level of involvement you are hoping for, so that they are neither overwhelmed with your input nor disappointed in your remoteness. In any growing family, each member may have their own set of expectations and capabilities as their role changes. Uniting the two generations’ vision of shared family life is the goal. For grandparents, finding the right balance as you approach this important stage of life is a team effort. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the City Council and Public Works Director Editor: While street sweeping is conducted by a Public Works Department professional driving a very expensive street sweeping machine, our city’s street sweeping program is run like an amateur volunteer activity. Effective street sweeping requires that the machine sweeps up fallen leaves in the gutters, otherwise those leaves wash down into our storm drains and clog them. Yet, cars routinely park on streets scheduled for sweeping, so the machine just sweeps around them, missing most of the gutter leaves. Why do cars remain on streets during sweeping days? The answer is because clearing the streets depends upon an intensive and frustrating volunteer effort. Local residents have to find out and remember when their street is scheduled for sweeping. Then, volunteer residents have to tie or tape cardboard “no parking” signs to trees or poles in front of their houses. Then, they have to call the Public Works Department to report that they have mounted the temporary signs. And the report must be made three full days before the scheduled street sweeping day. On the street sweeping day, the volunteer has to see if any cars are parked where the signs were posted, and if so, call the Piedmont Police to report a violation. Then they have to wait to see if a cop will come out to ticket the violating parker. Whew! Most neighbors don’t have time to actually go through this process. Last year my wife followed the city protocol to the letter because a lot of leaves had been accumulating. She raked the leaves away from the gutter into the street to help the machine collect them. In spite of her efforts, four cars parked on the street, ignoring the signs she posted. This is not the way to run a professional city service, and, the lack of adequate sweeping costs our city extra expense to clean out clogged storm drains. The solution is not rocket science; it just requires looking at what most other cities do. Residents have pushed the city to provide more accessibility with City officials. “We are so glad you are here and we so need your services,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the council meeting. “We dreamed about you,” added Council member Conna McCarthy. “Yes, for years,” Mayor King confirmed. “Expectations have grown. People used to just get news from local newspapers. Now they [also] want direct contact with the city,” said Schneider. Five years ago, the City of Berkeley created its version of the position, titled Digital Communications Coordinator. Schneider was the first to be hired. She developed Berkeley’s program, which has grown to a staff of four. When the pandemic hit she was appointed as Manager of COVID- 19 communications for Berkeley’s Public Health Department. “Echa comes to Piedmont with deep experience in local government,” said Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “She led the internal and external COVID-19 communications for Berkeley’s Public Health Department and city-wide pandemic response. Think about that for a moment, because that’s not what she signed up for, that’s not the job she originally took.” The Piedmont job posting listed the following duties for the new position: • Plan, organize, and execute comprehensive communications and public outreach programs for the City. • Develop Citywide strategic and ongoing communications, social media, branding, and media efforts. • Prepare a variety of written, oral, and multimedia communications. • Provide complex and responsible support to the City Clerk. • Supervise the operations and staff of KCOM, the city government access television station. Among her many new responsibilities Schneider understands that housing in Piedmont and the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) will be a major issue. “Development is controversial everywhere. [Berkeley and Oakland] have had more time, 10-15 years, to discuss [the development of housing]. The hard conversations about development are newer here in Piedmont,” she explained. Schneider discovered a passion for city politics while reporting on Oakland city government for Oak Book and SFGate. Schneider has lived in Oakland for 20 years, founded and operated an award-winning local blog called “A Better Oakland” from 2007-2011. It covered Oakland City Council meetings and policy. “[The site] started off as my way to get my opinion out there, and that evolved into writing straight news articles,” she explained. Schneider will also look to improve the City’s website. She designed and launched the Oakland Public Library’s website in 2011, a design which served the library for over 10 years. Schneider will receive general direction from City Clerk John Tulloch.

articles.text: What is PRFO? Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) is a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization founded in 2004 to support the development and improvement of public recreational facilities serving Piedmont residents. In collaboration with the City of Piedmont, PRFO’s recent projects have included raising over $450,000 for the renovation and renaming of the Corey Reich Tennis Center in 2019, and over $850,000 for the new construction of Hampton Park in 2017. Once again, PRFO is proud to partner with the City of Piedmont to make the Piedmont Community Pool a reality. Architecture and Urban Design was awarded the contract for the project. Using the 2017 conceptual master plan as a springboard, ELS led our community through a design process, and the City Council approved our new concept in January 2022. Since Measure UU passed, however, hyperinflation has driven up costs significantly. Earlier this year, the pool building design was substantially revised to reduce the overall costs by $4 million. But construction costs continue to be high, and the city currently anticipates a $2 million shortfall. Without raising additional private funds, we will have to forgo key elements of the project design. In 2020, the City approved a $19.5 million bond measure. Why is private funding needed to raise an additional $2 million? In November 2020, with more than two-thirds of the vote, Piedmonters approved Measure UU, a $19.5 million bond measure to pay for the renovation and enhancement of the Piedmont Community Pool. In 2021, ELS Why can’t I donate directly to the City? The City can accept donations, but it does not have the staff resources to manage large numbers of individual donors. As a 501(c)(3) with enthusiastic volunteers, PRFO is able to assist the City with this important effort. Why donate when the community is already contributing through Measure UU? The Piedmont Community Pool Project has created the blueprints for a state-of-the-art aquatic center equipped to serve residents long into the future. If PRFO is able to meet one-time fundraising targets for this capital campaign, people of all ages will benefit for generations to come. Whether through swim lessons, sports and fitness, or simply using the space to relax and unwind, the new design suits a wide range of needs. The Piedmont Community Pool will also add tremendous value to all properties within the City. What will the additional privately raised funds be used for? articles.text: Each election cycle the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage for residents to learn about each candidate for informed voting. For this year’s races, the first four weeks of our coverage will alternate between City Council and School Board weekly. This week, City Council candidates received two questions and the following week two different questions will be asked of all school board candidates. When the election heats up in October the Post will asks questions of all candidates in both races, weekly. Week 1 Questions 1. If elected, what are your plans for housing in Piedmont? What would additional housing in Piedmont cost and what would it look like? (mixed use/ single family homes/ market rate apartments, etc.) 2. What do you see as some of Piedmont’s critical infrastructure needs and what are your plans for reinvestment or repair? The six city council candidates vying for three open seats were sent these questions on Friday, September 9, and were asked to reply with 150-word responses. BETSY ANDERSON, Incumbent 1) Housing My goal is to promote transparency and help Piedmont retain local control of our housing policies. Local control includes design standards necessary to maintain Piedmont’s charm and character. To keep local control, the City must comply with state housing laws. Every eight years, Piedmont, like all California cities, is required by the State to prepare a comprehensive Housing Element document. In this cycle, the City is required to identify where 587 units of new housing, representing many different income levels, could potentially be built. The City is not required to build housing - just identify where it could be built. It’s up to individual Piedmont property owners to determine if it is in their best interest to build additional housing on their property. It is speculative at this point to predict costs. My plan is to continue communicating with residents about this process and about the importance of retaining local control. 2) Infrastructure The short answer is that ALL of Piedmont’s city facilities are old and outdated. Over its one-hundred year history, the City has adapted to donated spaces and made relatively minor renovations to city facilities. Given the lack of investment, it is not surprising that many of our facilities are cramped, inefficient, and no longer meet the needs of our dedicated city staff and community members. During my time on Council, we have made a concerted effort to address our aging facilities. We have set aside significant funding for facilities maintenance, voted to pass a bond to rebuild the defunct Piedmont Community Pool, and we are now in the process of renovating the Police and Fire Dispatch Center. I want to help Piedmont successfully complete these projects and work with city staff and community members

This week, City Council candidates received two questions and the following week two different questions will be asked of all school board candidates. When the election heats up in October the Post will asks questions of all candidates in both races, weekly. Week 1 Questions 1. If elected, what are your plans for housing in Piedmont? What would additional housing in Piedmont cost and what would it look like? (mixed use/ single family homes/ market rate apartments, etc.) 2. What do you see as some of Piedmont’s critical infrastructure needs and what are your plans for reinvestment or repair? The six city council candidates vying for three open seats were sent these questions on Friday, September 9, and were asked to reply with 150-word responses. BETSY ANDERSON, Incumbent 1) Housing My goal is to promote transparency and help Piedmont retain local control of our housing policies. Local control includes design standards necessary to maintain Piedmont’s charm and character. To keep local control, the City must comply with state housing laws. Every eight years, Piedmont, like all California cities, is required by the State to prepare a comprehensive Housing Element document. In this cycle, the City is required to identify where 587 units of new housing, representing many different income levels, could potentially be built. The City is not required to build housing - just identify where it could be built. It’s up to individual Piedmont property owners to determine if it is in their best interest to build additional housing on their property. It is speculative at this point to predict costs. My plan is to continue communicating with residents about this process and about the importance of retaining local control. 2) Infrastructure The short answer is that ALL of Piedmont’s city facilities are old and outdated. Over its one-hundred year history, the City has adapted to donated spaces and made relatively minor renovations to city facilities. Given the lack of investment, it is not surprising that many of our facilities are cramped, inefficient, and no longer meet the needs of our dedicated city staff and community members. During my time on Council, we have made a concerted effort to address our aging facilities. We have set aside significant funding for facilities maintenance, voted to pass a bond to rebuild the defunct Piedmont Community Pool, and we are now in the process of renovating the Police and Fire Dispatch Center. I want to help Piedmont successfully complete these projects and work with city staff and community members See Candidates’ Q&A on page 30

articles.text: On Wednesday, September 7, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect continued their Climate Speaker Series featuring a presentation from fire reporter and founding member of Watch Duty Sarah Paul. She focused her presentation on how wildfires start and spread, how to prepare for potential wildfires, and ways to stay informed about climate hazards and threats. Watch Duty is a wildfire awareness app and nonprofit that aims to build a “free, open, and un-editorialized emergency alert system,” according to its website. Paul has spent most of her career focused on wildfire prevention and analysis, both as an Arson Task force member for communities throughout Sonoma County and as a Community Wildfire Mitigation Specialist. She initially became involved in the midst of the Tubbs Fire in 2017 when a friend in Sonoma County with little information about the encroaching fire, eventually made a perilous escape through the flames. Paul saw her friend’s ordeal as a critical opportunity to improve communication and connectivity in the face of natural disasters. To effectively overcome climate issues, it’s critical to understand how a wildfire starts, or understand its behavior, said Paul, who explained that the three main causes of fires are fuel, oxygen and heat. In light of these factors, Paul astutely identified defensible space and home hardening as keys to limiting a fire’s fuel and thus limiting its spread. Defensible space refers to exterior protection by removing or cutting back any dry vegetation around a structure that could provide fuel for a potential wildfire while home hardening refers to protection inside like strengthening the roof, structural beams, decks or fences to increase resistance to heat, embers or flames. In many instances, large wildfires will create ember storms that, when carried by summer of fall winds, can massively increase the spread and destruction of fires in rural or unincorporated areas. In the event that all these prevention methods do not withstand the natural elements, it is important to be as prepared as possible in the event of a catastrophe. As Paul identifies, it’s safe to assume that electrical power and cell service will be nonexistent and most roads will be clogged if not entirely impassable. It’s best, especially if you live in rural areas, to get to know your neighbors and have multiple escape routes in the event of rapidly spreading fire. In the event of a large wildfire, time is of the essence which makes clear, concise plans critically important. Paul refers to a company called Zone Haven which has contracts with several Bay Area counties to set up evacuation zones. Paul also points to portable batteries, N95 masks and air purifiers with HEPA filters as useful wildfire preparation items. Watch Duty can provide live updated information about fires from multiple sources. Often there are several entities reporting on a wildfire – some from a county, some from a fire department, some from the state. Watch Duty compiles all that information to give users the most complete picture about the fire and its spread. For more information about Watch Duty, go to watchduty.org. You can view Sarah Paul’s complete presentation on YouTube by searching for Wildfire Mitigation in the Bay Area: What Can Be Done? “Dude says we’ve matured from ‘Old Boys’ to ‘Old Geezers.”
articles.title: My Watch Duty – an app for being informed on fire danger

articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town on Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and is organized by Officer Tyler Petit. Last year’s Car Show had 120 vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 68 vehicles have signed up for this year’s Car Show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, 1987 Ferrari Testarossa, and possibly two Formula Ford race cars. The car show includes free coffee and donuts, and there is a rumor that a taco truck might arrive. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want their cars to be in the show need to register on the Eventbrite website as soon as possible at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/coffee-cars-cops-car-showtickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue between the high school and Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov.
articles.title: 3rd Annual Classic Car show in Piedmont on Sept. 24

articles.text: The Piedmont Harvest Festival will return in Piedmont Park for its 24th year this Sunday, September 18 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The festival will include some classic activities – the Edible Food Contest, Farmers’ Market, Scarecrow Alley, Jazz Festival, the popular Tri-School Kids’ Carnival, an art exhibit, and food trucks along Highland Avenue. The event is sponsored by the city and staffed by volunteers. Piedmont Education Foundation will have a silent auction for the purchase of the scarecrows. Edibles Contest The Edibles Contest in the Community Hall is one of the focal events at the festival. Every year, residents get to showcase the amazing diversity of their gardens and kitchens with exquisite dishes for families and friends. Anyone who lives or works in Piedmont is eligible to submit an entry and entries may be done by individuals, households, neighborhoods or groups. Any item that is submitted for a cooking category must have a main ingredient that could be feasibly grown in Piedmont. While the actual ingredient does not have to be grown within the borders of the city. There is no charge to enter. All entries must be delivered to the Community Hall between 7:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. on Sunday, September 18, with a completed entry form or proof of digital submission. Only one entry form is needed regardless of an individual or group’s number of items and all labels must be securely A flying saucer, complete with blinking lights, made its appearance on Scarecrow Alley in 2018. Keith Trimble and Village Market set up their annual Farmer’s Market in 2019. attached for entry. Cooked items must include the “main ingredient” clearly visible. The judging begins at 10 a.m. and is not open to the public. The Harvest Festival is an opportunity for the community to come together around food and show off the bounties of their gardens and kitchens. All entries will be cleared by 1:30 p.m. The Bill Drum Memorial Sweepstakes Prize will be awarded to the person or group that receives the most blue ribbons. For additional information about the Harvest Festival, or to download entry forms, go to piedmont.ca.gov to the Recreation Department. Jazz Festival Under the skillful organization of Greg Slatoff, the 22nd annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will feature four bands. While the Albany Jazz Band will headline the event, other performers, including Forte and Juvenoia will play as well. The Piedmont High School Jazz Band will kick off the music starting at noon under the baton of Andria Mullan, band director at the high school. Forte returns with its big band, to be followed by the Albany Big Band making its fifth appearance in Piedmont. The band has been performing across the Bay Area for more than two decades with a blend of contemporary, big band, Latin and pop music. Since 2005, the band has been led by Bob Levenson and continually draws members from throughout the Bay Area. New this year is Juvenoia, a Piedmont based rock trio composed of Jackson Lommen (bass and vocals), Alina Shahid, (guitar), and Torsten Olsen (drums). Schedule of bands 12:00 p.m. Piedmont High School Jazz Band 1:00 p.m. Forte (16-piece band) 2:00 p.m. Albany Big Band 3:00 p.m. Juvenoia The Jazz Festival, organized by Greg Slatoff, is free and provides the opportunity to celebrate Piedmont’s musical talent amid fun, food and friends. Scarecrow Alley This year’s Scarecrow Alley is a nod to musical genius Danny Elfman with a “This is Halloween” theme. The name is an homage to Elfman’s enjoyable score in the 1993 animated classic The Nightmare Before Christmas. Families and individuals can make a scarecrow out of any material, from straw to paper maiche. The scarecrows will eventually be sold in a silent auction later on Sunday. articles.text: In contrast to the weather-worn, unattributed aphorism, “There ain’t no such thing as a free lunch”, the California legislature approved and is now implementing a free breakfast and lunch program for all students in all grades in public schools. California is the first state to move forward with the ambitious program. To adhere to mandatory participation in the program to start the year Piedmont schools have eliminated food sales and are offering free meals only. Approximately 75% of the funding comes from the state and is augmented by a federal program. The two sources will reimburse Piedmont School District roughly $2.60 per breakfast and $4.50 per lunch. The school has set aside $250,000 in unrestricted funds to supplement the “$250,000 is what we’re earmarked. We’re hoping we won’t need to do that. At the moment that is our number, given the cost of food, I think we may need to increase our staffing,” said PUSD’s Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The combined number of free lunches given out at Piedmont’s three elementary schools was around 600 per day as of September 1, and the middle and high school combined for 500 free daily lunches. Approximately 350 free breakfasts were provided in the elementary schools, and an average of 300 breakfasts were given during the brunch period for middle and high school students. “There are a lot of different factors at play. Right now we’re just providing very basic offerings. I know that that’s going to get adjusted, because our goal is to get as many kids eating as possible,” said Alahydoian. Alahydoian explained that calculating the percentage of students having school lunches in the past is tricky. In previous years students would commonly buy a single drink or snack, and now they will receive a whole meal. Cafeterias in past years would break even or make a small profit, largely from single drink sales. Without that revenue, the school district faces the likely need for a $250,000 supplement. The nutrition program falls under Alahydoian’s responsibility because it is considered part of “business services.” She has been on the front lines of the program and helped serve food in the high school cafeteria to start the year. The school district has added another mid-management job to its payroll, and has hired Gitara Spinks as Director of Food Service, working under the direction of Alahydoian. Students at Beach Elementary School line up to grab their lunches under the new universal food program. Whole Wheat Pullman Bread or Roll Chicken Salad, Egg Salad, Sliced Roasted Turkey Chicken Caesar Salad w/ Caesar Dressing & Croutons At the elementary level, parents choose meals for their kids online. As of September 1, all high school meals were open with no requirement to sign up. In recent years, Piedmont School District has partnered with a vendor Choice Lunch, which delivered hot food to the elementary school if ordered in advance. To start the year Choice Lunch is not participating as a vendor in the state free lunch program, the district now uses the vendor Lunch Master. Since every public school must participate in the program, there has been an enormous demand, and vendors are scrambling to meet the need.

articles.text: The application deadline for students applying to be on the Piedmont School Board is this Friday, September 16. The School Board approved the addition of two student members of the board at its meeting on August 24. Students selected are able to receive course credits. The board is now accepting applications from students in the 11th and 12th grades. It plans to name two students, one from Piedmont High and one from Millennium High. They will not be voting members of the board. Previously, Associated Student Body members served in an ad hoc capacity, providing updates on school activities to the board. The participation of students was frequently cited as a favorite part of the meetings by elected board members. A board background document states: “Student Board member(s) shall be recognized at Board meetings as full member(s), shall be seated with other members of the Board, and shall be allowed to participate in questioning witnesses and discussing issues.” Student Board members will be able to make motions which can be acted upon by the Board, except on matters dealing with employer-employee relations. The selected students will serve from October 1 to June 30, 2022 and will be required to attend the regularly scheduled board meetings and attend a one-day orientation. Students will also need to study the agenda materials, consult with the Superintendent, and spend additional time attending selected advisory group meetings, student meetings, workshops, and conferences. Applications should be sent to Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans at: devans@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Students with questions may contact the Superintendent’s Office at 594-2614. For the application and more details visit: Piedmont.k12.ca.us/ wp-content/uploads/2022/08/ Application-Form-for-PUSD-Student-Board-Member-Final.pdf.

articles.text: Disruption has a negative connotation to it, e.g. the kid in class who keeps talking, or the dog barking outside. But industries have long lauded innovation so new and unique that it disrupts our lives and changes the way we as a society do things. Our lives as humans (children included) can use some disruption now and again too. Something to shake up our status quo and leave us with an undeniable better. When we detach from sneaky influences like cool kids, advertisements and what others view as valuable, we allow space for new identities to take root. For adults, disruption can come in many forms, from an Eat Pray Love style journey At Camp Augusta nearly all activities are based upon creativity, creating a sense of wonder. Summer camp challenges children’s preconceived ideas of themselves, allowing them to build a newer, truer identity. around the globe. to quitting social media for a week. For children, the idea of disruption is trickier; they simply do not have the same level of autonomy to make change in their lives. What children do have, however, is summer camp, which lifts children out of everything familiar and plops them down in a foreign landscape designed to both care for and challenge them. Camp disrupts the sneaky stories children tell themselves, ones often mistaken for truth because they came from parents, friends, or teachers. For example, a parent may accidentally send the message that being away from home is scary, which the child accepts as true and fears crying before bed. Then when they make it through the session without any tears, they realize they are braver and more independent than they gave themselves credit for. Take another common example. A child believes he is “Mr. Sport Guy” because he’s fairly athletic and gets a lot of positive feedback playing sports. At camp he ventures out a little, maybe some horseback riding. Then juggling. Then ceramics. The session ends with an incredible week of friendship and fun all without sports. Sports as the center of his identity is disrupted, leaving room for a new one with more room for enjoyment beyond talent or praise. We are often not aware of what’s holding us back, which can be especially true for children who turn to the grown-ups in their lives for assurance and direction. Disruption done right won’t eliminate stories, beliefs, or identities that serve, but will take those Blockbuster parts of us and leave us with HD streaming. Randall Grayson, PhD, is the Director of Camp Augusta, which sits nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Nevada City and is beloved by Piedmont families since its founding by Edwin and Charlotte Ehmann in 1931. Information about the camp’s summer programs and family camps can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

In the afternoon students were given picnic blankets, chicken sandwiches from Bakesale Betty’s and were free to peruse the many offerings at Seniorfest. The mechanical bull garnered a long line all afternoon, and the adult sized pedal go-carts were constantly in use for races around the Hampton Field perimeter. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross-country team opened its season at the Lowell Invitational in Golden Gate Park on Saturday, September 10. The team had runners entered at the varsity, junior varsity, boys’ sophomore, and girls’ frosh/soph levels. For the boys’ varsity, a 2.73- mile course, event, Piedmont finished eighth of 34 schools with 255 points. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse was Piedmont’s top finisher with a time of 14:06.3 to place 21st of 222 runners. Two places behind was senior Christian Taylor in 23rd, clocking a 14:10.4. Junior Julien Lee finished 45th in 14:32.4 followed by senior Parker Long in 47th, 14:35.7. Rounding out the top five was senior Alex Ware with a time of 15:42.78. Schulte-Sasse and Taylor have been two standouts for the boys’ team as leaders. They were also Piedmont’s top two runners in a recent scrimmage on August 27, when they finished third and fourth respectively on a threemile race. “I’m not sure who our ultimate front-runner is going to be, but both of them worked really hard over the summer. Xander did a lot of long runs and Christian did a lot of training as well,” said veteran PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. The girls’ varsity team had only three runners to allow their underclassmen to compete at their grade levels. Junior Josie Oesterer, was the top runner with a time of 18:08.23 on the 2.73 mile course, finishing in 50th of 167. Behind her was classmate Jamie Juniors Josie Oesterer (942) and Jamie Schwartz (943) finished 50th and 54th respectively out of 167 runners. Senior Christian Taylor was 23rd in 14:10.4 at the Lowell Invitational. Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse led the way for Piedmont, clocking a 14:06.3 to place 21st of 222. Schwartz in 18:17.6, placing 54th. Also competing was senior Violet Lemley with a time of 21:26.7. Competing in the boys’ sophomore race on a 2.13-mile course, Piedmont placed 11th of 21 schools. Evan Byun came in 33rd of 230 runners with a time of 11:45.4. Finishing 50th was Simon March-Cunningham, coming across the line in 12:05. From there, Henry Horsley placed 74th in 12:29.9, Oliver Horsley was 81st in 12:43.1, and Lucas Chau at 111th in 13:09.6. In the girls’ frosh/soph race, Piedmont’s team had an impressive run to finish sixth of 18 schools with 176 points. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont struggled to deal with Berkeley’s Zada Sanger (left) in Monday’s loss. Shelby Cavenaugh (13) and Elena Stevens (11) go up for the block. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team took a 3-1 loss against league opponent Berkeley on Monday, September 12 at home . Five days earlier they lost by the same score to Skyline in a non-conference match at the Titans’ home gym. The pair of matches brings Piedmont’s record to 5-5. “This week, we’re going to practice a whole lot more on serve and receive. We were struggling a lot in that and that’s really the bread-and-butter of the game. I don’t think we were ready for fast-paced balls like we faced here. The tempo of Berkeley is zero-tempo and we’re working on faster-tempo sets so we can match that same energy,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. 3-1 loss to Berkeley The Yellowjackets won the first set 25-13 and took the second set 25-16. Piedmont bounced back in the third set to win 25-20 but dropped the fourth 25-15. Berkeley’s attack was led by an onslaught of spikes by outside hitters Zada Sanger and Elle Walker, who accumulated 28 total kills between them. The program is also led by former Piedmont coach and assistant Athletic Director Alison West, which marked her third win in as many attempts against the Highlanders. “Berkeley has two big time hitters and we tried to change up our rotation a couple of times to be successful. First set, we weren’t prepared; second set, we moved some things; third set we were ready and in it, but fourth set we got a bit distracted with outside factors. We need to learn to control what we can control,” said Cardenas. In the first set, things started 2-2 between the two sides but Berkeley jumped to a 6-2 lead and never looked back. The Yellowjackets eventually went on an 11-2 scoring run to extend the gap to 14-6 and closed the set by taking four of the final six points, 25-13. Piedmont led 8-5 at the start of the second set and held its last advantage at 11-10. From there, BHS scored four straight to go ahead 14-11. The Highlanders narrowed the deficit to one-point at 16-15 but the Jackets went on a 7-0 scoring run to jump ahead 23-14 and finished with two of the last three points. In Piedmont’s 25-20 win in the third set, they got off to a 3-1 start thanks to a service error, a block by Shelby Cavenaugh, and an ace by Sadie Town. With the set at 7-5, PHS went on a six point run which included kills by Tara Kothari and Maddy Mullin. Berkeley eventually battled back to tie the set at 18-18, but scored the final seven of nine points with kills by Elena Stevens, Cavenaugh, and a set-winning block by Eden Lorin. In the fourth set, Piedmont led 2-1 but couldn’t retain the lead. The two sides traded points until Berkeley led 9-8, at which point they went on a 9-1 scoring run to go up 18-9. At 19-11, BHS scored six of the last 10 points. Final stats: Kothari had five kills. Cavenaugh had seven kills and two blocks. Town four kills, one block, and two aces. Stevens had two kills and two blocks. Lorin had three kills, one ace, and one block. Mullin had two kills and a block. Bree DeYoung had one kill. Bauer Peterson had one ace. 3-1 loss to Skyline Piedmont’s trailed after the first two sets, falling 25-18 and 25-18 in back to back sets. The Highlanders battled back to a 25-20 win in the third set, but lost the clinching third set win for the Titans, 25-15. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-5 overall, 1-1 league) has another tough match tonight, Wednesday, September 14 at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland at 6:30 p.m. Sadie Town had four kills, one block, and two aces against Berkeley.

articles.text: Win vs. Pinole Valley; losses to Alhambra, Berkeley Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Newark Memorial Tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 9-10. Their sole victory came against , Pinole Valley 10-3 in the opening round on Friday, They followed with an 8-2 semifinals loss to Alhambra on Saturday and a barnburner 5-4 loss in the 3rd place game with Berkeley later in the day. The win over Pinole Valley marked PHS’ first of the year. Impressive performances came from Katarina Melian and Odessa Dando, who combined for 10-3 win over Pinole Valley The Highlanders scored the game’s opening goal when Melian sent in a shot from the hole set position with 5:28 left in the first quarter, coming six seconds after drawing an exclusion penalty. Melian scored again in close range with 3:10 left in the quarter and two minutes later landed her hat trick goal with 1:06 remaining. Odessa Dando made it 4-0 on a solo breakaway with 37 seconds on the clock. In the second quarter, Piedmont struck again shortly after forcing a turnover when Julia Montes sent an assist to Rosie Feldman to make it 5-0 with 5:16 left in the second quarter. Two minutes later, Feldman forced a turnover by stealing a sloppy pass before assisting Dando, 6-0. About 30 seconds later, Montes scored on a lob from the left wing to make it 7-0. At the 2:23 mark, Anne Reardon scored on a rebound off of the goalie, 8-0. Pinole Valley scored with 2:04 left to finally break the shutout, 8-1 going into halftime. Piedmont made the game 9-1 after a minute and a half when Sonja ten Grotenhuis fed Alicia Bernales for the goal. After backPiedmont gained its first win of the season with a 10-3 victory over Pinole Valley. and-forth possessions, Pinole Valley made it 9-2 with 1:44 left. Bernales scored once more with 44 seconds left in the third quarter, 10-2. In the fourth period, Piedmont used its defense to kill the clock and limit shot attempts. Pinole Valley scored with 1:48 left in the game for the final score, 10-3. Final stats: Melian had three goals. Dando scored twice and had two steals. Bernales scored twice as well. Feldman and Montes had a goal and assist. Reardon had an individual goal. Ten Grotenhuis had an assist. 8-2 loss to Alhambra Alhambra led 2-0 by the end of the first quarter and 5-0 by halftime. Alhambra made it 7-1 to start the fourth quarter with Piedmont’s goal scored by Dando. PHS’ Bernales scored in the fourth, but AHS added one more. Final stats: Dando had one goal and three steals. Bernales had one goal. Feldman had three steals. Melian, Reardon, ten Grotenhuis, Kate Meyjes and Annika Nilsson had individual steals. 5-4 loss to Berkeley In the battle for third place against the Yellowjackets, the Highlanders quickly jumped to a 2-0 advantage with goals by Melian on an assist by Feldman after 56 seconds. They scored again with 3:56 left in the quarter, Photos by Nancy Brahm but Berkeley scored with 1:27 left in the quarter and jumped into the lead in the second quarter with three more goals, 4-2 at halftime. After a scoreless third quarter, Piedmont had a couple of chances to score in the final going but Melian was denied on a shot by the goalie and Feldman was thwarted on a five-meter penalty shot. Dando then narrowed the deficit with 2:27 left to play, 4-3, but the Yellowjackets extended the gap to 5-3 with 1:50 to play. Macie Gard scored 30 seconds later to make it 5-4. In the waning seconds, Gard nearly tied the match but her shot slammed against the crossbar and Berkeley was able to hold on for the victory. Final stats: Melian scored twice, while Dando and Gard had individual goals. Feldman had an assist and a steal. Ten Grotenhuis also had a steal. Tuesday vs. San Leandro The Highlanders traveled to San Leandro on Tuesday, September 13 and celebrated their six seniors on the roster, including Odessa Dando, Rosie Feldman, Macie Gard, and Annika Nilsson, Molly Ashton, and Morgan Hunt. details. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3) will travel to American HS in Fremont on Thursday, September 15 for a 6:30 p.m. match. Katarina Melian had three goals against Pinole Valley and two vs. Berkeley. Odessa Dando finished the tournament with four goals.

For more information on Golden State Rowing Club and its programs, visit www.GoldenStateRowing.org. Photos courtesy of Golden State Rowing Club Golden State Rowing Club is a new club program started by James Kwan, a Piedmont High grad in 2010. The newest entry into the sport of crew (rowing) is Golden State Rowing Club. Founded by James Kwan, Piedmont HS Class 2010, and a former Princeton rower, the club is already attracting athletes around town by providing a personal experience. “What I’ve observed is that rowing is an amazing sport that needs to get spread out to more kids. It’s also putting forth a different experience with the sport. In my experience through high school, clubs, and in college, the rowing experience isn’t personalized. At times, you can feel like a cog in a wheel. Our goal [at Golden State] is to provide a community-based experience to make them successful in the sport and beyond,” said Kwan. Kwan formerly was with Oakland Athletic Rowing Society (OARS) and helped them achieve great heights over the summer. At the Junior National Championships in June, Kwan coached a quadruple scull to a third-place finish. The same pair won the Southwest Regional Championships in May, considered the sports’ State title. His goal with Golden State Rowing Club is to provide a more inclusive and community oriented program for athletes while still providing a premier destination for top competition. “Right now, I’m off to help one of our athletes study [for] the ACT and then go work on college essays. We want to build a full program that helps young adults take their next step,” said Kwan. “Starting Golden State Rowing was to create a community-based experience that doesn’t exist widely in sports. It fills some of the gaps that we see elsewhere. It definitely pushes you hard and at the same time fits in with whatever our athletes are doing in high school, It helps develops them into a well-rounded person,” he continued. Although Kwan has helped students win medals at prestigious events, he confirms that Golden State is open to all skill levels from grades 8th through 12th. “We are open to every kind of athlete. We row all different boat classes with boats from one-person to as many as nine. However, it’s my belief that developing in one- or two-person boats help build the critical skills you need to be fast in any team boat,” said Kwan. “Another part is that we build athletes who continue to love and are excited by the sport. We think we can get students introduced to the sport and reach the next level by developing them in the one, two, and four-person boats,” said Kwan. It would be far from the first time Kwan developed rowers without any experience in the sport. One example is PHS junior Zachary Feldstein, who qualified for the Junior Nationals last spring in the single scull in his first year of rowing. “Rowing is a sport which many athletes tend to find later on in life. A lot of the competitors have, at most, three or four years of experience. By getting a lot of individualized attention, you can make a lot of progress in your rowing technique in a year or less, like we had with Zach. I’ve had many athletes throughout the last few years, who had no rowing experience at the start of the year, and end the year at the National Championships, Regional ChamJames Kwan (right) after the OARS U17 quadruple scull placed third at Junior Nationals. Golden State Rowing Club aims to provide a community-based rowing program.

articles.text: The Mosquito Fire in the Tahoe and El Dorado National Forests expanded on Tuesday, September 6 outside Foresthill and as of Tuesday night is now up to 50,330 acres – over 78 square miles – with 25 percent containment. It has officially destroyed 46 structures. Smoke from the blaze blanketed the Lake Tahoe region over the weekend, causing the cancellation of a scheduled high school football game with Piedmont and North Tahoe HS in Tahoe City. “The Mosquito Fire continues to advance steadily to the east in heavily forested areas with extremely dry vegetation. Crews continue to construct indirect lines and utilize existing road systems ahead of the advancing fire to cut off the fire’s growth to the east,” wrote CalFire on its incident report. As of yesterday, September 13, fire officials stated that the fire picked up in activity due to high winds in the area. “Fire behavior Tuesday was active, consisting of uphill runs, group torching, and short-range spotting. As expected, the inversion lifted and the air cleared early, resulting in fire growth, particularly on the east and northeastern sides of the fire. Breezy southwest winds throughout the fire area increased fire activity,” according to Inciweb.org, an official government database for wildfires. Fire behavioral analyst Jonathan Pangburn describes that the recent winds pushed smoke out of the region which enabled fire to spread faster due to fresh oxygen. “Unfortunately, we’ve had a turn of events and the southwest winds is starting to move the Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service Winds on Tuesday, September 13 caused a large plume of smoke from the Mosquito Fire. Photo courtesy of YubaNet Fire News The Mosquito Fire has been raging for the last week and has now covered more than 50,000 acres. Photo courtesy of YubaNet Fire News The blaze is near Foresthill in Placer County. smoke out of area, which allows fresh oxygen to the area. That unfortunately is going to lead to a slight uptick in the fire behavior,” said Pangburn. The Placer County Sheriffs Department has evacuated a total of 6,258 residents with 90 declining evacuation orders. According to Cal Fire spokesman Scott McLean, yesterday’s events caused concern from officials that the blaze was quickly approaching Foresthill while some residents have refused to leave. “They have the right to stay, and the sheriff in both counties has made it very clear, (if) you leave your property in an evacuated area and the sheriff sees you, you will be escorted out or dealt with appropriately. We get it, we understand it. But the best thing to do is leave,” said McLean, in the Sacramento Bee. The fire increased containment from 18 percent to 25 by Tuesday night. Cal Fire operations section chief Landon Haack said they’ve been able to contain things south of Foresthill Road through “significant” efforts. “As of right now, the fire is still contained to the south of Foresthill Road and ridge below Todd Valley,” said Haack. “There’s a pretty significant firefight going on out there. They’re trying really hard to hold that fire in that box right there. As of right now, we don’t have any reports of fire on the north side of Foresthill Road.”

articles.text: Musical by Lin Manuel Miranda plays until October 16 Berkeley Playhouse is currently performing Lin Manuel Miranda’s musical, In the Heights. Directed by Melissa Martinez, it will be at Berkeley Playhouse through October 16, In the Heights is the second musical theater production developed by Miranda. His first production, Hamilton, told the story of Alexander Hamilton and federalism with a modern tune. This production draws on similar musical themes but tells the story of growing up in the Washington Heights neighborhood of New York City. The Berkeley Playhouse offers a season pass for avid theater fans or single show passes. The theater is located at 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. For tickets or season passes visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/ or call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351. Tickets purchased at the door are cash only. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently performing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. pages.text: Wednesday, September 14, 2022 17 By Paul Hertelendy Berkeley composer John Adams has made a welcome attempt to bring under control the unwieldy “Antony and Cleopatra” story out of Shakespeare. Evolving from there, past composer Samuel Barber’s grand 1966 Met failure, to Adams’ world premiere, it has been boiled down from some 40 scenes and two dozen solo voices (ouch!) to Adams’ sleek, late-model version in three hours, two acts. It debuted September 10 to mark the 100th year of the San Francisco Opera. If you were waiting for gooey Pucciniesque scenes of the two lovers, this was not your opera. Instead of affairs, Adams focused on affairs of state, plus ensuing conflicts, in a historian’s more formal way. This Antony and Cleopatra is a chess match turned civil war between the ancient Romans Caesar (Augustus) and Antony, with the alluring queen Cleopatra running all over the chess board and resetting all the clocks with impunity. The punchy, highly rhythmic score festooned with electric outbursts of brass and percussion was all Adams, making no concession to popular expectations (nor any semblance of the silver screen’s Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton pairing). His music is at its best conveying scenes of high tension, which the opera provides in abundance. If there was more than the normal quota of opera-house dissonance, how else to portray the would-be hero sonically walking away from two wives, moving in with a minority woman from North Africa, and taking up arms in a power struggle? Historical severity was there John Adams’ new opera Affairs of State, not affairs on all counts. And Eun Sun Kim’s orchestra was aboard to make it all happen. Antony hops in and out of so many bedrooms and marriages, with yet more disasters in real combat, you wonder how ancient Rome ever survived anything. Well, civil wars are as good a way as any to start or to bring down the greatest dynasties (here, pitched battles leading to the victorious Caesar becoming the first emperor of the Roman Empire). The cast turned out much better than expected, given the cancelation of the original Cleopatra, Julia Bullock, due to pregnancy. Lyric soprano Amina Edris stepped in smartly with a sterling high range and the look of an Egyptian queen – at least, as close as you might get with this 1930s setting of 2,000-year-old history. We could certainly have done well without those 1930s perms, or films of early Ford touring cars, right, Caesar? In the early going, the Antony of baritone Gerald Finley was the night’s apex, getting strong support from tenor Paul Appleby (Caesar) as the opponent, an emperor outfitted in a plain modern business suit that deserved at least a few epaulets. Stage Director Elkhanah Pulitzer and the various designers made it work with minimal tools like sliding panels and a couch or bed, all allowing for rapid scene changes. Working with a dramaturg but no credited librettist, Adams leaned on cherry-picking scenes and texts out of Shakespeare, plus adding snippets from Plutarch and Virgil. articles.text: The 22nd annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park this Sunday, September 18 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. as part of the city’s annual Harvest Festival. A large stage will be installed in the Main Park, making viewing and listening easy for everyone. This year’s festival will feature Forte, a Latin tinged force of nature that includes strong vocals and a tight horn section. Forte played the Festival several years ago and literally “blew a fuse” in the sound system such that the show had to stop for several minutes while the sound technicians adjusted the equipment to capture Forte’s sound. Newly emerged from a pandemic hiatus, the Festival will be an opportunity for the public to hear Forte and their tight high-powered sound. Forte will be followed by the big-band sound of the Albany Jazz Band in its fifth appearance in town. The band has been performing at concerts and dances in the San Francisco Bay Area since 1996 performing a repertoire that includes instrumentals and vocals that span classic and contemporary big band music, Latin, and pop. The Albany Jazz Band performs as its original 20-piece Big Band format and in a newer 10-piece format. Since 2005, the Albany Jazz Band has been led by Bob Levenson as music director. Band members are drawn from throughout the Bay Area. The bands rehearse every week and both maintain active performance schedules. Sunday’s festival will open with the Piedmont High School Jazz Orchestra under the baton of Andria Mullan, band director at the high school and middle school, and a talented horn player. Also appearing this year will be Juvenoia, a Piedmont based rock trio composed of Jackson Lommen (bass and vocals), Alina Shahid, (guitar), and Torsten Olsen (drums). Schedule of bands 12:00 p.m. Piedmont High School Jazz Band 1:00 p.m. Forte (16-piece band): 2:00 p.m. Albany Big Band. 3:00 p.m. Juvenoia The Jazz Festival, organized by Greg Slatoff, is free and provides the opportunity to celebrate Piedmont’s musical talent amid fun, food and friends. Forte, a 14-piece Bay Area band, will be one of the headliners at this year’s Piedmont Jazz Festival this Sunday, September 18 in Piedmont Park.

A friend of mine knew Queen Elizabeth from the time that she was a little princess until 1985. My friend was known in diplomatic circles as His Excellency, the Duke of Baena. He was, in fact, a Spanish nobleman and one of Spain’s most important diplomats for the better part of the 20th century. Even though we were friends for many years, I always addressed him as Your Excellency. His first job was as gentleman in waiting to the Court of King Alfonso XIII of Spain. Then he became the minister of culture during the Spanish Republic. Serving on his committee were the important Spanish composer Manuel de Falla and the poet García Lorca. The catastrophe of the Spanish Civil War caused him to leave for safety in France. When “peace” was established by Generalissimo Franco, the Duke was appointed ambassador to England. It was during these years that he established a close friendship with the entire royal family of England. The. Duke had the greatest respect for Queen Elizabeth as well as her mother. Queen Elizabeth was, in the Duke’s words, “perfect in every way.” When his service as ambassador ended, the queen mother and young princess Elizabeth personally drove the Duke to the airport in London. He maintained a correspondence with the ladies of the royal court until he died in 1985. Proof of the friendship were the enumerable autographed pictures and letters which he kept in his living room. In contrast to his close relationship with England’s royal family, he despised Spanish dictator Franco. The Duke was overjoyed when Juan Carlos became King of Spain. articles.text: In his early teens, Duane Allman regularly “borrowed” his younger brother Gregg’s Sears Silvertone guitar and played it endlessly. When Duane wrecked his little Harley 165 motorcycle, he sold the remnants to get enough money to buy a Les Paul Junior guitar. He ended up primarily playing Les Paul guitars. Early bands founded by Duane and Gregg include The Misfits, The Allman Joys and Hour Glass (with Paul Hornsby). In Jacksonville, Florida in 1969, Duane and Gregg formed The Allman Brothers Band. The most notable musicians in The Allman Brothers Band were Duane Allman, Dickey Betts and Chuck Leavell. Duane played slide blues guitar, in open E tuning (E-AE-G#-B-E) and open A tuning (E-A-E-A-C#-E) and also played in standard tuning. Duane was influenced by Robert Johnson, Elmore James Junior Wells, Muddy Waters and the Miles Davis album Kind of Blue. He wouldn’t copy phrases from them verbatim, but would listen and reflect. Duane recorded with Eric Clapton, King Curtis, Aretha Franklin and others. Gregg played the Hammond organ, guitar and sang. Dickey Betts played a standard-tuned six-string guitar. He grew up listening to bluegrass, country and Western swing. Dickey’s composition In Memory of Elizabeth Reed showed harmonic and modal influences of The Allman Brothers Band jazz artists like Miles Davis and John Coltrane. Pianist Chuck Leavell joined the Allman Brothers in 1972 and played on their album Brothers and Sisters. His great rock piano solo from the song Jessica (arranged for guitar) is included in the improvised examples linked near the end of this column. Since 1985, Chuck has regularly toured and recorded with The Rolling Stones, Eric Clapton, John Mayer, George Harrison and David Gilmour. Chuck is also an expert in sustainable forestry and wrote Growing A Better America: Smart, Strong, Sustainable. Duane was killed in a motorcycle accident in 1971 at a time when the band was in the middle of recording their next album. The remaining band members named the album Eat a Peach, to summarize Duane’s answer to the question “How are you helping the revolution?” Duane replied, “I’m hitting a lick for peace, and every time I’m in Georgia I eat a peach for peace. But you can’t help the revolution, because there’s just evolution. I’m a player. And players don’t give a damn for nothing but playing….” Listen to and read my improvised examples for this column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/ PostColumns.pdf The following are notes on the improvised examples. Stormy Monday improv is in The Allman Brothers style with a bit more jazz. Jessica piano solo is Chuck Leavell’s piano solo arranged for guitar. Wahoo slide solo is a friend’s original song with my Duane Allman style slide guitar. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510)923- 9522, text (510)435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com

Musical success in half Moon Bay On another note, a brief weekend trip to Half Moon Bay was an artistic revelation. While the Piedmont politicos are making things very difficult musically speaking, the seaside town of Half Moon Bay is entirely supportive of its arts. A delightful concert of Brazilian music served to renew the life blood of the musical scene with a concert in the excellent Public Library. They are so well organized in Half Moon Bay that they even have a society which funds concerts. You heard that correctly: the musicians actually get paid. The concert on Sunday afternoon was dedicated to Brazilian music. Dominique Gagne was the flutist and Cesar Garabini was the featured guitarist. Both were exemplars of a fluid and easy technique. The program was a total delight because, in addition to being excellent musicians, they were also excellent speakers. This is a very rare combination indeed. Every aspect of the concert made you smile. Some of the pieces caused the audience to dance. Others were soul-searching in a sensual way. That is the nature of Brazilian music. The audience overflowed the auditorium and extra seats had to be placed outside in the courtyard to accommodate everyone.
