articles.text: A joint art show will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from October 1-9. Ellen Dreibelbis, a figurative artist, and John Q. McDonald a landscape painter, will have an exhibit titled Something about the Light. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, October Dreibelbis of Oakland creates figurative paintings that illuminate and celebrate the beauty and Peruvian Boy, by Ellen Dreibelbis, pastel on archival paper, 18” x 14” wisdom of the world’s people. She is often deeply moved by the way the light illuminates an object, bringing forth its power and mystery. From that evocative beginning comes a journey full of risk, uncertainty and restatement, through which she strives to build the aesthetic architecture combining composition, value, color, and edges which anchor the more intangible qualities that emerge in the process of painting. As each painting seems to have its own voice, she has learned to be still and listen to it rather than imposing her own ideas, and never knows how a painting will turn out until all parts ring true. McDonald of Pleasanton uses light to enhance the graphical drama of landscapes in California and beyond. Inspired in part by modern landscape painters such as Robert Bechtle, Gerhard Richter, Georgia O’Keefe and Edward Hopper, his work tends to focus on the interaction between memory, the humanmade and the natural in our landscape. An astronomer by trade and therefore used to relying Warming Hut SF by John Q. McDonald, Oil on Canvas, 16” x 12” upon light, he endeavors to capture in his painting the unique quality of light found in the different places he has visited and inhabited, particularly the bright light of California and the West. He seeks to express the manner in which the things we create, the places we build, establish their meaning and presence in our environment. Friends for years, this is their first joint art show.

articles.text: Come enjoy a wide range of music, art and special events throughout the year. Saturday, September 17, 7:30 p.m. POSTPONED Chamber Music Society of S. F. Due to a medical condition, the concert will be postponed until Sunday, October 30 in a matinee performance at 1:30 p.m. at the Center for the Arts. Tickets already purchased will be honored on the new date, and CMS of SF will contact ticket-holders with other options. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Opus 132, String Quartet in A minor, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. In this and other late works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The program will also include Mozart’s String Quartet in C Major (“Dissonance”), and Caroline Shaw’s Valencia. This accomplished string quartet is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences, and passionate about concertizing in intimate settings to create close connections between performers and listeners, drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music. Don’t delay getting your advance tickets at https://bit.ly/3TpKMUZ for this 90-minute concert which opens CMSSF’s 10th season. Sunday, September 18, 3:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert celebrating the rich colors of Autumn Leaves with a selection of ballads, swing and jazz blues arrangements, nodding along the way to honor Mexican Independence Day with two special medleys. The concert will be a great way to spend part of a relaxed late summer Sunday afternoon and is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing PCA’s magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets are $20 at the door, or at https://bpt.me/5316993. Seating will be limited to the first 70 attendees. Saturday, October 1, 11:00 a.m. Dreibelbis, McDonald art An exhibit by two local artists, entitled “Something about the Light…” is comprised of figurative paintings by Ellen Dreibelbis that celebrate the beauty and wisdom of the peoples of the world. It also features paintings enhancing graphical drama in landscapes by John Q. McDonald, exploring the relationships between human structures and their natural surroundings. Some pieces in the show will be available for purchase. Entrance to the show is free. Gallery hours are Saturday and Sunday, October 1-2 and October 8-9 from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events. All public events at piedmont center for the arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside.

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum featuring exbibit by Carlos Villa

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Gardens in Woodside will continue its Summer Nights events on Thursday evenings through September 22. The Garden is open until 8 p.m., and the historic house open until 7 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance garden to the south. All admission, including for Summer Nights, must be reserved in advance. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ for more information and to reserve tickets.
articles.title: Filoli Summer Nights events continue to Sept. 22

San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more. Filoli Summer Nights events continue to Sept. 22 Filoli Historic House and Gardens in Woodside will continue its Summer Nights events on Thursday evenings through September 22. The Garden is open until 8 p.m., and the historic house open until 7 p.m. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance garden to the south. All admission, including for Summer Nights, must be reserved in advance. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ for more information and to reserve tickets. articles.text: Johnny Depp reprises his role as Captain Jack Sparrow in Pirates Of The Caribbean: On Stranger Tides. Review by Chris Honoré Pirates Of The Caribbean: On Stranger Tides is Johnny Depp returning once again to his signature role as the charming, strangely androgynous and ever resourceful Captain Jack Sparrow. His costume, his line delivery, his sashaying walk, his raccoon-like eyes are pure, campy genius. And his performance is close to the sole reason to see this fourth installment of what has been a wildly successful franchise. Audiences, of course, are ever hopeful that they will be present for the reincarnation of something as captivating as the Curse of the Black Pearl. Alas, of the films that followed the 2003 Pirates debut, a solid story has been elusive. All of the sequels, regardless of their subtitles, have been either decidedly convoluted or so thin in plot that it’s tempting to just forget the story and simply enjoy the characters. In this latest film the plot has been simplified: find the fountain of youth for England before the Spaniards find it and do something rash. Rumor is, there’s a map. That’s it. The meaning of the subtitle, “On Stranger Tides,” is a mystery. In fact, there are few strangers on any tides in this film. Okay, there is Blackbeard (Ian McShane), who is a nasty piece of work. Also new is the alluring, if duplicitous, Angelica (Penelope Cruz), with whom we’re told Jack has history. Seems that a broken heart was involved. Captain Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush), Jack’s nemesis, returns. As does sidekick, Joshamee Gibbs. They’re all great characters, wonderfully portrayed, and the photography is stunning. But, like its antecedents, with the exception of the original Black Pearl, the current journey of Captain Jack Sparrow seems pedestrian – with the exception of the first 15 minutes that involve an escape by Sparrow and stalwart Joshamee Gibbs. But then, swashbuckling adventure films must have an opening with a huge Wow factor – it’s de rigueur. Often, that first action setup can be the best part of the franchise ride. The reality is that any sequel that follows the first Pirates film is a tough climb. The initial introduction of Captain Jack Sparrow and company was fresh and original, with a winning story, despite the film being named after a Disneyland attraction. The burden of replicating that initial excitement is no easy trick. As demonstrated by On Stranger Tides. Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides. Starring Johnny Depp, Penelope Cruz, Ian McShane, Geoffrey Rush, Kevin McNally and Keith Richards. Directed by Rob Marshall. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Remarkably, a short story by the science fiction writer Philip K. Dick, adapted for the screen as The Adjustment Bureau, turns out to be the best romance of the year. A different love story to be sure, crafted from an unusual premise. However, because Hollywood has served up an endless string of trivial nonsense, this film comes as a welcome surprise. It begins with Elise Sellas (Emily Blunt), a ballet dancer, and David Norris (Matt Damon), a hotshot politician running for the state senate, meeting cute in the men’s room of the Waldorf Astoria. David is preparing to deliver a very difficult speech. Certain that he’s alone, he begins rehearsing. Suddenly, Elise steps out of one of the stalls. They begin a gentle, smart badinage and their mutual attraction is quickly evident – to them and the audience. But all that has happened to them is part of a greater plan. If either deviates from the plan, a small adjustment will be necessary. Enter stage left, the Adjustment Bureau: men in snap-brim hats, dark suits, and narrow ties, who warn David that he cannot pursue a relationship with Elise, for reasons that are not disclosed. David, impulsive and a bit reckless, is not inclined to cooperate, sensing that in Elise he has met someone unlike anyone before. Perhaps you have to suspend your disbelief to be fully engaged by the story. You must be willing to give the story sufficient latitude, all in the interest of being intrigued and perhaps even surprised. It helps that the fantasy/sci fi aspects of the film are handled so seamlessly that it never seems contrived or in any way jarring. It all fits nicely together. As David grows more intent on pursuing a relationship with Elise, the story delves into the existential question of free will. Do we design our own lives or are there forces greater than ourselves that guides us? Should David be allowed to choose? Are any of us truly free to choose? Of course, in the world of Philip K. Dick the ability to make choices is an illusion. During those periods in history when the Bureau stepped back and let mankind truly choose, the result was the 20th century, one of the most violent in history. Hence, the Bureau concluded that it was time to re-engage and guide. So, David falls down the rabbit hole (where would sci-fi/fantasy be without it?) and sets in motion a test of wills between himself and the Bureau which insists that she cannot be part of his destiny. Acts two and three involve an escalation of tension, some well choreographed chase scenes, as pieces of the puzzle begin to fall into place. If your threshold for such storytelling is high and if your imagination is captured by such a premise, you will find The Adjustment Bureau a solidly entertaining film, a perfect blend of romance and the improbable, nicely imagined and well acted. The Adjustment Bureau. Starring Matt Damon, Emily Blunt, John Slattery, Anthony Mackie and Terrance Stamp. Written and directed by George Nolf. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Nº 58 in a series Queen Elizabeth died peacefully at age 96 on Thursday, September 15, at Balmoral Castle in the Scottish countryside. She proved the longest serving monarch in English history, having celebrated her Platinum Jubilee reign of 70 years on June 5. The French government turned to paying tribute to the Grand British Dame. The Eiffel Tower with its typically bright display, a mesmerizing lightshow, went dark into the night. President Emmanuel Macron appeared at the British Embassy in Paris to pay tribute to the queen. He spoke in English to address the British public: “We are grateful for Elizabeth’s deep affection. She is a longtime friend and the closest of allies. Queen Elizabeth mastered our language, loved French culture, and touched our hearts,” he said. He remarked that she visited France more than any other nation. He signed the book of condolences, and First Lady Brigette Macron shared her “very, very great emotion and respect” for the late sovereign. “She was very important to us. For me, she was, she is, and she will remain the queen.” The world responded with condolences to her British subjects. The Italians laid flowers outside Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip. Queen Elizabeth in graceful majesty. Duke of Windsor Edward and wife Wallis at home in Paris in the early 1960s. the British Embassy in Rome. Pope Francis sent “heartfelt condolences.” At the White House in Washington D.C., the flag was lowered to half-mast. German Chancellor Olaf Scholz paid tribute to the Queen’s wonderful humor and her role for reconciliation after the Second World War. The Bundestag observed a moment of silence. The German Federation president Frank-Walter Steinmeier said, “Her Majesty was held in the highest esteem throughout the world.” Brussels lowered its flags to half-mast, and President of the Council of Europe, Charles Michel, commented about Elizabeth II’s statesmanship, and her monumental presence through the great conflicts of our time. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the Queen had been a reassuring presence through decades of change as the United Nations held a moment of silence in respect to the queen. Despite becoming a queen by accident, Elizabeth’s reign spanned the terms of seven U.S. Presidents. The princess was age 10 in 1936 when her uncle, King Edward VIII, abdicated the throne, setting in motion her carefully crafted life. Her father became king, crowned George VI, and her heart broke for him in his private struggle to overcome a lifetime of stuttering. (Colin Firth played him in The King’s Speech). Elizabeth dealt with a gripping fear of queen presumptive, while her carefree younger sister Margaret was flippant. Elizabeth was the insular, shy first-born, while Margaret was bold, confident, and boiling-over with envy. The teenage Princess Elizabeth gave a first-time public address over radio airwaves, a patriotic message to her war-torn nation, and her uncle, always quick to lacerate to make a deep wound, chortled over his niece’s high-pitched and childish voice, and pet-named her Shirley Temple. Her uncle Edward’s abandonment of the royal throne was unimaginable to the child princess. She couldn’t fathom his fixation on the American socialite Wallis Simpson, and his reckless scrambling of the succession risking public wrath and ridicule and thrusting her much-loved, unprepared father onto the throne. Why wouldn’t Edward simply behave? Her grandparents, King George V and his Queen Mary, had refused to receive Wallis Simpson after a single meeting. To the young Elizabeth, the twice-divorced American would A portrait of Queen Elizabeth at the time of her coronation. The young Queen wore a magnificent, bejeweled headpiece from the Crowned Jewels collection. somehow wreak havoc over the dignified royal office. Decades later, the issue of divorce and remarriage reared again. Princess Margaret would be devasted by Queen Elizabeth’s refusal to battle the Church to permit Margaret to marry the love of her life, Royal Air Force Captain Peter Townsend, a married man tangled up in divorce. The Church decree was unbending: no royal could marry a divorced person. King Charles III is married to a divorcée, Camilla. Elizabeth’s long reign changed the queen, relaxing tradition, slightly. Absolutely devoted to the crown with an extraordinary work ethic and literally dying on the job, she embodied her credo, “You don’t give up, you don’t abdicate, you endure for England.” Yet, Elizabeth made small but significant concessions. She protected her children. She lowered the flag to half-mast at Princess Elizabeth and her husband Prince Philip. Charles III, the oldest king in British history at age 73, waits to address Parliament. Charles III, with Camilla, Queen Consort acknowledge mourners at his mother’s death.

articles.text: Part 52 in a biweekly series As we have mentioned before in this column, one of the great pleasures of walking around town is discovering, observing and reflecting on the many fine conventional and idiosyncratic design elements found throughout Piedmont. All of these illustrate to some degree the various built environment principles we have been discussing, Many carry interesting historical or personal background stories behind their development and construction. What is most important however, is the personal concern and involvement so many people have in not only their own properties but in the entire city, from important historic buildings, to new residential proposals, to architectural, landscape architectural, and urban design details, such as new curb cuts and street bollards. In all of the walking around and photographing of examples I have been involved in over the last few years, absolutely everyone I have come in contact with has been friendly, cooperative and willing to share information about their homes, gardens, streets and neighborhoods. I think this is a real indicator that people take pride in their city and is a big part of the successful appearance and sense of community that exists here. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. This is a clever charging solution that precludes a tripping hazard chord over the sidewalk. Photos by Will Adams The trellis that visually links the new high school STEM building with the adjacent new theater is a nod to the famous East Bay architects Bernard Maybeck and Julia Morgan. It’s good to see that Wisteria vine has been planted and will quickly soften the strong horizontal lines, add color, and enhance this fine punctuation point in the town center. Street trees – what an asset to a city. In addition to so many other advantages, properly spaced street trees can punctuate the pedestrian experience for walkers by providing shade, separation from cars, and a “sense of enclosure” on a simple sidewalk. Nicolas Haralambides fashioned this interesting abstract (historic) sculpture for his garden in Piedmont. A closer look reveals it comes from the melted innards of his grand piano, lost, along with the entire previous house, in the huge Oakland firestorm of 1991.

articles.text: Sleek white quartz complements the cabinetry in this modern kitchen. McCutchen Construction In kitchen remodeling, there are many selections to consider for not only a well-designed, functional space but also one that is timeless and beautiful. Among one of the most important steps in remodeling is your choice of countertops. With so many possibilities, the process of selecting the right material can be overwhelming. While there are many options today for a great looking countertop not all will suit your family’s needs. Some popular materials today are Quartzite, Quartz, Marble and Granite. To help you decide the right material for you and your family, let’s explore these options for their strengths as well as their challenges. Quartzite is a natural stone. It’s highly durable and is available in many options aesthetically. This natural stone does require sealing to help protect it from heavy use and to ensure its longevity. It’s best to have it sealed once or twice a year to keep it performing and looking its best. The earth tones of this granite help create a refined, contemporary kitchen design. Classic marble is the star of this vintage style kitchen. Quartz is popular these days and rightfully so. It’s highly durable, scratch and stain resistant, made to last. This is an engineered stone that’s made from small stone particles or powder and combined with resin. Because it’s manmade, it does have less variation in appearance than natural material. Even so, it’s often difficult to tell the difference between this and natural stone once installed, and the cost is much less. Marble is classic, well-loved for its timeless beauty and elegance. articles.text: Once again, it’s the season for football games and backto-school activities. And if you work for a medium-size or large employer, it will soon be open enrollment season – the time of year when you can review your employee benefits and make changes as needed. What areas should you focus on? Actually it’s a good idea to pay close attention to all your benefits. Some of the offerings may have changed from last year – and you might have experienced changes in your own life, too, which might lead you to look for something different from your existing benefits package. Health insurance You may want to start with your health insurance. If you’re satisfied with your coverage, and it’s essentially the same as it’s been, you may well want to stick with what you have. However, many employers are increasingly offering high-deductible health plans, which, as the name suggests, could entail more out-ofpocket costs for you. But high-deductible plans may also offer something of benefit: the ability to contribute to a health savings account (HSA). Your HSA contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, so they can reduce your taxable income for the year. Also, your earnings grow tax-free, and your withdrawals are taxfree, provided the money is used for qualified medical expenses. (Withdrawals taken before age 65 that aren’t used for qualified medical expenses are taxable and subject to a 20% penalty; once you reach 65, the penalty no longer applies, although withdrawals are still taxable as income if not used for a qualified expense.) Life insurance Your next benefit to consider: Life insurance. Your employer may offer a group life insurance plan, but you’ll want to evaluate whether it’s sufficient for your needs, especially if you’ve experienced changes in your personal situation over the past year, such as getting married or adding a new child. There’s no magic formula for how much life insurance you need – you’ll need to consider a variety of factors, such as your income, family size, mortgage and so on – but it may be necessary to supplement your employer’s coverage with a private policy. Disability insurance Your employer may also offer disability insurance as a benefit. Some employers’ disability policies are fairly limited, covering only short periods of time, so you may want to consider a private policy. Retirement plan Beyond the various insurance policies your employer may offer, you’ll also want to closely look at your 401(k) or similar retirement plan. Typically, you can make changes to your 401(k) throughout the year, but it’s important to make sure your investment selections and contribution amounts are still aligned with your risk tolerance and goals. Also, are you contributing enough to earn your employer’s match, if one is offered? And if you’ve already receiving the match, can you still afford to put in more to your plan if such a move makes sense for you? Your employee benefits package can be a valuable part of your overall financial strategy. So, as open enrollment season proceeds, take a close look at what you already have, what’s being offered, and what changes you need to make. It will be time well spent. articles.text: Campers gather at the electric wood carving station. Scores of campers, parents and counselors gathered at Hampton Field on a warm Sunday afternoon, September 11, for Camp Augusta’s Campathon, a fundraiser for the non-profit camp established in 1931. The event, which aimed to raise $150,000 to change its ropes course to a pole course, featured more than a dozen stations, which included electric wood carving, acoustic guitar instructions and sword fighting. There were also a photo booth, bracelet making and balloon animals stations. Additionally, the event had more camp-specific games like gaga ball and the Augusta Knowledge Bowl, which asked campers questions about camp history and facilities. Correct questions equaled a punch card mark and ten punch card marks equal a level bracelet. Campers continued leveling up into the early evening. Arguably, the most important feature was Lazy Dog Ice Cream and its giant drumsticks. Based near the camp in Nevada City, Lazy Dog has become a staple for campers and counselors for years. They have unique flavors like strawberry shortcake and sour patch kids. Campers and parents played games one-handed while working through their oversized drumsticks. Lazy Dog even makes specialty cones exclusively for the camp. This was the first in-person fundraising event Camp Augusta has held since the COVID-19-related lockdowns “It felt incredible to be back in person,” said Board President Jason Ring, who touched on the family tradition at the camp and on display at the event. “We have friends in the community whose kids all went to the camp.” Randy Grayson, the Camp Augusta Director, echoed this sentiment and spoke to the Post about the benefit of the transition, the incredibly diverse staff and the unique activities that differentiate Augusta from other summer camps. Grayson also expressed deep gratitude to be returning to in-person events and the unique activities that campers experience at Camp Augusta. “We want to do all things that don’t exist anywhere else in the world. So, with every one of the 25 elements [on display at the Campathon], we want them to be unique, and we want them to have multi-functions. You could do it as a team, you could do it individually, you could do it in a small group, with all sorts of different layered challenges,” Grayson explained. He confirmed that Augusta has long broken away from the cookie-cutter approach to summer camp. “With the constellation of trees [surrounding the camp], we didn’t have all the elements interact with each other in varied ways,” he said. He explained how Augusta’s unique approach to activities and international coalition of counselors keep kids and families coming back year after year. “We do the one event, because the staff are from all over the world. Right now we have [counselors from] six different countries here,” Grayson said. Grayson, whose personal favorite activity is probably the faux sword fighting, will oversee the budgetary responsibilities and big picture considerations of the installation of a new zip line and ropes course using 80-foot poles instead of trees. According to Grayson, the camp has lost nearly 80 percent of its tallest trees in the last 20 years. Ronnie, who Photo by Ian Firstenberg The sword fighting station is ready for campers. Two campers square off for a sword fight while a counselor referees. Counselors teach a camper some riffs in the acoustic guitar booth. hails from Scotland, is the Ropes Course director and will be in charge of logistics, design management and production responsibilities. Sustainability is chief among the benefits of the innovative renovation. The project is slated to cost between $150,000 and $175,000. Construction will be handled by Challenge Works and should begin in early 2023. “On a long-term basis, sustainability is the key because the poles won’t die,” Grayson said. Overall, the Sunday fundraiser in Piedmont was a tremendous success. Kids and parents, full of ice cream, left with smiles knowing that Camp Augusta will continue to provide unique and innovative opportunities for campers, families and counselors. “A big focus of Augusta is creative expression and creative experience. We do the clinic activities like archery, but a large focus is how we make sure kids have a creative experience that they don’t have in their normal lives,” Grayson said. articles.text: Diana’s death in 1997, compelled by the public’s extreme outpouring of grief. Her much-adored father, Albert, becoming George VI in his first act as king, installed his older brother as Duke of Windsor, a made-to-order title, adding an honorary title of duchess for his bride. The couple carried their titles resentfully to their ending days yet managed to enjoy the good life while exiled in Paris. Edward, the once-king, narrowed his dealings with the crown to asking for bigger royal stipends, as there was never enough. Adopting her parents’ original stance against Edward’s disruptive tendencies, Elizabeth handled her uncle firmly: His considerable royal income would be threatened if he should ever return to Britain without an invitation. Elizabeth was crowned queen at age 26, a year after her father, a very heavy smoker, died in 1952 from lung cancer. She was a young, inexperienced royal with two small children and a restless and unruly husband, Philip Mountbatten. Now, at her death, elder son Charles is king, immediately. English doctrine of rex nunquam moritur, “the king never dies,” means there’s no interregnum: “The King is dead. Long live the King.” The Queen has died, long live Charles. The coronation and pomp will follow, but Charles’ first duty was to Parliament, stating his resolve to follow his mother’s stylebook of selfless duty. In a nod to heir presumptive Prince William, his father states plainly he intends to rule to the end of his life. Prince William expressed his deep honor accepting the title of Prince of Wales from his father who held it for more than 50 years. With his wife Princess Catherine (Kate), he expressed a deep affection for Wales, where they spent the earliest months of their firstborn Prince George’s life at Anglesey during an idyllic stay. The Netflix award-winning series, The Crown, closed production on September 8 in tribute to Queen Elizabeth’s passing. Season Five is in post-production following a two-year hiatus, and features an all-new celebrity cast

JENNIFER LONG, Incumbent 1) Housing Housing development in Piedmont requires careful, thorough planning that will enhance our safe, beautiful neighborhoods, and ensure continued strong property values. It is also essential to have as many community members as possible weighing in on how best to create housing in our city. Further, Piedmont residents must understand what California law requires of the city (and what it does not) and how we can make our compliance with state law work for our community. Currently, Piedmont has no specific plans to build housing and is under no obligation to pay for housing development. However, the City is mandated by state law to create a plan which identifies potential sites upon which housing might be built. The City is currently working diligently on this necessary step, which ensures that Piedmont will be able to maintain local control over the future of our beloved city. 2) Infrastructure I recently voted with my fellow council members to begin the design process for the renovation of Piedmont’s police and fire dispatch center. This dispatch center is a critical part of our city’s excellent police and fire services. Public safety will continue to be my top priority. Piedmonters are aware of the much-anticipated new community pool. Bringing this plan to fruition in a fiscally sensible manner is one of my goals. The civic center buildings (Veterans Hall, City Hall, and the police and fire buildings) are in need of critical infrastructure work. It is important that we upgrade these facilities to continue to be a well-run city. Finally, there are other projects underway such as upgrading our streets and sidewalks to be ADA compliant, and updating infrastructure to help meet our climate action goals. All of these investments will help our city continue to deliver high-quality services while advancing sustainability. TOM RAMSEY 1) Housing We have the responsibility and legal obligation to create a plan to integrate affordable housing into our beautiful town, but not to be a developer. Our town is not in the housing construction business, nor should it be. Here are two examples of what we can do: 1. Create Objective Design Standards for potential duplexes and lot splits allowed by state law. There are great examples of historic multi-family housing in Piedmont hiding in plain sight today. Let’s control negative impacts of SB9 by creating thoughtful Design Standards specific to Piedmont. 2. Look for opportunities for Public Private Partnerships that provide affordable housing and leverage public improvements for parks and city infrastructure. These collaborative efforts could provide non-City funding. I’ll use my 30 years’ experience as an architect and seven years serving on the Planning Commission to assure that our housing efforts preserve the character of our town. 2) Infrastructure We have great public services in Piedmont with dedicated staff and first responders. However, our infrastructure and facilities do not reflect the same quality. Our police and fire stations do not meet minimum building code requirements for essential facilities. For example, a 2020 review revealed that fire apparatus could be trapped inside the garage following an earthquake. Our work ahead should include: 1. Updating our Civic Center Plan 2. Evaluating existing conditions, options, costs, and phasing. Estimates suggest that rebuilding the fire station is less expensive than remodeling – Let’s vet all assumptions with the current market. 3. Evaluating efficiencies by combining redundant support facilities. 4. Working with the Budget and Finance Committee to determine appropriate funding options. 5. Evaluating a Public Private Partnership approach. 6. Implementing the proposed Emergency Operations Center Improvements. As an architect, I’ve spent my career tackling these issues. I’ll put that experience to work for Piedmont. BRIDGET HARRIS 1) Housing If elected, I would delay submission of the Housing Element to the state until residents of Piedmont clearly understand the impact on traffic and safety of locating 587 additional housing units in Piedmont. I would outline the consequences of delaying the submission, and provide options to be voted upon by the community in a special election. Should the current city council submit a plan to California without a vote of our citizens, I would still move to require a vote because the current proposed plan is a de facto re-zone and our city charter requires that any re-zone be approved by a vote of the community. We must protect our scarce open spaces, such as Blair Park. Any construction of multi-family units in the center of town would negatively impact school safety, traffic, pedestrians, and parking. We need to further explore re-zoning other areas near Park Blvd and Grand Ave. 2) Infrastructure The Piedmont community greatly values its police and fire departments, yet both operate in outdated and unsafe facilities. articles.text: In the Competition Pool, funds will support regulation length and depth for water polo play, diving well with two diving boards, scoreboard, timing system, sports lighting, and starting blocks and toe ledges. Recreation Pool amenities requiring additional funding include three standard-length lap lanes, an expansive shallow area for play and swim lessons and a poolside room for parties and gatherings. Why can’t the City fund the shortfall from general funds? The City relies on general funds to conduct its routine activities, including repairing sidewalks, maintaining parks and other public spaces. At present, the City does not have extra funds available for a major capital project such as this one. What is the deadline to raise the additional funds? Funding needs to be secured by October 16, 2022. What will happen to the pool if we cannot raise the $2 million? If the $2 million is not raised, the Piedmont Community Pool Project will continue, but specific features will be value-engineered out of the scope. Rather than have three standard-length lap lanes in the Recreation Pool, for example, the city may only be able to afford two. Will the facility still be allelectric? The new Piedmont Community Pool is designed to be fully electric. Funding for this design will not come from Measure UU nor from the PRFO fundraising campaign. There is a separate fundraising effort to pay for the increased construction costs for all-electric heating.

The roof at the Recreation Center needs replacing. Council awarded $222,884 for this repair. Underground electricity: as our city ages so do our utility poles. Downed wires can be deadly. The city should explore the means for installing underground utilities throughout the city. Underground wiring adds safety and beauty to our city. Crosswalks/Sidewalks: Many crosswalks/sidewalks are hazardous and open the city to liability. Crossings near the schools and parks need enhancements to alert drivers that children are present. Many sidewalks are a trip hazard and need repair. NANCY BOSTROM No response Pool News Continued from page 1 In the Competition Pool, funds will support regulation length and depth for water polo play, diving well with two diving boards, scoreboard, timing system, sports lighting, and starting blocks and toe ledges. Recreation Pool amenities requiring additional funding include three standard-length lap lanes, an expansive shallow area for play and swim lessons and a poolside room for parties and gatherings. Why can’t the City fund the shortfall from general funds? The City relies on general funds to conduct its routine activities, including repairing sidewalks, maintaining parks and other public spaces. At present, the City does not have extra funds available for a major capital project such as this one. What is the deadline to raise the additional funds? Funding needs to be secured by October 16, 2022. What will happen to the pool if we cannot raise the $2 million? If the $2 million is not raised, the Piedmont Community Pool Project will continue, but specific features will be value-engineered out of the scope. Rather than have three standard-length lap lanes in the Recreation Pool, for example, the city may only be able to afford two. Will the facility still be allelectric? The new Piedmont Community Pool is designed to be fully electric. Funding for this design will not come from Measure UU nor from the PRFO fundraising campaign. There is a separate fundraising effort to pay for the increased construction costs for all-electric heating. Will the new facility be open to non-Piedmont residents? What will be the fee for an Annual Pass? The new facility will be open to residents of Piedmont and the general public. articles.text: On Tuesday, September 6. Piedmont recorded a high temperature of 103.3°F at Piedmont City Hall, according to Weather Underground. Temperatures on Labor Day, September 5, also surpassed 100°F, as the entire West Coast continues to experience a heat wave. The forecast for today, September 7, is for a high of 92°F. As the first evidence of fog was seen late Tuesday afternoon, the temperature began to drop somewhat. Thursday’s high is forecast for 95°F, and Friday slightly cooler at 88°F. High temperatures are projected to be 80°F or lower over the weekend. “We have not had any heat-related calls,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “The wind is low and the humidity is high, so we are not in red flag conditions.” Red flag conditions are issued for weather events which may result in extreme fire behavior. Much of the West Coast has been under a heat advisory for excessive temperatures for seven days, and the state is under a heat advisory until Thursday evening. More than 50 million residents were under either Excessive Heat Warnings or Heat Advisories as of Tuesday. According to the National Weather Service “An upper level ridge of high pressure over the western U.S. continues to support an extensive heat dome up and down the West Coast.” The City of Piedmont’s website advises the following during the heat wave: • Drink lots of water, even if you don’t feel thirsty. Avoid alcohol and caffeine. • Limit physical activity overall and avoid physical activity during the hottest time of the day (10 a.m.-3 p.m.). • Never leave people or pets in a closed, parked car. • Cool off by taking a bath or shower. • Wear lightweight, light-colored, loose fitting clothing to help stay cool. Stick to breathable fabrics like cotton. • Older adults and individuals with chronic medical conditions are at greater risk during hot weather. Call and check in on friends, family, and neighbors to make sure they’re okay. An unrelenting heat wave has affected the Bay Area for one week with historic high temperatures.
articles.title: Triple digit heat wave hits Piedmont

articles.text: Dads Club hosts 17th annual Pancake Breakfast plus Arts Fund’s Chalk Art Festival The wait is nearly over for Beach School’s Dads Club’s big event this Sunday, September 11, the 17th Annual Pancake Breakfast at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. The fundraising event runs from 9:00 a.m.-12:00 noon in conjunction with the Chalk Art Festival, that invites artists to create colorful drawings on the school playground. The day is a great way for kids and adults to catch up with old friends and make new connections. Enjoy a plate of madefrom-scratch buttermilk, blueberry, chocolate chip, or oatmeal pancakes, plus sausage, bacon, fresh fruit and Alibi Coffee – all prepared by the Beach Dads. “It’s quite a big effort with all the dads involved,” explained current Dads Club President Peter The Beach School’s Dads Club in action during the 2019 Pancake Breakfast. Jaeschcke. “Their tasks range from frontline pancakes flipping on the six grills, to kitchen prep and coffee serving. And then there is all the behind the scenes for everything that goes into the event early that morning and days before,” Tickets can be purchased at the event. The cost is $10 for adults and $5 for kids and seniors. Funds will go to the Beach Parents Organization which pays for Staff photos Last year’s Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast drew hundreds of participants, with Will Rogan serving as Padre Grande.

articles.text: Ladies and gentlemen, this past week we have been slammed by a heat wave. And as someone who goes to school in Lafayette, I am no stranger to scorching heat all year round. But the heat does get to me from time to time, so without wasting another second, here are my five favorite ways to stay cool in the heat. In our number one spot, is one of my all-time top picks – frozen grapes. I am sure to some readers this is pretty familiar. It’s such a quick and easy hack, all you do is grab a bunch of grapes from the bag, put them in a bowl and stick them in the freezer for at least two hours. After two hours, just take the grapes out of the freezer and bon appetit! It’s one of my favorite way to stay cool because not only are you eating something cold, you are eating something that tastes sweet and is pretty healthy. For parents with toddlers, this is for you, because believe me this is going to save you a couple of tantrums because of the heat. Next on the list is another alltimer – spraying yourself with a hose. And all you have to do is put on a bathing suit, grab a hose, the closest parent, sibling, or pet, and have a blast. While you are getting soaked from the hose, if the sunlight hits the water droplets the right way, you can see a rainbow appear on the water. I don’t know about you, but that sounds like an absolute blast to me. But it is important to remember we are in a drought, so don’t overboard on the amount of water. On the bright side, you can water your plants while you are having a water fight. Coming in at number three is, filling up your bathtub with water to cool down the house. articles.text: 10th Annual Piedmont Artisanal Beer Festival is October 7 The Piedmont Center for the Arts will host one of its most popular events of the year the first weekend of October. On Friday, October 7, the 10th Annual Piedmont Beer Festival will take over the Center for the Arts for a celebration of Artisanal brewers and their finest home brews. In addition to sampling the best of local home brewers, guests are invited to have a legitimate German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center, with freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. Food is provided by Dave Larson at Piedmont Grocery. A panel of Piedmont celebrity judges will award prizes to home brewers for Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, Best IPA, and Best in Show. This year’s celebrity judges are Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson. Brewers already registered include Piedmont brewers Matt Gerhardt, Carter Dunlap, Trevor Fleshman, Zachary Jones, Ed Sweeney and Case Gardner. In addition, a 2021 winner, Kyle Blomseth, has also signed up. He won last year’s best specialty beer with a Belgian Style Ale. To enter home brews, contact Center for the Arts board member Carter Dunlap at carter@dunlapclan.net, or Jay Russell at jayrussell35@gmail.com. Include your name, phone & e-mail address and the type of beer you will bring. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue.

articles.text: After two years of meeting teachers through Zoom, it was wonderful to return to the classroom for Back-to-School night this year. We felt especially heartened to hear from teachers about how they plan to incorporate social justice and identity into the curriculum, from reading diverse, award-winning books to exploring geography, culture and current events through multiple perspectives. Many parents in the community didn’t have the fortune of a multicultural education when we were growing up. Now our children do. Our children are still learning literary analysis, the components of persuasive essays, critical developments in world and U.S. history — the nuts and bolts at the core of their education. But they’re doing so through a wider, more inclusive and equitable lens. Including diverse perspectives doesn’t mean sacrificing the quality of their education. Rather, it increases rigor, helping our children open up their field of view beyond Piedmont. Improving the educational experience for all students in the community isn’t as easy as flipping a switch. It takes time, training, funds, resources and planning — especially if we want to do this work well. For this reason, the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) advocated for a Director of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. A new position in Piedmont School District. That position has been filled by Dr. Marguerite Wyngaard, and we are thrilled to include her as an important part of our community. We believe her leadership, expertise and guidance are critical and necessary in navigating the challenge of creating a more culturally diverse learning experience. Students must prepare to be active members of an increasingly multicultural community, to live, work and grow within that community. Piedmont’s efforts to incorporate diversity, equity and inclusion in schools means that we are cementing our commitment to academic excellence. Join PADC for its next general meeting in September. Subscribe to its newsletter for updates and details at https://www.padc.info/ subscribe. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will host its third annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town on Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and is organized by Officer Tyler Petit. Last year’s Car Show had 120 vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 68 vehicles have signed up for this year’s Car Show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, 1987 Ferrari Testarossa, and possibly two Formula Ford race cars. The car show includes free coffee and donuts, and there is a rumor that a taco truck might arrive. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want their cars to be in the show need to register on the Eventbrite website as soon as possible at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/coffee-cars-cops-car-showtickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue between the high school and Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: Piedmont’s popular annual Harvest Festival returns to Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 18 with games, activities and a jazz festival from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The festival will feature all the traditional mainstays and activities, including Village Market’s Farmer’s market, the Edibles Contest, Scarecrow Alley, carnival games for kids, the annual Jazz Festival, an art exhibit at the Japanese Tea House, and food trucks lined up on Highland Avenue. The all-volunteer event is sponsored by the city. Scarecrow Alley will be set up in the main park, with more than a dozen creatively designed creatures. A silent auction allows viewers to purchase scarecrows at the end of the day. A robust carnival will take place in the Community Hall parking lot, with games and treats for kids of all ages. Edibles Contest The popular Edibles Contest has occurred every year since the Festival’s founding in 1998 by Susan Hill and Bill Drum. The contest features the best homeThe Edibles Contest has been popular since the Harvest Festival’s founding in 1998. grown and homemade foods from residents. There are many categories to choose from, including: biggest pumpkin, best sweet bread, most unusual vegetable, best apple pie, best jam, best salsa – even best compost. Entries may be submitted by individual residents, households, neighborhoods or groups. There is no charge to enter. All entries must be delivered to the Community Hall between 7:30 and 10:00 a.m. on September 18. To submit an entry form online, visit https://piedmont. ca.gov/community_ _ _events/ special_events/harvest_festival. Jazz Festival Local musicians will perform live jazz to conclude this year’s festival. Musicians will take the stage at noon and play until the festival ends at 4 p.m. The line-up will be announced in coming days and will be posted on https://piedmont.ca.gov/community___events/special_events/ harvest_festival. Scarecrow Alley This year’s Scarecrow Alley theme is “This is Halloween,” a nod to Danny Elfman’s score for the popular 1993 film The Nightmare Before Christmas. Families can create a scarecrow out of any material, from straw to papier mache. Scarecrows are usually created by grade school students, scout dens and troops, and frequently the Fire Department. For more information about this year’s silent auction, contact Amber Brumfiel at amberrye@ hotmail.com. Not all scarecrows are scary. These Minion scarecrows are from 2019. Art Exhibit Piedmont residents are invited to submit art for consideration. For details, contact Jane Reed by phone at (510) 654-2670.

articles.text: On Thursday, September 1, this reporter walked down memory lane at Piedmont High, his alma mater, to do an Inside the Classroom feature on Melanie McCauley’s Yearbook class. Instead of merely observing, McCauley called me to the front of the class to go over the basics of reporting, interviewing, camera operations, privacy law and caption writing. The production of the Yearbook requires its staff to be at every important school function during the year, with emphasis on taking plenty of photos and writing captions for each. I began my talk with a couple of tips on the use of the Post’s Nikon camera. The camera was passed to Sohrab “Seb” Ford to take some photos for the story. Hoping to save the future journalists from future woes, I pointed out how to change out the lens which has reverse threads and abides by “Lefty Tighty, Righty Loosey.” Another helpful tip was learning to use “Aperture Priority Mode” on the camera for preventing blurred photos when there is motion. We moved on to a discussion of California’s laws on consent to record people and “fair use” for taking photos in public. I demonstrated how we do the Question Man feature in the paper by invitPhotos by Seb Ford Reporter Jay Russell demonstrates to Piedmont High School students in Melanie McCauley’s Yearbook class how to attach a long lens to a camera. ing six students to be subjects of Question Man this week, allowing them to see how to politely, but effectively get candid answers in public. After students browsed through the paper, questions arose. “How much does this size of advertisement cost,” asked senior Ginger Gardner. “For a photo caption of a group, how many people do you need to identify by name?” asked McCauley. I explained that the Post does its best to identify everyone pictured by first and last name, but that for groups six or more, often the caption will be general and not include the names of everyone. The glaring exception is the inclusion of names of all the people pictured in the weekly Walking on Wednesdays articles. My visit ended with some irony, as I scooted aside some of the brand-new computers in the STEAM lab classroom to plug in my 1986 Brother Typewriter. Students lined up to try their hands on the archaic device. I challenged them to write one sentence each, and to keep a narrative going based upon the previous sentence. The students had a little too much fun writing about friends and the difficulty of Mr. Savage’s science courses. So much so, that when it came time for McCauley Staff Photo Melanie McCauley talks to her students about the events they will be covering for the high school yearbook this year. The Post’s Question Man, Jay Russell, asks senior Edin Lorin the Question of the Week while Yearbook students take part in a discussion.

articles.text: Ready to pick up an instrument, develop some musical ability and learn what piobaireachd means? A Beginning class on playing the bagpipe is being offered by Piedmont Adult School starting next week, September 14. The Bagpipes class is taught by long-time Adult School instructor Lynne Miller. Beginning students will learn the basics of reading music and playing bagpipes by playing a practice chanter, the preparatory instrument for bagpipes. As students progress, they will have the option of working with more advanced students. This year the class will include an introduction to piobaireachd, the classical music of the bagpipe. Separately, the Adult School is also offering a course in beginning guitar. Beginning Guitar A class in beginning guitar will be taught by Elizabeth Klute. If you have found basic guitar chords difficult to play, this class is for you. Using traditional folk songs and modified chord shapes, students will progress at their own pace to playing full chords. Basic music theory, melodic playing and improvisation will be covered. To register and for more information, visit Piedmontadultschool.org, call the Adult School office at 594-2655, or stop by the Adult School office near the entrance to Millennium High at 760 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: Storytelling is an important part of early childhood development. School is back in session and everyone is learning their math, science, language arts skills and hopefully some play. My favorite part of school has always been story time. This activity happens in the classroom at all age levels, from circle time for the littles all the way to Socratic seminars for the bigs. Storytelling is important from the very beginning of life. There is much research stating that storytelling is key for the developing brain including creativity, imagination, vocabulary and communication. This early exposure to letters, words and structure help children to read and write. Almost more importantly, storytelling and sharing aids children in telling their own stories allowing them to process and understand their own experiences, often reflecting their culture, language and history, contributing to the formation of identity. At Fairyland I watch children enjoying the stories being told at the puppet theatre. So much is manifesting in a short 15-minute show — the recognition of a story with characters, values, emotions and drama. This is evidenced by laughter, clapping, gasps and questions. As they build language The puppet show at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland. and communication, stories also spark curiosity and engage us in realities other than our own. This trip into another reality gives us valuable perspective on our own experiences. What can you do to support storytelling in your little people? • Talk a lot. For babies and toddlers, narrate what you are doing or what you will be doing and integrate voice inflection to help the story flow. • Share who you are. Tell family histories or stories illustrating who you are as a unit. • Write it down. Take dictation from your young storyteller and read it back to them. It often grows or gets clarified. • Act it out. Help young storytellers dramatize the stories they tell by adding movement. Although the structured environment of language arts in the classroom is crucial, storytelling outside of the classroom is also important. Storytelling directly impacts the development of our children, and the effects have a powerful impact on our community. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 7, 2022 Bagpipes and Guitar classes start soon at Piedmont Adult School By Jay Russell Ready to pick up an instrument, develop some musical ability and learn what piobaireachd means? A Beginning class on playing the bagpipe is being offered by Piedmont Adult School starting next week, September 14. The Bagpipes class is taught by long-time Adult School instructor Lynne Miller. Beginning students will learn the basics of reading music and playing bagpipes by playing a practice chanter, the preparatory instrument for bagpipes. As students progress, they will have the option of working with more advanced students. This year the class will include an introduction to piobaireachd, the classical music of the bagpipe. Separately, the Adult School is also offering a course in beginning guitar. Beginning Guitar A class in beginning guitar will be taught by Elizabeth Klute. If you have found basic guitar chords difficult to play, this class is for you. Using traditional folk songs and modified chord shapes, students will progress at their own pace to playing full chords. Basic music theory, melodic playing and improvisation will be covered. To register and for more information, visit Piedmontadultschool.org, call the Adult School office at 594-2655, or stop by the Adult School office near the entrance to Millennium High at 760 Magnolia Avenue. Thinking Outside the Classroom The power of storytelling By Kymberly Miller Storytelling is an important part of early childhood development. School is back in session and everyone is learning their math, science, language arts skills and hopefully some play. My favorite part of school has always been story time. This activity happens in the classroom at all age levels, from circle time for the littles all the way to Socratic seminars for the bigs. Storytelling is important from the very beginning of life. There is much research stating that storytelling is key for the developing brain including creativity, imagination, vocabulary and communication. This early exposure to letters, words and structure help children to read and write. Almost more importantly, storytelling and sharing aids children in telling their own stories allowing them to process and understand their own experiences, often reflecting their culture, language and history, contributing to the formation of identity. At Fairyland I watch children enjoying the stories being told at the puppet theatre. So much is manifesting in a short 15-minute show — the recognition of a story with characters, values, emotions and drama. This is evidenced by laughter, clapping, gasps and questions. As they build language The puppet show at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland. and communication, stories also spark curiosity and engage us in realities other than our own. This trip into another reality gives us valuable perspective on our own experiences. What can you do to support storytelling in your little people? • Talk a lot. For babies and toddlers, narrate what you are doing or what you will be doing and integrate voice inflection to help the story flow. • Share who you are. Tell family histories or stories illustrating who you are as a unit. • Write it down. Take dictation from your young storyteller and read it back to them. It often grows or gets clarified. • Act it out. Help young storytellers dramatize the stories they tell by adding movement. Although the structured environment of language arts in the classroom is crucial, storytelling outside of the classroom is also important. Storytelling directly impacts the development of our children, and the effects have a powerful impact on our community. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the poer of storytelling. Article reprinted from Piedmont Post in October 2021. articles.text: A new Piedmont High School tradition – the Great Chili CookOff – was held for the second year on Wednesday evening, August 31 in the Student Center on campus. Ten teams of students, parents, teachers and school administrators served up their best chili to a large crowd of satisfied samplers and judges. “We started cooking right after school, and the actual cook time was 60-70 minutes,” explained Guzdar. “Our teammate Jane Hempeck had a homemade chili powder on hand and we kind of eyeballed the rest. I have no idea what’s in it – it’s a secret powder,” Guzdar added. As juniors, the “Girls on Fire” will likely look to defend its title next year. Former PHS Principal Adam Littlefield created the fun event in 2019 as a fundraiser for PHS Technology. After two silent years due to Covid-19, the cookoff returned, this time as a community-building event. It included cornbread, sour cream, hot sauce and cheese as condiments for the chili. articles.text: PHS tops Mission San Jose, Clayton Valley, Newark Memorial, Cal High Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team started its season with a bang on Friday and Saturday, September 2-3, defeating four teams in the Labor Day Bash to claim the tournament title. Their victories opened with a 15-7 win over Mission San Jose on Friday, then 7-4 over Clayton Valley in the second round. They trampled Newark Memorial 13-5 in the semifinals, and then closed with a sudden-death overtime victory over California High, 10-9. Their finals victory featured rallying from a 9-6 deficit in the fourth period. George Stein scored the tying goal with 11 seconds left, and Declan Linnane scored the game-winner with 2:47 left in overtime. “It comes down to grit and determination. The entire team showed that,” said head coach Rik Krumins. “The fourth game in a tournament is always challenging physically. There were a lot of things not going on our way in the beginning of the game, but they really turned it around and stuck to the game plan as we made adjustments. Cal High played a press and we made adjustments late in the second. Things started turning around in the fourth quarter,” he said. Linnane was named tournament’s Most Valuable Player after scoring nine goals, four assists, and four steals. Peter Krumins and George Stein also earned first-team all-tournament honors. “They were all interchangeable and Declan really started taking over the finals game. Our motion on offense was on point; we were driving in the right position and were making the correct passes. We talked a lot about doing the little things to become successful, and the whole team stepped up to do them,” added Krumins. 10-9 finals win over Cal High Quincy Scherman scored the opening goal after nearly four minutes of action, but Cal High took the lead with a pair of goals in the final minute of the first quarter, including one as the buzzer sounded at the quarter’s end. In the second quarter, Cal High went ahead 3-1 after drawing a man-advantage and was up 4-1 with 3:37 to play. Finn Burke made it 4-2 for PHS but Cal High took a 5-2 lead by halftime. Cal High extended its lead to 6-2 two minutes into the third period, and Stein chipped away at the lead to 6-3 after PHS drew a penalty with 4:54 to go. The Grizzlies answered with a goal a minute later, but Krumins scored for 7-4 with 2:31 remaining. Krumins scored again less than a minute later for a 7-5 score, but Staff Photo Declan Linnane earned the tournament Most Valuable Player award. Photo by Nancy Brahm George Stein earned first-team all-tournament honors. Cal High scored against 15 seconds later at 1:30. Stein scored after 13 seconds for 8-6, but Cal High put one in with 30 seconds on the clock to retain a 9-6 lead heading into the final period. In the final period, Piedmont’s comeback began when Linnane netted one with 5:06 remaining. With 2:30 left, Stein scored with a man-advantage to make it 9-8. And then with just 11 seconds on the clock, PHS drew another penalty, allowing Stein to tie the match at 9-9. Piedmont won the sprint at the start of the three-minute sudden-death overtime and quickly called a timeout. Coach Krumins drew up a play, and after nine seconds, Linnane scored the game-winner by sending a lob over the goalie’s head. Final stats: Linnane scored three goals and one steal. Stein had three goals and two assists. Krumins scored twice. Scherman and Burke had individual goals. 13-5 over Newark Memorial In the semifinals, Piedmont closed the first quarter up 4-1 and went into halftime with a 5-2 lead. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team lost its season-opener 10-5 loss at Newark Memorial to start its season on Tuesday, August 30. After three minutes without any goals, Newark netted a shot with 3:58 to go in the first quarter. Annika Nillson had a shot ring off of the crossbar for Piedmont, but it broke a counter attack goal for the Cougars, 2-0 in the later minutes. Piedmont answered with a goal in the closing seconds when gaining a player-advantage, allowing Rosie Feldman to score with 4:22, making it 9-5. Newark tacked on one more in the closing minutes. Final stats: Feldman had a goal and two assists. Dando had two goals and an assist. Nillson and Melian had individual goals. Burke had one assist in her varsity debut. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team swept Hayward 3-0 on Wednesday, August 31 by scores of 25-6, 25-11, 25-13. It marked their fifth victory after winning four matches the previous week in a tournament in Morro Bay. There’s a clear difference in the attacking mindset in this year’s team. “Our focus right now is utilizing every opportunity from every player. We’ve been working on back row attacks, quick balls outside, right side, and the middle. Nothing is going to be vanilla,” said coach Maria Cardenas. Piedmont’s kills have clear velocity on them, another big change from the previous season. Cardenas’ message to the team through their offseason training has been to hit the ball as hard as possible. “I don’t care if it hits the wall or breaks a window all the way up in the ceiling. I want them ripping the ball; I want them fast and I want them to hit it hard. I want them to continue working on that fast-paced ball,” explained Cardenas. Middle hitter Bree DeYoung reiterated that they’ve been working on putting more pace on their shots, while also keeping successful defensive rotation to allow their offense to have more attempts. “We’ve just working on getting balls faster and quicker to our hitters. We’ve worked on our offense as well as our defense; having both sides play well has really helped us,” said DeYoung. There is also a clear fluid style of play for the Highlanders with successful fakes and attacks at the net. “We want to be up in the air and timing our balls better so we can see the court. We’ve been working on getting every player more trick plays. We middles like to have shots closer to the net, but when we switch to the right side, we’ll cross and the middle will go hit a slide,” added DeYoung. Game Recap The Highlanders opened the match with a resounding 25-6 victory in the first set, after jumping in front 8-1. With the score at 10-6, Piedmont reeled off 15 straight points to win the set, which included two aces by Sadie Town and kills by Town, Tara Kothari, Eden Lorin, and Molly Wagener. In the second set, a 25-11 win, PHS and Hayward traded points until the Highlanders held a 7-5 lead. From there, Piedmont scored 12 of the next 13 points to jump ahead 19-8. They closed out Bree DeYoung goes up for a spike against Hayward. Staff Photos Sadie Town makes a kill against the Farmers. the next six points with two kills by Maddy Mullin, and individual spikes by DeYoung and Klara Zietlow. The third 25-13 win, 25-13, started with Piedmont taking a 12-1 lead. Hayward battled to make it 22-13 with four straight points, but Piedmont closed with a nice block by Elena Stevens, a kill by Shelby Cavenaugh, and a Hayward error for the final point. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-3) plays at Skyline HS in Oakland today, Wednesday, September 7 at 6:30 p.m. Klara Zietlow in Piedmont’s game with Hayward.

articles.text: Piedmont’s varsity football team suffered a 42-0 shutout loss to the visiting Del Norte Warriors last Friday, September 2 at Witter Field. Del Norte from Crescent City is currently among the topranked Division 4 teams in the North Coast Section after reaching last year’s NCS Finals as a Div. 5 (small enrollment) team. Piedmont will also play as a Div. 5 team in non-conference play this year. “Everything is a learning experience,” said first=year coach Jordan Seiden. “A loss is a loss, but I just hope we learn and grow. We have to work a little bit harder and a little bit more every time,” said The lopsided loss provided Piedmont with a look at a top team. Del Norte’s roster includes 17 seniors and 11 juniors. PHS has only 22 players – nine seniors, five juniors, and eight sophomores. “We’re a young team and we have to learn to win like that. They were a senior heavy team and we’re a sophomore-heavy team. In a couple more years, we’ll be in a similar position with experience. I don’t think they are 42 points better, and I still think we’re a very athletic team. We have to keep a high amount of effort in every single play,” said Seiden. Piedmont will dust itself off and look ahead to playing on the road 200 miles away at North Tahoe High School in Tahoe City. North Tahoe is coming off a 26-14 loss to Quincy on August 26. articles.text: Highlanders sweep Arroyo 7-0, lose 8-1 to Miramonte Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team split its opening two matches of the season, losing 8-1 to non-league opponent Miramonte in Orinda on Tuesday, August 30, and shutting out league opponent arroyo 7-0 the following day. “We lost to Miramonte. They always have a strong team. “We lost to them 7-2 last year,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. ‘Then we swept Arroyo 7-0. The match was very one- sided with all of our matches won in decisive, straight sets.” 7-0 win over Arroyo Carolina Romanczuk started the day with a 6-0, 6-0 win at No. 3 singles. Asha Byers and Abigail Call followed with a 6-2, 6-1 win at No. 3 doubles. The freshman combination Arianna Kortum and Kate Jumper won handily at No. 2 doubles, 6-0, 6-4, while Talia Blumberg won 6-2, 6-1 at No. 4 singles. At No. 1 singles was Anne Jumper, won easily, 6-0, 6-1. Annika Gilliland won by the same score at No. 2 singles, and seniors Mara LaForte and Sophia Kalamas, in their first time as doubles partners, won at No. 1 doubles, 6-2, 6-1. “It was nice to have Talia Blumberg who hadn’t seen any action yet, winning at singles. Anika Gilliland started regaining her form as well. Our doubles saw the good playing and debut as a team of two of our seniors: Mara LaForte and Sophia Kalamas. They won handily,” said Landes. 8-1 loss to Miramonte Piedmont played nine matches with the Matadors, a Division 1 school. The only win on the afternoon was Romanczuk at No. 6 singles in a heated three-set match, 7-5, 2-6, 13-11. Piedmont’s No. 1 starter Tanya Kononova lost a razor-thin match in three sets, 6-3, 3-6, 11-9. Anne Jumper at No. 2 lost 6-2, 6-0. At No. 3, LaForte, lost in two sets, 6-0, 6-3. Michaela Bini at No. 4 and No. 5 Gilliland both lost by the same score. In doubles, Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon lost 7-6 (6-4), 6-2, Kortum and Kate Staff Photos Anne Jumper played at No. 1 singles against Arroyo, winning 6-0, 6-1. Carolina Romanczuk is currently undefeated with wins over Miramonte and Arroyo. Jumper lost 6-3, 6-0 at No. 2, and Kalamas and Ellie Broscow lost 6-4, 6-3 at No. 3. “Carolina Romanczuk got our sole victory winning 13-11 in the tiebreak. She pulled it out against a good opponent and a tough crowd. Our doubles teams all played well but lost in straight sets against some very good teams,” said Landes. articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team lost 35-2 to visiting Del Norte on September 2. Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team was knocked down by Del Norte 35-2 at Witter Field in the second game of the season on Friday, September 2. Del Norte, from Crescent City in far northern California, dominated early and often with four touchdowns in the first half Athletic Director Bradley Smet, who has taken over as JV coach, commented that Piedmont needed to show more physicality in tackles and blocks to prevent mistakes. “One of the things that we really need to work on next week is our overall physicality and staying lower. Our guys were staying straight up and down and not able to block and tackle properly. That’s why we saw they missed so many tackles,” he said. Piedmont’s defense showed some spirit by preventing a touchdown in the third quarter by tracking down a Del Norte running back after he had sprinted 60 yards downfield. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s offense found some success when quarterback Brandon Dicke threw a 32-yard pass to receiver Vincent Arbit. Photos by Sophie Hess Dash Water Worthen turns a reception upfield. However, PHS was eventually stopped when Del Norte intercepted the ball on the one-yard line. Piedmont’s only points came near the end of game when Albert Bellingrath sacked the Del Norte quarterback in the end zone for a safety. “We didn’t have a whole lot of success in the first half,” said Smet. “It was really good to see our kids coming back when we were already down by 28 points, still fighting, still trying to work hard. Not giving up was definitely good to see.” NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) goes on the road this weekend to Tahoe City to take on North Tahoe High School on Saturday, September 10 in Tahoe City at 10:00 a.m. The Scots’ offense struggled with consistency against an aggressive Del Norte defense.
articles.title: JV team loses to Del Norte

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ golf team begins its season this week, playing a tri-match with Castro Valley and San Leandro at Redwood Canyon Golf Course in Castro Valley on Thursday, September 8. “Our women’s varsity golf team is back in action. pages.text: Wednesday, September 7, 2022 13 JV team loses to Del Norte Piedmont’s JV football team lost 35-2 to visiting Del Norte on September 2. By Sophie Hess Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team was knocked down by Del Norte 35-2 at Witter Field in the second game of the season on Friday, September 2. Del Norte, from Crescent City in far northern California, dominated early and often with four touchdowns in the first half Athletic Director Bradley Smet, who has taken over as JV coach, commented that Piedmont needed to show more physicality in tackles and blocks to prevent mistakes. “One of the things that we really need to work on next week is our overall physicality and staying lower. Our guys were staying straight up and down and not able to block and tackle properly. That’s why we saw they missed so many tackles,” he said. Piedmont’s defense showed some spirit by preventing a touchdown in the third quarter by tracking down a Del Norte running back after he had sprinted 60 yards downfield. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s offense found some success when quarterback Brandon Dicke threw a 32-yard pass to receiver Vincent Arbit. Photos by Sophie Hess Dash Water Worthen turns a reception upfield. However, PHS was eventually stopped when Del Norte intercepted the ball on the one-yard line. Piedmont’s only points came near the end of game when Albert Bellingrath sacked the Del Norte quarterback in the end zone for a safety. “We didn’t have a whole lot of success in the first half,” said Smet. “It was really good to see our kids coming back when we were already down by 28 points, still fighting, still trying to work hard. Not giving up was definitely good to see.” NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) goes on the road this weekend to Tahoe City to take on North Tahoe High School on Saturday, September 10 in Tahoe City at 10:00 a.m. The Scots’ offense struggled with consistency against an aggressive Del Norte defense.
