articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents the world premiere of Berkeley composer Johns Adams’ latest opera, Antony and Cleopatra, on September 10. Significantly it was chosen to open the company’s 100th season and was commissioned by the San Francisco Opera for its centennial. Amina Edris, an Egyptian lyric soprano, will sing the lead role of Cleopatra, with Canadian bass-baritone Gerald Finley as Antony. The cast also includes Paul Appleby, Alfred Walker, Elizabeth DeShong, Brenton Ryan, Taylor Raven, Hadleigh Adams, Gabrielle Beteag, Timothy Murray and Bay Area favorite Philip Skinner. articles.text: The American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749-2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ passengers/.
articles.title: ACT premieres Passengers on September 15

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, now celebrating its 10th anniversary, returns to Piedmont for a concert on Saturday, September 17 at 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon and Clio Tilton will perform a program to include Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, op. 132, Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465, and Caroline Shaw’s “Valencia”. For tickets click on: https://bit. ly/3TpKMUZ. Beethoven’s opus 132 string quartet is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Op. 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, the San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, the Oakland Symphony and many others. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau and Jodi Levitz. For more information see: www.chambermusicsocietysf.org.
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF to perform concert in Piedmont Sept. 17

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is showing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on the book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 ®

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notable in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more. Artist Carlos Villa

Sunday, September 18, 3:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert celebrating the rich colors of Autumn Leaves with a selection of ballads, swing and jazz blues arrangements, nodding along the way to honor Mexican Independence Day with two special medleys. articles.text: Natalie Portman stars in Black Swan. Black Swan is an intense, gripping psychodrama that moves along a precipice between the transcendent art of ballet and a dark decent into madness. The performances are astonishingly good. First, ballet, no matter its patina of delicacy and seemingly fragile beauty, composed of movement to music that stirs and inspires, is also a sport practiced by athletes who give new meaning to the concepts of preparation, brutally hard work, and unflinching commitment. It is this aching sacrifice that is, ultimately, at the center of Black Swan. A young woman, Nina Sayers (Natalie Portman), has been insulated most of her life by the constraints of ballet and by a controlling, domineering mother, Erica (Barbara Hershey). To her astonishment, she is cast as the prima ballerina in the dual role of the black swan (Odile) and the white swan (Odette) in Swan Lake. The role is an obvious metaphor for this young woman, who is naïve, protected, talented, and now challenged by the Director, Thomas Leroy (Vincent Cassel), to explore her dark side, to find the visceral and the real in the role of Odile. When she dances as the white swan she is controlled perfection. But it’s when she dances as the black swan that she is bound by restraint and even fear. Great art, Leroy tells her, means letting go. And so Nina’s metamorphosis begins and the film moves incrementally into layers of brilliant, wrenching dysfunction. What is real and what is delusional becomes increasingly blurred as she descends into a world of such pressure that her ability to cope begins to fray. Hers is a brittle soul in a world that can be harsh; red flags of overwhelming anxiety and madness ignored in the name of an enchanted story about a woman transformed into a swan by a mad sorcerer, a tale elevated to the sublime by the music of Tchaikovsky. But this film is more than a deliberative, psychological study of a compelling, fragmenting character. Black Swan is, at times, unhinged, yet also lovely and compelling. Black Swan. Directed by Darren Aronofsky. Starring Natalie Portman, Mila Kunis, Barbara Hershey, Winona Ryder and Vincent Cassel. 1 hr., 48 min, Rated R. Released in 2010. articles.text: In 1979, James Baldwin, noted author, playwright and essayist, sent a detailed proposal to his agent – some 30 pages long – for a book he titled Remember This House. It was a work of nonfiction that was intended to connect three men: Malcom X, Martin Luther King, and Medgar Evers. Less than 10 years later (1987), Baldwin died, never having written more that those 30 pages. It proved to be, in its own right, a powerful essay on race. Director Raoul Peck used those pages (and some notes and essays) to craft not a biographical documentary about Baldwin, but instead a film about race using Baldwin’s transcendent words. The content was drawn from interviews on television and in print and from countless college podiums and used to frame in I am Not Your Negro an issue that has resisted resolution since the first slaves were brought to Jamestown in 1619. Our national identity is embedded in our response to what has been referred to by some scholars as a “Peculiar Institution,” which, as Baldwin explains, is part of our nation’s desire to create a fantasy that is only applicable to one segment of society, and not to all. The denial of what was perpetrated for three centuries continues to haunt us, a truth that Baldwin returns to time after time in this powerful film. He refers to our unwillingness to grapple with the impact of slavery as our “moral monster,” beginning not only with the antebellum South, but during the decades following the Civil War when segregation and Jim Crow were codified. The war was over, the North won, but the attitudes toward black people were deeply and intractably entrenched. Peck includes as part of the film, stark black and white photos of “Negroes,” a word that Baldwin uses repeatedly, who were lynched with impunity, to include children and men as well as women. What is chilling to the core are the looks on the faces of the men and women who were present at those hangings and bore witness. Their faces flash with a rictus smile, the rising tide of violence and death seemingly irresistible, something that refuses to touch their souls. Peck also reveals that same look, that same rage in the faces of men and women, in footage captured when schools in the South were desegregated. We see a single girl, surrounded by state marshals, making a harrowing journey from the street to the doors of the school building, her bravery beyond description. She is reviled and denigrated and threatened and yet she puts one tentative foot in front of the other. The faces of the protesting crowds are twisted with a hatred that could only be born out of the same impulses that killed Dr. King and Evers, a murderous resistance to our constitutional commitment to civil rights, tempered by the aspirational belief that every person should be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin. It is a concept so elegant and so profound that its beauty is often missed by large segments of society. The national truth is that we have yet to make that journey toward equality, at least not fully. Peck includes contemporary footage of Ferguson, Mo., demonstrating that America’s social fabric continues to be frayed, rooted in slavery. Slavery and all that followed, like a stone dropped into a wide pond, continues to be felt as the ripples move ever outward in concentric circles. The harm done continues. As an aside, James Baldwin, for reasons never fully explored in I am Not Your Negro, chose to leave America and reside in France. But as the Civil Rights Movement began to take form, as men such as Martin Luther King took on its purpose and weight, Baldwin felt its gravitational pull and returned, if only to bear witness to all that was occurring in America as this momentous struggle coalesced. And continues to this day. I am Not Your Negro. Documentary. Directed by Raoul Peck. Narrated by Samuel L. Jackson. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Netflix/Prime.

articles.text: Filmmaking technology has evolved to the point that Kong indeed now looks like the real deal. First, I have to acknowledge that I resisted screening Kong: Skull Island. Look up “reboot” in the dictionary and you will find Kong (1933, 1976, and 2005). movie theaters, you have sat in a large dark room and looked into the massive, rheumy brown-gold eyes of Kong. You’ve heard his roar, looked into his pink cavernous mouth and took note of those massive canines. And not to forget his incredible strength. Regarding Kong (1933, et al.), all that has changed (other than the narrative, which has been tweaked) is filmmaking technology that has evolved to the point that Kong indeed now looks like the real deal. This incarnation has a different hook, which is actually interesting. It takes place as the Vietnam War is coming to a close. A scientist convinces a senator to send an expedition into the farthest reaches of the South Pacific in search of an uncharted island. Hence, a quasi-military scientific group is formed, consisting of almost a dozen helicopters and a mixed group of soldiers and civilians, to include a war photographer, Mason Weaver (Brie Larson) and a mercenary, James Conrad (Tom Huddleston). This set up lasts some 40 minutes as the choppers skim the tree-tops of this never before seen island. Or so they assume. Suddenly (that’s the operative word for this film), out of the haze they are confronted with Kong and it’s no contest. The choppers are helpless and everyone is in serious harm’s way. Let the games begin. And whatever exposition is delivered at the start of the movie, well that was it. What follows is one very intense escape from Kong Island. It’s all one long, adrenalin-inducing chase across an island where creatures, to include spiders and water buffalo, lizards and birds, are the size of motels. Nothing is as it should be, starting, of course, with Kong. To his credit, what director Vogt-Roberts decides to do make sure that Kong: Skull Island is fun – a real ride. It becomes a long riff on very scary creatures that are intent on snacking on any member of the group that happens to drift away from the others. Of course, there are some subplots that never break the focus of the film. For example, chemistry between Weaver and Conrad is suggested. But there isn’t much time for even a hug. I think they hold hands in a moment of panic, but that’s it. This is about survival, and each scene is, well, breathtaking in a kind of basic way – can they get out of this without too much damage being done? But there is also a Conradian Heart of Darkness aspect to the story (Huddleston/Conrad); even shades of Apocalypse Now are present. (I kept waiting for someone to say they loved the smell of napalm early in the morning.) When the credits rolled at the end, I was glad I saw it. I love movies and I knew this was a big screen film and would not translate to the smaller screen. Kong is after all Kong, and he’s way larger than life. Kong: Skull Island. Directed by Jordan Vogt-Roberts. Starring Brie Larson, Tom Huddleston and Samuel L. Jackson. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Prime/ HBO Max/Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Dreamworks animation’s Turbo. Turbo is a Dreamworks animated feature film, ideal for 7-year-olds. It tells the story of a suburban tomato garden snail named Theo (or Turbo) who considers his life grindingly dull. He is, however, obsessed with the idea of speed. In fact he yearns to be the world’s greatest racer. No surprise, the snails who also live in the garden, a place called the Plant, ridicule Theo when he talks of going faster, especially when he tells them that his hero is Guy Gagné (Bill Harder), an arrogant French world class racer. Despite the doubts of his fellow mollusks, Theo is convinced he will one day compete in the Indianapolis 500, hear the roar of a crowd cheering him on (he’s watched the race on a dusty TV tucked away in a garage), and he’ll do this competing against real human drivers. But not now. Today he is feeling blue after being repeatedly discouraged by his good friend Chet (Paul Giamatti), and almost being run over by a lawn mower. Theo slowly makes his way to a nearby freeway, hoping to watch the cars speeding by. He feels the need for speed. What he’s not prepared for is to be sucked into the engine of a Camaro, a muscle car. Due to this freakish accident, he is saturated in nitrous oxide, which transforms him, to his immense surprise, into a snail with amazing speed akin to the fast and furious. Chet is filled with disbelief until he is snatched by a passing crow but is rescued by Theo who uses his newfound unexpected speed. As a result, the two bros end up in a shopping mall in Van Nuys where they meet a cohort of streetwise snails, voiced by Samuel L. Jackson, Maya Rudolph, Snoop Dogg, Ben Schwartz, and Mike Bell. The gang practices engaging in slowmo races around a very small track in the Starlight Plaza. Theo also gets the help of Tito Lopez and his brother Angelo (Luis Guzman), both humans, who have a food truck at the mall. They get the idea that they might get some publicity for Dos Bros Tacos if Theo can only win the 500. And so, escargot meets street racers – and they’re off to the competition. Keep in mind that the snails can talk to one another but can’t speak to humans. It will take the extraordinary imaginations of the young audience to appreciate a snail in a car race. But the kids will be entertained by Theo, aka Turbo. Turbo. Directed by David Soren. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Ryan Reynolds, Paul Giamatti, Michael Pena. Rated PG. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Prime/peacock/ apple tv.

Let the games begin. And whatever exposition is delivered at the start of the movie, well that was it. What follows is one very intense escape from Kong Island. It’s all one long, adrenalin-inducing chase across an island where creatures, to include spiders and water buffalo, lizards and birds, are the size of motels. Nothing is as it should be, starting, of course, with Kong. To his credit, what director Vogt-Roberts decides to do make sure that Kong: Skull Island is fun – a real ride. It becomes a long riff on very scary creatures that are intent on snacking on any member of the group that happens to drift away from the others. Of course, there are some subplots that never break the focus of the film. For example, chemistry between Weaver and Conrad is suggested. But there isn’t much time for even a hug. I think they hold hands in a moment of panic, but that’s it. This is about survival, and each scene is, well, breathtaking in a kind of basic way – can they get out of this without too much damage being done? But there is also a Conradian Heart of Darkness aspect to the story (Huddleston/Conrad); even shades of Apocalypse Now are present. (I kept waiting for someone to say they loved the smell of napalm early in the morning.) When the credits rolled at the end, I was glad I saw it. I love movies and I knew this was a big screen film and would not translate to the smaller screen. Kong is after all Kong, and he’s way larger than life. Kong: Skull Island. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 7, 2022 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers continue to explore million dollar homes By Dick Carter On August 24 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed looking at some beautiful homes for sale in Piedmont. There were eight homes with listing prices ranging from $2,450,000 to $18,500,000 that the group wanted to see, but they ran out of time and could only walk to five of them. One week later, August 31, the group took a look at the remaining three houses. The first was 317 Sea View Avenue. On the way they observed a Caterpillar land mover carving a hole in the steep hillside in front of a house on Crocker Avenue at the intersection of Wildwood. The house was designed by Albert Farr and built in 1906. At that time a garage was not considered a necessity, and one was not built for the house. Now, 116 years later, that is changing. As the walkers stopped to look, the contractor explained that it is common today for owners of old homes to make a cut in their front yards in order to add a garage. Proceeding past Crocker Park, the group turned onto Sea View and admired the always beautiful flowers in the yard of the Reich family. The yellow dahlias were particularly wonderful. Wednesday Walkers pause for a photo in front of 199 Lafayette Avenue. Pictured are: Larry Olsen Nancy Olsen, Jim Kellogg, Sarah Johnson, Pat Keller, Matt Gerhardt, Ann Quinby, Ian Morgan, Elizabeth Richter, Lisa Euphrat, Phil Witte, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Tally, Charlene Louie, Lois Price, Mary Hedley, Meghan Bennett, Albert Chen, Nadine Guffanti, Alan Goldhammer, Mike Henn, Jim Kuo, Rob Smith, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Bob Wong, Christen Calliste, Edith Lee, Cheryl Stanton, Peter Persoff, Alicia Rivera, Emma Sangil with K-9 best friend Olive, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Garrett Clifford. We Are Always Accepting New Patients! The group crossed La Salle Avenue and came to 317 Sea View, a 3- bedroom, 3-bath 1,952 square foot home designed by Sidney B. Newsom and built in 1914. This is the first time in 45 years the home is on the market and is listed at $2,450,000. The walkers continued up Sea View and crossed the Oakland-Piedmont city line, where the street becomes Ashmount Avenue. The story was shared of how the city of Piedmont was incorporated with the state in 1907, and its border was geographically defined based on a sewer map. This map was all that was available for the city’s founding fathers, and they used it to beat the city of Oakland’s attempt to annex Piedmont. This sewer map is why Piedmont’s boundary is often irregular with split parcel homes. The group turned on Mandana Boulevard and were quickly back in Piedmont on Crocker Avenue. Another quick left turn put the walkers on La Salle Avenue looking for their next house, 35 Muir Avenue. The Tudor style house was built in 1932 with 5,899 square feet, 5 bedrooms, and 5 bathrooms, with a classic half-timbered façade, a slate roof and an ornamental chimney. The next stop was just up the street at 256 La Salle, a 4-bedroom, 3-bathroom house built in 1922 with 3,765 square feet and in a Spanish Mediterranean design. The home has great views of San Francisco and is listed for $3,595,000. The last stop on the tour was further up La Salle as it becomes Lafayette Avenue. 199 Lafayette is a 3-bedroom/5-bath, 4,583 square foot home, built on .4 acres in 1915. It has views of the Golden Gate Bridge, a pool with a Jacuzzi, and a guest house, and is listed for $5,950,000, The group had completed their walking tour of all the homes on their list, and it was time to get back to their starting point in the city center. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Part 2 of a 2-part series loads of dark fruit and a touch or leather. Plenty of tannins on the finish ensure that this wine has a long life ahead of it. In my last column I shared some of the winning wines from the Family Winemakers of California tasting held in Oakland. This week finishes coverage of this outstanding event with another batch of winners. On August 21 the Family Winemakers of California held their first ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/ medium size operations making under 10,000 cases per year. As I meandered through the table-filled venue, I focused on small wineries with which I was unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. But the following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. They are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines in California are created in small, out of the way places by wineries that are fueled by family love and devotion. • 2020 Ca’ Momi Cabernet Sauvignon This Napa Valley Cabernet opens with notes of black cherries, currants plus hints of herbs and dusty soil. Medium to full-bodied, the palate delivers an appealing black fruit mélange with approachable, chewy tannins and a pepper and herbs-laced finish. • 2020 Field Chardonnay Russian River Valley Field has produced a delicious style of Chardonnay with hints of peach, pineapple and citrus blossom. This medium to full-bodied Chardonnay has terrific acidity, to go with the apple and pear fruit and a long finish. A well-balanced wine that is a role model of what California Chardonnay should be. • 2019 Noria Pinot Noir Valentine Vineyard The fruit for this lovely wine comes from the Russian River AVA. Pale to medium purple colored, it smells of black and red cherries, nutmeg and cinnamon followed by nuances of violets, chocolate and earth. Medium bodied on the palate, it is wonderfully elegant and well-poised with effortlessly fragrant red fruit and a long, intense finish. • Berghold Petite Sirah This Petite Sirah hails from the Sierra Nevada foothills. It is dark and brooding with aromas of plums and blackberries. In the mouth it is full-bodied and luscious with boat- • 2018 Lava Cap Petite Sirah Lava Cap is a 40-year-old winery located in the Sierra Foothills blessed with volcanic soils. Their Petite Sirah reveals classic aromas of blueberries, blackberries, smoky oak and earth. Very full-bodied it is packed with dark fruit flavors and a tannic finish. This wine should improve in the cellar for up to two decades. • 2018 Prager “Royal Escort” Port Prager has long been one of the only California wineries specializing in port. The grapes come from a Petite Sirah vineyard in St. Helena. It is made in what in Portugal is called “vintage style” – the biggest, most robust of the ports. It has a beautiful, extravagant bouquet with copious black fruit, spice and hints of menthol and orange rind that unfold wonderfully in the glass. The palate is beautifully balanced with velvety smooth tannins, copious black fruit with a harmonious finish that is a decadent delight. • 2018 Peche Merle Pinot Noir Laguna de Santa Rosa This Russian River Pinot has a classic nose of cherries and cranberries with notes of cola, tea leaves and flowers. Light to medium-bodied, it fills the mouth with warm luscious strawberry jam notes with an integrated vein of baking spice framed by very finely grained tannins and juicy, mouth-watering acidity, finishing long and spicy.
articles.title: Family Winemakers host tasting in Oakland

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Peaches and Cream Cake is a great way to cool down during the summer. This is my version of a German-style peach kuchen, written on a 3 x 5 inch recipe card in a penmanship style I abandoned decades ago. All to say, I no longer recall the origin of it to give proper acknowledgement. Whilst we are into September, it’s still officially “summer” for a couple more weeks. The farmers at the market say they will likely be harvesting late-crop peach varieties until early October, so there’s time to give this a try. Later you can easily swap out the peaches for another fruit – figs, plums, even apples and pears if this recipe moves you into autumnal fruits. This version yields a soft, tender cake with a soft topping bursting with fruit flavor. There’s a two-stage baking process; first the cake layer, then you take it out briefly to add the cream and fruit layer. The second bake time is only 15 minutes, so if you substitute a denser fruit like apples or pears, you may want to give them a brief sauté in a couple tablespoons of butter, sugar, and warming spices (cinnamon, ginger, or nutmeg), then letting them cool slightly before arranging them on the cake. articles.text: A History Fair will be held from 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. this Saturday, September 10, at the historic Camron-Stanford House at 1418 Lakeside Drive in Oakland. More than 20 Bay Area history-centered organizations and museums will participate. Each organization will have a booth for people to learn more about how to connect to the past. Browse sample exhibits, engage in fun activities, and get a sneak peek at upcoming events. Participating organizations include Peralta Hacienda, USS Hornet Museum, West Oakland Mural Project/Women of the Black Panther Party, and the Friends of Oakland Public Library. Many know the Camron-Stanford House by sight for its proximity to Lake Merritt and to the Main Library across the street. It was built in 1876 and is the last of the beautiful Victorian mansions that once surrounded the lake. By Deborah Quok This is my version of a German-style peach kuchen, written on a 3 x 5 inch recipe card in a penmanship style I abandoned decades ago. All to say, I no longer recall the origin of it to give proper acknowledgement. Whilst we are into September, it’s still officially “summer” for a couple more weeks. The farmers at the market say they will likely be harvesting late-crop peach varieties until early October, so there’s time to give this a try. Later you can easily swap out the peaches for another fruit – figs, plums, even apples and pears if this recipe moves you into autumnal fruits. This version yields a soft, tender cake with a soft topping bursting with fruit flavor. There’s a two-stage baking process; first the cake layer, then you take it out briefly to add the cream and fruit layer. The second bake time is only 15 minutes, so if you substitute a denser fruit like apples or pears, you may want to give them a brief sauté in a couple tablespoons of butter, sugar, and warming spices (cinnamon, ginger, or nutmeg), then letting them cool slightly before arranging them on the cake. Peaches and Cream Cake Makes one 9-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the cake: • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 1 Tablespoon baking powder • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 1 extra-large egg, slightly beaten • 1/2 cup whole milk • 1/3 cup unsalted butter, melted Thoroughly butter a 9-inch square baking pan, or line with parchment paper if you plan to lift the entire cake out of the pan for serving presentation. Use two sheets of parchment paper, placed crosswise in the pan with plenty hanging over the top to easily lift out the cake. Place an oven rack in the center position and preheat the oven to 350° F. In a medium mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, 1/4 cup granulated sugar, baking powder and salt. In a small bowl, combine the first beaten egg, milk, and melted butter. Add the wet mixture to the flour mixture and mix until just combined with no streaks of flour showing. But don’t over mix. Spread this batter evenly into the prepared 9-inch pan and bake for 15 minutes. Meanwhile, prepare the topping by adding the remaining beaten egg, 1/4 – 1/3 cup of granulated sugar, and sour cream together in a small bowl. Mix well. Slice the peaches and set aside. After the initial 15 minutes, remove the partially baked cake from the oven and set on a heatproof surface. Spread the sour cream mixture evenly over the cake then arrange the peaches in a single layer. Sprinkle with cinnamon. Return to the 350° F oven and continue baking for another 15 minutes. Cake is done when a toothpick inserted in the center of the cake comes out clean. Do not overbake. Serve warm or chilled. Camron-Stanford House to host History Fair this Saturday. articles.text: Mary Wood, a longtime member of the Piedmont community passed away on August 29, 2022 with loved ones by her side. Born Mary Simmonette Traude on October 1,1941, she was the daughter of Kenneth and Sara Traude of Villapark, Illinois. Mary moved to Alameda at age 3 and has been a California girl ever since. She attended Alameda High School and the University of California at Berkeley. While at Cal she met Edwin “Ned” Wood, whom she married on December 15, 1962. He claims it was love at first sight. They have resided in Piedmont for over 55 years. During Ned’s army duty, they were stationed in El Paso, Texas where Ned Junior was born. After returning to California, they welcomed their daughter Sally Thayer. Mary had a gift for making things beautiful, whether as a decorator, antique dealer, floral designer, gardener or a photographer. Her talents brought joy to many. She was amazing at taking single items, putting them together, and creating beauty. Her home and her garden were her sanctuary and those who had a chance to visit were in for a treat. In recent years, Mary became an avid bridge player, playing several times a week with in Africa, a sailing trip to the Galapagos or a trip to see grizzlies or polar bears, she was in heaven among all creatures big and small. The hummingbirds and squirrels who were fed daily on her porch could not have had a sweeter friend. Above all, Mary was a special friend to many, a wonderful wife and mother, and the perfect “gammie’ to her four beautiful grand-babies. Her grandchildren will forever have memories of multiple trips to Stinson Beach, the great K-L fishing trip, and their one-on-one trips with Gammie and Papa while in middle school. Mary is survived by Ned, her loving husband of 59 years, her son Ned Jr. and daughter in law Kelly, and her grandchildren Sam, Jane (Lane Karney), Jed and Jack Wood. She is predeceased by her beloved daughter Sally, her father and mother and many pups. A celebration of Mary’s life will be held at the Claremont Country Club on Sunday, September 25 from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests memorial donations in Mary’s name to: National Wildlife Federation (nwf.org), Piedmont Garden Club, or the charity of your choice. Mary was a longtime member of the Piedmont Garden Club, where she held various board positions. She was certified to judge in both the horticulture and photography categories and traveled throughout the U.S. judging at Garden Clubs of America events. articles.text: A memorial service will be held at 11 a.m. this Saturday, September 10, for Ernest Knell at St. John’s Episcopal Church, 1707 Gouldin Road in Montclair. The longtime Music Director and organist at the church, died on March 14, 2020. The memorial was delayed due to Covid-19. Ernest Fredrik Knell 1942 - 2020 Mr. Knell’s musical career spanned several increasingly responsible roles at the San Francisco Opera, including that of Associate Chorus Master. He served for 25 years as Minister of Music at St. John’s Episcopal Church in Oakland and he organized the Berkeley Bach Cantata Group, which met bimonthly over 30 years to read through the great composer’s many choral works. From time to time he conducted operas for local companies including Sacramento Opera, West Bay Opera, North Bay Opera, Pacific Repertory Opera, and West Edge Opera (formerly Berkeley Opera). Ernest is survived by his wife, Julianne Booth Knell, his daughters Sarah Booth Betts and Emily Knell Spaeth, their spouses Jonathan Betts and Shaffer Spaeth, his granddaughter Sadie Caroline Spaeth, grandsons Henry Arthur Spaeth and Theodore Corwin Betts, and his beloved Welsh Springer Spaniels Merywen and Briar Rose. For more about Ernest’s rich and accomplished life, see an extended obituary at https:// www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/ sfgate/name/ernest-knell-obituary?id=2152746. Members of the San Francisco Opera Chorus, the Berkeley Bach Ernest Knell, longtime Music Director at St. John’s Episcopal Church in Montclair. Cantata Group, and the Chancel Choir of St. John’s will provide the service music at the upcoming memorial service. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 7, 2022 Obituary Mary Wood dies on August 29 Mary Wood, a longtime member of the Piedmont community passed away on August 29, 2022 with loved ones by her side. Born Mary Simmonette Traude on October 1,1941, she was the daughter of Kenneth and Sara Traude of Villapark, Illinois. Mary moved to Alameda at age 3 and has been a California girl ever since. She attended Alameda High School and the University of California at Berkeley. While at Cal she met Edwin “Ned” Wood, whom she married on December 15, 1962. He claims it was love at first sight. They have resided in Piedmont for over 55 years. During Ned’s army duty, they were stationed in El Paso, Texas where Ned Junior was born. After returning to California, they welcomed their daughter Sally Thayer. Mary had a gift for making things beautiful, whether as a decorator, antique dealer, floral designer, gardener or a photographer. Her talents brought joy to many. She was amazing at taking single items, putting them together, and creating beauty. Her home and her garden were her sanctuary and those who had a chance to visit were in for a treat. In recent years, Mary became an avid bridge player, playing several times a week with in Africa, a sailing trip to the Galapagos or a trip to see grizzlies or polar bears, she was in heaven among all creatures big and small. The hummingbirds and squirrels who were fed daily on her porch could not have had a sweeter friend. Above all, Mary was a special friend to many, a wonderful wife and mother, and the perfect “gammie’ to her four beautiful grand-babies. Her grandchildren will forever have memories of multiple trips to Stinson Beach, the great K-L fishing trip, and their one-on-one trips with Gammie and Papa while in middle school. Mary is survived by Ned, her loving husband of 59 years, her son Ned Jr. and daughter in law Kelly, and her grandchildren Sam, Jane (Lane Karney), Jed and Jack Wood. She is predeceased by her beloved daughter Sally, her father and mother and many pups. A celebration of Mary’s life will be held at the Claremont Country Club on Sunday, September 25 from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests memorial donations in Mary’s name to: National Wildlife Federation (nwf.org), Piedmont Garden Club, or the charity of your choice. articles.text: Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s summer camp in the Sierra foothills since 1931, will have a Campathon fundraiser at Hampton Park this Sunday afternoon, September 11, from 3:00-5:00 p.m. Enjoy Lazy Dog ice cream while completing playstation-style activities that recreate your camp favorites - including a Gaga Ball tournament. Have tons of fun while raising money for many projects at camp. Including a new high ropes pole course. Ask parents, friends, neighbors and extended family members to sponsor you for Campathon. Minimum $100 donation is required per participant. No need to be a camper to participate. During the Campathon complete as many play stations and activities as you want, purchase some ice cream and enjoy reliving camp highlights. The event is also a great way to check out what Augusta is all about and to meet some of its staff members. As a non-profit, the camp needs to raise significant funds to finance a new Ropes Pole Course and support ongoing creative activities at Camp Augusta. One of the most unique aspects of Camp Augusta is the high ropes course elements nestled amongst the pine trees. The trees have been greatly affected by the drought of the last few years and some of the most beloved climbing elements have had to come down for safety. Camp Augusta has a new opportunity to expand and continue to challenge our campers and build confidence and teamwork with the installation of a new Ropes Pole Course. pages.text: Wednesday, September 7, 2022 25 HIKING WITH JON A hidden gem in Oakland: Middle Harbor Shoreline Park By Jonathan Comeaux Tucked away in the Port of Oakland is a hidden treasure that even local residents cannot seem to find. Middle Harbor Shoreline Park is a public reserve with sweeping views of the Bay, the Bay Bridge, and San Francisco. Better yet, there are never a lot of people. Aside from the awe-striking views on each trail, the park has BBQ pits, an amphitheater, viewing platforms, and even a small rock climbing structure for children. It’s considered a wildlife sanctuary for birds of several varieties in the surrounding cove with informative panels which detail each breed you spot. Directly from the parking lot is a small sandy beach, a perfect place to eat lunch, and a an elevated viewing tower with binoculars looking out toward the harbor. Following the road from the parking lots leads to the Chappell Hayes Observation Tower, and along the way are some historiYou can spot seabirds like pelicans, Caspian terns, gulls, and cormorants in the shallow harbor waters. The Chappell Hayes Observation Tower is a great two-story overlook of the bay. Atop the Chappell Hayes Observation Tower are binoculars and a nice shady place to soak in the view. Staff Photos Middle Harbor Shoreline Park provides an epic view of the Bay, the shipping cranes of the Port of Oakland, the Bay Bridge, and city of San Francisco. The trails at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park have a great view from every angle. cal facts about the stone training walls along the shoreline. The stone wall (see photo) is a replica of a former historic jetty that was designed in 1874 extending from the Port of Oakland into the bay. The jetties were designed to keep Oakland’s shipping channels open. Prior to their creation, ships had to wait until high tide to enter the shallow waters of the Oakland Estuary. The Chappell Hayes Observation Tower is a two-story tower with more informational panels about the surroundings. It provides a beautiful overlook of the Bay, the Port of Oakland, the Bay Bridge, and. San Francisco. The location’s namesake, Chappell Hayes, was an activist and environmentalist, becoming a driving force for the Clean Air Alternative Coalition. The trails by the observation tower provide another terrific view. You’ll often see boats and ferries coming to and from the Estuary. You can also see iron bars in the ground from a former railroad that led toward the water. The tracks lead to the location of the old Western Pacific Mole, dating from the early 1900s. The station was considered a brazen challenge to the Southern Pacific Railroad’s monopoly of Oakland’s waterfront. Southern Pacific sued, but the court ruled against them in 1907. If you want to add to your day, a half mile down 7th street is Port View Park, a fishing station that also has a clean children’s park Pictured is a replica of a historic “training wall,” which was a jetty dating back to the early 1900s. An old train track at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park leads to the former location of the Western Pacific Mole, a historic railway for Oakland. and information center. A short walk from there is the Port View Park Fishing Pier, which is a stunning place for anglers. Walking around Middle Harbor Shoreline Park, to the fishing pier and back to the parking lot is about 4.5 miles. It’s a great location for senior walkers, children, and anyone looking for a secluded view of the Bay. Punch in Middle Harbor Shoreline Park to your GPS device to find the park, which is a short 13-minute drive from Piedmont via 580 West. Port View Park is another hidden, quaint location with great views. It’s also a good spot for fishing.

Editor: We have been Piedmont residents for over 20 years and are writing to the City Council about the recent construction of the accessible pathways, curbs, ramps, sidewalks and storm drains at the corners of Manor Drive and Holly Place. In view of the execution of the City Standards to these corner intersections as of September 6, 2022, we raise these points: 1. Alterations were made to private properties without due process for notification and permission of owners. 3. Neighbors, including school children living in the area, use these intersections and therefore should have been notified of the City’s plan before implementation of changes to seek input. 4. articles.text: The 24th annual Piedmont Harvest Festival returns to Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 18 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The festival will feature all the traditional mainstays and activities, including Village Market’s Farmer’s market, the Edibles Contest, Scarecrow Alley, carnival games for kids, the annual Jazz Festival, an art exhibit at the Japanese Tea House, and food trucks lined up on Highland Avenue. The all-volunteer event is sponsored by the City. The Piedmont Education Foundation will oversee the popular “Scarecrow Alley” and a silent auction for purchase of the scarecrows, as well as a robust carnival in the Community Hall parking lot, with games and treats for kids of all ages. Edibles Contest The popular Edibles Contest has occurred every year since the Festival’s founding in 1998 by Susan Hill and Bill Drum. The contest features the best homegrown and homemade foods from residents. There are many categories to choose from, including: biggest pumpkin, best sweet bread, most unusual vegetable, best apple pie, best jam, best salsa – even best compost. Entries may be submitted by individual residents, households, neighborhoods or groups. There is no charge to enter. All entries must be delivered to the Community Hall between 7:30 and 10:00 a.m. on September 18. Photo by Amber Brumfiel Wildwood School’s kindergarten students created “Kai,” the red Ninjago, for Scarecrow Alley at last year’s annual Piedmont Harvest Festival.
articles.title: Harvest Festival takes over Piedmont Park on September 18

articles.text: Crow’s contact with PG&E line causes 24,000 buildings to lose power A crow came in contact with and damaged Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) equipment on the morning of August 25, causing a temporary outage that affected 24,000 customers in Alameda County. The outage occurred on Thursday morning at 11 a.m. and affected residents and business owners in the Oakland Hills, Montclair, Piedmont, Oakland, and Mills College. Traffic lights were out at the main intersection in Piedmont at Oakland and Grand Avenues. “Several intersections were without power affecting traffic signals. Portable stop signs were brought out to control traffic, and police staff monitored intersections for any issues,” confirmed Piedmont Police Department Commander Lisa Douglas. “The police department building experienced a brief power outage, but generators provided emergency power. articles.text: Are cattle chutes in the future for residents? The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I am a long-time resident of the Piedmont Manor neighborhood on York Drive. I want to express my deep concerns about the new sidewalk and curbs being installed at Holly Place and Manor Drive. The selected design decision was clearly made without regard to the function of sidewalks and streets in this pedestrian-friendly and bikefriendly neighborhood. There is clearly no citywide consistency in design standards, and I urge you to direct Public Works to install infrastructure that meets the needs of users. My objections to the partially completed concrete infrastructure are: • Safety is degraded • Pedestrian flow is reduced • Green space is reduced Safety degradation The previous design was pedestrian-friendly, with wide and minimally-sloped transitions from sidewalk to street. The new infrastructure requires almost a 90-degree turn by each pedestrian, and only one person at a time, almost like cattle being slotted into a narrow chute. People do not move in this manner, and most will step up on the new curb, go across the new concrete and down the other step into the deeply-guttered street. This movement involving new hazards is almost required by the current design. Pedestrian flow degradation Holly Place and the public cutthrough from Holly to Ricardo Avenue is a conduit for hundreds of students headed to Beach School, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School every day. The movement of young students with parents toward Beach School is made in groups, and the new design squeezes the flow into a single-file, one-way movement. This is not feasible for parent and children, or groups with bikes, scooters, wheelchairs or strollers. The natural work-around will be to use the street for group movement, which will be worse than the current situation. Green space reduction The city will be moving against its own environmental policies by turning green space between the sidewalk and street into concrete. This location is best served with wide, minimally-sloped transitions from sidewalk to street. I see many Piedmont sidewalks with date stamps from the 1920s and 1930s. Please do not move forward with a design that degrades safety, pedestrian flow and green space for the next 100 years. –Ellen Smith 460 Boulevard Way, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS

articles.text: Sara Paul of Watch Duty opens series on September 7 Sara Paul of Watch Duty will be the guest speaker for Connect’s speaker series on September 7. The Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV) and Piedmont Connect are co-hosting a climate speaker series, beginning with guest speaker Sara Paul from Watch Duty. Her talk will be on Wednesday, September 7 at 4 p.m. The speaker series will continue through May 2023. Watch Duty launched in August 2021 as a smartphone application and interactive map that shows where wildfires are burning across the state in realtime with information gathered from a variety of channels and agencies. Watch Duty covered Sonoma, Napa and Lake counties in its inception, and has since expanded to include all 58 counties in California. Paul manages Sonoma County Fire Updates for the app and will speak on wildfire mitigation at next week’s Zoom event. “Watch Duty fills an important gap as a source of reliable fire information provided in a timely manner,” said Paul. “Our target audience is anyone living in fire country in California. In 2022, that’s all of us.” The Watch Duty team monitors a network of sources to bring information directly to the user. Among its trusted channels are flight patterns of California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE), the statewide network of ALERT wildfire camera, and satellite data. The speaker series aims to educate constituents on a range of important topics with a focus on environmentalism and sustainability. Paul’s presentation will be followed by a question-and-answer session. Sign up for the speaker series at https://lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx?page_id=4002&club_ id=601389&item_id=1765943. The event begins at 4 p.m. Registration is free and open to all. The program will be recorded and can be watched after the fact on LWV’s YouTube channel. The app Watch Duty delivers real-time information on wildfires across the state. business hours.

articles.text: The city of Piedmont held a final community workshop on its draft housing element, published on April 8 this year, prior to City Council review. The hybrid informational session was held in City Hall and on Zoom on August 18. City Administrator Sara Lillevand and Planning Director Kevin Jackson facilitated the meeting. Piedmont is a member of the Association of Bay Area Governments (ABAG), which allocates housing mandates to each jurisdiction based on multifaceted methodology. Piedmont did raise concerns numerous times during ABAG’s housing mandate process with questions as to where the methodology was headed, Lillevand explained. This cycle’s methodology largely considered access to opportunity and proximity to jobs - Piedmont is considered a “high resource area” and is close to transit hubs, which increased its allotted regional housing needs allocation (RHNA). “All of Piedmont is considered a high resource area, with [access] to great schools, city services and amenities which contribute to positive outcomes - and as a result, Piedmont was allocated more units [this cycle],” Lillevand said. Proximity to jobs across the Bay Area was also a factor ABAG considered when handing Piedmont a total of 587 low to moderate income units. Lillevand said she considered where city and school employees fall under the income based allocation, and found that nearly 80% of city workforce falls under the low-income category, with less than $110,000 of household income. Piedmont is not alone in this challenge, Lillevand said - Albany, Emeryville, Orinda, Sausalito, Tiburon, and more cities that fall under ABAG’s mandate process all saw dramatic increases in their RHNA. “If the city is not in compliance with state housing law, it will be ineligible to receive grants and loan programs, and will be unable to issue building permits, conditional use permits and design review permits,” Jackson explained. “[Incompliance] leaves the city vulnerable to costly litigation from housing rights organizations, developers and HCD.” “If the city is not in compliance, it will only have one year

articles.text: 10th Annual Piedmont Artisan Beer Festival is October 7 On Friday, October 7, the 10th Annual Piedmont Beer Festival will take over the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a celebration of Artisanal brewers and their finest home brews. In addition to sampling the best of local home brewers, guests are invited to have a legitimate German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center with freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. Food is provided by Dave Larson at Piedmont Grocery. A panel of Piedmont celebrity judges will award prizes to home brewers for Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, and Best in Show. This year’s celebrity judges are Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson. Brewers already registered include: • Piedmont brewers: Carter Dunlap, Trevor Fleshman, Matt Gerhardt, Zachary Jones • Defending Winner: Kyle Blomseth, Belgian Style Ale • Winners from the Bay Area Mashers Club To enter home brews, contact Center for the Arts board member Carter Dunlap at carter@dunlapclan.net, or Jay Russell at jayrussell35@gmail.com. Include your name, phone & e-mail address and the type of beer you will bring. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue.

articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town on Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and has been organized by Officer Tyler Petit since the retirement of Sgt. Steve DeWarns. Last year’s Car Show had 120 vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 65 vehicles already have signed up for this year’s Car Show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, 1987 Ferrari Testarossa, and possibly two Formula Ford race cars. The car show includes free coffee and donuts, and there is a rumor that a taco truck might arrive. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want to include their vehicles in the show need to register on the Eventbrite website at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ coffee-cars-cops-car-show-tickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue between the high school and Piedmont Park. To sign up and for more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov. A row of Porsches, Lamborghinis, Ferraris and other exotic cars from last years car show. Photo by Rob Yelland

articles.text: A volleyball subcommittee, consisting of Recreation Commissioners Dick Carter, Lisa Gardner, and Aamir Virani, conducted a citywide survey to gauge interest in beach volleyball courts in town. Although the survey found that there is interest in the sport, funding and space constraints have halted the project. There are no dedicated outdoor volleyball or beach volleyball courts in Piedmont. A group of Piedmont parents, including Kim DeYoung, Kiel Murray, and Zoa Town, advocated creating beach volleyball courts in town, with the primary focus of finding a practice and competition space for a future Piedmont High School girls’ beach volleyball team. The Recreation Department offers recreational volleyball opportunities for girls and boys aged 7 to 18 during the fall, spring, and summer, but none for those over 18. Based on the group’s strong interest in beach volleyball, the Recreation Commission formed a volleyball subcommittee in January. “The advocates got up to speed really fast and figured out a way to move the ball forward,” said Virani. “[Based on a citywide survey] we found that there is community interest in beach volleyball and the development of courts.” Virani added that the survey was informal, although there were 272 responses. The subcommittee then met over six months to discuss survey findings and next steps. “It was interesting to work on this project, with lots of discussion. We tried to get as much information as we could when we put this together,” Virani said. The subcommittee considered that city space is at a premium and found concerns regarding adding programming to “already strained resources from the perspectives of facility sharing, historical usage, adaptability of facilities, and noise impacts,” according to the survey results report. “When the master plans for city parks are revisited, at that time, the city, park commission and recreation commission should work together, along with the recreation department, to consider beach volleyball courts at that time,” Virani said. City parks master plans are revisited when funding allows, with no set date at this time. “This is disappointing, but not entirely surprising,” Town said to commissioners at an August 17 meeting. “We are focused on working with PUSD to get the facility we need. It’s slow, it’s like hitting a heavy volleyball through the wind, but it’s moving forward.” DeYoung echoed Town’s sentiments. “I ask for advocacy and support,” she told commissioners. “It’s hard being parents of high school students. I know the high school is trying to identify more athletic opportunities for female athletes. Beach volleyball was the number one sport of interest [for female students].”
articles.title: City plan for adult beach volleyball halted

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Commission established an Older Adult Programming Subcommittee at an August 17 meeting. Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen will serve as staff lead for the subcommittee. “We heard from the community that there is increased interest in more [older adult] programming,” Phalen said. “The goal is to figure out what people are looking for and in what structure.” Some classes and meetups have been successful, Phalen added, like Walking on Wednesday, organized by Recreation Commissioner Vice Chair Dick Carter. “I’m excited about this and have lots of ideas,” Phalen said, and added that the department is interested in opening up programming to individuals beyond Piedmont. “This has been an area of interest of mine for some time,” Carter said, who wrote a proposed program in 2018 to address older adult recreational programming. “There are about 2,350 people over the age of 65 in Piedmont, according to the census. That’s up from about 1,600 in 2010, so our population is growing older.” Walking on Wednesday and an established reading group have been successful. Over 140 people have signed up for Walking on Wednesday, with an average of 30-35 per week. Carter and commissioner Lisa Gardener were the first to volunteer to be on the subcommittee.
articles.title: Rec. Commission establishes committee to consider older adult programs

articles.text: Anne Valva began her tenure as Beach School Principal one week ago after being confirmed by the Piedmont School Board on August 24. Valva’s first year as a principal follows 30 years of experience in education. She has been at Beach since 2013 as a fifth grade teacher and Math Intervention Specialist. “My first few days as principal have been so much fun,” said Valva. “The students and families have been so welcoming and the teachers are very supportive. I am constantly learning.” The top position at Beach opened when Michael Corritone committed to a principal position in Walnut Creek on August 1, just nine days before Piedmont’s school year began. The school district quickly posted the job on Edjoin to field applicants. After two rounds of interviews Valva was named the top choice. “The main reason I applied for the job is that I want to continue the great work the teachers, staff and students do at Beach School every day,” Valva explained. Valva’s career path began to finding her home at Beach School. After teaching 5th grade at Beach for four years she became the school’s Math Intervention Specialist, a role she has enjoyed from 2017 until the first week of this year. “She comes highly recommended from fellow staff and families and I look forward to watching her build on an already thriving school community,” said Piedmont Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. Valva has served Beach in many roles that will serve her well as Principal, including being a member of the school’s Leadership and Response to Intervention Teams. She has worked at the elementary and District-levels analyzing and interpreting assessment data and passing on the information to fellow teachers to more successfully implement classroom curriculum. Beach School has a storied history, which Valva intends to continue. Beach School was founded as The Lake Avenue School in 1913, two years after Piedmont’s first elementary school, Havens, was built. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a check for $3,350,402 to the Piedmont School Board on August 24. The funds represent the culmination of fundraising campaigns from last year (2021-2022) principally through the Giving Campaign. “We are humbled by the generosity of our community,” said Amelie Kappes, Chair of the Foundation’s board. “Once again, Piedmont has shown its commitment to our schools and our students.” A total of 1,216 families contributed to the 2021-2022 Giving Campaign with an average gift of $3,075. The grant provides 42,000 hours of instructional and student support and represents an $2,316,000 in teacher salaries, $925,000 in student support staff, and $109,000 in teacher professional development, instructional technology, and classroom supplies. The grant also includes funding for mental health counseling, tutoring, and libraries. For more details, visit piedmontedfoundation.org/our-impact/grantsschool-support/. “We are thankful for the hard work of our Giving Campaign chairs, Colleen Allan and Christine Wente von Metzsch, and to the whole Giving Campaign team for their record-breaking success,” said Heather Frank, PEF Executive Director. “They really brought our community together to share the importance of giving to our schools.” Megan Pillsbury, the School Photo by Jane Violich Giving Campaign Chairs: Dana Murray (left), Katie Sharafi, and Julia Ruthven. Board Vice President, accepted the check on behalf of PUSD. “A huge thank you as always. With government funding restrictions, we just couldn’t operate the way we do without PEF,” said Pillsbury. This year’s campaign begins Sept. 20 The Education Foundation has announced that Dana Murray, Julia Ruthven, and Katie Truitt Sharafi will be co-chairs of this year’s Giving Campaign. “We are honored to be able to represent the Giving Campaign this year, and to give back to the community in a way that feels meaningful,” said Murray. “This year’s campaign will focus on investing in student success,” added Sharafi. “Funds from the Giving Campaign help ensure our students have the teachers and classes needed for a fulfilling and challenging education. We are really excited to build on last year’s momentum.” The Foundation and the Giving Campaign committee invite the community to celebrate the launch of this year’s campaign with a popsicle party in Piedmont Park and a separate party near Beach School on Tuesday, September 20 from 3-4 pm. Popsicles will be donated by Mulberry’s Market. Photo by Brian Killgore Piedmont Education Foundation board members present a check to Piedmont School Board on August 24. Pictured are: School board member Veronica Thigpen (left), Giving Campaign Co-Chair Katie Sharafi, School Board member Megan Pillsbury, Giving Campaign Co-Chair Julia Ruthven, Education Foundation Executive Director Heather Frank, School Board member Hilary Cooper, Education Foundation Board Chair Amelie Kappes, and Giving Campaign Co-Chair Dana Murray.
articles.title: Ed Foundation supports Piedmont schools with annual grant of $3,350,402

articles.text: Piedmont School District began its weekly COVID count on August 6, four days before the start of the 2022 school year. In the three weeks since then, through August 26, there have been 106 reported student cases and eight reported teacher cases. Student and Teacher Combined Weekly Average: 38 cases/ week These case counts at Piedmont are similar to Spring Break on April 9-17 and the weeks following. There were 130 student and teacher cases reported during the four weeks including Spring Break and the next three weeks. Cases reported during Spring Break and following weeks showed a student and teacher combined weekly average of 32.5 cases per week. The highest totals of COVID cases came during and after the Winter Break spanning December 17, 2021 to January 10, 2022. The district estimated roughly 228 cases were reported by teachers and students in that three and a half week (25 day) period. Student and Teacher Combined Weekly Average: 64/week. Indoor masks have been recommended but not required since March 14, 2022. School nurses are working the same number of hours this year as last (2.2 full time salaries paid), but their staff has been reduced to three health clerks, half of last year’s total. If case counts are still significant in school, what is different? For one, COVID is less of an unknown now; many people are contracting it for a second time. With vaccinations and treatment available, the possibility of a serious or life-threatening cases has decreased. For better or worse, it is largely the attitude around COVID-19 that has changed.

articles.text: Are your kids ready for school? With 2022 back-to-school already upon us, our children are experiencing a wide range of individual experiences. Some variability is due to differences in educational settings and pandemic related factors. But not all. What constitutes “school readiness”? A wide body of research has examined the neurodevelopmental elements required for a child to be ready for school. Is it certain pre-academic skills? Is it social aptitude? Emotional maturity? Review of the literature shows that a child’s ability in one kindergarten readiness area prior to school entry is predictive of continued success in that same academic area. For example, a child’s preschool alphabet and phonics skill level is predictive of their reading level later on. But is there an indicator that predicts skill acquisition both within and across domains? For example, we know that foundational pre-math skills at preschool predicts a child’s ability in that subject, but do preschool math skills correlate with success in any other academic or social domains? Analysis of children’s assessment data taken before kindergarten entry, and again in the first, third and fifth grades, reveal that language ability has the most wide-reaching effects on school readiness and ongoing academic success. That is, researchers found that the language skills a child exhibited before entering school predicted not only that child’s school-aged level of communication skills, but also their overall levels in reading, writing, math and to some extent social skills. Researchers hypothesize that language skills are correlated with so many other key areas, because language serves as a set of tools that helps children acquire other skills. For example, we use our language comprehension to understand numeracy and vocabulary concepts, which leads to stronger math and reading skills. We also use our expressive abilities to connect with others and explain our thinking, which may be why stronger language skills support our social skills. So, what does it actually mean to be ready for school? Perhaps it means language! For some at-risk children, this could mean we focus on prevention. For some children with speech and language delays, this could mean we focus on treatment. And for most children this could mean we focus on language enrichment. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will host a Community Academy which will teach residents about law enforcement operations, enhance community relations, and promote community policing by supporting and encouraging citizen involvement. Classes are scheduled for 10 weeks, and each session lasts four hours. The deadline to apply is this Friday, September 2. The academy will be presented over 10 consecutive sessions tentatively beginning September 6, from 6:00-10:00 p.m. every Tuesday in September, and every Wednesday in October and November until November 9. The weekly classroom setting builds momentum and becomes more intriguing as the participants meet the various instructors and eventually ends with an opportunity to play the role of these everyday officers on scenario night. Topics will include: Communications and Technology. Community Policing. Crime Prevention. Crimes against persons and property. De-escalation. Elder Crimes. Defensive Tactics & Arrests. Evidence Collection Financial Crimes, Investigations. Juvenile Law. Laws of Arrest. Mental Illness. Narcotics. Patrol Procedures. Search and Seizure. Traffic Enforcement. The application deadline is Friday, September 2. Applications are available online at: Piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/police/community_programs. Participants must be at least 18 years old, successfully complete a background check, sign waiver forms and be approved by the Chief of Police. These opportunities have helped me understand the needs of different stakeholders in the district, which will be invaluable in achieving my goals. Lindsay Thomasson My education and qualifications are: As the parent of students currently at PMS, Havens, and in preschool. I have held numerous volunteer roles over the past five years, giving me a robust understanding of how our district works, its strengths and weaknesses. I served as Havens’ Parent Club President, on the LCAP Committee, Superintendent Community Advisory Committee, and Wellness Center Committee, to name a few. As a member of PUSD’s Board of Education, my priorities would be to ensure PUSD has the leadership and resources to provide students an excellent, well-rounded academic experience, including the hiring of a superintendent aligned in our goals, and attracting and retaining well-qualified, diverse, engaged educators. This will allow PUSD to truly equip students with the essential critical-thinking, STEAM, and language arts skills needed to succeed at the universities and in the careers of their choosing. I have attended California public schools my entire life, culminating in degrees from Cal Berkeley and UCSD. Piedmont schools are the foundation of our community, yet the past three years have been divisive. To move forward we must engage in meaningful community dialogue, be pragmatic and creative, ensure all stakeholders are engaged in our decision-making processes, and always put students first. Shirley Hooi COVID-related online learning has forced PUSD students to endure an unprecedented period of educational losses and mental stress. Now is a crucial period to help our students get back on track. I believe that parent, student and community member involvement in school board decisions is critical. Their opinions should be considered in the selection of the superintendent, along with issues regarding school curriculum and teacher retention/recruitment. As a product of the Oakland Unified School District, PUSD was regarded as the epitome of an exceptional public school education. Families strived to move to Piedmont to raise their children in a community in which a public school education was comparable to the local private schools. Unfortunately, this has changed, and PUSD continues to lose students to local private schools every year. My immigrant parents instilled in their children the belief of education and hard work as a path out of poverty. Now as a PUSD parent, it is my role to instill the same beliefs upon my children. If you support this philosophy, now is the time for me to be your voice on the school board. Get Involved: www.shirleyhooi.com.

articles.text: Betsy Andersen, incumbent My priorities on the Piedmont City Council have been community health and safety, financial stability, and strong city-school relations. During my time on Council, we have renovated Hampton Park and the Corey Reich Tennis Center, invested $3.75M for future pension needs, facilitated in-town COVID-19 testing, allocated funds to modernize police and fire dispatch, and maintained a balanced budget. Currently, we are rebuilding the city-owned Piedmont Community Pool, thanks to voter-approved Measure UU. As a lifelong resident, I appreciate the challenges and opportunities as we develop strategies to meet our climate action goals, address the state housing crisis, and replace aging infrastructure. Prior to serving on Council, I volunteered on the Public Safety Committee to promote emergency preparedness and chaired the Recreation Commission with a focus on improving recreational facilities and opportunities for all ages. I attended Piedmont public schools, majored in Public Policy at Duke, earned my law degree from UCLA, and practiced law for nearly two decades. My husband, Robert, and I raised our daughters here, Jane (PHS ’18) and Ellie (PHS ’21). If re-elected, I will continue to listen thoughtfully to all voices as we work together to strengthen the community we call home. Jennifer Long, incumbent I am running for City Council to serve our beautiful community and maintain its greatness as it grows and evolves. With an impending pool build, critical infrastructure repair (and or replacement) and housing development, Piedmont is poised to be a city with the future in mind. In these unprecedented times, our city needs leaders who understand the interests of our citizens
