articles.text: Piedmont’s football team came up one touchdown short in a season-opening 27-20 loss to Seaside on Friday night, August 36 at Witter Field. Tied 7-7 at halftime, Seaside pulled ahead 21-14 in the Staff Photos Piedmont senior Matteo Costa scored on an interception against Seaside in the opening game of the football season. third quarter, but the Highlanders rallied to narrow the score to 21-20. The Spartans scored the clinching touchdown in the final quarter “It was a tough one,” commented first-year Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. “We really thought we had control of the game and then all of a sudden, we were down a touchdown. We’ve got to get more physical and tackle better. All the plays like long bombs, long runs, interceptions are beautiful and fun to watch, but football comes down to blocking and tackling. Those things got in our way tonight,” he said. PHS battled in the second half to keep the game close. but with only 20 players. Many playing both offense and defense, fatigue became a factor. With the lack of a full offseason training camp due to the school abruptly canceling, then reviving the varsity team during the spring months, Seiden was forced to progressively install his system s in a short amount of time. Friday’s game was the first of Piedmont’s full-speed action without an opening scrimmage game, and some of that came into play on Friday night. “We weren’t really able to Jack Nelson had 150 total yards and over 20 carries as a running back. get into contact drills because of the numbers. This was essentially our scrimmage. For some of our guys, this was the first time they’ve actually played a live football game,” Seiden said. “There are certain things you can’t replace, and one of them is full contact,” he added. But there were some high points. Running back Jack Nelson carried the load for the offense with nearly 150 total yards. “Jack is a helluva player, especially for someone whose focus in high school has been on lacrosse. He’s a true warrior and represents what we want our kids to be; he brings it all to the table.” Said Seiden. Sophomore quarterback Markos Lagios recorded his first two passing touchdowns to classmate Sam Shelby, playing varsity for the first time. “Sam is a kid we knew would be a heavy contributor; he made some plays on both sides and is a player we can count on. He is a key cog to what we’re building,” said Seiden. Game Recap Piedmont started the game by recovering an onside kick and drove down to the 11-yard line, but turned the ball over with an interception that first tipped off of the hands of a PHS receiver. Seaside got to the PHS eight yard line but turned it over on downs. Piedmont was first to score, a 70-yard catch and run by Shelby on a 4th-and-10 with 2:40 left in the first quarter. One minute later, Seaside answered with a 60-yard touchdown, leading to a 7-7 tie at halftime. In the third quarter, Piedmont took a 14-7 lead in the third quarter when safety Matteo Costa intercepted the ball on the 30-yard line and ran it back 70 yards for a touchdown with 7:01 left. But once again Seaside responded with its own touchdown drive for a 14-14 tie. Seaside scored again with 29 seconds left in the third period after forcing a Piedmont turnover on downs at the Highlanders’ 37 yard line, going ahead 21-14. Piedmont got back on the board with 7:56 left in the fourth quarter, driving 65 yards for a six-yard pass to Shelby in the end zone. Seaside blocked the extra point kick, and remained ahead 21-20. On the next possession the Spartans scored with 2:31 left in the game, but this time. Piedmont blocked the extra point attempt point to stay within one point, trailing the visitors 27-20. The Highlanders were able to drive to their own 46-yard line with around 30 seconds left in the game before an interception closed the game. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1) hosts Del Norte of Crescent City this Friday, September 2 at 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field. Sophomore quarterback Markos Lagios made his first two touchdown passes of his high school career, both going to sophomore classmate Sam Shelby.

articles.text: Waters Worthen The Junior Varsity Highlanders preformed big in the season opener on Friday, August 26 against the Seaside High Spartans at Witter Field, cruising to a 28-0 shutout victory. Piedmont scored when quarterback Brandon Dicke hooked up with Ethan Alering for an 18 yard touchdown pass with running back Cash Panico scoring a two point conversion to make it 8-0—which was the score to enter halftime. The Spartans ensued possession coming back from the half, but Piedmont was able to stop its drive. Just three plays later Panico burst a 40-yard run to make It 14-0. Vincent Arbit scored the final two touchdowns for PHS. As a quarterback, he tossed an eight yard pass, and followed up on the defensive side with a fumble recovery returned to the house for the final score, 28-0. The outstanding defense hounded the visiting Spartans, as contributors like Cash Elmquist and Albert Belingrath wreaked havoc, preventing Seaside from ever breaching the Piedmont 30-yard line for the entire second half. NEXT UP Piedmont host Del Norte on Friday, September 2 at 4:30 p.m. Photos by Mike McConathy Cash Panico with a carry against Seaside. He had a 40-yard touchdown run in the game. Piedmont’s Albert Bellingrath (36) pounces on the ball carrier with Adan Soleto (56) in pursuit.

articles.text: An article in the August 24 edition of the Piedmont Post incorrectly identified a member of the Piedmont High School tennis team as a Russian exchange student. Freshman Arianna Kortum is a longtime resident of Piedmont and not an exchange student. The Post offers its apologies to the Kortum family for the error.

articles.text: Wearing purple and white as Piedmont High’s No. 1 singles starter on the tennis team this coming fall season, Tanya Kononova will be a new face on the team. She never could have imagined coming to California as a high school student prior to February 24, the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived in Piedmont with her mother just one month ago on July 22 from Odesa, a city on the southern shore of Ukraine. Kononova, a junior at PHS, showed up one week later at a tennis clinic being run by varsity coach Jim Landes, and instantly impressed him. “It was the week I had a warm-up clinic for high school girls. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. The first time she hit, right then and there I knew she was a very good player. It was also a good time for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Having to leave your country is an unimaginable experience. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could into two suitcases and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russians invaded. Her father is still in Ukraine as men under the age of 60-years old were required to stay and help in Ukraine’s war with Russia. To enter Moldova, Tanya and her mother had to wait at the border for 13 hours. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova, They stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months but after the building of the town administration was targeted by Russian artillery, they decided to flee to Bulgaria, where they would stay from May through July. It would be their last stop before flying to the U.S. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived – my mother, my grandfather and grandmother and me. My grandparents are still in Bulgaria now,” said Kononova. When initially leaving Odesa, she and her family were forced to quickly throw together their belongings because of fear that the Russians would siege the city. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically narrowed things down to what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. There was a moment when Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week in order to grab more belongings. She and her friend went to a mall when a rocket struck a building close by. In a recent interview, Kononova details the emotions she experienced. “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s where it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were told to go to a shelter because they detected a missile, but we paid no attention. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions, and it was one of the days they bombed one of the residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Since then, Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe. Tanya and her mother, meanwhile, moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids. I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” said Kononova. Now enrolled in high school as a junior and on the school tennis team, she is playing tennis for the first time since February. “She is playing with my racket,” said PHS coach Jim Landes with a wide smile. Piedmont High School junior Tanya Kononova, the school’s No. 1 singles starter on the tennis team, discusses her experience as a Ukrainian refugee. Tanya began playing tennis when she was six years old and continued at the club level through her teenage years. She instantly made friends with her Piedmont teammates, though the concept of playing on a team is new to her. Tennis is, after all, an individual sport. “It’s completely different from the places where I was before. But it’s a nice place and it feels like you are safe here. The people are quite happy to see you… Playing on the team definitely makes me feel like someone stands for me. You’re not alone and it’s less stressful. “It’s also more fun,” Kononova added. Coach Landes adds that the team has already taken well to her. “I think all the teammates really like her. It’s a new school for her, so having this activity helps her meet people and bond with them. If she wasn’t a tennis player and just went to this new school without being an athlete, I think it would be much more difficult. She already knows a bunch of girls,” said Landes. Tanya already has set a goal for this season, and it’s an ambitious one. “I don’t want to lose a single match,” said Kononova with a smile. The Post welcomes Tanya and her mother to Piedmont and thanks Tanya for her courage in being willing to describe her experiences of the past six months. articles.text: The Piedmont Post is seeking interns to cover Junior Varsity football and water polo for the fall semester. The position offers budding sports journalists professional experience in covering events and learning the trade. Interns will work remotely with the Post’s sports reporter, Jonathan Comeaux, who will advise and provide feedback to interns wanting to publish their articles. Playing experience is not a requirement, only an eagerness to learn and have stories published in a timely manner. Jonathan will give young writers tips on how to cover sporting events, including interviewing and writing profiles of players. Parents or PHS students may reach out to news@piedmontpost. org, or JonathanCX525@gmail.com.

articles.text: Head coaches switch; Krumins to take lead, Savage to assist Piedmont’s defending WACC Championship boys’ water polo team returns for the fall season, but with a couple of changes. John Savage has stepped down as head coach entering his 10th year at the helm in favor of assistant coach Rik Krumins. Savage will continue as the varsity assistant and be the head coach of the junior varsity team for at least the 2022 season. The two have coached together for six years, share a mutual philosophy. The change in title will allow Krumins to coach his son, Peter Krumins, a junior. He was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2022.. “We’ve decided that we’ll be co-head coaches, essentially, and that’s been the dynamic for a while. With water polo, only one coach is allowed to stand during games, so he’ll be the one standing and yelling. So, he can yell at his son,” added Savage with a laugh. Krumins enters with a wealth of experience. He played on nationally ranked water polo teams at the University of California in the 90s and went onto play for Team U.S.A. He’s been an assistant coach alongside Savage since 2016. “We’ve really looked at ourselves as side-by-side as co-head coaches. John brings a lot of triathlete experience to the table in training the team, and I bring water polo aspect with Xs and Os. At the end of the day, it’s just who stands up on the deck. My son is a junior on the team as well, and John understands the scenario in life where there are not a lot of times where you get to do this. I really appreciate that,” said Krumins. The Highlanders return after going 19-6 last season and set school history by winning the program’s first-ever WACC Title with a big 12-8 win over No. 1 seeded Berkeley on October 30. They went into the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs with the No. 3 seed and received a firstround bye. They defeated Terra Linda 18-13 in the quarterfinals on November 6 before falling to No. 2 Marin Academy 7-4 in the semifinals on November 10. Back as a leader from 2021 is goalie Dariush Kashani, who was the Post’s honorable mention for 2021 Sophomore of the Year and was named 2020 Freshman of the Year. He earned a first-team Photo by Nancy Brahm Rik Krumins has been named head coach for the boys’ water polo team, with John Savage switching roles as assistant coach. The two have coached together for six years. All-League selections in 2021 as a junior and 2019 as a sophomore. He undoubtedly would’ve received one as a sophomore if the league offered postseason awards in the pandemic shortened season. “Dariush will anchor our defense. He allows us to play any style of defense that we want. By having that, it calms a lot of nerves as a coach because we know we have an anchor at the back and it creates opportunities for everybody else,” mentioned Savage. After the graduation of Antonio Rivera, Piedmont will have to identify a new Hole set player. Both coaches describe that they will likely go with a “by committee” approach. “We have three or four guys who are very talented offensively. We don’t have a superstar but we have a very balanced team. It will be a little bit of “Hole set by committee,” we have guys who we can rely on and that’s pretty valuable for us,” said Savage. Both coaches named several players to keep an eye on, including Declan Linnane, George Stein, Farris Saffouri, Finn Burke, Elles Krieckhaus, and Krumins. “Finn Burke has really impressed me over the training camp. George Stein, Decland Linnane and Peter will all get time in Hole set, and that gives us some flexibility,” added coach Krumins. NEXT UP Piedmont’s season starts at the Labor Day Bash on September 2. They will play multiple matches at several locations including Mission San Jose, James Logan, and Newark Memorial. Start times and opponents have yet to be announced. Peter Krumins will be a key player after being a starter last season. Goalie Dariush Kashani is the rock of Piedmont’s defense with multiple first-team All-League awards from previous seasons. articles.text: With the new school year officially here, the Class of 2023 looks toward the upcoming sports calendar for the fall, winter and spring seasons to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. LIAM CAMPBELL Football & Baseball Liam Campbell is currently a starter on the football team and will also have a key role on the baseball team in the spring. On the gridiron, Campbell lines up at cornerback and wide receiver. In baseball, he is an outfielder. In last Friday’s opening football game, Campbell had two receptions and converted one for a first down. This is his second year as a starter. Last spring, Campbell had a .304 batting average in baseball, with seven hits, six RBIs, 10 runs scored, five walks, and two stolen bases. MADDIE HILL Basketball Staff Photos Liam Campbell is currently a starting defensive back and receiver on the football team and will be a key member of the baseball team in the spring. son. She was a major part of taking PHS to the North Coast Section Finals and a No. 2 ranking. The team earned a No. 1 in the Div. 2 CIF State tournament, but she suffered an injury in the NCS Semifinals and was unable to appear in the finals or CIF tourney. It marked the team’s first NCS semifinal berth in 11 years. Prior to her injury, Hill recorded 19 points in a 76-50 NCS quarterfinals win over St. Mary’s and 13 points in the opening round against overmatched No. 15 Swett. Maddie Hill is a four-year starter on Bryan Gardere’s squad. She earned a second-team AllLeague selection last winter and was an Honorable Mention as a freshman. With water polo, only one coach is allowed to stand during games, so he’ll be the one standing and yelling. So, he can yell at his son,” added Savage with a laugh. Krumins enters with a wealth of experience. He played on nationally ranked water polo teams at the University of California in the 90s and went onto play for Team U.S.A. He’s been an assistant coach alongside Savage since 2016. “We’ve really looked at ourselves as side-by-side as co-head coaches. John brings a lot of triathlete experience to the table in training the team, and I bring water polo aspect with Xs and Os. At the end of the day, it’s just who stands up on the deck. My son is a junior on the team as well, and John understands the scenario in life where there are not a lot of times where you get to do this. I really appreciate that,” said Krumins. The Highlanders return after going 19-6 last season and set school history by winning the program’s first-ever WACC Title with a big 12-8 win over No. 1 seeded Berkeley on October 30. They went into the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs with the No. 3 seed and received a firstround bye. He undoubtedly would’ve received one as a sophomore if the league offered postseason awards in the pandemic shortened season. “Dariush will anchor our defense. He allows us to play any style of defense that we want. By having that, it calms a lot of nerves as a coach because we know we have an anchor at the back and it creates opportunities for everybody else,” mentioned Savage. After the graduation of Antonio Rivera, Piedmont will have to identify a new Hole set player. Both coaches describe that they will likely go with a “by committee” approach. “We have three or four guys who are very talented offensively. We don’t have a superstar but we have a very balanced team. It will be a little bit of “Hole set by committee,” we have guys who we can rely on and that’s pretty valuable for us,” said Savage. Both coaches named several players to keep an eye on, including Declan Linnane, George Stein, Farris Saffouri, Finn Burke, Elles Krieckhaus, and Krumins. “Finn Burke has really impressed me over the training camp. articles.text: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco is exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work now through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to Artist Carlos Villa learn more.
articles.title: Carlos Villa exhibit on view at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: The Albany Jazz Band will perform at the annual Piedmont Jazz Festival on September 18 at 2 p.m. The 23rd annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park on Sunday, September 18 as part of the annual Harvest Festival. Schedule of bands 12:00 p.m. Piedmont High School Jazz Band 1:00 p.m. Forte (16-piece band): 2:00 p.m. Albany Big Band. 3:00 p.m. Juvenoia The Jazz Festival, organized by Greg Slatoff, is free and provides the opportunity to celebrate Piedmont’s musical talent amid fun, food and friends. Albany Jazz Band The Albany Jazz Band’s performance at this year’s Piedmont Festival on Sunday, September 18 in Piedmont Park will be its fifth appearance in town. The band has been performing at concerts and dances in the San Francisco Bay Area since 1996 performing a repertoire that includes instrumentals and vocals that span classic and contemporary big band music, Latin, and pop. The Albany Jazz Band performs as its original 20-piece Big Band format and in a newer 10-piece format. Since 2005, the Albany Jazz Band has been led by Bob Levenson as music director. Band members are drawn from throughout the Bay Area. The bands rehearse every week and both maintain active performance schedules. For more information, see the website: www.albanyjazzband.org.
articles.title: Albany Jazz Band to headline Piedmont Jazz Festival

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, now celebrating its 10th anniversary, returns to Piedmont for a concert on Saturday, September 17 at 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton will perform a program to include Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, op. 132, Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465, and Caroline Shaw’s “Valencia”. For tickets click on: https://bit. ly/3TpKMUZ. Beethoven’s opus 132 string quartet is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Op. 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creatNatasha Makhijani (left), Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton comprise the principal quartet of Chamber Music Society of San Francisco. ing close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, the San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, the Oakland Symphony and many others. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau, and Jodi Levitz. For more information see: www.chambermusicsocietysf.org. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: The chorus line in the musical Follies. San Francisco Playhouse’s production of the award-winning musical Follies continues until September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by multiple award-winning stage and film composer Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army. Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The original production is the second-most costly production performed on Broadway to date. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and PhylPhoto by Jessica Palopoli lis were showgirls in the Follies, both in failing marriages. The San Francisco cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/ to obtain tickets, or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street.
articles.title: Last 2 weeks of Follies at SF Playhouse

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently showing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on the book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Goddess playing through Sept.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749- 2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/passengers/. articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents the world premiere of Berkeley composer John Adams’ latest opera, Antony and Cleopatra, on September 10. Significantly it was chosen to open the company’s 100th season and was commissioned by San Francisco Opera for its Centennial. It is set in a universe where “ancient Egypt meets Old Hollywood.” Adams tackles the Shakespearean equivalent of a celebrity romance and gives it a 21st century spin. Amina Edris, an Egyptian lyric soprano, will sing the lead role of Cleopatra, with Canadian bass-baritone Gerald Finley as Antony. The cast also includes Paul Appleby, Alfred Walker, Elizabeth DeShong, Brenton Ryan, Taylor Raven, Hadleigh Adams, Gabrielle Beteag, Timothy Murray and Bay Area favorite Philip Skinner. The opera will be conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim. Seven performances are scheduled from September 10 to October 5 at the War Memorial Opera House. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/operas/antony-and-cleopatra/ to purchase tickets. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on the book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. The chorus line in the musical Follies. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse’s production of the award-winning musical Follies continues until September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by multiple award-winning stage and film composer Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army. Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The original production is the second-most costly production performed on Broadway to date. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and PhylPhoto by Jessica Palopoli lis were showgirls in the Follies, both in failing marriages. The San Francisco cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/ to obtain tickets, or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street. John Adams’ Antony and Cleopatra premieres at SF Opera Sept. 10 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Opera presents the world premiere of Berkeley composer John Adams’ latest opera, Antony and Cleopatra, on September 10. Significantly it was chosen to open the company’s 100th season and was commissioned by San Francisco Opera for its Centennial. It is set in a universe where “ancient Egypt meets Old Hollywood.” Adams tackles the Shakespearean equivalent of a celebrity romance and gives it a 21st century spin. Amina Edris, an Egyptian lyric soprano, will sing the lead role of Cleopatra, with Canadian bass-baritone Gerald Finley as Antony. The cast also includes Paul Appleby, Alfred Walker, Elizabeth DeShong, Brenton Ryan, Taylor Raven, Hadleigh Adams, Gabrielle Beteag, Timothy Murray and Bay Area favorite Philip Skinner. The opera will be conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim. Seven performances are scheduled from September 10 to October 5 at the War Memorial Opera House. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/operas/antony-and-cleopatra/ to purchase tickets. ACT premieres Passengers on September 15 By Allyson Aleksey American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749- 2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/passengers/. articles.text: Berkeley-based violinist Dan Flanagan. Everyone knows the old joke: How do I get to Carnegie Hall? Answer: Practice! Dan Flanagan is a local violinist of notable achievement. He is going to Carnegie Hall. His path is very interesting. It even has a title: “The Bow and the Brush”. Music and art are comfortable companions. Can you picture the way Mussorgsky put music to his composition, Pictures at an Exhibition? How about the extraordinary swatches of color at the beginning of Walt Disney’s Fantasia? Long before these examples, composers were writing music that conjured up vivid imaginations. Things like The Cat’s Fugue by Scarlatti, and the songs of birds. These have always been great inspirations to musicians, artists, poets, and movie makers. To Dan Flanagan, art inspires music which inspires art. It can be the other way around too. When violinists play soli programs, they usually perform music by Bach, Telemann and Ysaye. But Flanagan’s program was completely new. He rode no war horses, but he rode to victory, nonetheless. The road to Carnegie Hall; the road to perdition Every composition was modern. I must admit that I am not always enthusiastic about contemporary music. Too many violinists these days emphasize the ugly. Flanagan always emphasizes the beautiful. And that’s the way it was from beginning to end. With playing like this, his success at Carnegie Hall is almost assured. The road to perdition An article in the Post last week presented the case for teaching music to all students. It was in the Back to Schools section on page 12 and entitled “the importance of music for students”. What I write here is a follow-up to those beautiful words. This is one teacher’s opinion on why all schools should teach music. The ancient Greeks had no problem integrating music and athletics. They even included mathematics and logic in the mix. If the ancient Greeks could do it, we can also. But our educational system is losing ground rapidly. What is the stumbling block? There is a huge difference between teachers and educators. Teachers do the teaching. Educators are not teachers. Educators must relinquish the territory they stake out. Will they be able to do it? Probably not. Therefore, the general public needs to become aware of the benefits of integrating music with other subjects and to re-educate our educators. Get them out of their offices and onto the front lines. Every kid needs to be in a music education class. They need to sing every day in elementary school. When I was teaching in San Francisco schools, I went to every classroom every week. One year I had 1200 students. We sang, learned to read music, played recorders, and knew every instrument of the orchestra. It is generally acknowledged that we are experiencing more problems all the time. Music is an acknowledged antidote. We must initiate the change ASAP. Get involved and speak up. articles.text: Come enjoy a wide range of music, art and special events throughout the year. Saturday, September 17, 7:30 p.m. Chamber Music Society of S. F. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Opus 132, String Quartet in A minor, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. In this and other late works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California is celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, in a display on view through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artists’ career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” The exhibit examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than fifty years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo by Christina Cueto A collection at Oakland Museum of California showcases Edith Heath’s ceramics.

articles.text: Elizabeth Banks and Russell Crowe in The Next Three Days. The Next Three Days is, in some ways, similar to the decidedly harrowing Unstoppable. While any comparison may seem a stretch, both films are polished B-movies with A-list actors. This represents an encouraging change. B-movies have long been the repository of second-tier talent as well as writing that lacks, well, complexity. But thankfully, this genre has experienced a renaissance of sorts over the last decade. B-movies represent, increasingly, raw and edgy filmmaking. Unlike Unstoppable, which quickly gets up to speed, The Next Three Days involves a long and complex setup. John Brennan (Russell Crowe), a local college teacher in Pittsburg, is living a nightmare. His wife, Lara (Elizabeth Banks), has been tried and convicted and recently sentenced to 20 years in prison for murder. Two years have passed since the crime. He is raising his son, with the help of his parents and trying to understand how he and his wife might ever wake up from this debilitating horror. A plan begins to take shape in John’s mind. The only alternative, he concludes, is to break Lara out of an impenetrable maximum security prison. The question is: how? Soon the wall in his dining room is filled with maps, bold notes regarding passports, escape routes, locations, times, and elaborate strategies. The wall becomes the nexus of the film and, as it fills, the tension builds. This is high risk, high gain planning and seems all but impossible from every angle. Not to forget that John is a teacher of literature and clearly unprepared to cobble together a Quixotic escape (actually, there is a nice scene where he is teaching Don Quixote to his students, something about belief in virtue is more important than virtue itself). Knowing that John is an amateur adds hugely to the sense of foreboding that gives this thriller its impetus. There is not one moment when the conclusion is foregone. This will not have a right ending. How could it? John will end up in jail along with his wife and his parents will then have to raise his son. What’s wonderful about top drawer B-movies – this one was written and directed by the highly acclaimed Paul Haggis (“Crash,” “Million Dollar Baby,” “Letters from Iwo Jima”) – is that they are focused on solving an external problem. With solid actors such as Crowe and Banks delivering exceptional performances, the entertainment payoff can be gripping. As it is in The Next Three Days. The Next Three Days. Starring Russell Crowe, Elizabeth Banks, Brian Dennehy and Liam Neeson. Directed by Paul Haggis. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13, Released in 2011. articles.text: Papa: Hemingway in Cuba was the first film shot on location in Cuba since 1959, the year that Fidel Castro came to power. The scenery is beyond beautiful, a rainbow of colors, topaz waters and classic cars. As well, many of the interior shots are actually filmed in Hemingway’s Finca Vigia, located in Havana and now a lovingly cared for museum, testimony to the Nobel and Pulitzer Prize-winning author’s prodigious talent and extraordinary life. But the promise of this film, which is never fulfilled, resides in the fact that it takes place in the late 50s (on the cusp of the Cuban revolution) when Hemingway is approaching his 59th birthday. He receives a letter from a young Miami Globe reporter, Ed Myers (Giovanni Ribisi), who shares with the aging writer how much his prose meant to him as a young person who had been abandoned by his father during the depression and grew up in a Catholic orphanage. He later went on to become a journalist and war correspondent. Not unlike Hemingway. To Myers’ surprise – initially disbelief – Hemingway calls him and thanks him for the letter and invites him to come to Cuba and go fishing. While sitting on a beach with Hemingway’s fourth wife, Mary, he tells them that he has never had a family. Hemingway (who insists on being called “Papa”) says that he and Mary will be his family. It is a moment that the young journalist could only have imagined; yet, there he is, sitting on an idyllic beach with the man who had previously only gazed back at him from a book’s dust jacket and wrote words that made all the difference. What Myers could not fully comprehend – how could he? He gazed at Hemingway through a worshipful prism – was that the renowned writer was also a mean, cruel drunk, a verbally abusive husband, and increasingly paranoid (he was convinced the F.B.I. was tailing him). He was also a man in decline. And it is that reality that is sadly missing in this film. The scaffolding of Hemingway’s life was language. Words mattered and he wrote them sparingly and beautifully. Again and again. This film needs long moments of exposition, such as discussions while sitting at dinner tables or bars or on a sunswept beach. It begs for reflection. Hemingway grappled with the reality that he was no longer the man he remembered. And he seems powerless to reframe his life, to find a path into old age that he could embrace, absent the distortions created by too much booze. Instead he sank into depression, dwelled in dark corners of regret and anger and loss and contemplated suicide seemingly daily. (He committed suicide 18 months after leaving Cuba). In one scene he puts the barrel of a gun into his mouth. This was not the man that Myers thought he was going to visit. But this was Hemingway as he approached 60. And yet the film seems unable to risk more than dwelling on Hemingway’s surface torment, absent what is behind it. Hence he says things like, “The only value we have as human beings are the risks we’re willing to take.” What does that truly mean? What was he saying about life and about himself? Clearly, the risk Hemingway was unwilling to take was that of growing old. Which may take more courage than stepping into a bullring with only a ceremonial cape and sword. Papa: Hemingway in Cuba could have been a revelation, an intimate look at the man and all of his imperfections, a man tormented by demons that formed a crucible of memories tempered by regret for all that had passed and couldn’t be changed. To my surprise, there is no mention of one of his finest and most iconic works, the elegant and beautifully written, The Old Man and the Sea – a book, a metaphor, triumphant and painful. It was his last major novel. Papa: Hemingway in Cuba. Directed by Bob Yari. Starring Adrian Sparks, Giovanni Rib, Joely Richardson. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Released in 2016. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/peacock.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, August 31, 2022 MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Next Three Days – top drawer acting by Crowe, Banks Elizabeth Banks and Russell Crowe in The Next Three Days. By Chris Honoré The Next Three Days is, in some ways, similar to the decidedly harrowing Unstoppable. While any comparison may seem a stretch, both films are polished B-movies with A-list actors. This represents an encouraging change. B-movies have long been the repository of second-tier talent as well as writing that lacks, well, complexity. But thankfully, this genre has experienced a renaissance of sorts over the last decade. B-movies represent, increasingly, raw and edgy filmmaking. Unlike Unstoppable, which quickly gets up to speed, The Next Three Days involves a long and complex setup. John Brennan (Russell Crowe), a local college teacher in Pittsburg, is living a nightmare. His wife, Lara (Elizabeth Banks), has been tried and convicted and recently sentenced to 20 years in prison for murder. Two years have passed since the crime. He is raising his son, with the help of his parents and trying to understand how he and his wife might ever wake up from this debilitating horror. A plan begins to take shape in John’s mind. The only alternative, he concludes, is to break Lara out of an impenetrable maximum security prison. The question is: how? Soon the wall in his dining room is filled with maps, bold notes regarding passports, escape routes, locations, times, and elaborate strategies. The wall becomes the nexus of the film and, as it fills, the tension builds. This is high risk, high gain planning and seems all but impossible from every angle. Not to forget that John is a teacher of literature and clearly unprepared to cobble together a Quixotic escape (actually, there is a nice scene where he is teaching Don Quixote to his students, something about belief in virtue is more important than virtue itself). Knowing that John is an amateur adds hugely to the sense of foreboding that gives this thriller its impetus. There is not one moment when the conclusion is foregone. This will not have a right ending. How could it? John will end up in jail along with his wife and his parents will then have to raise his son. What’s wonderful about top drawer B-movies – this one was written and directed by the highly acclaimed Paul Haggis (“Crash,” “Million Dollar Baby,” “Letters from Iwo Jima”) – is that they are focused on solving an external problem. With solid actors such as Crowe and Banks delivering exceptional performances, the entertainment payoff can be gripping. As it is in The Next Three Days. The Next Three Days. Starring Russell Crowe, Elizabeth Banks, Brian Dennehy and Liam Neeson. Directed by Paul Haggis. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13, Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Bill Campbell and Alan Arkin in The Rocketeer. The Rocketeer, based on the graphic novel written by Dave Stevens, should appeal to a whole new generation of kids. Sure, it’s retro, set in 1942, and carried with it the hope that it would be the beginning of a superhero franchise. Alas, for reasons that remain inexplicable, it failed to find an audience, and never caught the imagination of those kids for which it was intended. Hence, no Rocketeer II. But, after a quarter of a century since its release, strangely, after a bevy of superhero movies, its special effects and energetic story can seem fresh and compelling, even with the absence of CGI, to which kids have grown so accustomed. Set in Los Angeles. The year is 1938. The film opens with Cliff Secord (Billy Campbell), a test pilot and barnstormer, finds in his crashed bi-plane a strange looking dual rocket pack with a leather harness. He takes it to his favorite mechanic, Peevy Peabody (Alan Arkin), asking him what he can make of it. It’s only later that Cliff comes to realize that the pack was stolen from Howard Hughes (Terry O’ Quinn) by a gang of thieves (who had hidden the pack in Billy’s plane to begin with) who are led by one gangster-type named Eddie Valentine (Paul Sorvino). Predictably, not only does the U.S. government want the package, but is also being sought after by a cohort of nefarious Nazis who immediately see the potential in creating an army of rocket men using the package as a weapon to take over the U.S. Of course, Cliff and Peevy figure out how to tweak the rockets, and Cliff soon finds himself going vertical, launched into the sky. It’s a rush. And thus is born what became known as the Rocketeer. Unfortunately, the baddies (the thieves and the Nazis) hear that Cliff found the package and so begin the chase to get it back. There’s even a big thug wearing a rubber mask who works for Valentine. And there’s an exciting battle between Cliff and the Nazis on top of a zeppelin. Not surprisingly, Cliff has a gorgeous girlfriend, Jenny Blake (Jennifer Connelly), who wants to become a movie star in a film with a third-rate actor, Neville Sinclair (Timothy Dalton) who also has some designs on the rockets. However, Jenny helps cliff avoid those who are desperate to get their hands on the rockets. Even Sinclair. There are lots of special effects and excitement, car chases and gunfights. There is an Indiana Jones quality to the movie, an adventure film to this day that has stood the test of time. I have a feeling that The Rocketeer, a film reminiscent of the once popular Saturday matinees, will appeal to kids of all ages and stands up well even today. The Rocketeer. Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Bill Campbell, Jennifer Connelly and Timothy Dalton. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 1991 by Walt Disney. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Captain America: The First Avenger is, at least initially, set in New York City. The year is 1942. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and his best friend, Sgt. Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), are downtown attending a future technology exhibition, and happen to pass a military recruitment station. War is in the air, Bucky is about to ship out for Europe, and countless men are enlisting, with the exception of Steve, who suffers from asthma and weighs in at some 98 pounds. It’s not for trying that he’s not in uniform. To his chagrin he’s been rejected multiple times. As it happens, also attending the exhibition is Dr. Abraham Erskine (Stanley Rucci), a brilliant inventor and genetic scientist, working on a special “super soldier” experiment for the Strategic Scientific Reserve. The project is under the command of Col. Chester Phillips (Tommy Lee Jones). Dr. Erskine happens to overhear a conversation of regret between Bucky and Steve. Looking at the scrawny Steve , he Steve might be perfect for his special serum and what are referred to as “vita rays.” Pulling a few strings with Col. Phillips, the scientist manages to get Steve into the program. Ever hopeful, willing to try anything to enlist, he agrees. Stretched out on a table, machinery begins to hum and spark, the serum/vita rays are administered, and to his surprise, Steve emerges much taller, more muscular, with an ability to now run at a tremendous speed. In other words, he has been indeed transformed into a super soldier. Amazing at the result, the army decides to dress him in stars and striped tights, hood, provide him with a shield and send him cross-country to advertise for war bonds using the name Captain America. The best part of Captain America is the transformation of weakling Steve Rogers into his alter ego. He’s now a square-jawed, humble, even shy superhero who soon is sent out to fight for truth, justice, and the American way. Soon he confronts his uber-nemesis and Nazi provocateur, the villainous, megalomaniac Red Skull (Hugo Weaving) and his army of thugs called Hydra, all ensconced in Red Skull’s alpine forest retreat where he is conducting his own experiment: a blue-cube that will enable him to take over the world. The story is a big, bold, razzle-dazzle adventure, and has plenty of action, chase scenes, shootouts, a submarine, aircraft, and even a fight on top of a Nazi blimp, all leading to a spectacular showdown between Captain America and Red Skull. And there’s even a touch of romance between MI 16 Brit spy, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), who has been assigned to the Strategic Reserve. Kids will love this origin film, one that will soon be followed by The Avengers, introducing lots of superheroes. Stay tuned. Captain America: The First Avenger. Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, and Hugo Weaving. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now Streaming on VUDY/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: On August 21 the Family Winemakers of California held their first ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/medium size operations making under 10,000 cases per year. As I meandered through the table-filled venue I focused on small wineries with which I was unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. But the following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. These are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines in the state are created in small, unknown, out of the way places by wineries that are fueled by family love and devotion. Robert Keenan Winery is one of Napa Valley’s Cabernet pioneers. Cabernet Franc is deep garnet in color and it leaps from the glass with notes of blackberries, black cherries with hints of bay leaves and earth. Medium to full-bodied, nicely poised, very fresh and beautifully elegant, it has a solid frame of fine-grained tannins and a long, berry-laced finish. Impressive. • 2018 Elaine Pinot Noir Calypte Vineyard The Russian River AVA is famous for its complex, textured Pinot Noirs and this delicious wine is a textbook example. Concentrated yet restrained, the wine is deep, rich, and promising with blueberry and dark cherry fruits, spice and forest floor. It is a beauty with great balance and symmetry. Enriquez Muscat is a rare and enchanting wine. • 2017 Enriquez Muscat Windsor Oaks Vineyard This wine reminded me of the wonderful dry Muscats produced in France’s Alsace region. On the nose it is so floral and opulent with aromas of honeysuckle and gardenias that you think it is going to be a sweet wine. But on the palate, you get citrus lemon and lime and apple, and the finish is totally dry and clean. Unfortunately, it is rare to find Muscats like this in the U.S. It would be a perfect partner with Asian food of all kinds. • 2018 Keenan Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve This is the 42nd vintage for Robert Keenan Winery – one of the true pioneers in classic Napa Cabernet. This blend of 95% Cabernet Sauvignon and 5% Oakville Ranch is a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. • 2015 Oakville Ranch This is Oakville Ranch’s signature wine, a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. A brilliant wine, it unwinds in the glass with aromas of cassis, dark berries, and cigar box mingled with subtle hints of loamy soil. Full-bodied, deep and concentrated, it’s seamless and exquisitely balanced, with beautifully refined tannins, bright acids and a long, penetrating finish. The wine is impressively endowed, with a dark purple hue and intense bouquet of cassis sprinkled with aromas of chocolate and herbs. Full-bodied and extracted viscous flavors that exhibits great ripeness this structured full-throttle Cabernet Sauvignon is built to last for decades in the cellar. Worth seeking out. • 2018 Ehret Cabernet Sauvignon Hillside Reserve This Knights Valley Cab exhibits an opaque, purple/black color, a huge nose of black raspberries, minerals, and smoke, as well as exceptional concentration and expansiveness on the palate. One of the most concentrated, well-balanced Cabernets I have recently tasted, it has potential to last for at least two decades. • 2019 Hawk and Horse Petite Verdot This Petite Verdot has a very fragrant nose with macerated black cherries and crème de cassis enveloped in a veneer of creamy oak that does not impede the fruit. The palate is full-bodied with a salacious dark, creamy cassis and chocolate-tinged fruit on the entry. It is beautifully balanced, with a long, sensual finish that demonstrates just what this esoteric variety can do in the right hands. It should last for 15 years in the cellar. • 2018 Nove Malbec Hailing from Lake County, the deep colored Nove Malbec offers excellent sweetness, medium body, fine purity, and ripe fruit in both the mid-palate and the finish. This big creamy blackberry fruitball will drink well for 7 to 8 years. • 2015 Brooklyn West Tempranillo This Rioja styled wine is made from fruit from the Sierra foothills. Crimson-colored, it presents aromas of smoke, spice box, roses, leather and cherry. Elegant on the palate in a racy style, the Robert Keenan Winery is one of Napa Valley’s Cabernet pioneers. Cabernet Franc is deep garnet in color and it leaps from the glass with notes of blackberries, black cherries with hints of bay leaves and earth. Medium to full-bodied, nicely poised, very fresh and beautifully elegant, it has a solid frame of fine-grained tannins and a long, berry-laced finish. Impressive. • 2018 Elaine Pinot Noir Calypte Vineyard The Russian River AVA is famous for its complex, textured Pinot Noirs and this delicious wine is a textbook example. Concentrated yet restrained, the wine is deep, rich, and promising with blueberry and dark cherry fruits, spice and forest floor. It is a beauty with great balance and symmetry. fruit is balanced by lively acidity and the flavors are ripe and savory. With 7 years of age, it’s drinking perfectly now and cries out for a nice paella. • 2017 Greyscale Cabernet Sauvignon Deep garnet-purple colored the Greyscale Cabernet from Rutherford AVA opens with profound black and red currant cordial notes over an undercurrent of spices, chargrill, earth and bay leaves. Medium-bodied with wonderful intensity and depth in the mouth, it has a firm frame of tannins and compelling freshness finishing long and layered. • 2018 Sarah’s Vineyard Syrah Besson Vineyard A dynamite effort, the saturated, opaque, purple-colored Sarah’s Vineyard Syrah offers aromas of bacon fat, mocha, licorice and blueberries. This full-bodied unctuously-textured, stunningly rich, robust Syrah is tremendously satisfying. Quite youthful, it promises to age gracefully for 10-15 years. • 2018 Ladera Cabernet Sauvignon This cuvee was assembled with grapes from various vineyards on Atlas Peak, Howell Mountain, and Calistoga. It is wonderfully supple and fragrant. Silky tannins frame a core of expressive plum and blackberry fruit. Floral and spice notes are nicely woven throughout. This textured, balanced, gracious Cabernet Sauvignon should continue to age gracefully for at least 15 years. • 2019 Justin Isosceles Hailing from Paso Robles, Justin’s Isosceles is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot. The wine reveals vibrant cassis, plum, and raspberry notes with a hint of damp soil, cedar and a waft of lavender. Full bodied with plenty of lively crunchy black and red fruits, this big boy packs over 16% alcohol but in no way seems hot or clumsy. It has a firm frame of grainy tannins and a long, youthful finish. Give it another few years in the cellar and drink over the next two decades. • 2018 Aphelion Tempranillo Produced by the Sakura Winery in Livermore, the Aphelion Tempranillo reminds me of the great Pesquera wines from Spain’s Ribero del Duero. It is purple-colored with an expressive perfume of earth, leather, spice box and blackberry. Layered on the palate, it has ample savory fruit, good richness and 3-5 years of cellaring potential. • 2020 Landmark Vineyards Chardonnay Damaris Reserve The Landmark Damaris Reserve Chardonnay reveals notes of lemons, lime cordial and fresh peaches with touches of honeysuckle. Medium to full-bodied, the palate is sporting oak-inspired flavors, complementing the citrus and stone fruit layers, finishing long and refreshing. • 2019 Glunz Zinfandel Dante Dusi Vineyard This Paso Robles vineyard is one of the state’s most famous Zinfandel hot spots. The Glunz Zin unfurls scents of blueberries, pepper, charcuterie and herbs. The full-bodied palate explodes with spicy fruits, offering powerful yet defined flavors, light tannins, bright acidity and a very long, mineral-driven finish. This would be great with some BBQ pork ribs. • 2021 Navarro Gewurtztraminer Cuvee Traditional This is a classic dry Alsatian style Gewurtz from legendary Navarro winery in the Anderson Valley. it has aromas of lychees, tropical fruit cocktail and roses with a hint of allspice. Medium to full-bodied and dry on the palate, it packs tropical fruit and spicy flavors with enough refreshing acidity to balance, finishing long and savory. • 2017 Blair Estate Pinot Noir The Reserve This Pinot Noir comes from Monterey County and is the premier bottling of Blair Winery. It sports a beautiful nose of potpourri, orange peel, granite and lavender with blueberries and dark cherries. The medium-bodied palate offers good concentration of perfumed fruits, a sturdy frame and juicy freshness to lift the long finish. Can’t imagine a better partner to grilled salmon. • 2017 Cabana Petite Sirah Lodi is the home of this sumptuous Petite Sirah. It has an opaque purple color and aromas of plums, chocolate, violets, and herbs. Full-bodied, it floods the mouth with luscious, spicy fruits with a chewy frame but great acidity to counter, finishing long and unexpectedly elegant. Try with a grilled rib eye steak. • Rack and Riddle North Coast Sparkling Rose At a retail price of $22 this sparkler is a good value. It has a luscious nose of strawberry and melon. In the mouth it is bright and cheerful with very small bubbles and a refreshing bone-dry finish. A perfect companion on a warm summer afternoon. Enriquez Muscat is a rare and enchanting wine. • 2017 Enriquez Muscat Windsor Oaks Vineyard This wine reminded me of the wonderful dry Muscats produced in France’s Alsace region. On the nose it is so floral and opulent with aromas of honeysuckle and gardenias that you think it is going to be a sweet wine. But on the palate, you get citrus lemon and lime and apple, and the finish is totally dry and clean. Unfortunately, it is rare to find Muscats like this in the U.S. It would be a perfect partner with Asian food of all kinds. • 2018 Keenan Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve This is the 42nd vintage for Robert Keenan Winery – one of the true pioneers in classic Napa Cabernet. This blend of 95% Cabernet Sauvignon and 5% Oakville Ranch is a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. • 2015 Oakville Ranch This is Oakville Ranch’s signature wine, a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. A brilliant wine, it unwinds in the glass with aromas of cassis, dark berries, and cigar box mingled with subtle hints of loamy soil. Full-bodied, deep and concentrated, it’s seamless and exquisitely balanced, with beautifully refined tannins, bright acids and a long, penetrating finish. Its structural refinement is such that it’s delicious to drink now, yet patience will be rewarded. • 2018 Frog’s Tooth Alicante Bouchet I was delighted to discover that Frog’s Tooth had bottled one ADVERTISE IN THE POST You know she loves her morning walk, struggles to take her medicine on time, and is fiercely independent. We’ll know that, too. WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. articles.text: You probably won’t see it on your calendar, but September is Life Insurance Awareness Month. And it is indeed important to be aware of the importance of life insurance. Are you adequately insured? Many people aren’t. About 40% of Americans face some type of life insurance gap, either because they’re uninsured or underinsured, according to a 2021 survey by the research and advocacy groups LIMRA and Life Happens. The need for life insurance is pretty straightforward: If something were to happen to you, would your family be able to continue their same lifestyle? Would the mortgage still be paid? Would your children still be able to further their education? So, if you decide that you should acquire or strengthen your life insurance, how much do you need? Your employer may provide you with some insurance as an employee benefit, but it may not be sufficient. You might have heard that you should have coverage worth seven or eight times your annual salary. But this estimate is just that — an estimate. Everyone’s situation is different, and there’s really no one formula that can tell you how much insurance you require. To determine the coverage you need, you’ll want to consider several factors, including your age, number of dependents, your income and that of your spouse and the size of your mortgage. Knowing how much coverage you need is obviously important, but you’ll also want to consider what type of life insurance is right for you. You have two basic choices: term or permanent insurance. As the name suggests, term insurance provides coverage for a specified amount of time, such as 10, 20 or 25 years. Term insurance only offers a death benefit — there’s no buildup of cash value in your policy. Generally speaking, term insurance is considered to be quite affordable, especially when you’re young. Permanent insurance, on the other hand, offers a death benefit and the opportunity to build cash value. Because of this, premiums for permanent insurance – which includes “whole life” or “universal life” – are considerably higher than those for term life. Which type of insurance should you choose? articles.text: What makes piano music “classical?” Piedmont Adult School is offering a new course, Classical Piano Appreciation, for anyone interested in expanding their knowledge of this important genre. Students will learn what elements define classical music and how the piano has evolved to remain relevant in the 300 years since invention. They will become familiar with the most famous composers and pianists and their best-known works, as well as the misconceptions and misunderstandings about classical piano music. The class will be discussion-based and responsive to specific student interests. Piano experience is welcome but not required. Instructor Daniel Finnamore has taught piano lessons for 47 years, beginning with the Oakland Conservatory, located in the historic Sherman and Clay Building in downtown Oakland. Piedmonters may know Daniel Finnamore, the instructor of the new course Classical Piano Appreciation, from his performance at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in 2014. He made his public solo debut at age 20. His San Francisco debut, a benefit concert for the Liszt Society, was favorably reviewed by future Time magazine music critic Michael Walsh. Daniel has made five CDs of piano music by Brahms, Debussy, Liszt and various classical Spanish composers. He performed a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in December 2014.

Some financial experts advise people to “buy term and invest the difference” – that is, use the money saved on the lower term insurance premiums to invest in stocks and mutual funds. Insurance can even play a role in your estate planning, as you determine the best way to distribute assets to your family members and any charitable organizations you support. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 32 walkers and one K-9 best friend. They admitted that they find the local real estate market pretty interesting. There are currently a number of beautiful homes for sale in Piedmont. Eight homes with listing prices ranging from $2,450,000 to $18,500,000 could be walked in a loop that would take the group to the top of Glen Alpine Road, a great street that the walkers hadn’t been to this year. There was some elevation gain, but anyone not wanting to climb to the top could peel off at Hampton Park. There was also some Piedmont history associated with this walk. The walkers headed off for the first house at 21 King Avenue by going up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Lincoln Avenues, and turning down King. About midway down the street they spotted a Sold sign. It. The home was built in 1925, and. The group had fun making guesses on this 4 bedroom/3 bath, 3760 square foot home’s listing price, which was $3,250,000. The group retraced its steps back to Lincoln and went up to Sea View Avenue. Turning right, they came to 70 Sea View. a 5 bedroom/7 bath, 7,162 square foot home designed by Claude B. Barton and built in 1923 on roughly 1 acre. The group also made their guesses on the listing price, which is $10,800,000. Continuing on Sea View they passed more beautiful homes, including two having construction work done. The walkers then turned up Hampton Road to view the house at 395 Hampton, known historically as Hampton House. It is a 1928 Albert Farr-designed, 8 bedroom/9 bath, 11,150 square foot mansion on .93 acres and has an ADU next door at 1 Glen Alpine Road. At $18,500,000, this was the walking tour’s highest listed priced home and a spot worthy of the attached group photo. At the top of Glen Alpine was another Albert Farr mansion, 75 Glen Alpine. It is a 5 bedroom/8 bath, 11,938 square foot, French revival chateau built in 1926 on 1.62 acres, and listed for $11,500,000. It’s an impressive home, sitting at the top of this impressive street. Will Adams, who is a planner, urban designer, and architect, and writes regular “Walking Piedmont” articles in the Post, made some comments on Farr’s exterior design. In 1914 James Tyson, a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman, purchased 30 acres here to build his estate, which he named “Oakmont.” The property is house is now 70 Sotelo, but the Oakmont mansion was demolished in 1964. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife could live temporarily while supervising the construction of their new home, which was completed in 1916. This carriage house is the lovely home at 45 Glen Alpine that the walkers passed on the way up the hill. To the right of 75 Glen Alpine are Tyson’s original, two sandstone pillars which marked the entrance to the long driveway to Tyson’s now-gone mansion. The walkers descended on Sotelo Avenue, which forms half of the loop road above Tyson Lake, another Tyson creation. After he built Oakmont he dammed a small creek that ran through his property and created this reservoir, which is now owned and managed by a neighborhood association. The house at 7 Sotelo provided another surprise. This is a 3 bedroom/3 bath, 2,945 square foot home built in 1948. It was the first time this home was on the market, as it was built for the great grandparents of the sellers. At a listing price of “only” $2,750,000, it seemed like a bargain to the walkers. Everyone had enjoyed the walking tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to return to the center of town. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers pause for a photo in front of 395 Hampton Road on August 24. Pictured are Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Pat Keller, Martin Levy, Alan Goldhammer, Renee Goldhammer, Noemi Alvarado, Harriette Louie, Melba Yee, Stella Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Adrienne Hamlin, Christine Calliste, Bob Wong, Charlene Louie, Will Adams, Albert Chen, Tracy Lee, Sarah Johnson, Karin Fetherston, Shirley Nakao, Edith Lee, Gloria DaSilva, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, Lisa Euphrat, Elane Rehr, Jim Kuo, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Bill Ahern.

Will Adams, who is a planner, urban designer, and architect, and writes regular “Walking Piedmont” articles in the Post, made some comments on Farr’s exterior design. In 1914 James Tyson, a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman, purchased 30 acres here to build his estate, which he named “Oakmont.” The property is house is now 70 Sotelo, but the Oakmont mansion was demolished in 1964. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife could live temporarily while supervising the construction of their new home, which was completed in 1916. This carriage house is the lovely home at 45 Glen Alpine that the walkers passed on the way up the hill. To the right of 75 Glen Alpine are Tyson’s original, two sandstone pillars which marked the entrance to the long driveway to Tyson’s now-gone mansion. The walkers descended on Sotelo Avenue, which forms half of the loop road above Tyson Lake, another Tyson creation. After he built Oakmont he dammed a small creek that ran through his property and created this reservoir, which is now owned and managed by a neighborhood association. The house at 7 Sotelo provided another surprise. This is a 3 bedroom/3 bath, 2,945 square foot home built in 1948. It was the first time this home was on the market, as it was built for the great grandparents of the sellers. At a listing price of “only” $2,750,000, it seemed like a bargain to the walkers. Everyone had enjoyed the walking tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to return to the center of town. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Your son and his partner are having a baby. You’re very excited and can’t wait to hear whether it’s a boy or a girl. They must be dying to know, too, so you’re certain that they will take advantage of the earliest medical tests available to determine the baby’s sex. Of course, they will. Wait, what? Your son tells you that he and his partner have chosen not to learn the sex of the baby before birth. OK, that’s fine. They just like surprises, right? It will be exciting to learn when the baby is delivered. Wrong again. You’re stunned to learn that the expectant parents will not be sharing the baby’s sex before birth, nor will they announce this bit of information after the baby arrives. Like a growing group of parents, they believe that assigning sex at birth is wrong, that every child should be able to discover their own gender identity for themselves, and that they should be allowed to express that identity freely in any way that they choose. What is meant by gender identity? For an excellent explanation of this term and others, please visit www.thinkorblue.com. assigned by a medical professional at a baby’s birth depending on the visual inspection of the newborn’s genitals. Gender identity is often defined as how a person perceives their own gender – whether they feel that they are male or female. This is something that a person learns about themselves over time and is not something that can be determined by others. Today’s parents are raising families in a world that in many ways bears no resemblance to the one in which you raised your children. Terms such as gay and lesbian may be familiar to you, while genderqueer, cis & trans, transgender, transmasculine, transfeminine, gender non-conforming, non-binary, gender-neutral, gender-fluid, etc., may not be. Yet these are likely to be common words in your children’s vocabulary, and the sooner you learn their accurate definitions, the better. Almost every family will have a loved one who identifies outside the stereotypical gender norms. If you have not yet experienced this in your family, you probably will one day. As you watch your adult children raising their families, keep in mind that it’s their turn. How you respond to your children and your grandchildren’s perspectives and lived experiences around the issue of gender identity is no different than anything else. Be open to what your loved ones feel and believe, no matter how much it may differ from your own beliefs. Lovingly support the free expression of their inner selves and think before assuming stereotypical gender roles for them. Be the first one to let them know they are loved just the way they are. The communities in which we live may take a long time to bring equity and inclusion to all persons. But you can begin this process of loving acceptance at home even before your grandchild is born.
