articles.text: A professional caregiver can become like a member of the family over time as they provide meaningful home care services when some are at their most vulnerable. However, they likely start out as a stranger to not only the person who is receiving care but also that person’s family. Here are five ways to break the ice and get to know your caregiver better so that caregiving becomes familiar and builds a stronger relationship. 1. Ask them how they became a caregiver. Often people get into the caregiving business after caring for a loved one at one home and seeing the profound impact of one-on-one care for someone who is recovering from a surgery, living with the symptoms of a chronic condition, or just adjusting to changing abilities with age. This might spark a conversation about different jobs you had in life. The key to building any lasting relationship is sharing, so if they seem shy, take the first step and talk about any caregiving experiences of your own. 2. Find out about their skills. Feel free to ask if they have done any meal preparation before if that’s something you or your loved one might need. Or ask if they have experience in caring for someone with a specific condition such as dementia, Parkinson’s Disease, diabetes, or something else. Caregivers may attend to many clients for short visits or work with just one client each day over a few years, so backgrounds and experience will vary. 3. Do they have hobbies? Everyone has something they are interested in outside of what they get paid to do, even if it’s a favorite TV show they watch regularly or talking with a relative at a predictable day and time. Care can be a two-way street with one person receiving and one person giving, but it is best when each person gets something out of it. Maybe you both love antique cars and go to a local museum or car show and share knowledge with one another. You may like the same TV show and watch it together or discuss the latest plot points and characters. These commonalities are a way to develop a bond outside of the tasks they are there to perform. 4. What information goes into the plan of care? A plan of care is a record of the tasks completed as well as details about someone’s preferences, so that their care can be customized as needs change. With a person-directed approach to care, it can be helpful to know how often this information is updated as it might inform how much or how little care is needed. Home care services evolve with needs, as well as preferences, so when the caregiver can be open about what notes they are sharing, it strengthens the back-andforth of this dynamic. 5. How do they handle challenges? In the best-case scenario home care is arranged in order to help prevent emergencies, but life happens. Making sure your caregiver has basic CPR and First Aid training can be a great help in the event of emergencies. If you or a loved one is living with a condition in which there are challenges with swallowing, for example, choking should be something that the caregiver should be trained to handle. Since each person is unique, this means that the caregivers have their own strengths and weaknesses when they come work. Good communication is key to most relationships. Caregiving is oftentimes a hybrid relationship spanning elements of professional and personal lives. And know that while sometimes a caregiver may be perfectly trained, they may not be a good fit. It’s okay to try someone else if the match is not there. Look for those soft traits, such as common interests or similar backgrounds, that can overcome differences in age or gender. For more information and ideas, contact Homewatch CareGivers, locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.

Dear MacMama: When my neighbor set up my new iMac, he asked me if I would like to use iCloud to back up my files. What does that exactly mean? I think my contacts and calendars are on iCloud already. Lissa D., Oakland Dear Lissa: iCloud, Apple’s proprietary sync and storage system has been around in one form or another for several years. If you have more than one device, meaning your iMac, an iPhone and an iPad, making sure that your contacts and calendars are synced with iCloud makes things easier to keep all devices current. For instance, if you change an address on your phone, it is automatically changed on all other devices that have iCloud enabled. iCloud can also back up and synchronize your photos. In this case, your entire photo library is backed up in iCloud. Meaning that if your computer is lost, stolen, or just breaks, your photos are safe. To enable iCloud, you sign into your device with your Apple ID (which is your iCloud account) and password, and through the settings, check the items that you want synced. iCloud also has the possibility of storing and backing up your documents and the items on your desktop. When this is enabled, you can access the files in your documents folder and on your desktop from any device that is also signed into your iCloud account. This means that you can access your desktop files from your phone, iPad, or a web browser like Safari. You simply would go to icloud.com, sign in with your Apple/iCloud ID and password, and then access your photos, files, contacts, etc. Or on your phone or iPad, go to Files to find your stuff. In most cases, if you want to store and back up most of the items on your computer on iCloud, you would have to increase the free storage amount that you get when you have an Apple ID, which is 5 GB. So, then you would sign up for what is called iCloud plus to increase the storage. Offered first in 2017, the costs for extra storage are quite reasonable, $.99 a month for up to 50 GB, and $2.99 a month for up to 200 GB. You can even get 2 TB for $9.99. And with a good back up plan, meaning a time machine back up, this cloud backup gives you extra safety and redundancy. I know sometimes clients are worried about the safety of cloud back up, but Apple uses industry standard methods for securing data in iCloud. When they first came out with the ability to back up photos and data, there were definitely a few bumps in the road, but I feel good enough about it to do it with my own data. Of course, it can be daunting to incorporate a new system of backing up to the cloud, but so much is stored in the cloud by our banks, Social Security the IRS, and other organizations that require security. And in our area where earthquakes are reality, and fires are a danger, cloud back up just makes sense. Google Drive, Dropbox, and Microsoft One Drive are other examples of cloud storage and back up possibilities. In reality I use iCloud, Dropbox and Google Drive seamlessly. Drop box in google drive are excellent, but no replacement for iCloud which offers benefits not available on the other services, like syncing all of your Apple devices. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com. articles.text: Piedmont Seniors outside the Charles Schultz Museum in Santa Rosa: (front) Larry Singer and Gregory Jurin (left); (middle) Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Tanya Hu, Carol Jones, Yorkman Lowe, Mona Jamieson, Sandra Curach, Pati Singer, Irene Westler; (back) Susan McCreary Elene Manolis, Penny Robb, Larry Hu, Janet Epstein, Not pictured: Jim Ayotte. On a beautiful, sunny June day 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors group visited the Charles Schultz Museum and the Luther Burbank Home & Gardens in Santa Rosa. This year is memorable: it marks 100 years since the birth of Charles Schultz, aka “Sparky”, the cartoonist of the comic strip Peanuts. He was born in Minnesota in 1922 and knew from an early age that he wanted to draw “funny pictures”. His comic strips have appeared in over 2600 newspapers worldwide and his books have been translated into 25 languages. Schultz wanted to name his strips “L’ll folks” but there was concern about possible copyright infringement with a cartoon called Little Folks by Tack Knight published in the 1930s. Schulz suggested Charlie Brown or Good Ol’ Charlie Brown, but the syndicate decided upon Peanuts. The name “Peanuts” was likely chosen because it was a well-known term for children at the time, popularized by the live television program “Howdy Doody Show” with an audience section for children called “the Peanut Gallery”. The Schultz Museum is very modern and inviting. The museum even has a theatre, where one can look at the posted schedule on the wall and then choose to watch films which rotate on a regular basis. The Piedmont Seniors were fortunate to have a wonderful and knowledgeable docent who had a wealth of information about Schultz and his endeavors. Schultz most identified with Charlie, a boy who never caught or kicked the football, but kept trying. Schultz created over 70 distinct characters in the Peanuts strip. Schultz most likely had a beloved blanket, much like Linus, and, let’s face it, who doesn’t know someone like the bossy Lucy? The characters are based upon Schultz’s own experiences. He once said, “almost all of the characters are mine, including the wishy-washiness of Charles and the sarcasm of Lucy”. The beauty of the comic strip is that it is timeless and appeals to people of all age. When the tour was over, the group headed across the street to the Warm Puppy Café for reserved box lunches, in a relaxed outdoor setting. There is a large, inviting gift shop also on the property with something for everybody. You can even see Snoopy’s World War One Sopwith Camel airplane hanging from the store’s ceiling as Snoopy pretends his doghouse is the airplane used to fight the Red Baron. The last stop before returning home was a visit to Luther Burbank’s Home and Gardens, also in Santa Rosa. Just a short distance from the Schultz Museum, the Burbank museum is a step back in time. It is a city park containing the gardens, greenhouse, home and grave of one of the most famous American horticulturists. Visitors can see how Burbank lived from 1906 until his death in 1926. Burbank was so famous that Arbor Day is celebrated on March 7 in honor of his birthday. He became an early media celebrity as he welcomed visitors from around the world to his home and gardens. Burbank introduced hundreds of new plant varieties, including his famous spineless cactus. The trip is certainly worth the 1-hour drive to see all of Burbank’s accomplishments. Tours are available for his house and gardens where o can learn about horticulture as well as his gardening experiments with fruit trees as well as plants. The Piedmont Seniors had a wonderful day learning about two famous people who contributed so much to the history of Sonoma County. The Doctor is In: Mona Jamieson and Penny Robb. Charles Shultz with his famous cartoon characters Charlie Brown, Lucy, and Snoopy at the Hollywood Star of Fame.

articles.text: At the August 24 School Board Meeting Piedmont Unified School District will recommend the hiring of Anne Valva as the new Beach School Principal. Valva has been a fifth grade and math intervention teacher at Beach since 2013. If her appointment is ratified tonight by the board, she will begin her tenure tomorrow Thursday, August 25. Valva is set to replace Michael Corritone, who had his final day at Beach August 19 and now is the principal at a Walnut Creek Elementary School. Commenting on her teaching experience, Valva said, “My past 23 years of teaching in multiple grade levels in four districts and holding diverse leadership positions in Piedmont have prepared me to take on this challenge. I would like parents to know that all of my own children graduated from Piedmont schools and that I feel like I am part of the community.” PUSD Experience 2017- Present | Math Intervention Specialist, Beach School 2013-2017 | Fifth Grade Teacher, Beach School 2011-2013 | Fifth Grade Teacher, Havens School Education and Degrees UC Riverside | M.A. Education - Curriculum and Instruction, Tier I Administrative Credential UC Riverside | Clear Multiple Subject Teaching Credential UCLA | B.A. Economics On August 1 when Corritone announced his departure, the school district posted the open position for Beach Principal on Photo courtesy of PUSD Anne Valva is expected to be confirmed as the new Beach School Principal at tonight’s School Board meeting, August 24.

articles.text: Piedmont teachers gathered outside their school sites during student drop-off on Tuesday morning, August 23, to bring awareness to their upcoming salary negotiations with the school district, scheduled for Monday, August 29. Teachers are pleading for salary increases to help them cope with 9% inflation and the difficulty of being able to afford living in the Bay Area. At all Piedmont school sites teachers demonstrated their support by wearing red and waving signs asking for community support. A similar rally was held at schools last spring. Salary negotiations between the Association of Piedmont Teachers, the teachers’ union, and the district office broke off in May 2022 with no agreement. Teachers returned to their classrooms this fall without any salary increase. The last two years have seen record numbers of teachers resigning in Piedmont, including one who resigned just days before the start of this school year because other districts offered $30,000 more than Piedmont’s salary. Over the summer Piedmont School District’s budget showed a surplus of $2,200,000 as the state of California projected a record $128 billion going to schools. Historically, Piedmont teachers receive small raises typically 1-3%, but this year their message is loud and clear: larger action is needed. A teacher shortage throughout the state has existed for nearly three years, since the start of the pandemic. Many Piedmont teachers see the issue as simple economics: the increase in demand should increase their value. Middle school teachers prior to the start of the school day rallied in front of the school to highlight the need for teacher raises.
articles.title: Teachers rally for raises ahead of Monday’s salary negotiations

articles.text: PRFO campaign aims to close construction funding gap The city of Piedmont will launch a campaign focused on funding 20 heat pumps required to heat the new Piedmont Community Pool using electricity. The city council approved the authorization to proceed with fundraising efforts at an August 15 meeting. “Cost estimates have held steady since the significant design revisions undertaken in March to combat construction hyperinflation. Based on council direction in May… we will proceed with an all-electric facility,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. The overall estimated construction funding gap is $2.1 million. “When we add in all the safety maintenance and competitive equipment, as a well as a timing scoreboard and sports lighting, we are projecting a total potential funding gap of $2.6 million to deliver the community pool facility,” Lillevand said. “These are projections based on estimates, and we won’t know the real costs until we open [construction firm] bids in six to eight weeks.” Funding for the project will primarily come from Measure UU General Obligations Bonds; to front the added costs, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) is ready to launch a robust community pool fundraising campaign with donor levels and potential naming opportunities within the facility, Lillevand explained. “This has the potential to close the entire funding gap,” she said. articles.text: Only 32 recognized across the nation In a ceremony in the courtyard of Piedmont Community Church on August 18, longtime Piedmont resident and active Scout participant Anne-Marie Lamarche received one of the highest honors that can be bestowed upon a volunteer in Scouting, the illustrious Silver Antelope Award. Only two volunteers are recognized from the territory annually and only 32 throughout the country. The Silver Antelope recognizes adult Scouters whose work affects Scouting at the territory level. Piedmont is in Territory 3 which covers all of California and Hawaii. Valva has been a fifth grade and math intervention teacher at Beach since 2013. If her appointment is ratified tonight by the board, she will begin her tenure tomorrow Thursday, August 25. Valva is set to replace Michael Corritone, who had his final day at Beach August 19 and now is the principal at a Walnut Creek Elementary School. Commenting on her teaching experience, Valva said, “My past 23 years of teaching in multiple grade levels in four districts and holding diverse leadership positions in Piedmont have prepared me to take on this challenge. I would like parents to know that all of my own children graduated from Piedmont schools and that I feel like I am part of the community.” PUSD Experience 2017- Present | Math Intervention Specialist, Beach School 2013-2017 | Fifth Grade Teacher, Beach School 2011-2013 | Fifth Grade Teacher, Havens School Education and Degrees UC Riverside | M.A. Education - Curriculum and Instruction, Tier I Administrative Credential UC Riverside | Clear Multiple Subject Teaching Credential UCLA | B.A. Economics On August 1 when Corritone announced his departure, the school district posted the open position for Beach Principal on See Anne Valva on page 29 Photo courtesy of PUSD Anne Valva is expected to be confirmed as the new Beach School Principal at tonight’s School Board meeting, August 24. Piedmont High School teachers bring their message of a needed salary increase to parents’ attention at dropoff on Tuesday, August 23. Teachers rally for raises ahead of Monday’s salary negotiations By Jay Russell Piedmont teachers gathered outside their school sites during student drop-off on Tuesday morning, August 23, to bring awareness to their upcoming salary negotiations with the school district, scheduled for Monday, August 29. Teachers are pleading for salary increases to help them cope with 9% inflation and the difficulty of being able to afford living in the Bay Area. At all Piedmont school sites teachers demonstrated their support by wearing red and waving signs asking for community support. A similar rally was held at schools last spring. Salary negotiations between the Association of Piedmont Teachers, the teachers’ union, and the district office broke off in May 2022 with no agreement. Teachers returned to their classrooms this fall without any salary increase. The last two years have seen record numbers of teachers resigning in Piedmont, including one who resigned just days before the start of this school year because other districts offered $30,000 more than Piedmont’s salary. Over the summer Piedmont School District’s budget showed a surplus of $2,200,000 as the state of California projected a record $128 billion going to schools. Historically, Piedmont teachers receive small raises typically 1-3%, but this year their message is loud and clear: larger action is needed. A teacher shortage throughout the state has existed for nearly three years, since the start of the pandemic. Many Piedmont teachers see the issue as simple economics: the increase in demand should increase their value. INSIDE City launches fundraising efforts for all-electric pool PRFO campaign aims to close construction funding gap By Allyson Aleksey The city of Piedmont will launch a campaign focused on funding 20 heat pumps required to heat the new Piedmont Community Pool using electricity. The city council approved the authorization to proceed with fundraising efforts at an August 15 meeting. “Cost estimates have held steady since the significant design revisions undertaken in March to combat construction hyperinflation. Based on council direction in May… we will proceed with an all-electric facility,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. The overall estimated construction funding gap is $2.1 million. “When we add in all the safety maintenance and competitive equipment, as a well as a timing scoreboard and sports lighting, we are projecting a total potential funding gap of $2.6 million to deliver the community pool facility,” Lillevand said. “These are projections based on estimates, and we won’t know the real costs until we open [construction firm] bids in six to eight weeks.” Funding for the project will primarily come from Measure UU General Obligations Bonds; to front the added costs, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) is ready to launch a robust community pool fundraising campaign with donor levels and potential naming opportunities within the facility, Lillevand explained. “This has the potential to close the entire funding gap,” she said. articles.text: Drought is an urgent issue for Piedmont Editor: The city of Piedmont is making an effort to reduce the city’s carbon footprint, which is commendable. However, there is a more urgent and immediate issue we’re not addressing, and that is the drought. I believe the city should start a campaign urging people to reduce their water consumption and the wasteful use of water. Looking around, you see more lawns in Piedmont than anywhere in other East Bay cities. I know it’s not up to Piedmont to set limits – that’s up to EBMUD and the state – but as responsible citizens we must realize how critical it is to save water, and not just by putting bricks in our toilet tanks. At the very least, reduce the number of days you water those lawns, and lower the amount of water per day. If you see water running down the street, you’re watering too much. If you see your neighbors watering too much, consider saying something about it. Even better, remove lawns and replace them with native plants, which use far less water, and attract native insects and birds. We should acknowledge that we live in a partial desert. Consider creating dry gardens with succulents and cacti. I realize that, even if EBMUD raises rates for overuse, many of us in Piedmont can afford to pay whatever it costs to keep those lush green lawns. But we must think of others less fortunate and help reduce our wasteful use of water before severe quotas are mandated for everybody. A number of towns and counties in the North Bay are close to running out of water. The Colorado River and the two largest reservoirs it supplies are running at the lowest levels in history. Even Los Angeles with its thousands of swimming pools, may have to initiate water rationing. – Ken Greenberg Piedmont

articles.text: An algal bloom in Lake Merritt prompted Oakland Public Works Department to post warning signs along the lakeshore near the 1200 to 1400 blocks of Lakeshore Avenue on August 4. The agency warned the public that low levels of contaminants associated with the algal bloom have been discovered and cautioned pedestrians, children and pets to stay away from the water. On August 4, Oakland Public Works received a report from a concerned resident of brownish red water in the lake. “The reddish color of the material in the water indicates it could be a Cyanobacteria bloom, also known as a harmful algal bloom, which can produce toxins that are harmful to humans and animals,” the agency said in a press release. “Oakland Public Works staff are conducting additional inspection of the area and will submit a report to the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board.” Oakland city staff have confirmed that ongoing testing will continue. The most recent scheduled testing date was Monday, August 22. The algal bloom is potentially caused by increased inputs of nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers and human or animal wastes, low water flows, stagnant water, increased intensity and duration of sunlight, and sustained high temperatures, the City of Oakland explained in a press release, adding that current research suggests that the rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns caused by climate change are a catalyst for their growth. The Alameda County Environmental Health Department issued a similar warning. “It is highly recommended that people and their pets stay out of the water until the blooms dissipate,” said the Alameda County Environmental Health Department in a statement. “Contact with the algae blooms can cause skin irritation and burning eyes to humans and can cause more dangerous effects to dogs.” The algal phenomenon is occurring throughout the Bay Area, said San Francisco Baykeeper Executive Director Sejal Choksi-Chugh. San Francisco Baykeeper is an environmental group based in Oakland that has investigated marine pollution in the Bay and its watershed since 1989. The group’s team of lawyers, scientists, and environmental activists have worked to strengthen laws that protect Bay Area waters and hold polluters accountable. Choksi-Chugh explained that, after conducting tests of impacted areas, that the algal bloom is caused by a bacteria known as Heterosigma akashiwo. “Our scientists have been monitoring the situation and are in communication with relevant agencies and researchers. Both the California Department of Public Health and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration have identified the dominant algal species forming the bloom as Heterosigma akashiwo– a species known to form ‘red tides’,” said Choksi-Chugh. “The US Geological Service and San Francisco Estuary Institute report high densities of H. akashiwo further south, as far as Newark.” The algal bloom in Lake Merritt and the Oakland Estuary extends across the East Bay’s shoreline, including to the Richmond and Berkeley marinas and the Albany Bulb, San Francisco, and into the South Bay. Although the City of Oakland has not yet released the findings of its August 22 test, the city and San Francisco Baykeeper warns against coming in contact with the water.
articles.title: Algal bloom in Lake Merritt; public asked to stay away

articles.text: Virtually all statewide and citywide mandates on masking and showing proof of vaccination have been lifted as of April 2022, two years after Gov. Gavin Newsom issued a state of emergency in response to the COVID pandemic. These safety protocols are still required in limited settings. According to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), masks are required in public healthcare settings, emergency shelters, jails and prisons, homeless shelters, and long-term care facilities. Schools The state has lifted its mask mandate in schools. However, both the CDPH and Piedmont Unified School District have issued statements advising that masks are strongly recommended. “While there are no current indoor masking requirements for schools in California or Alameda County, the wearing of masks in indoor school settings remains strongly recommended. All students and staff are encouraged to wear masks indoors, and in any situation where social distancing is limited,” said Piedmont Interim School Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans. Proof of vaccination against COVID is no longer required in Piedmont public schools. The CDPH announced in April that it would no longer include the COVID-19 vaccine in its list of mandated childhood vaccines for public schools. Piedmont School District mandated COVID-19 vaccination for all students from kindergarten through 12th grade in September 2021. On April 27, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Brad Seligman struck down the case, which led to a settlement agreement. Under the agreement, the school district cannot consider any similar mandates in the future. “COVID vaccinations remain the best defense against the virus and a valuable tool in keeping our schools open,” said Dr. Evans. “We thank our community for its partnership in helping create a safer school environment by receiving COVID vaccinations and boosters at one of the highest percentages in the country. PUSD continues to strongly recommend all who are eligible to get vaccinated.” Traveling Masks are not required, but are strongly recommended for California public transit riders, and commuters in stations, terminals, and airports. The Centers for Disease Control no longer enforces masking on public transportation conveyances and at transit hubs at the federal level. U.S District Judge Kathryn Kimball Mizelle in Tampa struck down the requirement in April, ruling that the CDC had overstepped its authority in issuing a mask mandate on transportation. The CDC responded in a brief asking the appeals court to reverse the district’s court decision. “It is difficult to imagine a more direct way to control the spread of communicable disease than a measure that traps infectious particles to prevent their spread,” the agency stated. The U.S. Justice Department filed the brief as part of the case appeal to the U.S 11th Circuit Court Appeals and added that the law granting CDC authority to rollout public safety mandates has been “used to prohibit the capture, distribution, or release of certain animals to prevent the spread of monkeypox.” “I’m at the point where I can’t remember the difference between net and gross.”
articles.title: Where masks & vaccines are still required in California

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is offering free compost for Piedmont residents. The site is open every Friday and will be open, weather and conditions permitting, each Friday after 8:00 a.m. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes the City of Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, Carbon dioxide, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products Staff photo The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. To pick up compost, bring a shovel, a container, and gloves for loading the material. Pickup trucks must use a tarp covering. The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. For more information on the self haul pilot program, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/services_ _ _departments/public_ works/recycling_organic_waste_ garbage/s_b_1383. PUSD continues to strongly recommend all who are eligible to get vaccinated.” Traveling Masks are not required, but are strongly recommended for California public transit riders, and commuters in stations, terminals, and airports. The Centers for Disease Control no longer enforces masking on public transportation conveyances and at transit hubs at the federal level. U.S District Judge Kathryn Kimball Mizelle in Tampa struck down the requirement in April, ruling that the CDC had overstepped its authority in issuing a mask mandate on transportation. The CDC responded in a brief asking the appeals court to reverse the district’s court decision. “It is difficult to imagine a more direct way to control the spread of communicable disease than a measure that traps infectious particles to prevent their spread,” the agency stated. The U.S. Justice Department filed the brief as part of the case appeal to the U.S 11th Circuit Court Appeals and added that the law granting CDC authority to rollout public safety mandates has been “used to prohibit the capture, distribution, or release of certain animals to prevent the spread of monkeypox.” READ IT IN THE POST “I’m at the point where I can’t remember the difference between net and gross.”

articles.text: Urban Compassion Project volunteers will gather this Saturday, August 27, at 5th and Webster Street in Oakland to assist with a weekly scheduled urban cleanup. The Project, founded by Vincent Ray Williams, hosts cleanups every Saturday morning at various locations in Oakland. Piedmont residents have joined Williams in his humble mission since the group’s inception. The organization seeks to build community between the unhoused and housed community through these simple acts of kindness. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland. “We approach [cleanups] with compassion and kindness and build bridges between volunteers and our unhoused community,” said Williams. The cleanup will be held from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Volunteers should wear a mask, closed-toe shoes and gloves. articles.text: Piedmont’s Boy Scouts of America (BSA) council sent its Order of the Arrow (OA) Lodge to the University of Tennessee to participate in a week-long conference in August. Piedmont’s OA Lodge, Hungteetsepoppi, was one of over 250 lodges that participated in the National Order of the Arrow conference (NOAC). The Order of the Arrow was founded over 100 years ago to recognize Scouts who showed expertise in camping. It is now the recognized service arm in the BSA, dedicated to camping and service. Candidates are elected by their peers and wear a white sash with a red arrow to signify their membership in the OA. This 2022 conference had more than 6,500 members from across the country participating for a week of amazing activities and fellowship. Piedmont’s Hungteetsepoppi Lodge brought a contingent of six youth and three adults, with an additional adult serving on staff. For most of the crew, their journey started in Manitoba, Canada, where they were completing a canoe and backpacking summer trip. Getting to Knoxville involved three flights and 19 hours of travel, but all would say it was well worth it. The week-long convention’s slogan was “Tomorrow Begins Today” and focused on important topics of reform, restructuring, and the future of the Order Scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 6 arrive in Knoxville, Tennessee for the National Order of the Arrow conference. Pictured are Jeff Green (left), Lisa Gros, Bryan Gros, Vincent Pickering, John Cumbelich, Kevin McKillop, JD Sellman, Lenny Gustavson, and Jack Gros. articles.text: Piedmont continues to honor the 50th anniversary of the passage of Title IX, the federal law which guarantees that no person will be discriminated against on the basis of sex in their education, including school sports. Around town, you can see girls, women, and many boys and men showing their support for Title IX with their black and gold t-shirts and hoodies. Piedmont’s Title IX celebration committee is using the funds from the merchandise sales and donations to raise awareness about the law and to advocate for improvements for girls’ sports at PUSD. The Education Speaker Series kicks off this year on Tuesday, September 13, at 7:30 pm with Kim Turner, Positive Coaching Alliance’s Director of the Gender Equity Initiative, speaking about the Pursuit of Equity: Why Title IX Matters. She is a coach, athlete, advocate, and former nonprofit Title IX attorney who has spearheaded lawsuits around the country bringing school districts and universities into compliance with Title IX and affording hundreds of thousands of girls a chance at a full educational experience. “We’re excited to have Kim Turner this anniversary year of Title IX to educate the community and show our girls that they should have every opportunity in athletics just like the boys,” said Dana Lung, Piedmont Education Foundation board member and chair of the Education Speaker Series. “I’m proud to support Title IX,” said Dan Cavenaugh. “It is essential for our daughters to know and feel that their opportunities and experiences are the same as our sons. These impressions impact the trajectory of every aspect of their lives.” Even elementary students will learn about Title IX this year, as the celebration committee plans to use some of its funds to purchase age-appropriate books for each of PUSD’s school libraries. The books will be chosen by the school librarians and will include titles such as Nike is a Goddess: The History of Women in Sports. Meanwhile, the Title IX celebration committee continues to advocate for Piedmont School District to come into compliance with Title IX. The first-ever audit conducted by the school district over the course of 2021-22 showed significant deficiencies between the boys and girls athletic experiences in Piedmont. Piedmont offers 55 fewer slots for girls to participate in high school sports than boys. “Athletics provide significant benefits for girls and boys alike, and Piedmont girls want that opportunity,” said Mary Wells, a volunteer on the committee. “I´m happy the district conducted an audit last year and promised to follow up annually.” For those interested in buying a t-shirt or hoodie, sales at the Piedmont Store will continue through August 26. Tickets to the Title IX Education Speaker Series event may be purchased at https:// piedmontstore.org/ Stay tuned for details on the Appreciating Diversity Film Series, which will screen a pair of short documentaries (The Queen of Basketball and Mink!), and the spring of 2023 Readmont book, which will focus on Title IX.
articles.title: Title IX: Celebrating equal opportunities for girls in school sports

articles.text: Highlands Preschool is in high gear preparing for a magical 2022-2023 school year. Director Deanna Johnson, well-known for her love of glitter and ability to make each and every child feel loved, is putting the final touches on this year’s curriculum. Along with Head Teacher Angela Livermore, Johnson ensures that Highland’s playbased curriculum is shaped in a way that celebrates the diverse array of holidays, customs, and cultures celebrated by the Highlands community. In addition, the teachers incorporate letters, words, numbers, and science into their lessons while staying true to the play-based philosophy of the school. Community is key to Highlands, a co-op preschool. Parents volunteer in the classroom and play an active role in their child’s experience. Having parents in the classroom helps make the classroom run more smoothly, keeps tuition low, strengthens the relationship between the home and school environments, and provides a window for parents to observe their child’s life at school. Highlands Preschool still has a few openings left for the current school year. To learn more and schedule a tour, visit their website at: https://www.highlandspreschool.org/.
articles.title: Back to School at Highlands Preschool

articles.text: Registration for Piedmont Language School’s (PLS) Mandarin classes is open until September 2, and classes begin September 6. Fall semester classes run from 3:20-4:20 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays at the Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. The Mandarin program helps children learn a language through social interaction, hands-on activities, and creative teaching based on themes. PLS believes in immersion learning and using Mandarin as much as possible in the classroom. Chinese culture is also a significant component of language learning, so the class introduces songs, stories and the celebration of Chinese holidays across all levels. Under new Director Jennifer Poole, Piedmont Language School is revamping its curriculum and is now working with parents to organize carpools to the church and bridging gaps in afterschool care. For more information e-mail Poole at piedmontlanguageschool@gmail.com. Five different levels of Mandarin classes are offered to kids in grades TK through 6th. PLS is partnering with East Bay Chinese School to offer in-person Mandarin classes. Families can sign up at Ebchinese.corsizio.com.

articles.text: Piedmont parents hosted a Back-to-School Carnival for all sixth graders at Piedmont Middle School on Thursday, August 18, the second week of school. A total of 175 students attended the optional afterschool event, replete with carnival games, sporting competitions, food and raffle prizes. The event, held at the Piedmont Middle School courts, is a long-standing tradition and rite of passage for students entering middle school as sixth graders. As the first social event of the school year, it allows students to come together as a class not divided by elementary school sites. Kids enjoyed ring-toss, plinko, and an inflatable carnival long distance basketball hoop. “The atmosphere at the Carnival today was pure excitement; games, pizza, ice cream, music, Staff photos Students eagerly gathered around in hopes of hearing their name announced as a raffle prize winner at the 6th grade Back-to-School Carnival. Parent volunteers Susan Fizzell (left), Angela Anastasi and Abha Kothari helped organize the event and announce the lucky raffle winners. 6th graders Sam Town, Ellia Sharafi, Havia Leonard, and (top right) Leila Weinstein preferred ice cream snacks and conversation to the hullabaloo of the raffle. 6th graders earned raffle entry tickets by competing in carnival games, including the stacked can knock down game. Inflatable soccer, basketball and football targets brought out friendly carnival competition. and raffle prizes felt refreshingly post-COVID,” said Parents Club Rep. Susan Fizzell .“It’s really a great community-building event, for the kids and even for the parent volunteers and supporters who had a chance to meet or reconnect. These kids have been through so much; it’s great to see all their smiling faces.” Donations by 35 families funded the event including gift cards for Mulberry’s, Target, Starbucks and See’s Candies. Kids earned raffle tickets by participating in carnival games and 45 lucky winners took home gift cards. PMS Parent Club 6th grade representatives Susan Fizzell, Julia Ruthven, and Becca Posamentier were this year’s key organizers. An additional dozen parent volunteers helped out.

articles.text: Registration for ALPS’s Student Learning Circles has been extended through Sunday, August 28. ALPS (Advancing Learning For Piedmont Students) created the programs to foster the joy of learning for Piedmont students in grades 3 through 8. “Learning Circles are an opportunity for our students to deep dive into learning about their areas of passion in a small group setting with an academic mentor,” said Ella Grossberg, the program creator and this year’s ALPS co-president. ALPS has added some interesting new programs this fall, starting the first week of September. including: • Discover Artificial Intelligence • From Steph Curry to Serena Williams: The Science of Health in Sports • Introduction to Mind Reading • Shell-abrating Sea Life: Exploring our Big Blue Backyard In addition, ALPS continues to offer its popular core classes of math enrichment and creative writing. This year, ALPS has a new lineup of fun and enriching afterschool offerings, called Learning Circles. Accompanying these changes, ALPS rebranded itself as “Advancing Learning For Piedmont Students” to reinforce its new broader educational focus and offerings for all learners who seek deep and joyful learning. ALPS was previously known as “Advanced Learners Program Support.” Registration and content details are available at Piedmont ALPS.wordpress.com. Questions may be directed to Piedmont ALPS@gmail.com .

articles.text: A large crowd gathered for last year’s Open House hosted by members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Teens and their parents are invited to attend an open house and Fall Kickoff hosted by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) on Sunday August 28 at 4 p.m. Sign up to attend at: https://forms.gle/4iJmyPA5CRrmmMcT7 Come meet current crew members and youth leaders. This will be a fun, social event with refreshments along with presentations about the crew and how members and their parents can benefit. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led organization, provides teens with the skills and opportunities to make lasting impacts in their community. As a youth-led, co-ed venturing crew under the Piedmont Council BSA, founded 18 years ago, we provide many leadership and volunteer opportunities that cater to most interests, in a lowstress, fun and nurturing environment. Middle school kids and their parents may register with the companion Piedmont Service Club (PSC) where they partake in everything offered by PCSC that is age appropriate. PCSC partners with organizations across the Bay Area to create dynamic and diverse volunteering events multiple times each week. These range from cooking meals for people in underserved communities, building and renovating homes, working with underserved children, and nature immersive clean-up projects. We remain active over summers, striving to have a summer service trip that is planned by our youth. Together, our members gain various skills and experiences that bring them closer into becoming well-rounded individuals in our community. One of PCSC’s most popular events is the annual project with Rebuilding Together Oakland (RTO). Each year 100 or more crew members collectively put in over 1,000 hours into renovating an elderly person’s home in Oakland. Through this project participants learn a range of skills, from fundraising, project planning and teamwork; structural repairs, improvements and then cleaning and repainting the entire house. Above all, crew members learn the value of gratitude and giving back as they work with the homeowner. PCSC members Vale Prieto Black, Elena Stevens, Klara Zietlow, and Sofia Prieto Black describe the work the Crew does and the many benefits for its teen members. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Registration is still available for the Piedmont Soccer Club’s Fall teams in all age levels, from Under-6 through Under-19. PSC offers a fun and challenging soccer experience for more than 1,000 players in Piedmont and the immediate area. It is the soccer club of choice for nearly half the student population. Though the official period of registration has closed, some space is still available for most age groups. The Fall season begins the last week of August. The recreation-level teams serve soccer players from beginners to more experienced players. Under-6 and Under-8 teams participate in-house with short weekly practice sessions for U-8, and fun 4 v 4 and 5 v 5 unscored games on the weekend. All games for U-8 and younger take place in Piedmont. Players on Under-10 and older teams participate in games in the Jack London Youth Soccer League and play a 10-game schedule with teams from Piedmont, Oakland, and Alameda in the fall. Teams may also elect to play in the spring season as well. Teams are led by volunteer coaches, supported by the 24-7 UK Soccer Academy curriculum and their professional coaches. Players in the recreational program may choose to attend professional coach-led programs (SkillSKOOL, Goalkeeping) held during the year in locally. PSC is an active community partner, supporting local initiatives like this year’s inaugural “Play Like a Girl” event, designed to encourage girls’ participation in youth sports, and the conversion of a Bern Court at Piedmont Middle School to a soccer-ready turf field. PSC is also a partner of the Oakland Roots, the professional soccer team in Oakland. The club sponsors an annual PSC “Roots” night where players can attend their game in uniform and play a fun scrimmage for the crowd at halftime! For more information about Piedmont Soccer club and registration, see www.piedmontsoccer.org. Kids enjoy being on soccer teams in Piedmont in the Piedmont Soccer Club players in action. fall.

Benefits of music have been well researched and include better communication skills, outlet for emotional release, decreased anxiety, improved cognitive function and mental health, and connections to Studies have linked early participation in music to increased grades in high school exam scores in English, mathematics and science, including exhibiting higher executive function supporting increased academic achievement. Learning music and theory supports skill sets such as memorization, interpretation and improvisation, building blocks of higher learning. Music is a great creative outlet as students navigate academic and social challenges. Listening to and playing music provides an opportunity for self expression. Playing a musical instrument has been shown to lower cortisol levels and decrease anxiety levels. Creating music involves a sense of camaraderie, as music is a collaborative endeavor. Teacher-student interactions and learning a piece with peers teaches how to work together towards a common goal, gaining skills to connect with those around us. Collaboration is a significant life skill needed as our students move through college, the workplace, and personal relationships. A local hub for learning music provides an opportunity to be a part of their community, introducing them to other students who share the same passions. We find the benefits of music to be crucial in students’ lives, and strive to meet the needs of our community. With one child through Piedmont schools and one in high school, we see the benefits of art, music, theater and creative outlets in tandem with STEAM, an opportunity for children to experience and discover their strengths. Among our many services, we offer individual and group music lessons for a wide variety of instruments, both in-person and online, and have a stage for practice and performance. We rent instruments to individuals and those in bands along with our sister-store, Rockin’ Robbie’s. It is our mission to make the benefits of music accessible for local students, all family members and the community at large. It marks the Piedmont debut of firstyear head coach Jordan Seiden. “Our theme this week is ‘focus and finish.’ Focus on the game, focus on what’s in front of us and finish every rep and all of our kids to contribute in some form or fashion,” said Seiden. “We have a good group of kids and are learning fast, their confidence is high, and people are feeling good.” Piedmont will play this season as an independent school this fall after dropping from the Western Alameda County Conference after debate arose about whether to continue the varsity program in 2022 due to low signups. The team will return to the WACC in 2023. This year’s team is still light on numbers, with only around 20 players available throughout training camp. It’s going to require contributions from every player on the team, including those playing varsity football for the first time. “I expect most if not all of our kids to play and participate. It’s going to be a big moment; we have several players who haven’t played high school football before. We’re going to count on some of those kids and we really believe they can handle their responsibility and do their job,” said Seiden. Seiden’s offense will be in the “pro-style” mold. They have been progressively installing their system throughout the summer with this week driving home what to expect on Friday. “It’s good. They are picking up stuff fast. It’s helpful that we run a pretty modern offense with similar concepts to last year but with our own twists. Some of the playmakers identified by Seiden are running back/safety Matteo Costa, running back/linebacker Jack Nelson, running back/defensive back Sam Shelby, tight end/linebacker Tommy Ashton, and quarterback Marcos Lagios. Having guys like Dom and Liam step up and make plays will be big for us. Jack is obviously another person who will be important for us,” said Seiden. A strong backfield is the hallmark for any high school program. It will be headlined by a strong trio in the backfield: Jack Nelson, Sam Shelby, and Matteo Costa. “Jack is going to be really crucial for us, with Sam being a great 1-2 punch, while Matteo is the ‘hammer’ of the three. All three of them will contribute. Sam is the outside, perimeter guy, Jack is more of a slasher, and Matteo is more of the hammer,” said Seiden. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team gets its season started next Tuesday, August 30, with a match against Miramonte in Orinda. The Highlanders return after going 18-9 last season, finishing second in the Western Alameda County Conference behind Bishop O’Dowd. PHS coach Jim Landes is expecting more healthy competition against the Dragons this season. “We’re building, and we’re not bad In terms of the league, I think we’ll be good. It should be a good season,” said Landes. Returning varsity players include three four-year starters, Anne Jumper, Michaela Bini, and Mara LaForte, the incumbent team leaders. “They are three seniors that we’ve had since their freshman year. They have a lot of experience and are going to be our leaders of the team,” said Landes. Jumper will return to No. 2 in the singles lineup, LaForte is set to be the No. 3 and Bini the No. 4. But the big news is the arrival of Tanya Kononova, a Ukranian refugee and junior at PHS, who will be the team’s No. 1 singles player. She comes to Piedmont as an international transfer student. “At the very top is a surprise. She showed up a month ago. I was teaching on a Sunday and she showed up with her mother and said she wanted to play. It turns out she’s very good, so right now she’s our number one. It’s great to have her – she’s a nice addition,” said Landes. The doubles lineup will include junior Ceclia Defazio and sophomore Emma Eisemon most likely as No. 1. The two were a strong tandem last season, winning 11 doubles matches. “I think they’ll be a solid group again. They may be our top doubles team,” said Landes Landes will hold some challenge matches to determine the rest of the doubles lineup. “I’ve been talking things over with Corey (Reich, assistant coach), and we may move some things around with some singles players,” said Landes. Also cracking the varsity Michaela Bini returns as a fouryear varsity starter. lineup are two talented freshmen, Kate Jumper, Anna’s younger sister, and Arianna Kortum, a Russian exchange student. “We have two freshmen who are doing well. Kate is really good, and we have a translator for both Arianna and Tonya, whose English is limited. Piedmont played in a preseason match against Las Lomas yesterday, Tuesday, August 23, but results have not been posted. articles.text: Piedmont High senior A.J. Harris has been plugging through the summer and offseason with his AAU basketball club, the Lakeshow. On Saturday, August 20 at Modesto Christian High School, the former school of twins Courtney and Ashley Paris and their siblings. Harris won a 3-point shootout against some of the best players in the state. He’s been working hard at his craft since last winter’s season, studying film, and putting in plenty of hours on the court. “It was definitely nice to get some recognition because I’ve spent a lot of hours working on my shot. I go early in the morning before school at the YMCA just working on my shot. There’s also a lot of other aspects that go into shooting, like watching film on my form and try to fix any issues I see. There’s also a lot of mental game to it, learning to not get frustrated when things aren’t going in.” “It’s nice to get some recognition as one of the best shooters in NorCal,” said Harris. The shootout featured four rounds in a first-to-11 buckets format, resulting in Harris defeating Jamari Phillips of Modesto Christian 11-8. Phillips is rated as a four-star recruit by 247Sports, which slots him in as the No. 19 overall player in the U.S. “I played against Jamari Phillips, who is one grade below me. He’s [being looked at] by some major schools in the country, like Oregon, Texas Tech, Gonzaga, and Kansas. He’s a super good player,” said Harris. Simply Basketball, the organizer, also hosted a game called the Battle of Norcal, where Harris represented the Bay Area and helped them reach the Finals. “I was on team Bay and we played against the best players from the Central area. In the championship, we played against the best players from Stockton. I felt like I was able to hold my own and show that’s where I belong,” said Harris. During the offseason, Harris has been training with Lakeshow, an AAU team with several Piedmont players, JoJo Murphy, Luke Barrett, and older brother Luke Harris. Last June, Harris dominated Vanden by scoring 53 points, 11 rebounds, and three assists. PHS senior A.J. Harris recently won a 3-point shootout hosted at Modesto Christian High School “I’ve just been working on my conditioning, my ball-handling skills, quickness, and being more athletic in order to guard more point guards. Playing with Lakeshow and AAU in the summer is a huge bonus and super helpful to prepare for the season. You travel around the West Coast to play some of the best players out there who have major offers. You can’t be scared of anything and it teaches you to be tough,” said Harris. Aside from competing with Lakeshow, Harris has been spending time perfecting his shot by working with his father Jason Harris, the assistant coach at Piedmont. “I’ve been training a lot with my dad. Ever since I was little, he’s helped me. He was a really good shooter when he was younger, so he’s helped me get my form in the right place. Whenever he notices something I can work on, we’ll just go to the gym and get a bunch of shots up to identify whatever is wrong,” said Harris. Harris is a four-year varsity member and three-year starter with the Highlanders. He mentioned that his goal for the upcoming winter season is to help bring home another North Coast Section title to Piedmont after watching the 2020 team win one as a freshman on the bench. “When I was a freshmen, I played JV and was called up to the varsity team for the playoffs. I saw that varsity team win the first-ever NCS championship in school history, I’m just trying to get back there and get another one for us,” said Harris. A.J. Harris is hoping to bring home another North Coast Section title to Piedmont.

articles.text: Piedmont High senior Audrey Lam has accomplished something all soccer players strive to achieve – being a member of their national team. Lam qualified for the Under-17 U.S. Women’s National Team earlier this summer, and currently is playing international friendlies in Madrid against the national teams of Spain and Germany. Lam played her first match against Spain yesterday, August 23, and will play the Spanish squad again on Thursday, August 25, before facing Germany on Wednesday, August 31. She played 30 minutes in Tuesday’s match, which the U.S. won 2-0. “It’s everything I’ve dreamed of,” said Lam recently. “Ever since I was little, my goal was to be on the National Team, and this is just one step closer to achieving that goal. I’ve worked pretty hard and this just shows that. It’s really just a dream, I feel honored to be given this opportunity,” said Lam. Her inclusion in the lineup is possibly an auspicious sign. The U-17 FIFA Women’s World Cup is in India October 11-30. Many of the current U.S. players recently competed in the CONCACAF Women’s tournament in May. “I’m looking forward to playing with these players and against these other teams. This leads to the U17 World Cup and hopefully if I play well, I’ll get called up again. As long as I stay disciplined and focused, I think I can achieve this,” said Lam. This marks her second opportunity with the U.S. Women’s National Team after taking part in a U-15 development camp in Kansas City in 2019. It is her first time competing in games with the team. To be called up to the U-17 team, Lam credits impressing coaches at a showcase in Oceanside earlier this summer where she scored three times and turned the heads of coaches. “I practice four times a week with my club and practice by myself as much as I can outside of practice, and it all leads up to the showcases. This past summer at Oceanside. a few scouts came out. I just tried to put everything out there. I tried to show my footwork and I think that got their attention, I scored a few times, which is something they obviously like to see,” said Lam. Lam trains with Lamorinda Soccer Club and competes on their Women’s Soccer Premier League team, Lamorinda United, Audrey Lam, Class of 2023, is currently competing abroad in three international friendlies with the U-17 United States Women’s National Team. Audrey Lam (No. 7) is a central attacking midfielder and plays on Lamorinda Soccer Club’s WPSL team. under head coach Mohamed Mohamed. He’s been coaching Lam for six years and says Lam is a player who makes “everyone better.” Audrey Lam competed on the Piedmont High team last winter and earned first-team All-League honors. “She is extremely talented and a hard worker, not just offensively but defensively as well. She’s the type of player who other players look up to. She’s an extremely humble person and the type of athlete that you want to have on your team. She’s an amazing teammate and we are so proud of her to reach this level and also watch her grow,” said Mohamed. Lam is currently committed to play collegiately at Brown University in Rhode Island with plans of playing professionally and one day making the senior U.S. Women’s National Team. “My goal was to always be on the National Team or go professional. Another goal is to play collegiately and get my degree. After I graduate, my goal is to play professionally wherever I can in the U.S. or Europe, and hopefully continue with the National Team,” said Lam.

articles.text: With the new school year officially here, the Class of 2023 looks toward the upcoming sports calendar for the fall, winter and spring seasons to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. ANNE JUMPER Tennis Anne Jumper, a senior, is fouryear varsity tennis player. She was mentioned as a team leader by coach Jim Landes after earning an honorable mention for AllLeague honors as a singles starter last year. Jumper is set to be the team’s No. 2 at singles this fall. In 2021 she helped Piedmont reach the quarterfinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section team playoffs as the No. 4 seed. PHS defeated No. 12 Justin-Siena in the first round with Jumper winning her match at No. 2 singles in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. In the quarterfinals, Piedmont narrowly lost 4-3 to No. 5 College Prep, while Jumper battled to a three-set loss despite fighting stomach cramps, 5-7, 7-5, 6-3. He had a .216 batting average with 11 hits, two doubles, six RBIs, and scored 14 runs. ZOE WOLFERS Soccer WILL SPRAGUE Baseball Will Sprague earned firstteam All-League honors in baseball last spring after helping the team win the Shoreline Division championship and post an overall record of 19-9. Piedmont advanced to the quarterfinals of the North Coast Section playoffs. Sprague contributed as a pitcher and infielder. On the mound, he threw 23 innings in nine appearances, accumulating Zoe Wolfers will step into the winter season as a key player on coach Dan Chubbock’s attack. She worked hard to get minutes last season as a junior, often appearing as a striker and central attacker. Last season Piedmont finished 7-5-6 overall and earned the No. 6 seed in the Division 4 NCS Playoffs. They defeated No. 11 College Prep 4-0 before losing 2-1 to No. 3 Sonoma Academy. PHS is expected to return a group with a wealth of starting experience from last winter, including attacker Emily Fitzgerald, goal keeper Morgan Hunt, midfielder/fullback Hailey Marshburn, fullback Cameron Lorin, and center backs Sofie Hebert, Charlotte Davies, and Amy Derr. articles.text: What inside sources at the club are saying about the move A huge development occurred on Thursday, August 18, with Oakland Roots announcing that they placed their head coach Juan Guerra on administrative leave. This came shortly after Phoenix Rising FC mutually parted ways with its coach Rick Schantz the previous day. Sources indicated to The Post that Phoenix had been engaged in discussions with Guerra without permission. He is under contract with Oakland Roots SC, which deemed it “disruptive to the organization.” The news came one month after it was initially reported that Guerra was a candidate for the Phoenix job, and the wheels have seemingly been turning since then. Two days ago, on Monday, August 22, Phoenix officially announced Guerra had been hired as its new head coach. Oakland Roots stated in a press released that it had come to an agreement to part ways with its former coach after releasing him from his contract. Sources indicate that Oakland received an extensive offer from Phoenix, which included purchasing his remaining contract, buying assistant coach Marcos Reina, and giving Roots rights to allocated roster slots that value at over $200,000. But all this raises the question of what tampering standards were breached by Phoenix Rising FC contacting and negotiating a deal with Guerra while he was under contract. Bylaws of USL Championship, the league in which both teams play, states “players, agents, or representatives cannot engage in any contract negotiations other than with the players’ current club in regards to a future deal.” The rules further state that the league may prohibit the club or player from entering an agreement and may declare the deal null and void. It is unclear if the same bylaws pertain to manager contracts as well. LOCAL SPORTS Oakland Roots’ coach Juan Guerra hired by rival Phoenix What inside sources at the club are saying about the move By Jonathan Comeaux A huge development occurred on Thursday, August 18, with Oakland Roots announcing that they placed their head coach Juan Guerra on administrative leave. This came shortly after Phoenix Rising FC mutually parted ways with its coach Rick Schantz the previous day. Sources indicated to The Post that Phoenix had been engaged in discussions with Guerra without permission. He is under contract with Oakland Roots SC, which deemed it “disruptive to the organization.” The news came one month after it was initially reported that Guerra was a candidate for the Phoenix job, and the wheels have seemingly been turning since then. Two days ago, on Monday, August 22, Phoenix officially announced Guerra had been hired as its new head coach. Oakland Roots stated in a press released that it had come to an agreement to part ways with its former coach after releasing him from his contract. Sources indicate that Oakland received an extensive offer from Phoenix, which included purchasing his remaining contract, buying assistant coach Marcos Reina, and giving Roots rights to allocated roster slots that value at over $200,000. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749-2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ passengers/. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently showing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on a book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Goddess playing now through September 25.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is currently performing the musical Follies through September 10. The show is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army, Blood, Sweat, and Stanley Poole (1961). Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim. It was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre. Sally and Phyllis, the lead characters, are showgirls in the Follies and both in failing marriages. Cast members include Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. To obtain tickets see: https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/, or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street. Cast members of San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Follies. Photo by Jessica Palopoli
articles.title: Follies playing at SF Playhouse through September 10

articles.text: Ballet Folklorico will perform with San Francisco Symphony at Davies Symphony Hall on September 15. In celebration of “Fiesta Patrias” and Hispanic Heritage Month, the world-famous dance company Ballet Folklorico de los Angeles will perform with San Francisco Symphony at Davies Symphony Hall on Thursday, September 15. Enrico Lopez-Yanez will lead the Symphony with music by Mariachi Garibaldi de Jaime Cueller and vocals by singer-songwriter Lupita Infante. Fiesta Patrias (patriotic holidays), are traditional celebrations of Mexican national pride, independence, and culture that take place in Mexico and across the United States. These celebrations coincide with National Hispanic Heritage Month, which is observed from September 15 to October 15 every year. The performance begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/FiestaPatrias. You can also call the Davies Symphony Hall box office at (415) 864-6000. articles.text: Dan Flanagan, Principal 2nd Violin of Berkeley Symphony, and a composer and art collector, will perform his debut concert at Zankel Hall at Carnegie Hall in New York on October 3. Titled The Bow and the Brush, the recital of solo violin pieces is inspired by paintings and sculptures in Flanagan’s private collection. All music being performed will be world premieres, commissioned or composed by Flanagan, with images of the art projected during the performance, designed by Nancy Johnson. The concert integrates visual arts with new music. Flanagan will premiere many of his 20 commissions at Carnegie Hall, with a follow up performance at Hertz Hall in Berkeley on October 16 and performances across the U.S. and Europe. All pieces will be recorded and shown with the art that inspired them for Youtube. Local composers and artists are indicated below with an asterisk. articles.text: Hey, George. The first thing we need to do is to confirm your credentials. You were a music critic, weren’t you? My name is Bernard. Pronounce it with the accent on the first syllable, BERnard. And, yes I was a music critic from my youth until the last year of my life. I was always opinionated, and I loved to use the most expressive language I could. Sometimes my readers didn’t even know what I was talking about. I was also contentious. My nom de plume was Corno di Bassetto. In the words of my good friend Charles Dickens, I witnessed the best of times and sometimes the worst of times. OK, Bernard, tell us about the best of times. My favorite violinists were señor Pablo de Sarasate and the young Jascha Heifetz. Their playing was ever so expressive and they stood like marble statues allowing the music to speak for itself. I also liked the young Thomas Beecham, the famous conductor who later was knighted. He had a wicked sense of humor. OK, Bernard. Do you know much about the musicians of the present day? Yep, I certainly do. The great actress Sarah Bernhardt would make a great conductor these days. As for violinists, they remind me of the French vaudevillian Le Petomane with his deep knee bends. Well, Bernard, you certainly are opinionated. Contentious also, it seems. Did you hear about what’s happening in sports? Maybe you know about the basketball player who got a $19 million raise. Any opinions on this? Yep, I sure do. In my day, $19 million was just about the total budget for an entire country. PerPlaywright and music critic George Bernard Shaw. haps you heard that I am a “share the wealth” kind of a guy. I liked John L Sullivan a whole bunch because he earned every dollar the hard way –you know, going into a bar and challenging everybody. I think the French call that egaliterianism. As you know I started playing music as a little kid. I always advocated for music education at every level. Music teaches everybody all the principles of life. It is certainly the most autobiographical of all of the art. Let me not mince words. Society is on the wrong path. It kind of reminds me of the last days of Rome. And we know how that ended, don’t we? I think I understand what you’re saying, Bernard. Do you have any last words? Yes, as a matter fact I do. I would advise people to get their priorities straight. Thank you GBS. Here’s a “heads up” These days music lovers need to find out about concerts via the grapevine. Our Piedmont Center for the Arts is our great resource. But every once in a while there are some good shows elsewhere. Let’s start with a forthcoming noontime concert entitled “majesty of the spiritual” in Herbst Theater on August 28. It will be a complete overview of gospel music in one concert. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org
articles.title: George Bernard Shaw as a music critic

articles.text: Exhibition now on view at Treasure Island Museum Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage, is currently exhibiting Portal to the Pacific in War and Peace. The museum is open Monday through Friday each week from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. The exhibition presents Treasure Island’s dynamic and unique history in a series of banners and panels on display throughout the Building One lobby. The panels feature many previously unpublished color photographs of the island. This is a fixed exhibition on view during the island’s monthly lecture series, but it is temporarily removed when events are held in the lobby. Reference the museum’s calendar at https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ exhibitions before visiting. The exhibition is free and open to the public. The museum is located at 1 Avenue of the Palms #111 on Treasure Island. Treasure Island Museum also offers several online exhibitions throughout the year. A permanent exhibition is located in the lobby of the Treasure Island Museum.
articles.title: Portal to the Pacific in War and Peace

articles.text: A scene from Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs was released in 2009 and adapted from the children’s book by Judi and Ron Barrett. The story is set in the small town of Swallow Falls. For years its economy has been dependent on catching and selling sardines. But unexpectedly the demand for sardines takes a steep dive and the denizens of Swallow Falls find themselves with an economic problem. To the rescue comes Flint Hardwood (Bill Harder), a bright teen who loves to invent stuff like spray on shoes, or a television with legs that can walk over to you if you want to change the channel. Flint’s gruff dad, Tim (James Caan), owns a bait and tackle shop and is feeling the effects of the lack of demand for sardines on his business. Flint puts his inventing cap on and decides he wants to help the town and sets about creating a machine that converts water into food. Somehow his invention is suspended in the sky (don’t ask), and when it starts to rain, well, it’s not rain but cheeseburgers, hotdogs, soup and mashed potatoes, jell-O molds that kids can bounce on, and any other type of food Flint orders from his computer. The folks of Swallow Falls are delighted, especially the town’s youngsters who get to enjoy a morning snow fall of ice cream. Plus there’s Sam Sparks (Anna Faris), a local weather girl, who is a bit confused about what to forecast. And there’s the ever-hungry Swallow Falls mayor (Bruce Campbell) who can’t wait for the next food storm. But, as things turn out, the residents get greedy and begin demanding bigger portions. As a result, Flint’s machine begins to go a bit haywire and strange things begin to happen. There’s a tornado of spaghetti, a blizzard of sherbet, a pancake falls on top of the school, and a giant cob of corn rolls downhill after a group terrified kids. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs is a lot of fun, filled with gags, interesting characters, and, of course, a few life lessons, such as follow your dream, believe in yourself, and know that your grumpy old dad, Tim, actually does love you. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. Directed by Chris Miller and Phil Lord. Voiced by Bill Harder, Anna Faris, Andy Sandberg, and James Caan. Animated. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime/VUDU.
