articles.text: Will Ferrell has constructed a successful career playing outrageous, exaggerated, slapstick caricatures. Recall Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, Step Brothers, or Talladega Nights. He has perfected the deer-caughtin-the headlights moment, the comedic intersection between plain, dumb obliviousness and a grudging, cranky awareness and has found a fan base. Ferrell has done straight drama far too infrequently. Surprisingly, he is an actor who can portray a certain character with subtlety and insight, pathos and humanity, as he so nicely demonstrated in Stranger Than Fiction, and in Everything Must Go. In fact, it could be argued that some of his best work is to be found in these two films and not in those banal comedies he has starred in following his years on Saturday Night Live. In Everything Must Go, his character, Nick Halsey, is a study in sadness, touched by an existential despair. He arrives home after an awful day – he’s been fired from his job as a mid-level sales executive because of an alleged drunken episode with a female employee and his ongoing battle with alcoholism – and finds the locks on his house changed and all of his stuff, soup to nuts, on the front lawn, including his favorite recliner. His marriage, evidently, is over and he has been moved out, if no further than the lawn. It’s his quiet and deliberate response that makes this film appealing. He begins to arrange all of the items as if the lawn were his rec room, then heads off to the local liquor store and buys two twelve packs of beer. He returns to his lawn and his recliner where he sits, contemplating his life and future. Such as it is. What’s intriguing about Nick is that he neither rages, nor becomes maudlin; instead, he drinks a beer (and then another and then another) and looks out at his neighbors, feigning a studied sense of normalcy – I now live outside the house and not inside the house – though life has dealt him a crushing defeat, his loneliness suddenly defined with a brutal clarity. Clearly it’s time to make some changes, and he starts by unloading his stuff, a metaphor for so much that has cluttered up his life and gotten in his way, perhaps insulating him from who he is, which, as it turns out, is a pretty decent guy. Good narrative cinema is rare. So much of what is sold by Hollywood as substantive is nonsense, likely based on the premise that character driven films will not attract an audience. Our loss. Based on a Raymond Carver short story, Everything Must Go is an evocative film, nuanced and engaging, an examination of life and the human condition, such as it is. As well, Ferrell is working with a talented ensemble of actors to include Rebecca Hall, a pregnant neighbor who is waiting for her husband to arrive from New York; Christopher Wallace as a young, at-loose-ends kid whose mother works in the neighborhood; Michael Pena, portraying Nick’s AA sponsor and a Scottsdale detective; and Stephen Root, delivering a nice cameo as a tightly-wound next-door neighbor. They’re all top drawer. Everything Must Go. Starring Will Ferrell, Rebecca Hall, Laura Dern and Stephen Root. Written and directed by Dan Rush. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated R. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Netflix/VUDU.

articles.text: The journey of Troop 6 Scouts finds its beginning around four years ago, when the idea of a troop excursion to Northern Tier first began circulating. Northern Tier is a canoe-based High Adventure trip offered by Scouts BSA, with separate locations in Minnesota and Canada. We planned a trip to the Manitoba base, deep in the buggy lowlands and miles away from the closest town because it was the most challenging and rugged of all the bases. Our roster of seven Scouts and four parents was decided in mid-2021, when we began getting gear, establishing training exercises, treating clothes with bug repellent, and reading emails rivaling libraries in their magnitude. We met often to discuss different aspects of our travel plans while also practice canoeing on Lake Merritt and at Del Valle. Early morning Zoom meetings to schedule flights were commonplace as the trip grew nearer. On Friday, July 15, we boarded a plane to Vancouver, then Winnipeg, where we stayed in a hotel overnight. The next morning we departed by bus to Bissett, a tiny The crew: Jack Throne, Jack Gros, Vincent Pickering, Bryan Gros, Lenny Gustavson, Lisa Gros, Jason Throne, Peter Ichimaru, JD Sellman, John Cumbelich, and Kristen Gustavson. Jack Throne and Kristen Gustavson work on their maps. Each boat was responsible for preparing its set of maps, marking all the portages. The trek this summer spanned three maps. Arriving at the canoe cache and selecting a canoe, hopefully with no holes. GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 The journey started with a float plane ride to Scout Lake. town in the north of Manitoba. There we met our guide, Matt, and went over the gear we had brought, which was packed down into impossibly small waterproof bags. We charted our course across the wilderness (60 miles total) in the Map Room, and prepared our crew’s gear before spending our final night in relative comfort on the base. The next morning, we quickly packed our gear and walked to a small lakeside dock. A floatplane came for us, and we were treated to an unforgettable and beautiful view of the untouched Canadian wilderness as we left civilization behind. Landing at Scout Lake, we retrieved our canoes from a cache and were off after some quick lessons in paddling and portaging, which consists of carrying the boat on one’s shoulders over land. Our convoy was made up of four canoes, with three people to each one. Paddlers in the back were responsible for steering the canoe, while paddlers in the front powered the boat forward. In the middle was the “duff” seat, where one just sits and navigates. We quickly got used to the rhythm of paddling, and our first few portages went off without a hitch. Little did we know, howGOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 ever, what was in store for us at our campsite. Our first night was spent on Lake Noname, on a mossy outcropping of a campsite. After bringing our canoes ashore and setting up camp, we began a read-aloud of the Princess Bride as storm clouds brewed in the distance. Less than an hour later we awoke to the most torrential downpour any of us had ever seen. Completely drenched, we retreated to our tents ready to spend the rest of the night cold and damp in our sleeping bags. Minutes later the rain stopped and was replaced by a gorgeous sunset. I suddenly knew what he meant when Matt told us this would be the best and hardest trip of our lives. The next few days were similarly action-packed. Day two’s calm waters were interrupted by a few baby rapids. I managed to nearly capsize my boat and fling our adult leader into the water. Day three’s camp was on the shores of the enormous Lake Sasaginnigak, where we spent an idyllic afternoon drying out clothes, catching fish, and swimming to nearby islands.
articles.title: Troop 6 Scouts enter Canada for summer canoe trip

articles.text: While the drought has created many problems, it has provided the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group with some lovely, sunny mornings to walk Piedmont streets. The forecast was for a cooler Wednesday, but it was a surprise to see that there had been some rain in the early hours pf August 17, and the sidewalks were wet that morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group has an informal objective of walking every safe Piedmont street during the calendar year. The less walked streets are generally towards the city’s border with Oakland. It was determined that 16 different streets hadn’t been walked this year. The group crossed Highland Avenue and went to Pala Avenue, with a plan to Walk the parallel streets of Mesa and Monte Avenues, which connect with Pala, Park Way, and Moraga Avenue. On Mesa the walkers found a surprise, a lovely, classic, vintage home built in 1907. On Monte the group enjoyed many homes with shingle exteriors that have been beautifully maintained and updated. The group recognized that by going down Park Way they were retracing some of the Key System Number 10 streetcar route of the first half of the last century. The group turned on Estrella Avenue and found two almost identical homes next to one another. Jim Kellogg, an architect, described them as California Mission style. The twin houses share a driveway. In front of the house next door, the walkers discovered a circular tablet that resembled a large coin. On it were Chinese characters that Jim Kuo and Albert Chen translated to say “welcome, good fortune, and money.” Turning onto Ramona Avenue and found the 107-foot set of steps that took them back to Park Way for a short walk to Dracena Avenue. They quickly came to a house that stopped them in their tracks. It had been recently redesigned and rebuilt. Jim Kellogg described it as a “contextually modern” home of a Japanese style. The house is very different from its traditional Piedmont neighbors, but Jim felt it still fits harmoniously with its surroundings. A mixture of roof levels provides some visual interest, along with appropriate exteriors, colors, and landscaping. Going down Blair, they spotted a large birdhouse attached to a tree on the exterior of Dracena Park at the corner with El Cerrito Avenue. The history of Walker Blair, the first European settler in this area during the second half of the 19th Century, was recalled. What is now Dracena Park was the enterprising Blair’s quarry, and at this corner was his dairy farm. At Oakland Avenue the walkers went up block-long Carmel Avenue that took them back to the street named in honor of Walker Blair. articles.text: 2020 Ridge Lytton Springs I consider this wine, along with their Geyserville, to be the flagships of Ridge’s Zinfandel portfolio. This bottling is blended with 11% Petite Sirah and 10% Carignane. This beautiful and compelling wine shows blackberries, graphite, leather and tar notes. The wine boasts fabulous balance in an extroverted style that is hard to resist. It is built to last and will easily develop over ten years in the cellar. • 2020 Ridge Evangelho This is a fascinating blend of 54% Carignane, 26% Zinfandel and 20% Mataro (Mourvedre). It comes from ancient sandy soiled vineyards near the town of Oakley in Contra Costa County. This unique old vine blend is a wine of tremendous character. It has hints of violets, currants and raspberries with a rich spice box note as well as leather and earth. The perfect companion to roast chicken and potatoes cooked in fat. • 2020 Ridge Zinfandel Benito Dusi This 100% Zinfandel from Paso Robles offers classic briery, mineral, spicy Zinfandel aromas. On the palate, the wine is dense, rich, and full-bodied, with copious quantities of glycerin, abundant plum/blueberry fruit, low acidity, and a fleshy, succulent finish. It’s a gorgeous Zinfandel to drink over the next five years.

articles.text: The family of Helen Robison-FitzGerald has announced with deep sadness her passing on August 7, 2022. A mother, engineer, and intellectual, she passed away after a valiant battle with pancreatic cancer and its consequences. She was 62. Born Helen Robison in Fort Worth, Texas, she was the daughter of William Robison, a West Point graduate and officer in the U.S. Air Force, and mother, Marianne Buttner Robison, a teacher. Helen lived in Texas, Alabama, Ohio, Virginia, Piedmont and Palo Alto. She enjoyed summers and Christmas vacations in Piedmont with her grandparents, Helen and Edgar Buttner. Helen was a student at Piedmont High School and won the annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest in 1978, leading to an appearance on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson. Helen earned an engineering degree from Stanford University and continued with graduate studies at the University of Chicago. She worked for Cisco Systems, CoastCom and Verizon, and made significant contribuFitzGerald, an engineer at Cisco Systems. Both were devoted to engineering and mathematics. Helen loved to cook and attended the San Francisco Culinary Academy. Thanksgiving and Christmas at Helen’s house were always greatly anticipated given her culinary skills. Helen developed pancreatic cancer in 2020. Despite grim prospects and with a will to survive, Helen pursued surgery and chemotherapy. In the end, cancer took Helen, depriving her of many years of life and the opportunity for family members to be in her company. Helen is survived by her daughter, Anna Stang, and by her husband, Cary FitzGerald. She is also survived by a brother, Tim Robison, and her mother, Marianne Robison of Piedmont. A memorial service will be held at the Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, at 2:00 p.m. on Sunday, August 28. articles.text: Editor: Over the last 50+ years that my family has lived in Piedmont, we have seen progressive changes in the city’s demographics. Our family moved to Piedmont in 1967 when most parents were having children when they were in their 20s and comfortably suviving on one salary. Today the social and economic structures of families in our community have drastically changed. For a majority of our city, two full-time incomes are often needed to purchase a home in Piedmont, and even with dual incomes, many of my fellow alumni returning to our community still needed help from their parents to purchase their homes. Enrollment in schools is drastically declining, reflecting young adults delaying parenthood until they can simultaneously afford a house and childcare in a city that doesn’t cater to working families. Many of our longer-term residents who raised children here couldn’t afford to purchase their own homes at today’s current rates. The need for more affordable housing in Piedmont for families, seniors, school, and city employees is critical. For all these reasons and many more, I believe we should embrace additional, yet gentle density housing in Piedmont as the state is requiring us to do. I agree with those who have voiced concerns about over-development. I believe we don’t need to drastically change the look or feel of Piedmont. We could add small multi-family units on top of the buildings already in dire need of structural upgrades, such as our city center, the plethora of antiquated and almost always empty brick-and-mortar banks, as well as Grand Avenue. Replacing the ever growing list of dilapidated and abandoned homes in Piedmont with affordable multifamily units would improve home values more than the homes with tarps covering the holes in the roofs and plywood over their broken windows. I want young people in their 20s and 30s to be able to move to Piedmont and eventually afford a home here. The problems we are experiencing are not unique. I would like to see Piedmont looking to the future to see how the benefits of creating more housing would strengthen the fabric of our community. I want our future generations to see that Piedmonters are wise, creative, and forward-thinking. Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak and a school board member conducted the second round of interviews. articles.text: Eric Havian, on behalf of PRFO, explained that the group began meeting in June to plan for fundraising campaign efforts. “We have pulled together a group of 20 residents working furiously [on this]. This is a short timeframe and will be a real challenge,” he explained to city council. “People have been phenomenal in stepping up, even in the middle of summer when Piedmont can become a bit of a ghost town.” Havian credited the powers of Zoom for allowing the PRFO to meet throughout the summer to plan. “We are looking forward to doing our part with the community to get you across the finish line,” Steve Collins, PRFO President, said on August 15. “We had fantastic private-public partnerships with the city. I’m optimistic that we will put together a successful fundraiser.” PRFO has identified three potential naming opportunities at the new pool facility for donations in the range of $500,000 to $1,000,000. These include the Poolside Room, the Pavilion, and the Competition Pool. Naming agreements would be brought before city council for final approval. For more information on PRFO’s Piedmont Community Pool Campaign, see https://prfo. org/piedmont-community-pool/. Separately, the city and its Sustainability Department will launch a campaign focused on funding the heat pumps required for the pool to be an all-electric facility. The proposed framework will be to reach the target of $500,000 by naming each of the 20 heat pumps with donations of $25,000.
articles.title: All-electric Pool

articles.text: An armed robbery involving an assault rifle occurred in Piedmont on Friday, August 19, shortly before 1 p.m. on Hillside Avenue between Blair and Oakland Avenue. While having lunch in their construction van, workers were approached by two suspects. described as Black men, tall and thin, dressed in dark clothes and wearing dark masks. One suspect brandished an assault rifle and the other revealed a handgun as the suspects demanded cash and tools from the victims. The victims were not injured. The suspects took $150 and a Makita drill from the construction crew, then fled the scene in a 4-door gold 1997 Lexus ES300 sedan. The gold car has gray lower trim, side and rear dark tinted windows, a number 2 sticker on the back left bumper and a license plate of 3TTW430. A few hours after the Piedmont robbery, the Lexus was pursued by San Francisco Police but evaded the patrol car and is still outstanding. The Piedmont Police Department is actively investigating this crime and requests any possible information. Those with information are asked to contact Detective George Tucker at (510) 420-3013 or (510) 420-3000. If this vehicle is seen, call 911 immediately. Surveillance cameras capture the image of the suspects’ gold 1997 Lexus ES 300.
articles.title: Daytime stickup with assault rifle

We came out of this portage hours later as different people than who had gone in, our high spirits shattered long ago. After a contemplative evening overlooking Scout Lake, we were picked up by the float plane on the morning of Day seven. Returning to base, we said our goodbyes and left a Troop 6 neckerchief hanging from the Dining Hall ceiling. With that, we were back to Winnipeg for a night and on a plane home the next morning. None of this would have been possible without the amazing Lisa Gros, who planned our trip, organized travel details, and supported us through every step of the way. Our other advisors included Bryan Gros, Kristen Gustavson, and Jason Throne, who were a huge source of motivation. Northern Tier certainly lived up to its name as a High Adventure base. CRIME REPORT By Jay Russell Daytime stickup with assault rifle An armed robbery involving an assault rifle occurred in Piedmont on Friday, August 19, shortly before 1 p.m. on Hillside Avenue between Blair and Oakland Avenue. While having lunch in their construction van, workers were approached by two suspects. described as Black men, tall and thin, dressed in dark clothes and wearing dark masks. One suspect brandished an assault rifle and the other revealed a handgun as the suspects demanded cash and tools from the victims. The victims were not injured. The suspects took $150 and a Makita drill from the construction crew, then fled the scene in a 4-door gold 1997 Lexus ES300 sedan. The gold car has gray lower trim, side and rear dark tinted windows, a number 2 sticker on the back left bumper and a license plate of 3TTW430. A few hours after the Piedmont robbery, the Lexus was pursued by San Francisco Police but evaded the patrol car and is still outstanding. The Piedmont Police Department is actively investigating this crime and requests any possible information. Those with information are asked to contact Detective George Tucker at (510) 420-3013 or (510) 420-3000. If this vehicle is seen, call 911 immediately. Surveillance cameras capture the image of the suspects’ gold 1997 Lexus ES 300. READ IT IN THE POST

Edible contests have been a part of the Piedmont Harvest Festival since the beginning in 1998. They showcase, for the appreciation of all, the amazing diversity of fruits and vegetables grown in Piedmont, and the talent of our residents in preparing and preserving these products for their families and friends. Eligibility Anyone who lives or works in the City of Piedmont may submit an entry. Entries may be done by individuals, households, neighborhoods or groups. Rules of Entry Any item submitted for consideration in a growing category must be grown within the borders of the City of Piedmont, CA. Any item that is submitted for a cooking category must have a main ingredient that could feasibly be grown in Piedmont. The actual ingredient does not have to have been grown within the borders of Piedmont. Items submitted for display only are not limited by the above rules. Non-residents are welcome to join the fun by bringing items for display only. No Fees There is no charge to enter. Prizes All participants will receive recognition and prizes will vary among categories. The Bill Drum Memorial Sweepstakes Prize is awarded to the person or group that receives the most blue ribbons. Number of Entries Any number of entries are allowed in each category by individuals or groups. Submission of Entries All entries must be delivered between 7:30am and 10:00am on Sunday, September 19, 2021 Please bring your completed entry form (or proof of digital submission) to the Community Hall. Use one entry form for all entries and be sure a label is securely attached for each entry. Labels for items in the cooking categories must have the "main ingredient" clearly visible. Additional forms are available at the Recreation Department, City Hall, or at www.piedmont.ca.gov Judging Judges for the contest will be knowledgeable in the areas they judge. Entrants are reminded of the objective of the Festival: to provide an opportunity for people to show the bounty of their gardens and kitchens, to provide a source of fun and to strengthen our sense of community. Judging begins promptly at 10:00am and is not open to the public. Any Item Not Picked Up by 1:30pm Will be Eaten or Recycled Due care will be taken to insure the safety of entries during the festival. However, neither the Recreation Department nor the Harvest Festival Committee can assume responsibility for any loss or damage that may occur. Entries will be cleared at 1:30pm Make Scarecrow Any individual or group (resident or non-resident) can make a scarecrow and donate it for the Silent Auction. Scarecrows must be family-friendly and proceeds will benefit the Tri-School Fund. For information, contact Amber Brumfiel (amberrye@hotmail.com) The Jazz Festival Come enjoy the Jazz Festival held in the Main Park. Pack a picnic or purchase your lunch from one of the food trucks. articles.text: Six residents have qualified as candidates for the City Council election on November 8. As of August 12, the deadline for filing papers with City Hall, names of the following individuals will appear on the ballot: incumbents Betsy Andersen and Jennifer Long, and candidates Tom Ramsey, Bridget Harris, Jeanne Solnordal, and Nancy Bostrom. Avnish Patel did not return paperwork prior to the deadline. City council members Andersen and Long are eligible to run for a four-year term. Long was appointed in February and is currently serving in an interim role. Mayor Teddy Gray King will term out after eight years on the council.
articles.title: Six candidates to run for city council

articles.text: Stop wasting taxpayers’ money Editor: No matter our political leanings, here’s something we can all agree on: Don’t waste taxpayer dollars. Neighbors around Nova and Magnolia are asking the City not to spend money on a project we do not want. In 2019, the City of Piedmont installed its first use of plastic bollards to calm traffic at the intersection of Nova and Magnolia. The bollards compromised the neighborhood aesthetic, and in letters and testimony at council meetings, neighbors urged the City to take a different approach. We were told the bollards were only temporary, simply a trial design for a landscaped solution. This eyesore was supposed to enhance safety but has not. The bollards have created confusion and posed their own safety risks. Neighbors have asked the City repeatedly to remove the bollards ASAP, but, even in the face of a petition signed by 120 residents, the bollards are still there. Now the City is proposing to install black and orange asphalt bumpers at a cost of $50,000 in lieu of the bollards. But these, too, are ugly and pose safety risks. Neighbors have done everything the City asked in order to get a landscaped solution. For example, we were told to go to the CIP, and nothing occurred. We were told to raise funds which we did but were rebuffed. Now we have some simple requests to the City: 1. Remove the bollards 2. Do not spend $50,000 of taxpayer money to foist on residents raised eyesore markers that are inappropriate to the neighborhood. Many of us are longtime residents and all of us are taxpayers. This intersection, which abuts a main Piedmont artery, deserves more than a slipshod solution. If we have to raise money, we need a good list of options and how much money each would cost. Perhaps nothing further is even needed. This is all common sense. Spending $50,000 would be folly. Let’s hope a majority of the City Council agrees. –Joy Koletsky Jacobs

articles.text: A weekend walk-in clinic offering monkeypox vaccinations opened at San Francisco General Hospital on Saturday, August 14. A quarter of the state’s monkeypox cases are in San Francisco. The federal government announced its national monkeypox vaccine strategy on June 28. Multiple federal agencies coordinated to implement a plan to inoculate at-risk individuals with a limited supply of vaccines. Long lines were reported at monkeypox vaccine pop-up clinics throughout the state when the Jynneos vaccine first became available. The Jynneos monkeypox vaccine is administered in two doses similar to the Moderna and Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine. San Francisco resident Joe Haley said he waited in line over three hours to receive his first dose at San Francisco General Hospital on August 1. Haley arrived at 5:30 a.m. as a walk-in patient and was given a patient information sheet to fill out, and then a number for inoculation: #149. “I showed up before the clinic opened and was expecting a lot of people. The [hospital] staff were efficient despite the long line and wait time,” Haley said. The patient information sheet required that each walk-in patient state their name, address and phone number, as well as sexual identity and sexual orientation. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said in a press release on May 18 that “anyone can spread monkeypox regardless of sexual orientation,” while also noting that early case tracking suggests “gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men make up a high number of cases.” Haley, who identifies as gay, said he sought out the vaccine after hearing of the first confirmed case of the virus in San Francisco. “The symptoms [associated with the virus] sound and look excruciating. There is definitely a sense of alarm in the gay community,” he said. Haley lives in the Castro District of San Francisco. San Francisco General Hospital is one of the closest pop-up clinics offering the Jynneos monkeypox vaccine. At the time of his first inoculation on August 1, Haley was not given a date to return for his second dose. The vaccine series is administered in the upper arm at least four weeks apart. According to the CDC, people who receive the vaccine have minor reactions such as pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site. Rare reactions such as nausea, chills, and fever have been reported. Vaccine supply is limited. San Francisco General Hospital received over 10,000 doses from the federal supply last week, allowing it to reopen and inoculate individuals seeking vaccinations. The vaccine is free and no health insurance is required. In San Francisco, gay, bisexual, and men who have sex with men; sex workers of any sexual orientation; persons who have been in close contact with someone with a suspected or confirmed case of the virus; and clinicians who have had a high-risk occupational exposure are eligible to receive the Jynneos vaccine. The San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH) explained in a statement that it will prioritize first dose of Jynneos vaccine “to as many at-risk people as possible and will defer second dose appointments until sufficient supply is received.” The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) has created a screening worksheet and urges all individuals with symptoms of Monkeypox to complete the worksheet, which requires the patient to send photos of rashes and collect specimens. The form is available at https://acphd-web-media.s3-uswest-2.amazonaws.com/media/ communicable-disease/monkeypox/docs/monkeypox-screening-form-2022.07.10.pdf.

articles.text: Editor: Hundreds of pages of technical analyses as well as scores of hours of public testimony regarding housing for low-income families in Piedmont boil down to a simple question: do we want to live in a segregated city in which low-income families reside, as a matter of public policy, in a concentrated enclave socially and physically isolated from the remainder of the community? Comments at public hearings suggest that some Piedmonters would answer “yes.” They suggest locating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park – noisier, more hazardous, more distant from schools, and more physically isolated than any site the city’s professional staff recommended the City Council consider. Fifty years of research into the costs and benefits of subsidized housing tells us, however, that concentrating low-income families in an area functionally separate from the remainder of the community is the worst choice a city can make. Indeed, federal, state, and local, including Piedmont, policy is to avoid such concentration. Ignoring those policies and concentrating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park would create a place that all Piedmonters will know as the “other side of tracks.” A stigmatized place that impedes rather than fosters participation in the larger community. And, yes, research also suggests that adding low-income housing to high income communities reduces property values, at least temporarily. But those effects are smaller and shorter in duration when cities “scatter” rather than segregate such housing. The State’s requirement that we accommodate 220 low and very low-income families means we cannot preserve all Piedmont neighborhoods as we now know them. We can, however, choose whether Piedmont will welcome or impede the participation of these families in the social and civic life of our community. This choice will profoundly influence how Piedmont families, regardless of income, come to view, and live with, each other. It will also affect how others in our region view us now and into the indefinite future. Do you prefer a segregated Piedmont to one that keeps open the possibility of creating a community, however imperfect, of which we can all be proud? If not, please let the City Council know your preferences in advance of the August 18 City Council meeting. –Ralph Catalano For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will be piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up on specific days, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than the recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul every Friday during the summer months. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located to the right of the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road, Piedmont, CA. The site will be open on Friday, May 26 and close for the season in the fall. The site will be open, weather and conditions permitting, each Friday after 8:00am. The site will close during periods of rain or when the site is at all muddy. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes the City of Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Learn more about the benefits and uses of compost here. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. San Francisco resident Joe Haley said he waited in line over three hours to receive his first dose at San Francisco General Hospital on August 1. Haley arrived at 5:30 a.m. as a walk-in patient and was given a patient information sheet to fill out, and then a number for inoculation: #149. “I showed up before the clinic opened and was expecting a lot of people. The [hospital] staff were efficient despite the long line and wait time,” Haley said. The patient information sheet required that each walk-in patient state their name, address and phone number, as well as sexual identity and sexual orientation. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said in a press release on May 18 that “anyone can spread monkeypox regardless of sexual orientation,” while also noting that early case tracking suggests “gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men make up a high number of cases.” Haley, who identifies as gay, said he sought out the vaccine after hearing of the first confirmed case of the virus in San Francisco. “The symptoms [associated with the virus] sound and look excruciating. There is definitely a sense of alarm in the gay community,” he said. Haley lives in the Castro District of San Francisco. San Francisco General Hospital is one of the closest pop-up clinics offering the Jynneos monkeypox vaccine. At the time of his first inoculation on August 1, Haley was not given a date to return for his second dose. The vaccine series is administered in the upper arm at least four weeks apart. According to the CDC, people who receive the vaccine have minor reactions such as pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site. Rare reactions such as nausea, chills, and fever have been reported. Vaccine supply is limited. San Francisco General Hospital received over 10,000 doses from the federal supply last week, allowing it to reopen and inoculate individuals seeking vaccinations. The vaccine is free and no health insurance is required. In San Francisco, gay, bisexual, and men who have sex with men; sex workers of any sexual orientation; persons who have been in close contact with someone with a suspected or confirmed case of the virus; and clinicians who have had a high-risk occupational exposure are eligible to receive the Jynneos vaccine. The San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH) explained in a statement that it will prioritize first dose of Jynneos vaccine “to as many at-risk people as possible and will defer second dose appointments until sufficient supply is received.” The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) has created a screening worksheet and urges all individuals with symptoms of Monkeypox to complete the worksheet, which requires the patient to send photos of rashes and collect specimens. The form is available at https://acphd-web-media.s3-uswest-2.amazonaws.com/media/ communicable-disease/monkeypox/docs/monkeypox-screening-form-2022.07.10.pdf. Free compost self-haul at Corp. Yard every Friday until Labor Day The City of Piedmont will be piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up on specific days, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than the recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul every Friday during the summer months. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located to the right of the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road, Piedmont, CA. The site will be open on Friday, May 26 and close for the season in the fall. The site will be open, weather and conditions permitting, each Friday after 8:00am. The site will close during periods of rain or when the site is at all muddy. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes the City of Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Learn more about the benefits and uses of compost here. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. By Ralph Catalano Editor: Hundreds of pages of technical analyses as well as scores of hours of public testimony regarding housing for low-income families in Piedmont boil down to a simple question: do we want to live in a segregated city in which low-income families reside, as a matter of public policy, in a concentrated enclave socially and physically isolated from the remainder of the community? Comments at public hearings suggest that some Piedmonters would answer “yes.” They suggest locating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park – noisier, more hazardous, more distant from schools, and more physically isolated than any site the city’s professional staff recommended the City Council consider. Fifty years of research into the costs and benefits of subsidized housing tells us, however, that concentrating low-income families in an area functionally separate from the remainder of the community is the worst choice a city can make. Indeed, federal, state, and local, including Piedmont, policy is to avoid such concentration. Ignoring those policies and concentrating 100 or more low-income families in Blair Park would create a place that all Piedmonters will know as the “other side of tracks.” A stigmatized place that impedes rather than fosters participation in the larger community. And, yes, research also suggests that adding low-income housing to high income communities reduces property values, at least temporarily. But those effects are smaller and shorter in duration when cities “scatter” rather than segregate such housing. The State’s requirement that we accommodate 220 low and very low-income families means we cannot preserve all Piedmont neighborhoods as we now know them. We can, however, choose whether Piedmont will welcome or impede the participation of these families in the social and civic life of our community. This choice will profoundly influence how Piedmont families, regardless of income, come to view, and live with, each other. It will also affect how others in our region view us now and into the indefinite future. Do you prefer a segregated Piedmont to one that keeps open the possibility of creating a community, however imperfect, of which we can all be proud? If not, please let the City Council know your preferences in advance of the August 18 City Council meeting. –Ralph Catalano Collecting photos for Where in the World For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany The Yulan Magnolia (magnolia denudate) in the forecourt at Piedmont Community Hall, is recognized in the city’s Heritage Tree program and will be included in the city’s tree inventory. Piedmont Public Works is conducting a citywide tree inventory of its urban forest, a project that will take two to three months. The City announced on August 10 that Davey Resource Group [DRG] will canvass and record the thousands of public trees in Piedmont. “During the inventory, DRG’s experienced, qualified urban foresters locate trees, planting sites, and stumps along maintained street right-of-ways and in public parks and properties,” said Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent. “The arborists will evaluate those trees and record the data specified by the city.” DRG’s staff will identify the species, location, diameter, and health of over 8,000 trees in the coming weeks. They began collecting data on August 9. “Residents will see arborists walking our streets and parks with their iPads reviewing the trees of our urban forest,” Kent said. “They will be identifiable by their safety vest and hard hats and will carry a badge.” Public Works Supervisor Nik Millosovich explained the importance of the tree inventory. “The city has not done a tree inventory since the mid-to-late 1980’s, and the city’s tree inventory has changed quite a bit in that time,” he said. Parks and public areas are maintained by the Public Works Department; the Park Commission, Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club contribute to the maintenance of the city’s diverse landscape. Millosovich confirmed that the majority of the city’s mature trees are Liquidambar and London Plane. Also included in the city’s public tree stock are Maples, Highland Poplars, Coast Redwoods, and European White Birches.
articles.title: Piedmont tree inventory underway

articles.text: The city of Piedmont anticipates construction on the Piedmont Community Pool to begin in late November or early December this year. Bid documents will be distributed to pre-qualified contractors this month and opening bids will begin in early October. “This marks an important milestone in the process of bringing a new community pool to Piedmont. We are ready to solicit bids for construction,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said to the City Council on August 16. The project defines a base bid that includes: a single-story pool building with an office, lobby, locker rooms, two gender neutral changing rooms and rooftop pavilion; 27-meter x 25-yard competition pool with diving well; 3,177 square foot Activity Pool with zero beach entry and three 25-yard lap lanes; an all-electric powered aquatic center, including building, site and pool systems; and right-of way improvements. “Due to the unique nature of the Community Pool Project, council members authorized city staff to prepare a pre-qualification request [RFQ] at the May 16 meeting to ensure that only contractors fully capable of successfully constructing the project would be invited to submit bid proposals,” Lillevand said. The RFQ was issued on June 1, and six bid proposals were received by the July 1 deadline. After a detailed review, two firms, Lathrop Construction Associates and S.J. Amoroso Construction Co., were pre-qualified to bid on the City’s Community Pool Project, Lillevand explained. The bid documents specify that the estimated time to complete the project is 335 working days, which keeps the project on track for opening in the summer of 2024. Photo courtesy of ELS Architecture and Urban Design Construction on the Piedmont Community Pool is expected to begin this winter, according to city staff.
articles.title: Pool construction to commence

articles.text: The following letter was sent on August 14 to Piedmont City Council. Editor: We are writing to you in your official capacities as mayor and city council of Piedmont because the recent curb work at the intersection of Manor Drive and Holly Place is unsafe and unsightly. The neighborhood was afforded absolutely no opportunity to weigh in on the design before it was adopted. In short, we went from a typical Piedmont curb allowing pedestrians to travel freely through the intersection to an ugly sunken maze of tripping hazards. Two days ago, we and over a dozen of our neighbors met with Daniel Gonzales of the Department of Public Works to express our concerns with the design. While Daniel acknowledged that communication “could have been better,” he said he didn’t think it was likely that he would agree to redesign the intersection. He also said that the street would be ground down and repaved “soon,” but couldn’t say when, locking in the poor design choices. There is some urgency to the matter. We are therefore asking you to instruct the Department of Public Works to develop and implement a design for the intersection that returns the sidewalk to its former level and provides safety when crossing the street for all residents. In the long run, making these changes now rather than letting them fester, will save the city money. To give you a sense of the changes, see the attached beforeand-after pictures. –Dr. Elizabeth McDonald and J High Corner of Manor Drive and Holly Place — Before. Corner of Manor Drive and Holly Place — After.
articles.title: Restore Holly & Manor curbs to normal

articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://cur. tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: Piedmont School District will conduct the second round of interviews for a new Beach School principal today, August 17. Michael Corritone, principal for the last eight years, leaves this Friday, August 19 to take a job as principal of Indian Valley Elementary School in Walnut Creek. Starting Monday, August 22, Superintendent Donald Evans and Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak will alternate overseeing operations at Beach until a new principal is hired. The district hopes to confirm the appointment at its August 24 board meeting. The district conducted a first round of interviews on August 12 with a panel of interviewers consisting of five Beach parents, four Beach teachers, four CSEA (non-teaching staff) members, elementary school principals, and school district cabinet members. The five Beach parents were selected from the Beach Parent Club, Site Council representatives, and PRAISE. “I know the Beach teachers on the panel are hoping to find someone truly devoted to elementary [students], with warm rapport and a community spirit, who prioritizes presence in classrooms and hallways, who embraces a collaborative approach, who communicates honestly and well, and has a philosophy that continues to help the school evolve and grow,” said teachers union President Elise Marks. Today’s second-round interviews will be conducted by Evans, Wozniak and a school board member. Only two round of interviews are scheduled, and the job was posted only for nine days, starting August 1 when Corritone announced his departure. A full recap of the interview and hiring processes will be presented at the school board meeting on August 24, when the board also plans to confirm the appointment of a new principal and announce the starting date.
articles.title: Second round of interviews today for Beach School principal

articles.text: The Annual Walk for Wellness, which raises money for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center, will take place the week of August 21-27. The Grubb Company is sponsoring a kickoff event with a boba truck supplying free drinks for the first 200 student walkers to sign up at the Exedra on August 21 between 1:00-5:00 p.m. Walk for Wellness is a community-wide event. Parents, teachers, students, and other community members will receive a list of community walks that will take place throughout the week. Participants are also encouraged to bring a friend and head out for a stroll. Participants can register for the walk or sign up to sponsor the event at Pef.schoolauction. Walk for Wellness Committee members Martha Joerger (left), Sarah Meyjes, Laurie Misra, and Lindsay Thomasson. net/wfw22. This year’s event is co-chaired by Martha Joerger and Lindsay Thomasson along with Wellness Center Support Committee Co-Chairs Sarah Meyjes and Laurie Misra. Last year’s event raised $50,000 for the Wellness Center and increased community, and particularly student, awareness of the services provided by the Center. To date, the Walk has over 50 family and corporate sponsors who have donated between $500- $10,000 each. There is a potential for nearly 400 walkers to join in the Walk during the week, a significant increase from past years. The Wellness Center provides confidential free counseling services to all Piedmont middle and high school students, including IEP-based counseling services. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one-third of high school and one-quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year.

articles.text: The new school year is underway as Piedmont athletes get set to hit the fields and courts. It can be easy to forget all that transpired the previous year as coaches turn the page and look toward their new rosters. There were several moments last year that made a strong impression on this writer. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite five events and memories from last year. 1 Boys’ Soccer’s North Coast Section championship Coach Todd Sullivan is among the most emotional coaches at the school during games, often shouting at referees and urging his players to achieve great results. Once the final whistle blew on that February 26 night at Witter Field when PHS defeated No. 2 University 1-0 for the Division 4 North Coast Section championship, Sullivan shot his hands in the air, gave me an embracing hug when congratulating him, and had his emotions on high during our postgame interview. In a rattling voice he described that he might break into tears any moment. Even a bucket of icecold Gatorade dumped on him on a cold February night brought no shivers. Instead, it produced an air of satisfaction knowing that that Piedmont had finally captured an NCS banner. 2. Boys’ Water Polo captures first league title It’s difficult to think of another person more deserving of a championship than water polo coach John Savage. Piedmont’s 12-8 win over No. 1 seeded Berkeley Staff Photos Boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan gets doused with Gatorade after Piedmont beat University to win the North Coast Section championship. Boys’ water polo coach John Savage pumps his fists after his team won the league championship for the first time in school history, on October 30 for the WACC title was a long time coming for the school that has churned out collegiate talent over the years. It was the team’s first league banner in 15 years. As the final whistle blew, Savage pumped his fists with clipboard in hand while his team celebrated in the pool. 3. “Daddy’s Money” game with Berkeley football 2021 was a difficult season for Piedmont football, which played a full season with a roster of only 19 varsity players and finished with a 2-7 record. But on October 8 at the Yellowjackets’ field, the Highlanders beat large-enrollment Berkeley 28-26 in a comeback. The Berkeley student section provided a hostile setting, chanting “Daddy’s money” toward Piedmont throughout. But PHS quarterback Adhi Bornstein drove the team 55 yards with 2:41 left in the game, completing the winning TD pass to receiver Ryan McConathy. Bornstein had his best game of the year with 261 yards, three touchdowns, and on defense, making an interception to seal the deal. The football team’s 28-26 win over Berkeley came in a hostile environment. Quarterback Adhi Bornstein led the team with 261 yards passing and three touchdowns. The boys’ lacrosse team captured its sixth straight WACC title in a heated 10-9 win over top-seeded Bishop O’Dowd, with new PHS coach Alex Yu defeating his former team.
articles.title: A look back: the Post’s top-5 in 2021-22

articles.text: Indoor teams struggling to find assistant coaches Piedmont High announced last spring that it would add Beach Volleyball to the spring sports calendar in 2023. The announcement came after students at PHS petitioned to add the sport “Our first season of Beach Volleyball will be in the spring,” confirmed Athletic Director Bradley Smet. The next steps will be to find a location for sand courts. Smet explained that there is not a set location for games to take place. The players are examining the possibility of playing in Moraga, Berkeley, and Alameda. “We will be renting courts for at least the first year. We are continuing to work with the city and the district to find the best solution for this. We have not set our final location for courts yet,” said Smet. articles.text: Next up: Cincinnati Masters, U.S. Open this month Photos courtesy of EuroSport Mackie McDonald recently competed in the Cincinnati Masters, making the Round of 32. Mackie McDonald is playing his way through the summer schedule in preparation for the U.S. Open later this month (August 29 to September 11). This week, McDonald reached the Round of 32 at the Cincinnati Masters tournament, nearly double-bageling Nikoloz Basilashvili 6-0, 6-1 on Sunday, August 14 but losing in straight sets to No. 3 seed Carlos Alcaraz on Tuesday, August 16, 6-3, 6-2. Against Basilashvili, McDonald recorded eight aces and won 90 percent of points on his first serve, while claiming six of 11 break point opportunities. It was a dominant win over the world’s No. 34 overall ranked player on the ATP World Tour. McDonald took three break points in the first set as the returner and another three in the second set. McDonald has played well against Basilashvili throughout his career. This marks his third career win over the Georgian. In the match with Alcaraz, the loss came against the world’s No. 4 overall ranked player and a teenage phenom at just 19 years old. Alcaraz started the first set by stealing a point as the returner, while Mackie battled to 4-3 in the first. However, the Spaniard won the final two games, including the sixth game as the returner. In the second set, the match sat at 2-2, but Alcaraz claimed four straight games to win, including two break points. Alcaraz finished with five aces and claimed four of seven break point opportunities. McDonald is now ranked No. 72 in the world after reaching a career high of No. 48 earlier this month. McDonald lost in three sets to No. 44 Emil Ruusuvouri in the Citi Open’s first round on August 2, 1-6, 6-4, 6-4. He also lost in the first round of the Canadian Open on August 8 to No. 39 Alex Molcan in a close match, 7-6 (7-1), 6-4. Looking ahead to the prestigious U.S. Open, the event in 2016 was McDonald’s Grand Slam debut, where he reached the first round. McDonald reached the second round in 2021, defeating No. 27 seed David Goffin 6-2, 7-5, 6-3 in the first round but lost to Kei Nishikori in the second round, 7-6 (7-3), 6-3, 6-7 (7-5), 2-6, 6-3. Mackie McDonald lost to No. 4 world ranked Carlos Alcaraz in the second round of the Cincinnati Masters. Mackie McDonald gears up for the next Grand Slam tournament, the U.S. Open from August 29-September 11.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald in middle of summer schedule

articles.text: 3 points back of playoff qualification zone, 9 matches left It was another tie for Oakland Roots, this time with Detroit City, after leading 1-0. Charlie Dennis’ scored for Oakland in the 50th minute, but Detroit equalized it with three minutes left in regulation on a goal by Francis Atuahene. The result brings Oakland’s record to six wins, 12 ties, and seven losses with nine games left in the season. With 30 points, it’s shaping up to be a thick race for a final playoff spot in the Western Conference. Following the weekend’s results, the Roots are in ninthplace and two points behind eighth-place Los Dos (which has one game in hand), three back of Las Vegas (one game in hand) in the seventh-place playoff barrier, and four back of sixth-place El Paso–which has played one more match than Oakland and plays again on August 20. Behind Roots, meanwhile, is Phoenix and Monterey Bay with 29 points each. Roots dropping points is a painfully common occurrence in 2022 with Saturday’s result being the eighth time Oakland has either tied or lost from a winning position. How valuable would’ve been those 24 points? Here’s a list Charlie Dennis scored for Oakland after being in position when Detroit’s keeper misplayed a pass. Staff Photos Roots coach Juan Guerra and players came away with their 12th tie of the season in a 1-1 draw with Detroit City. It marked the eighth time they dropped points from a winning position after leading 1-0. of those games: 3-2 loss to Monterey Bay, March 26; Roots led 2-1 after 49 minutes. 2-2 tie at New Mexico United, March 30; Roots led 1-0 after eight minutes. 1-1 tie at El Paso, April 23; Roots led 1-0 after 23 minutes. 1-1 tie at Las Vegas, May 14; Roots led 1-0 after three minutes. 2-1 loss to New Mexico United, June 15; Roots led 1-0 after 20 minutes. 1-1 tie at San Antonio, June 18; Roots led 1-0 after 29 minutes. 3-3 tie at Sacramento Republic, July 9; Roots led 3-2 after 70 minutes. 1-1 tie at Detroit City, August 13; Roots led 1-0 after 50 minutes. In Saturday’s draw, Roots had its chances and had better looks before and after the 50th minute goal. Dennis nearly had an early goal in the ninth minute when his left footed shot forced a diving save. In the 18th, Darek Formella had a shot on target saved after receiving a feed by Edgardo Rito on the counter attack. Dennis’ goal in the 50th came from a disastrous ball by Detroit keeper Nate Steinwascher, which went straight to Dennis, enabling him to uncork a left-footed shot into the net. Rito perhaps had the most clear look in the 65th with an opportunity to put Oakland up 2-nil when Dennis found him with a ball over the top, but Edgardo’s left footed shot (his weaker foot) skied by the left post. In the 82nd minute, Oakland subbed in Joseph Nane for Mikael Johnsen in a defensive move. But Detroit struck just five minutes later when striker Antoine Hoppenot went down the right side with the Roots’ defense strung out of position. The DCFC striker was able to find Atuahene with acres of space in a one-on-one situation, leading to the equalizer. It was an unfortunate turn after a solid game by the defense to not allow many clear looks. Detroit finished with 10 shots, three on target, after going into halftime with three shot attempts and none on target. Oakland, finished with 12 shots, three on target, five blocked and three big opportunities missed. Roots coach Juan Guerra shared his thoughts on Twitter, voicing optimism after playing in a difficult environment at Detroit’s Keyworth Stadium. “Tonight we were able to play our way in a very tough environment. I am proud of my players and staff. We will keep pushing forward, always believing in our
articles.title: LOCAL SPORTS Oakland Roots concedes late goal in 1-1 tie with Detroit City

articles.text: The largest fire in 2022 is just about out of the national spotlight and near full containment at 95 percent as of Tuesday night, currently at 60,392 acres burned— gaining just three acres in size over the last week. Firefighting efforts are still focusing on unburned vegetation within the containment lines. “Firefighters continue suppression repair efforts and are patrolling throughout the fire perimeter. Crews are paying particular attention to areas of unburned vegetation within the interior of the fire containment lines, which have been producing smoke and heat. Aircraft was brought in to conduct aerial suppression operations on one of these pockets in the southwestern fire area. Three hand crews and a strike team of engines also conducted ground suppression and the “hot spot” posed no threat to the containment lines,” wrote Inciweb, a federal fire information site. Inciweb continues that only two miles of the fire is considered uncontained, while fire prevention work has contructed 204 total miles of containment lines. “Additionally, firefighters have been granted access to the McKinney Creek Road area, and repair work will begin within the next few days. As of Sunday evening, firefighters have constructed 62 miles of containment line by hand, and heavy equipment has constructed 142 miles of containment line. Only two miles of the fire is considered “uncontained” at this time. Forward progression of the fire has stopped, but steep terrain and the abundance of hazard trees are making it difficult for firefighters to perform mop-up in this area. Crews will keep working as safety allows,” wrote Inciweb. Photo courtesy of Redding.com Firefighter efforts have helped contain the McKinney Fire to 95 percent. Photo courtesy of Redding.com Fire prevention efforts have created over 200 miles of containment lines.
articles.title: OUTDOORS McKinney Fire at 95 percent containment

articles.text: Aiden Morgan, an 8th grader at Piedmont Middle School, was named tournament MVP at the USSAA Gold Rush Classic baseball tournament in Ripon the weekend of August 6-7. Aiden plays on the Future Star Baseball team, a 13 & Under team based in Oakland. Their team took first place in the tournament, coming back from a 10-2 deficit in the championship game to win 13-10. During the tournament, Future Star beat U-Town Baseball Club from Ukiah 14 – 4, lost 9-4 to Izturis Baseball Academy from Rancho Cordova, and beat Lafayette Select 10-1 to advance to the finals. In the championship game they beat the Dublin Warlocks from Dublin 13-10. Aiden Morgan was named MVP in the Gold Rush Classic baseball tournament in Ripon on August 7.
articles.title: Local 13 & Under baseball team wins tourney in Ripon

Firefighting efforts are still focusing on unburned vegetation within the containment lines. “Firefighters continue suppression repair efforts and are patrolling throughout the fire perimeter. Crews are paying particular attention to areas of unburned vegetation within the interior of the fire containment lines, which have been producing smoke and heat. Aircraft was brought in to conduct aerial suppression operations on one of these pockets in the southwestern fire area. Three hand crews and a strike team of engines also conducted ground suppression and the “hot spot” posed no threat to the containment lines,” wrote Inciweb, a federal fire information site. Inciweb continues that only two miles of the fire is considered uncontained, while fire prevention work has contructed 204 total miles of containment lines. “Additionally, firefighters have been granted access to the McKinney Creek Road area, and repair work will begin within the next few days. As of Sunday evening, firefighters have constructed 62 miles of containment line by hand, and heavy equipment has constructed 142 miles of containment line. Only two miles of the fire is considered “uncontained” at this time. Forward progression of the fire has stopped, but steep terrain and the abundance of hazard trees are making it difficult for firefighters to perform mop-up in this area. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s free events on Friday Nights will continue this fall, with food trucks, music, and art activities inspired by the museum’s current exhibitions. Beginning at 5 p.m., an assortment of food trucks on 10th street between Oakland and Fallon Streets will be parked, with beer and wine available. The variety of food changes weekly. Activities and music will be available on the museum’s outdoor lawn. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the project design. Renovations were funded by a campaign to expand OMCA’s role in the community as a public gathering place. Outdoor games like “Giant Jenga” and “Connect-Four” will be available. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/fridaynights. Friday, August 19 5 to 7 p.m. - DJ Ron Reeser (Amphitheater) 6 to 8 p.m. - Textiles Remixed with Kalingafornia Laga Weaving Collective, Sheng Lor, and Amadi Greenstein (Garden) This program explores the practice of textile art with a series of demonstrations in the OMCA campus garden, featuring Bay Area artists Kalingafornia Laga Weaving Collective and Sheng Lor. Kalingafornia Laga is a weaving collective of Filipino American women in the San Francisco Bay Area who preserve, promote, and maintain indigenous backstrap weaving traditions from Kalinga. Sheng Lor is a Hmong American fiber artist whose practice is motivated by a desire to connect to cultural practices of her elders, which are rooted in shamanism and land stewardship. Amadi Greenstein is a passionate textile artist originally from Northern Virginia who creates original textile works that explain the narratives of her cultural identities and personal memories, along with discoveries of narratives from other identities. The artists and makers will remix concepts of identities, mythologies, and healing through braiding, weaving, and wrapping. Following the demonstrations, Carin Adams, OMCA Curator of Art, will lead a conversation about textiles. Friday, August 26 5 to 7 p.m. - DJ X-Ro (Amphitheater) 7 to 9 p.m. - Can I Kick It? Film Experience Presented by Shaolin Jazz, with screening of Black Panther (Garden) Visit OMCA’s expansive outdoor garden for an outdoor film experience. Can I Kick it? highlights Kung-Fu and action films and the music they inspired. At the screening, watch the popular Marvel film Black Panther scored with a live mixed blend of hip-hop, soul, funk. DJ X-Ro will play in the amphitheater from 5 to 7 p.m. Staff photo Oakland Museum’s outdoor lawn, renovated one year ago, hosts Friday Night programing beyond the summer.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse presents Follies onstage now through September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army, Blood, Sweat, and Stanley Poole (1961), written with his brother William. Other work for the stage includes A Family Affair, a collaboration with John Kander, starring Shelley Berman; Evening Primrose (1966), Oliver Twist (1982), Anna Karenina (1985), Anatasia: The Mystery of Anna (1986), and Tolstoy (1996). Goldman’s novels include The Man from Greek and Roman (1974), Myself as Witness (1980), and Fulton County (1989). Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The original production is the second-most costly production performed on Broadway to date. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and Phyllis were showgirls in the Follies, both in failing marriages. The cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. For tickets, vsit https://www. sfplayhouse.org/, or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents the musical Goddess from the critically acclaimed team that created Merry Wise for New York’s Shakespeare in the Park. The play opened on August 14 and will be performed through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, an ancient folktale passed down by generations in Africa. According to the tale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed, and an advocate for peace. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, and is based on a book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and lyrics are by Michael Thurber, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. Cast members include Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. Photo by Calvin Ngu Cast members in rehearsal for Goddess at Berkeley Rep.

articles.text: World premiere at Opera House September 10 San Francisco Opera presents the world premiere of Anthony and Cleopatra, written by Berkeley native John Adams, on September 10 and running through October 5. Anthony and Cleopatra opens San Francisco Opera’s 100th Season. The play, commissioned for the Opera’s centennial, is set in a universe where “ancient Egypt meets Old Hollywood.” Adams tackles the Shakespearean equivalent of a celebrity romance and gives it a 21st century spin. Amina Idris sings the role of Cleopatra and Gerald Finley will be Anthony. The cast also includes Paul Appleby, Alfred Walker, Elizabeth DeShong, Brenton Ryan, Taylor Raven, Hadleigh Adams, Gabrielle Beteag, Timothy Murray and Philip Skinner. Anthony and Cleopatra will be conducted by San Francisco Opera’s new Music Director, Eun Sun Kim. For tickets, visit https:// www.sfopera.com/operas/antony-and-cleopatra/. Berkeley composer John Adams’ new opera, Anthony and Cleopatra, will have its world premiere next month at San Francisco Opera.

Kalingafornia Laga is a weaving collective of Filipino American women in the San Francisco Bay Area who preserve, promote, and maintain indigenous backstrap weaving traditions from Kalinga. Sheng Lor is a Hmong American fiber artist whose practice is motivated by a desire to connect to cultural practices of her elders, which are rooted in shamanism and land stewardship. Amadi Greenstein is a passionate textile artist originally from Northern Virginia who creates original textile works that explain the narratives of her cultural identities and personal memories, along with discoveries of narratives from other identities. The artists and makers will remix concepts of identities, mythologies, and healing through braiding, weaving, and wrapping. Following the demonstrations, Carin Adams, OMCA Curator of Art, will lead a conversation about textiles. Friday, August 26 5 to 7 p.m. - DJ X-Ro (Amphitheater) 7 to 9 p.m. - Can I Kick It? Film Experience Presented by Shaolin Jazz, with screening of Black Panther (Garden) Visit OMCA’s expansive outdoor garden for an outdoor film experience. Can I Kick it? highlights Kung-Fu and action films and the music they inspired. At the screening, watch the popular Marvel film Black Panther scored with a live mixed blend of hip-hop, soul, funk. SF Playhouse presents Follies through Sept. 10 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse presents Follies onstage now through September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army, Blood, Sweat, and Stanley Poole (1961), written with his brother William. Other work for the stage includes A Family Affair, a collaboration with John Kander, starring Shelley Berman; Evening Primrose (1966), Oliver Twist (1982), Anna Karenina (1985), Anatasia: The Mystery of Anna (1986), and Tolstoy (1996). Goldman’s novels include The Man from Greek and Roman (1974), Myself as Witness (1980), and Fulton County (1989). Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The original production is the second-most costly production performed on Broadway to date. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and Phyllis were showgirls in the Follies, both in failing marriages. The cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. Goddess musical playing at Berkeley Rep By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents the musical Goddess from the critically acclaimed team that created Merry Wise for New York’s Shakespeare in the Park. The play opened on August 14 and will be performed through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, an ancient folktale passed down by generations in Africa. According to the tale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed, and an advocate for peace. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, and is based on a book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and lyrics are by Michael Thurber, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. Cast members include Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. Photo by Calvin Ngu Cast members in rehearsal for Goddess at Berkeley Rep. Anthony and Cleopatra opens San Francisco Opera’s 100th Season. The play, commissioned for the Opera’s centennial, is set in a universe where “ancient Egypt meets Old Hollywood.” Adams tackles the Shakespearean equivalent of a celebrity romance and gives it a 21st century spin. Amina Idris sings the role of Cleopatra and Gerald Finley will be Anthony. The cast also includes Paul Appleby, Alfred Walker, Elizabeth DeShong, Brenton Ryan, Taylor Raven, Hadleigh Adams, Gabrielle Beteag, Timothy Murray and Philip Skinner. Anthony and Cleopatra will be conducted by San Francisco Opera’s new Music Director, Eun Sun Kim. For tickets, visit https:// www.sfopera.com/operas/antony-and-cleopatra/. Berkeley composer John Adams’ new opera, Anthony and Cleopatra, will have its world premiere next month at San Francisco Opera.
