articles.text: There are thousands of stories out there. Columnists such as Herb Caen and Dwight Chapin engaged the readers’ interest every day. So did radio broadcaster Paul Harvey. Yes, everyone has a story. One of the most interesting stories in the history of music involves the duo of operetta composers W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan. A more interesting duo probably never existed. Another story of particular interest is the San Francisco-based Lamplighters Music Theater. They have been presenting Gilbert and Sullivan productions for 70 years. That’s quite a run. I took the opportunity to attend the Sunday performance of their most recent production, Iolanthe, in the Yerba Buena Center in San Francisco. The production was everything you would expect from the Lamplighters…The costumes were colorful, and the production was lively. The orchestra played with precision. Overall, the staging was excellent. My only criticism is that the diction was sometimes not as clear as it might have been. But when I moved to the second row, it seemed to improve. Gilbert and Sullivan knew how to thumb their nose at almost everybody in society and positions of authority. They also knew how to do it in such a way that the object of their humor did not respond with anger – something requiring extraordinary talent and skill. Iolanthe is a typical example of political satire. It’s kind of like the joke where someone asks someone in a high position if it is possible to be both ignorant and apathetic. The “self important person“ answers: I don’t know and I don’t care. Gilbert and Sullivan use this routine frequently. Iolanthe pokes fun at just about everybody. There was absolutely no doubt that English Prime Minister William Gladstone was the object of much of this barbed humor and perhaps surprisingly was delighted with what Gilbert and Sullivan had created. Sadly, times have changed. Many people in high places now can’t take a joke. . There is one final performance of Iolanthe next weekend in Livermore. I gibe it my highest recommendations. And now the food part When I first moved to San Francisco, you could find good dim sum in almost any restaurant. I usually went with Chinese friends and always had a good time. Over time, however, It became more difficult to find good dim sum. That changed last week when I went to the Saigon Seafood Harbor Restaurant on Pierce Street in Richmond. In the old days waitresses and waiters used to come around with carts and you’d pick what you want. This dim sum restaurant has menus, and, more importantly, has great food. I never had better roast duck. Everything on our gigantic banquet was superb. Another recent discovery was Pomella restaurant located at 3770 Piedmont Avenue. This is a popular Middle Eastern restaurant. Everything that my party ordered was delectable. If you park in the adjacent lot, please note that the meters are enforced until midnight. I didn’t read the small print… And I mean SMALL print… The parking fine is $30. Next week we might look at how opera uses revisionist history. Forget the Barber of Seville. Forget the Spanish background of Carmen. And as for Aida…forget about Egypt. Put on your thinking caps and study your geography. And then forget everything. Operetta composers Gilbert & Sullivan.

articles.text: Jimi Hendrix is the most significant rock guitar stylist. He created a liquid style with slurs, fluid rhythm and pedal effects like distortion, octavia (transposes up an octave), wah-wah and Echoplex (tape echo, invented by Les Paul). Born in 1942, to an African American father and an American Indian mother in Seattle, Jimi started playing guitar at age 15 In 1961, he joined the army to avoid going to jail for car theft. Stationed at Fort Campbell, KY with the 101st Airborne Division, he received an honorable discharge the next year. Now a civilian, Jimi moved to Nashville and started playing on the “chitlin circuit” throughout the East, South and Midwest. On the circuit, he learned double stops from Curtis Mayfield in the Impressions (playing pairs of notes on adjacent strings, keeping one note stationary while changing the note on an adjacent string with a hammer or pull off). Use the link near the end of this column, you can hear Hey Joe double stops. Jimi learned showmanship from King Curtis and Little Richard. In 1966, Jimi was performing with his band Jimmy James and the Blue Flames in New York with Randy California. Randy later formed the band Spirit. Keith Richards’ girl friend, Linda Keith heard Jimi in a club and tried to get Keith to go listen to him. Keith wasn’t interested. Linda told Chas Chandler, the bass player with Animals about Jimi, and soon Chas asked Jimi and Randy both to go to London to develop a performing and recording band. Randy’s parents insisted that Randy finish high school. Chas flew Jimi to England to Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix form the Jimi Hendrix Experience, hiring Mitch Mitchell on drums and Noel Redding on bass. Chas financed the band’s room and board and paid to record their first single, Hey Joe, before they had a recording contract. Before going to England, Jimi hung out with Bob Dylan in Greenwich Village and was impressed by his lyric writing and that Dylan carried an idea notebook. Jimi said “you must admire the guy for having that much nerve to sing out of key, but then I started listening to the words. That sold me.” Jimi’s lyrics were sometimes inspired by science fiction magazines. Purple Haze, as example, was inspired by a story about a purple death ray. articles.text: Quinton Aaron and Sandra Bullock in The Blind Side Review by Chris Honoré The trailer for The Blind Side, released in 2009, has the appearance of another slick Hollywood happy meal. The film will be a two-hour sports cliché, the audience leaving the theater feeling somewhat satisfied but also a bit empty. Instead, surprisingly, the movie proves to be a solid drama, with Sandra Bullock as can-do southern belle, Leigh Anne Tuohy, giving her best performance in years and redeeming herself after the disastrous All About Steve. The true story, based on the book by Michael Lewis, while blatantly sentimental, tells the appealing story of Michael Oher (Quinton Aaron), aka Big Mike, a homeless black teen from the projects (ironically named Hurt Village), who is enrolled in a private Christian school in Memphis, Tennessee. Late one wintry night he is spotted by Leigh Anne and her husband, Sean (Tim McGraw), walking on a busy road. It’s bitterly cold and Michael admits that he has nowhere to go. They take him home, thus beginning the transformation of Michael from an undereducated, silent mountain of a kid to a star athlete who is eventually drafted by the Baltimore Ravens. It’s a remarkable journey, tempered to be sure by Michael’s stoic silence and his reluctance to trust, at least initially, this most improbable family that has taken him into their hearts. But he learns. And in the process begins a completely new life. Is the feel-good ending telegraphed almost from the first frame? Of course. But no matter. The Blind Side is a sweet movie. The Blind Side. Directed by John Lee Hancock. Starring Sandra Bullock, Tim McGraw, Quinton Aaron, and Kathy Bates. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released in theaters in 2009; reviewed then in the Post. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ peacock
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Blind Side a sweet movie with Sandra Bullock

articles.text: Madagascar is filled with gags, risky escapes, Looney Toon moments, and, of course, some standard life lessons (the importance of friendship, and be careful what you wish for). The story is likely best suited for older kids and tweens. The narrative is set in the New York Zoo, at least that’s where the adventure begins. Marty the zebra (Chris Rock) is celebrating his 10th birthday and rather than feeling cheerful, he is cranky, bored with the zoo’s day-in and day-out routine. His best bud, Alex the lion (Ben Stiller), a zoo favorite, tries to cheer him up, but to no avail. Alex loves to perform for the visitors, as well as enjoying his daily diet of raw steaks. One day Marty, still moping around, hears that there’s a scheme in the works by the crafty penguins, Skipper (Tom McGrath), Kowalski (Chris Miller), Rico (Jeff Katzenberg), and Private (Chris Knight). But it turns out the group is planning an escape. Naturally, Marty is inspired. It seems the penguin cohort wants to take over a ship and head toward colder climes. Marty convinces his friends, Gloria, the sassy hippo (Jada Pinkett Smith), Melman the giraffe (David Schwimmer), and Alex to join him in the break out. But things don’t go quite as planned, and the foursome end up stranded on the sandy shores of Madagascar, a jungle island island off the coast of Africa. They soon discover that there’s a colony of lemurs living there, led by King Julian (Sasha Baron Cohen). They also discover that they are now in the middle of the wild, exactly the place Marty had dreamed of. But what the gang soon learns is that perhaps the zoo is not all that bad. The wild jungles of the island are not all that userfriendly, and from Alex’s point of view, those ready-to-eat steaks are nowhere to be found. Soon he starts to eye Marty’s haunch as hunger sets in. All he wants is a nibble. Luckily, the penguins find a way to feed Alex some sushi. Soon Marty begins to wonder about how they might return to the zoo. It’s not as boring as he thought and being pampered was not all that bad. All of this is silly, funny, frisky storytelling that begins from the minute that they arrive on the island. Madagascar. Dreamworks animation. Directed by Eric Darnell & Tom McGrath. With voices of Ben Stiller, Chris Rock, and David Schwimmer. 1 hr., 26 min. Rated PG. Released in 2005. Now Streaming on Vudu/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Madagascar a silly adventure from NYC to Africa

articles.text: Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary Buck Brannaman is the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. So Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them, leaving them scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To come even briefly to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck. Directed by Cindy Meehi. With Buck Brannaman, Gary Meyers, Bib Frazier. Documentary. 1 hr., 28 min. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv. Buck Brannaman stars as himself in the documentary Buck.
articles.title: Buck – a remarkable story

It’s not as boring as he thought and being pampered was not all that bad. All of this is silly, funny, frisky storytelling that begins from the minute that they arrive on the island. Madagascar. Buck – a remarkable story Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary Buck Brannaman is the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. So Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them, leaving them scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To come even briefly to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck. Directed by Cindy Meehi. With Buck Brannaman, Gary Meyers, Bib Frazier. Documentary. 1 hr., 28 min. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv. articles.text: If you’re like most people, your work has been a central part of your life. So, wouldn’t it be nice to have the flexibility to decide when you no longer want to work? Many people of retirement age have achieved this type of control. In fact, two-thirds of workers ages 65 and older say they work primarily because they want to, not because they have to, according to a 2021 study by Edward Jones and Age Wave. But that means that one-third of workers in this age group feel financially compelled to work. This doesn’t necessarily mean they dislike the work they do — but it’s probably fair to say they would have liked the option of not working. How can you give yourself this choice? You can start by asking yourself these questions: • When do I want to retire? You’ll want to identify the age at which you wish to retire. You may change your mind later and move this date up or back, but it’s a good idea to have a target in mind. • What sort of retirement lifestyle do I want? When you retire, do you anticipate staying close to home and pursuing your hobbies, or do you hope to travel the world? Would you like to spend your time volunteering? Open your own business or do some consulting? Clearly, some of these choices will require more resources than others, so you’ll want to follow a financial strategy that aligns with the retirement lifestyle you intend to pursue. • Am I saving and investing enough? As you chart your course toward your retirement journey, you’ll want to assess the sources of income you’ll have available. If you think you may be falling short of achieving your retirement goals, you may need to consider saving more. • When should I start taking Social Security? You can begin collecting Social Security benefits as early as 62, but your monthly payments will be much bigger if you wait until your “full” retirement age, which will likely be between 66 and 67. Your decision about when to take Social Security will depend on several factors, including your other sources of income and your family history of longevity. Of course, as you’re probably aware, the Social Security system is facing significant financial stress, so it’s possible that we may see changes to Social Security, based on actions Congress could take. In any case, you might want to be fairly conservative in estimating how much Social Security can contribute to your retirement income. of when you might reach the point at which work is optional. But you’ll also need to consider other factors, too, such as how much you enjoy working or when your spouse or partner is planning to retire. In any case, the sooner you start planning for this next phase of your life, the better position you’ll be in when it’s time to make the transition. articles.text: It was relatively quiet at the Exedra last Wednesday morning at 10:30 as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled for their weekly walk. Two hours earlier the frenzied, first-day-ofschool rush had just gone on at the Exedra. On another lovely morning, a strong turnout of 31 walkers and two K-9 best friends were ready to walk. The group decided to go to some “roads not taken” streets, inspired by Dave DeRoche and his baritone voice reading Robert Frost’s “The Road Not Taken” to the group. This poem ends with, “Two roads diverged in a wood, and I – I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.” It was noted that one of the great things about Walking on Wednesdays is that the group can take a less traveled Piedmont road one week, and then take the more traveled one the next Wednesday. The group headed for Bellevue Avenue by way of blocklong Sierra Avenue. They stopped to talk about two Julia Morgan designed homes that architect Will Adams had described on a tour he led last year. Turning onto Sheridan, they went to Caperton Avenue, then traveled Richardson Way and onto Lakeview Avenue, and the little-known Poplar Way, ending at Mountain Avenue near the intersection with Bellevue Avenue. The corner is marked by an historic redwood tree, site of the city’s first tree lighting ceremony. At the far end of Bellevue they came to a beautiful, large home with a long driveway, a majestic oak tree in the front year and a great view of San Francisco. The group continued on to Pacific and Hagar Avenues, enjoying fabulous, clear views of San Francisco along the way. On Bell Avenue, at the top of Piedmont, there were more great views. From Bell the group began its descent on Scenic Avenue to Alta Avenue and then down a 163-foot set of steep stairs to the lower portion of Scenic. On Scenic they saw the house inhabited around 1900 by artist Xavier Martínez, a well-known bohemian figure in San Francisco and the East Bay. This section of Piedmont was a bit of an artist colony during the turn of the century. It was then an easy return to the center of town via Blair, Pacific, Mountain, and Highland Avenues. It had been a two-mile walk in 90 minutes with beautiful homes and views enjoyed along many not-often-taken roads. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Participants on the Walking on Wednesday outing on August 10 included Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Elizabeth Richter, Jim Kellogg, Pat Keller, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Vivie, Alan Goldhammer, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Renee Goldhammer, Bob Wong, Kat Lang, Harriette Louie, Phil Witte, Melba Yee, Charlene Louie, Gloria DaSilva, Priscilla Wanerus, Dick Carter, Stella Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Pat Sheehan, Albert Chen, Dave DeRoche, and Meghan Bennett. The group was happy to have Nancy Olsen and Larry Olsen back for their first post-pandemic walks; as well as Siow Fang Tan and Christine Calliste now that their summer vacations are over.

Troop 6 Scouts hosted a luau on the beach, grilling teriyaki chicken, rib eye steaks, pineapples, and vegetables on a makeshift beach barbeque. On the Fourth of July, they went on a 3-mile beach hike, and along the way spotted bald eagles fighting with ospreys over fish. The hikers were also buzzed by a pair of Air Force F-15’s. They made a flagpole on the beach using driftwood, and posting the American flag and Troop 6 pennant as they temporarily claimed the beach for the Piedmont Council. Other Troop 6 traditions included nightly poker games, Dutch oven desserts, games of Uno and D&D, and the annual double-elimination Jenga Tournament. In campwide competition, the “older” six Scouts wiped the floor in the beach volleyball tournament. Four Troop 6 Scouts officially became members of the Dime Club, shooting five shots all within the circumference of a dime. Troop 6 Scoutmasters also brought glory to the troop with two successful egg-drop contraptions made of “found” materials, and building a catapult for the winning Scoutmaster team for a siege of the castle. Michael Bruin is a member of Piedmont Scouts’ Troop 6 based at Corpus Christi Church, St. Troop 6 Scouts play games at night at summer camp on the Oregon coast. James Drive & Park Boulevard. Troop 6 Scouts Sebastian Guzman, Vincent Doubrava, Gabriel Pierre, Peter Ichimaru, JD Sellman, Alexander Velasco, Jack Throne, and Martin Gustason squeeze into a hammock for a group photo at Camp Meriwetther. articles.text: Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand has announced she intends to retire in April next year, 2023. Lillevand has served as City Administrator since June 2019, when she was named to succeed former City Administrator Paul Benoit from a pool of over 40 applicants. Prior to becoming City Administrator she was the city’s Recreation Director for five years, from 2015 to 2019. Her earlier professional experience was as Athletic Director at Hayward State, as a collegiate basketball coach and kinesiology instructor. “I deeply appreciate the community of Piedmont. It is a special place with engaged residents and a genuinely committed, supportive, and indefatigable City Council. The staff are professional, dedicated, and caring; they respect each other and work as a team for the good of the community,” said Lillevand, a Piedmont native. “I am honored to have served as Recreation Director and City Administrator and will be forever grateful for both opportunities.” The city has benefited from Lillevand’s leadership since her appointment four years ago, Mayor Teddy Gray King said. “Throughout her time in Piedmont, she has put the community first. Since becoming City Administrator, Sara has deftly guided the City through the COVID-19 pandemic, and the uncertainties and changes that this time brought. She worked tirelessly to bring the Piedmont Community Pool project to fruition, through the design phase, and soon to construction. Sara’s efforts to maintain high service levels, excellent public facilities, and make Piedmont a better place for its residents will not soon be forgotten,” said Mayor King. “We will all miss her professional leadership and optimistic outlook and I will personally miss her guidance and friendship.” Lillevand will remain in her position until April 5, 2023 or until the position is filled, whichever is earlier. Recruitment for her replacement will begin immediately, the city confirmed. Piedmont City Administrator has announced her plans to retire next spring.
articles.title: City Administrator Sara Lillevand to retire in 2023

articles.text: Piedmont will hold its general municipal election on November 8. Three City Council seats and two School Board seats will be on the ballot. Seven residents have obtained nomination papers as of August 1 for city council, and three have obtained papers for School Board. One resident, Avnish Patel, has obtained nomination papers for both City Council and School Board. There are no Incumbent school board members running for re-election. City Council incumbents Betsy Andersen and Jennifer Long, and candidates Tom Ramsey, Bridget Harris, Avnish Patel, Jeanne Solnordal, and Nancy Bostrom also have obtained nomination papers for City Council. Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson obtained nomination papers for School Board. City council members Andersen and Long are eligible to run for an additional four-year term. Long was appointed in February and is currently serving in an interim role. She was appointed to the position by City Council following former vice mayor Tim Rood’s resignation in December 2021. Mayor Teddy Gray King is completing eight years on Council and is not eligible to run again. Former school board member Megan Pillsbury was eligible to run for an additional four-year term but moved out of town and is no longer eligible. Incumbent Amal Smith has termed out. The nomination period closes this Friday, August 12, at 5 p.m. If an eligible incumbent does not file nomination papers by August 12, the filing period for that office will be extended to August 17. articles.text: Because I love baseball, I preach an annual baseball-themed sermon This is the 2022 edition of my expression of love for the game. I love baseball. I love it because it fills me with many happy childhood memories. I love it because the goal of the game is to return home. I love it because a game proceeds at its own pace; it isn’t completely bound to a timeclock. I love it because, as a game in which failure abounds (the best hitters fail in their task seven out of ten times), it is a game I can relate to. I love it because it is a game of beautiful voices, among them Vin Scully, voice of the Los Angeles Dodgers from 1950- 2016. Vin died last week and I join with the millions of others who mourn his passing. In recent years my love for the game has taken the form of umpiring youth baseball games. Undeniably, my love for the game surpasses my skill as an officiant, but I try to do a credible job of helping young people and their families have a positive experience through the game of baseball. Every time I am on the diamond, I try to remember to take a deep breath and tell myself “It is a gift to be here.” Last fall, as part of a training series for umpires, we were taught that it would help us in our work if we remembered the letters E, L and M. • E for Effort. • L for Learning. articles.text: The Corey Reich Tennis Center was reopened after 12 days as new light standards were installed August 5. Of the city’s four principal tennis courts, the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Vista and Bonita Avenues is the only one with lights. Throughout the week residents can play tennis until 9 p.m. Installation of six new light standards and double light fixtures was performed by Oakland based Gil’s Electric, the same company that some years ago installed the necklace of lights encircling Lake Merritt. The total cost for the four courts in Piedmont was $69,800 according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The project included four new single-light fixtures, and new lighting controls with a digital time switch. “The new lights are designed to provide improved court illumination while reducing the offsite glare. They should be a huge improvement over the previous configuration and provide the school and Recreation Department with the facilities that they need for their programming needs,” Gonzales said. articles.text: When Piedmont’s Housing Element requirement was initially announced, the Piedmont Planning staff informed residents that, even though the requirement of 587 units was nearly 10 times the previous requirement, “Piedmont should take on accommodating 587 units as a challenge.” There was no mention of challenging the 587-unit number, despite the drastic increase from the previous General Plan. Why challenge the State HCD (Housing and Community Development Dept.) requirement? One reason is that the State Auditor was directed to evaluate the needs assessment process that the HCD uses to provide key housing guidance to local governments. The Auditor’s report, dated March 17,2022, concluded that the HCD does not ensure that its needs assessments are accurate and adequately supported. The HCD response to this very serious finding was that it would review their processes over the next year, but they would not commit to reviewing or modifying any of the current cycle of projections. The State Auditor’s findings and conclusions introduce enough uncertainty about HCD requirements to warrant a serious inquiry or as some other like-minded cities have done – that is to band together and legally challenge the HCD on their process and projections. It is very important to remember that the General Plan will need to be resubmitted in 2031 and that the State will surely impose another housing requirement on Piedmont then. How many units and where will those units go? What legacy will be left for the City Council of 2031? It is very important that we and other cities push back and demand more transparency and accuracy from the HCD now. Another reason – our Fair Share. In the Aug. 1 Council meeting, many residents stated their belief that Piedmont should provide its fair share of housing units. I wholeheartedly agree but I also believe that our fair share should be derived from a fair and open process and that there should be some recognition of Piedmont’s constraints – that it is predominately built-out and that the City faces reconstruction or new construction of its Essential Services Buildings which could significantly affect some of the few available parcels in the City. Another reason – numbers matter. Many of the objections to the Housing Element come down to the extraordinary means needed to accommodate 587 units. If, for example, Piedmont’s Housing Element were only a 3-fold increase over the existing requirement and Piedmont needed to accommodate 180 units, I believe that the Housing Element would now be approved and in our rear-view mirror. Numbers do matter and accuracy and fairness of process matter. That is why I strongly urge the City Council to listen to the residents and take on the challenge – to investigate, question, and push back against the HCD 587-unit requirement and demand a fair process. –Donald Chandler, AIA “Things are looking better. Slow-paying customers are replacing non-pay customers.”
articles.title: Piedmont’s housing mandate needs to be challenged

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band, led by majorette Elaine Lindenmayer, marches down Highland Avenue during the 4th of July parade, its only public appearance during the year. Part 2 of two-part series Piedmont Community Band members met on July 2 on Dracena Avenue for their only rehearsal of the year. Two days later they marched down Highland Avenue as a major participant in the city’s 4th of July Parade, their only public performance of the year. Mobilizing the band two days before the parade can be complicated, but this year With only about 30 musicians, ranging from amateur to professional, it was smooth sailing. Most musicians live in town, and some have been marching and playing with the band for well over 20 years. One family of musicians arrives from Minnesota as part of a family reunion. “This year, we did an [open call] for musicians. It can be hard to pin down volunteers who can perform in the parade and be there for rehearsal on July 2, so I’m always pleased by the level of participation,” band founder Jane Reed explained. The band includes musicians playing everything from trombone, trumpet, tuba, saxophone, clarinet, flute, to drums and even cymbals and a glockenspiel. “We sort of take whatever we can get,” Reed said with a smile. “We had a saxophone player’s wife play the cymbals this year.” The tradition of a one-rehearsal show has worked seamlessly, in part because the band plays the same three marches every year. The principal song is “On, Wisconsin!”, the high school standard. It is also an ode to Reed’s home-state of Wisconsin, where she learned to play The Piedmont Community Band near Piedmont Park. the alto saxophone growing up in high school. The band was led for a half dozen years by Ray Perman, a longtime percussionist in the band. He arranged for new neckerchiefs and caps for band members and was the first to connect all band members by e-mail and send music to everyone in advance. Resident Elaine Lindenmayer has led the band as majorette for 35 years. She first picked up a baton in high school and has twirled on and off throughout her life. In 1984, shortly after she moved to Piedmont, she heard the band practicing in front of her house on Highland Avenue. “When I heard them, I just wanted to march and twirl. I just have that percussion in my blood,” she said. Lindenmayer has held the baton since joining the band in its inception - taking off one year to give birth to son Evan in 1985. “I keep doing it because I have so much fun. Everyone lines up in front of my house year after year to rehearse (on July 4), and I know I could not sit in this house, hear that band, and not participate,” she said. Unlike playing from sheet music, Lindemayer’s routine changes each year. She said she tends to modify it during the parade. Her solo act – and the fact that she has been with the band since its very early days – gives her the creative liberty to explore different steps and twirls. Despite the absence of the city’s parade for two years due to COVID, the parade drew a large crowd this year. Lindenmayer said she noticed chairs lining the route as early as two weeks before July 4. The band picked up right where they left off in 2019. Reed credits the smooth sailing to the band members’ resilience and to its leader, Ken Kawaichi, who has led the band dressed as Emperor Norton for 36 years. The nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, who proclaimed himself “Norton, Emperor of the United States,” was joke that eventually became tradition - but added that Kawaichi, a skilled musician in his own right, leads the band every year with the same zeal. Photo by Ken DeCrosta Ken Kawaichi, dressed as Emperor Norton, leads the Piedmont Community Band in 2007 when it had more than 80 musicians.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Band, an original

Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show on Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops and has been organized by Officer Tyler Petit since the retirement of Sgt. Steve DeWarns. The car show includes free coffee and donuts to everyone. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have up to 120 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want to include their vehicles in the show need to register on the Eventbrite website at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ coffee-cars-cops-car-show-tickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue between the high school and Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov.

articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https:// cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: School will start slightly later for high school students this year, with classes beginning at 8:30 a.m., a half hour later than in prior years. The change is due to Senate Bill 328 approved by Governor Newsom on October 13, 2019. It applies to all high schools in the state. The last classes of the day will end at 3:25 p.m. on Mondays, and 3:35 p.m. on Tuesday and Thursdays. Classes will end at 2:50 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays. Piedmont High School conducted a pilot program for four weeks in January and February. During that time an additional period for office hours twice a week at the end of the day was tested and considered. It was learned that some upperclassmen with free 6th and 7th periods were asked to return to campus even after their last period. The additional periods are rescheduled this year to after brunch on Wednesday and Friday and will be called “Academy.” “There will certainly be a learning curve to start, but having gone through the pilot program last spring, we believe students and staff will grow into the new schedule quickly and take full advantage of its opportunities,” said school district Director of Communications Brian Killgore. The new state law also requires middle schools to start no earlier than 8:00 a.m. So while there was no requirement to change from the previous 8:20 a.m. start PMS did adjust its bell schedule on its own accord by moving the start time back to 8:40 a.m. Middle school will let out at a varying times throughout the week: Monday 3:24 p.m. Tuesday 3:08 p.m. Wednesday 2:41 p.m. Thursday 3:08 p.m. Friday 2:41 p.m. “Research shows that teenagers need more time to sleep at night for their well-being,” said PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami. “The benefit is for students to be in better spirits and well-rested when arriving on campus. This will not only help their mental well-being, but also with their academics,” she added. The school district said it will conduct evaluations throughout the school year and gather feedback from students, staff and families. A Bell Schedule Committee will reconvene in January for discussions and to plan for any adjustments for next year. articles.text: Application period for new Beach School principal closes today At 9:00 a.m. the morning of August 10, the opening day of classes for Piedmont schools, the school district closed the period for accepting applications for the position of new principal at Beach School. The Beach School principal Michael Corritone announced two weeks ago that he had accepted a similar position in Walnut Creek, but would stay at Beach until August 19. The district has not announced how many applicants applied for the position. To view the job posting which was open for nine days, visit: Edjoin.org/Home/DistrictJobPosting/1639933 The district has issued the following ambitious schedule for finding a new principal: • First Interview: August 15 • Second Interview: August 17 • Board Appointment: August 24 • Start Date: Following Board Appointment “Beach parents will be a part of the first-round interview process with a number of them sitting on the interview panel,” said Communications Director Brian Michael Corritone’s last day as the principal of Beach School will be August 19. Killgore. Corritone heads to Indian Valley Elementary in Walnut Creek, after announcing his decision to the Piedmont community on August 1. Corritone’s departure comes at a time when the school district also faced the retirement of PHS Principal Adam Littlefield, the departure of middle school principal Ryan Fletcher, and the resignation of Superintendent Randy Booker. Indian Valley Elementary is a TK-5 school with approximately 400 students. Its academic year also starts on August 10.

articles.text: This fall Piedmont Middle School will present the musical The Addams Family Young@ Part, a musical comedy with music and lyrics by Andrew Lippa and book by Marshall Brickman and Rick Elice. Directed and produced by Amy Moorhead, performances are October 21, 22 and 23 and will be held in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the PHS campus. All 6th, 7th, and 8th grade students at PMS are invited to audition. For more information about auditions contact amoorhead@ piedmont.k12.ca.us. Moorhead will also direct and produce a high school production of Hello, Dolly! With music and lyrics by Jerry Herman and book by Michael Stewart, Hello, Dolly! is considered to be one of the last of the Golden Age of Broadway musicals. Auditions will begin in late September with performances scheduled for February 2-5, 2023, in the Alan Harvey Theater. All PHS and MHS students are invited to audition.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District sent a letter to the school community authored by interim Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans on Thursday, August 4, detailing COVID-related guidance for students and parents. The school district is following California Department of Public Health (CDPH) guidelines. “While there are no current indoor masking requirements for schools in California or Alameda County, the wearing of masks in indoor school settings remains strongly recommended,” Dr. Evans said. “All PUSD students and staff are encouraged to wear masks indoors and in any situation where social distancing is limited.” Anyone experiencing symptoms associated with COVID is recommended to wear a mask even after testing negative, he added. Symptoms of COVID include fever, cough, chills, and diarrhea. Students exhibiting such symptoms should “stay at home,” but students who feel “otherwise well enough for school should confirm a negative at-home COVID test before returning to school.” Testing COVID tests are now widely available at pharmacies like Walgreens and CVS, and the City operates a COVID testing clinic near Community Hall five days a week in partnership with health services company Curative. The school district will offer testing as well. Tests will be available at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, 325 Highland Ave., from 7:45-8:15 a.m. and 8:45-9:15 a.m. on weekdays starting today, August 10 and continuing for at least the first few weeks of the school year. The district can provide a COVID test for home use, as supplies last. A daily health screener for COVID will not be used this academic year. Parents and guests are asked to self-assess before entering campus for symptoms associated with COVID. Tracking cases The school district will continue to track COVID cases in the school community. If your child tests positive, report the absence to their school and complete an online reporting form at http:// Tinyurl.com/pusdgotcovid. Students who test positive should isolate at home for five days, and up to 10 days if symptoms persist. Students testing negative after day five of absence may return to school provided they test negative.
articles.title: Masks at schools strongly recommended but not required

articles.text: Walk for Wellness, an annual fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center, will take place August 21-27 this fall. It is an inclusive series of walks around town and is open to all. The event focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. The Wellness Center, on the high school campus, provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Center also helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including but not limited to stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. According to Wellness Center staff, approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. Martha Joerger and Lindsay Thomasson will serve as co-chairs of this year’s event. To sign up or sponsor the event, visit https://pef.schoolauction.net/wfw22/homepages/show.
articles.title: Walk for Wellness begins August 21

Beach Principal Michael Corritone’s last day is August 19 Application period for new Beach School principal closes today By Jay Russell At 9:00 a.m. the morning of August 10, the opening day of classes for Piedmont schools, the school district closed the period for accepting applications for the position of new principal at Beach School. The Beach School principal Michael Corritone announced two weeks ago that he had accepted a similar position in Walnut Creek, but would stay at Beach until August 19. The district has not announced how many applicants applied for the position. To view the job posting which was open for nine days, visit: Edjoin.org/Home/DistrictJobPosting/1639933 The district has issued the following ambitious schedule for finding a new principal: • First Interview: August 15 • Second Interview: August 17 • Board Appointment: August 24 • Start Date: Following Board Appointment “Beach parents will be a part of the first-round interview process with a number of them sitting on the interview panel,” said Communications Director Brian Michael Corritone’s last day as the principal of Beach School will be August 19. Killgore. Corritone heads to Indian Valley Elementary in Walnut Creek, after announcing his decision to the Piedmont community on August 1. Corritone’s departure comes at a time when the school district also faced the retirement of PHS Principal Adam Littlefield, the departure of middle school principal Ryan Fletcher, and the resignation of Superintendent Randy Booker. Indian Valley Elementary is a TK-5 school with approximately 400 students. Its academic year also starts on August 10. Middle school to perform musical version of The Addams Family This fall Piedmont Middle School will present the musical The Addams Family Young@ Part, a musical comedy with music and lyrics by Andrew Lippa and book by Marshall Brickman and Rick Elice. Directed and produced by Amy Moorhead, performances are October 21, 22 and 23 and will be held in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the PHS campus. articles.text: School starts today, and summer is coming to an end. Your days will soon be filled with soccer and coding classes. But wait – there is one more activity you should consider throwing into the mix. Delivering for the Piedmont Post is a great opportunity for you to do a few things especially if you’re looking for a way to learn independence and reliability. I am one of their paper delivery girls and have to admit something. It’s not all about wearing a newsboy style cap while triumphantly flinging papers that miraculously land on the middle of the door mat. For starters, never fling your papers; no one has that good of an aim. Besides, there is so much more than just delivering papers. You develop life skills and learn personal management with your earnings. I think the best part is talking to all the people you meet along the way. Samantha Pell delivering papers for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Calling all new middle schoolers

articles.text: Just last week I was delivering papers to a house with a lot of steps. A neighbor came up to me and said, “I know they are on vacation, so let me take it for you.” I remembered this resident because of an interaction around Thanksgiving. He told me that when he was young he used to deliver papers. He then went on to describe how he did it. Apparently, he and a few friends used to stand on a platform on the back of a truck and would fling the papers to the houses. I said that it sounded like fun. “Oh it was,” he replied, “especially Sunday papers.” It’s connections like that that make me smile. One more thing that makes me smile is the memory of one time I was delivering a paper and as soon as I turned around the door opened. The resident called out “Thank you!” It’s the happiness - what people find and see in the paper, and in us, the people delivering the news to them. That’s what I like about delivering papers. For those who want to apply, send your name, grade in school, and contact information by e-mail to: news@piedmontpost.org. Samantha Pell is a 7th grader at Piedmont Middle School whose creativity and work ethic never falters. articles.text: Get a glimpse of the show at Chabot Space & Science Center this Friday Nothing says summer like a late-night firework show. Mixtures of strontium, calcium, sodium, and many other salts and metal compounds explode into the sky, producing a spectacular array of colors, and then a large BOOM! Fireworks light up the sky in celebrations across the world for Lunar New Year, New Year’s Eve, Bonfire Night, Diwali, and recently the 4th of July. Beyond these special holidays, Mother Nature creates her own beautiful firework displays around 30 times a year — through meteor showers. More about meteors What are meteors? And what are meteor showers? Meteors are small, typically icy rocks that are expelled from comets. When debris from an old comet or asteroid enters the Earth’s atmosphere, a meteor shower occurs. From Earth, we see meteors streak across the sky and leave a fleeting trail of light as they pass by. From July 17-August 24, the Perseid Meteor Shower will take over the sky as the Earth passes through debris from the massive comet, “Swift-Tuttle”. This annual meteor shower is named after the point of the sky where its meteors originate: the Perseus constellation. The Perseid Meteor shower was first observed about 2000 years ago— our ancestors discovered this naturally enchanting light show, and years later, we are still mesmerized by its beauty! Perseid Meteor Shower The Perseid Meteor Shower is the most popular annual shower and it’s easy to see why. Viewers usually can look forward to warm summer temperatures and 50-100 meteors passing by per hour. The best part? The shower can be seen with the naked eye. To get the best views of the celestial event, we recommend being far away from light pollution (streetlamps and other city lights). At Chabot Space & Science Center’s beautiful Observation Deck, which is located in a Redwood forest, our astronomers are hosting a Perseid Meteor Shower Watch Party with hot chocolate to celebrate Mother Nature’s enchanting fireworks. Don’t miss it: this annual shower is considered the best meteor shower of the year by NASA. Come out on the summer evening of August 12th to appreciate the fast and fiery show. Megan Hiller is a Marketing and Communications intern at Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement and located at 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Big meteor shower this month

articles.text: In 2019, Alameda County reported 0 homeless individuals in Piedmont. This year, the count accelerated to 42 homeless individuals. According to the report, four individuals were living in tents, nine sleeping in a car or van, 14 sleeping in recreation vehicles (RVs), and 15 living on the street or outside. The data comes from an annual survey of homeless individuals in the United States conducted by local agencies, called the Point-in-Time (PIT) count. EveryOneHome is the local, nonprofit organization that conducts the survey in Alameda County. The US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) requires that any community that seeks federal funding for homeless programs conduct a PIT count every two years. The PIT count compiles into the Annual Homeless Assessment Report, which is provided to Congress. The survey began in 2003 and is conducted entirely by volunteers. Alameda County conducted its count on February 23, 2022. The last count in Piedmont was done in 2019. The survey results rely purely on observation. Alastair Boone, a PIT count volunteer in Alameda County in 2019, noted that “individual people are counted one by one, but EveryOneHome uses a multiplier to determine how many people might be living inside tents and vehicles” in a 2019 Bloomberg news article. “This multiplier comes from field research conducted by outreach workers. A separate count is held to tally Alameda County’s homeless youth, and an additional survey is also used to gather more demographic information for the county’s homeless population, such as health conditions, veteran status, and housing history. This data, along with the number of people counted on the street by volunteers, comprises the totals reported in the PIT count,” Boone said. The number of 40 homeless individuals in Piedmont seemed to be inaccurate, according to residents quoted in a July 21 San Francisco Chronicle article “Piedmont saw its official homeless count spike. Now its unsheltered residents are nowhere to be found.” The article questioned whether volunteers mistakenly counted people in Oakland without knowing the city boundaries and added it to Piedmont’s count. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said that the department has received relatively few reports of people sleeping in vehicles, sheds, or backyards. “If the [call] is related to a significant crime, then we’re going to investigate the situation and take appropriate action irrespective if the person is unhoused or not. If the call is simply about someone who is unhoused, we will first treat the individual with dignity, respect, and empathy. If they are violating specific trespassing laws, then we will educate them and request they move from the private property,” he said. Chief Bowers added that all Piedmont Police Department officers are required to attend Crisis Intervention Training within the first year of their employment. “This training is important. It is common for some individuals who are dealing with homelessness to also be dealing with mental health challenges. We try to provide resources to individuals and partner with the county’s Community Assessment Transport Team (CATT) which pairs an EMT and mental health clinician to provide services for those who are dealing with mental health challenges,” Bowers explained.
articles.title: County reports 42 homeless individuals in Piedmont

County reports 42 homeless individuals in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey In 2019, Alameda County reported 0 homeless individuals in Piedmont. This year, the count accelerated to 42 homeless individuals. According to the report, four individuals were living in tents, nine sleeping in a car or van, 14 sleeping in recreation vehicles (RVs), and 15 living on the street or outside. The data comes from an annual survey of homeless individuals in the United States conducted by local agencies, called the Point-in-Time (PIT) count. EveryOneHome is the local, nonprofit organization that conducts the survey in Alameda County. The US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) requires that any community that seeks federal funding for homeless programs conduct a PIT count every two years. The PIT count compiles into the Annual Homeless Assessment Report, which is provided to Congress. The survey began in 2003 and is conducted entirely by volunteers. Alameda County conducted its count on February 23, 2022. The last count in Piedmont was done in 2019. The survey results rely purely on observation. Alastair Boone, a PIT count volunteer in Alameda County in 2019, noted that “individual people are counted one by one, but EveryOneHome uses a multiplier to determine how many people might be living inside tents and vehicles” in a 2019 Bloomberg news article. “This multiplier comes from field research conducted by outreach workers. A separate count is held to tally Alameda County’s homeless youth, and an additional survey is also used to gather more demographic information for the county’s homeless population, such as health conditions, veteran status, and housing history. This data, along with the number of people counted on the street by volunteers, comprises the totals reported in the PIT count,” Boone said. The number of 40 homeless individuals in Piedmont seemed to be inaccurate, according to residents quoted in a July 21 San Francisco Chronicle article “Piedmont saw its official homeless count spike. Now its unsheltered residents are nowhere to be found.” The article questioned whether volunteers mistakenly counted people in Oakland without knowing the city boundaries and added it to Piedmont’s count. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said that the department has received relatively few reports of people sleeping in vehicles, sheds, or backyards. “If the [call] is related to a significant crime, then we’re going to investigate the situation and take appropriate action irrespective if the person is unhoused or not. If the call is simply about someone who is unhoused, we will first treat the individual with dignity, respect, and empathy. If they are violating specific trespassing laws, then we will educate them and request they move from the private property,” he said. Chief Bowers added that all Piedmont Police Department officers are required to attend Crisis Intervention Training within the first year of their employment. “This training is important. It is common for some individuals who are dealing with homelessness to also be dealing with mental health challenges. We try to provide resources to individuals and partner with the county’s Community Assessment Transport Team (CATT) which pairs an EMT and mental health clinician to provide services for those who are dealing with mental health challenges,” Bowers explained. articles.text: Piedmont had several water polo players who competed in the recent U.S. Junior Water Polo Olympics from July 16-19 with CC United, a high-level water polo program in the East Bay. On July 18 at Independence HS in San Jose, they beat James Kappes (fourth from left in glasses), a 4th grader at Wildwood School, was on CC United’s 10U Black A team.

articles.text: From the NFL on down to the high school level, football training camp for the fall season is ramping up. At Witter Field, the Highlanders are strapping on their helmets and shoulder pads this week in preparation for an opening game with Seaside on Friday, August 26. “This is the best time of the year. All across the country, kids start putting their helmets on and getting in their pads, and feeling what it’s like,” said first-year head coach Jordan Seiden. “From a football perspective this is what you live for. The start of camp, putting on pads, and watching kids grow up on the field. They build up a toughness with their brothers every day. It’s great to see their excitement.” Monday, August 8, marked the first day for the players to put on their helmets, as they l progressively move into full contact drills by week’s end. Seiden wants to be sure they maintain the intensity of training and learn how to play the game safely. “Due to attrition, we don’t have a lot of numbers. We can’t get too physical because we can’t afford to lose players to injuries. Today [Monday] is helmets, tomorrow is will be shoulder pads, and Wednesday will be full pads. We definitely need to have full-contact days where kids are getting hit, tackled, and blocking – working out the physical part of football. You need to play safely and smart, added Seiden. Throughout the summer, Seiden, offensive coordinator Mike Dixon, and defensive coordinator Kerry Griffin have mentioned some players who have stood out: Matteo Costa, Bautista Costa, Sam Shelby, and Tommy Ashton, typically the first player to arrive at Witter. Sophomore tight end and inside linebacker Tommy Ashton has been impressive in camp. Football coach Jordan Seiden, in his first year at Piedmont, oversees the football team that begins strapping on helmets and pads this week in preparation for Week 1 of the fall season. – Jordan Seiden PHS head football coach Coach Jordan Seiden watches players work on a blocking sled. Offensive coordinator Mike Dixon talks with players following offensive drills. “It feels good to get the praise. I really enjoy playing football, and my teammates are really putting in work out here. We all have the same goal of winning, through all the pain and conditioning, I think we’re going to do well,” said Ashton. Conditioning has been a focal point of the summer. Ashton can see the difference since the start of camp in May. “At the beginning of the summer, everyone was kind of out of shape and lacked discipline. But our coaches have made us work hard and build strong discipline really quickly. We just want to see everyone continue working hard and keep developing plays and discipline in general. We have to make sure we’re ready for Seaside on August 26,” said Ashton. Though dealing with a smallsize roster, Seiden has been encouraged by the work ethic and camaraderie of his players throughout the summer. “We have a small group but an amazing group of kids. Most of the players between JV and varsity have been here most of the summer. As a coaching staff we have so much respect for them; I’ve never been in a program where the kids thank you after practice after dang near killing them. They never leave the field without thanking us for being there, it makes leaving practice hard,” said Seiden. Seiden and his staff are still focusing on conditioning to make sure the group has the stamina and toughness for a full 10-game schedule. “We’ve taken it pretty slow just from a perspective of understanding the concepts instead of just lining up and running a play. Our plays have concepts and ideas, a lot of situations that they have to understand. We have high IQ kids off of the field and it translates onto the field. They’ve been picking it up quickly. It’s now just learning the terminology and how we want to do things,” said Seiden. The Post will return to football practice in the week prior to the August 26 season opener against Seaside. Senior Matteo Costa turns upfield after a pass reception.

articles.text: With the new school year starting, Piedmont’s Class of 2023 looks ahead to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. HAILEY RONEN Softball Hailey Ronen earned an honorable mention for All-League last spring in the team’s march toward a WACC Shoreline title, 18-7 overall record and perfect 10-0 against league opponents. She lines up on the hot corner as coach Gene Denard’s starting third baseman. She scored one run in Piedmont’s 8-5 win over Encinal to capture the league banner on May 12, while she went 1-for-2 with two runs scored and a walk in PHS’ 10-1 win over No. 12 Arcata in the North Coast Section playoffs on May 17. In 2022, Ronen recorded 10 hits, one double, seven RBIs, seven runs scored, 11 walks, and three stolen bases. Staff Photos Hailey Ronen earned All-League honorable mention honors last season and is the softball team’s starting third baseman. NATHAN FREDERICKS Lacrosse Nathan Fredericks was the leading goal scorer and a captain on Piedmont’s WACC Championship winning lacrosse team, which marked the program’s sixth consecutive league title. He earned first-team All-League honors. Fredericks helped lift Piedmont to a 10-9 win over arch rival Bishop O’Dowd in the league title game on April 29 with three goals, concluding their season with a 9-8 overall record in their first season at the Division 1 level after previAUDREY LAM Soccer Nathan Fredericks led scoring for the lacrosse team last season and helped lead PHS to its sixth consecutive WACC title ously competing at D2. Fredericks also scored three times in PHS’ 21-7 loss against No. 4 Vista Del Lago in the first round of the D1 NCS playoffs on May 3 as the No. 13 seeded school. The lacrosse team will be poised to contend for another league championship in 2023 with a strong senior cast alongside him, including Soren Dixon, Jack Nelson, Henry Brayer, Bailey Cain, Keita Clear, Noah Lindenbaum, and Matteo and Bautista Costa. Audrey Lam earned firstteam All-League honors as an influential member of coach Den Chubbock’s squad as a central attacking midfielder last winter. She’s an accomplished athlete at the club level, has competed in several U.S. Development camps before joining the Highlanders’ 2021/2022 varsity roster, and is already committed to continue playing at Brown University. Piedmont finished with seven wins, five ties, and six losses and received the No. 6 seed in D4 NCS Playoffs last season, defeating No. 11 College Prep 4-0 on February 16 before losing a close 2-1 battle to No. 3 Sonoma Academy in the quarterfinals on February 19. She was among the most talented players on the roster with slick technical footwork, pressing defense, and a proven ability to draw fouls. In a 1-1 tie against Bishop O’Dowd on January 28, Lam drew two critical fouls including a free kick that led to a goal in the 56th minute and a penalty kick in the 64th. Soccer player Audrey Lam earned first-team All-League honors last winter and is a highly talented attacking midfielder.

articles.text: The Oakland Roots professional soccer team has 10 games left in its season. Currently it is four points back of El Paso Locomotive in seventh place, the final position for possible qualification to the postseason. The Roots currently have six wins, 11 draws, and seven losses with 29 points. “We have 10 Finals to play. For us, every game is important,” said coach Juan Guerra when speaking with the Post. In order to reach the playoffs, Oakland will require some good things to happen. Guerra knows his team will need to win at least five games wins and a draw in the final 10 matches.. “We want to reach 45 points. We believe that’s the mark that will get us into the playoffs. If we keep playing productively, I believe the boys will get us the points we need,” said Guerra. It’s a critical time for Roots supporters to watch scoreboards this week. Monterey Bay faces San Diego Loyal today, August 10. Of note, Monterey is just three games behind Oakland and has played three less matches. On Friday, August 12, third-place Colorado Springs Switchbacks plays El Paso—Oakland will be rooting for a Colorado win. Lastly, last place Orange County hosts ninth-place Phoenix Rising—which holds equal points and one game in hand on Roots. OCSC will need to upset Rising to help out Oakland. The Roots plays this Saturday on the road against Detroit City, its first match since tying 0-0 with Phoenix on July 27. Detroit has one of the most intimidating atmospheres, with its raucous crowds which often use obscenities and smoke bombs. Keyworth Stadium is a formidable venue. Following Detroit, Oakland travels to second-place San Diego Staff Photos Roots head coach Juan Guerra confirmed that the team has 10 games left in its season and is four points shy of the final playoff slot. on Wednesday, August 24 before heading to fifth-place Sacramento Republic on Saturday, August 27. Republic is a fierce rival of Roots and is eight points above them. However, Sacramento has yet to defeat Oakland. The Roots has one win, five draws, and no losses against Republic. Oakland returns home to Laney College on September 3, where it plays first-place San Antonio. The two teams last played to a 1-1 tie on June 18. After that Roots travels to Phoenix on September 10, back home against New York Red Bulls II on September 17, then to Colorado Springs on September 24, a home match with Birmingham Legion on October 1, before crossing the country to play Hartford Athletic in Connecticut on October 8. articles.text: The legacy of veteran distance running coach Len Goldman continues. Boys and girls in 4th through 8th grade may sign up for cross-country through what the Recreation Department is calling Piedmont Junior Running Club. It has been offered for many years at the middle school and has proven to be popular as an introduction to running. It will be offered at all elementary schools starting September 12 and will go until the end of October. Practices will be on Mondays and Wednesdays after school. On Mondays, the program will go from 3:15 to 4:30 and on Wednesdays from 2:00 to 3:15. Each session will include not only running, but active games, agility drills, and relay races. All practices will be supervised and directed by adults who are experienced runners and coaches. Middle School X-C team The Piedmont Middle School cross country is coed for all interested students in 6th, 7th and 8th grades. Not in its 17th season, the team practices 4 days a week, Monday through Thursday after school from 3:30 to 5:00 p.m. PMS is in a league with other schools in the East Bay. There will be a series of meets at various parks where students can enjoy friendly competition. Cross-country is a sport any kid can do. There are no plays to learn or athletic skills to master – just running. An experienced coaching staff will lead this program, headed by veteran middle school coaches, Minori Tsuge and Christine Chapon. Sign up for any of the programs being offered by calling the Rec Department at 420-3070, or register on its website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/ activityguide. Adults who would like to help coach are encouraged to contact Akil Danjuma, the Recreation Department’s Sports Coordinator at 420-3089 or by e-mail at adanjuma@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Rec. Dept. offering cross- country for 4th-8th graders

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is seeking interns to cover Junior Varsity football and water polo for the fall semester. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, August 10, 2022 A look ahead at the Class of 2023 By Jonathan Comeaux With the new school year starting, Piedmont’s Class of 2023 looks ahead to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. articles.text: With the Portola Redwoods State Park announcing this week that it is shutting down its campsites for the remainder of the summer, we return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021. When hiking in the park you will see groves of firstand second-generation redwood trees. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails, although some popular destinations are closed due to COVID-19 protocols – ;ike Tip Toe Falls. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bears its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within the park. Aside from the awe-inducing size, the thousandyear-old tree is among the few old growth trees to have survived the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill Staff Photos The Old Big Tree. a redwood tree estimated to be 1,200 years old, 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. Take the Summit Trail to start your loop. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. Hikers can still see char marks from fires from previous decades along the many first- and second-generation redwoods of Portola State Park. ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail. Turn left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. By turning right, you start a 1.5 mile hike to an historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to a width of less than 6-feet, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turned left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with a T. Turning right to make your way to Upper Escape Road, where you turn right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car – and a pleasant 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that we saw 18 hikers on the 0.6 mile out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Aside from towering redwoods in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the knocking of woodpeckers off in the distance. This column was originally printed in the Post in January 2021. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. Watch out for banana slugs, a common sight in coastal parks.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Walking through old growth trees in Portola Redwoods State Park

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Krcrtv.com Firefighters’ efforts have helped contain the McKinney Fire at 55 percent. The McKinney Fire in the Klamath National Forest near the Oregon border is now at 55 percent containment as of Tuesday, August 9. It was the first time that the blaze experienced no growth since the fire began on July 29. Firefighters were able to construct a line around the fire in an 80-mile perimeter to help extinguishing efforts. “After 11 days of arduous labor, firefighters have accomplished 55 percent containment in the McKinney Fire and have constructed initial line around the entire perimeter. The next step for our fire personnel is to continue to maintain this line by aggressive and thorough mop-up with the intention to gain depth and keep the fire in its existing footprint. Crews continue to patrol and evaluate alternate lines, should the firefighters experience rolling burning material or any spot fires that could challenge their primary line,” wrote Inciweb in a statement, which is a federal fire information site. As of Tuesday, the fire had been burning for 10 days, destroyed 185 structures, damaged another 11, caused 15 injuries, and resulted in four fatalities in Siskiyou County. It is the largest fire this year in California. The fourth reported fatality was longtime U.S. Forest Service employee Kathy Shoopman, who was 73 years old. She died in her home in the Klamath River community as a result of the fire. Siskiyou County was designated as being in extreme drought conditions and is still in red flag conditions. Fire personnel are still keeping a watchful eye on wind and extreme heat. “Anticipate high temperatures, reaching up to 100 degrees, in the Photo courtesy of Yubanet.com The McKinney Fire has caused four fatalities, including 73-year old U.S. Forest Service employee Kathy Shoopman. lower elevations and high 80s in higher elevations. Conditions are expected to be dry with the relative humidity reading 7-8 percent. Winds from the south/southwest could produce gusts up to 35 mph in high elevations. Large dust devils have been observed and are a hazard to look out for on the fire line from the unstable atmosphere. The fire remains in a red flag warning, keeping fire personnel on high alert for any other initial attacks in the area,” wrote Inciweb. Yesterday, August 9, was a critical day in firefighting efforts. It marked the last day of red flag warnings, per California Interagency Incident Management Team fire behavior analyst Dennis Burns. “(Tuesday) is our last day of red flag warnings. If we make it through, I’m starting to feel better that we’re going to keep it, and this fire is going to stay where it belongs,” said Burns. The blaze began on July 29 and rapidly grew in size due due to strong winds and lightning strikes in the area, spreading over 80 square miles in just a two-day span. Conditions have improved greatly since then. Photo courtesy of Wikipedia The McKinney Fire has now burned 60,389 acres, but considerable progress has been made since last week.
articles.title: FIRE SEASON McKinney Fire at 55 percent containment; 60,389 acres burned
