articles.text: The Asian Art Museum of San Francisco is currently showing the work of Filipino artist Carlos Villa now through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions created from the 1970s to 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; a juxtaposition most notably seen in the 1970s. The exhibition has been curated by the SF Asian Art Museum and the San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more. Photo by Rya Jetha A patron at San Francisco Asian Art Museum views the artwork of Carlos Villa.
articles.title: Exhibit of Carlos Villa on view at Asian Art Museum through Oct. 24

articles.text: American Conser vator y Theatre presents the UK-based production of Passengers at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll is the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area,” said Carroll, whose career started years ago at Club Fugazi in North Beach. “The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco. The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ Shana Carroll’s production of Passengers comes to San Francisco on September 15. that is unexpected and so often cut too short – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” Carroll is the co-founding artistic director of Montreal’s Les 7 Doigts de la Main (7 Fingers circus company), where she has directed and choreographed the company’s major touring shows, including Traces (Drama Desk nomination), Sequence 8, Loft, La Vie, Le Murmure du Coquelicot, Cuisine & Confessions, and Psy. Tickets for the Geary Theater production are available by calling the box office at (415) 749- 2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season
articles.title: ACT opens season with Passengers Sept. 15

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will perform the award-winning musical Follies through September 10. The musical is based on a book of the same name by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. The show opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim; it was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of a crumbling theatre in between the world wars. Sally and Phyllis were showgirls in the Follies, and both are in failing marriages. The current cast includes Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. To obtain tickets visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/ or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street. Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, and Emily Corbo appear as dancers in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Follies.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents musical Follies

articles.text: De Young Museum, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, opened a comprehensive exhibition of Faith Ringgold’s artwork on July 16 entitled “Faith Ringgold: American People.” The exhibition spans 50 years of Ringgold’s vision, featuring works that evolved to meet political and social change. Ringgold is a painter, writer, mixed media sculptor, and performance artist best known for her narrative and vivid quilts. This is the first West Coast retrospective of the 91-year-old artist and activist. Ringgold, from Harlem in New York City, currently resides in and works in New Jersey. Artist Faith Ringgold The exhibition will be on view through November 27. To learn more, visit https://deyoung. famsf.org/exhibitions/Faith-Ringgold-American-People. The museum is located in Golden Gate Park at 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223
articles.title: Faith Ringgold exhibition at de Young through Nov. 27

articles.text: The 18th annual Sculpture in the Garden continues at Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek through August 27. Live music by Zola will be performed on the final day of the sale beginning at 5:30 p.m. Sculpture in the Garden is an annual art show and sale that combines sculptural art with the natural sculptural beauty of the Garden. All sculptures are for sale. Admission to the event is free with regular garden admission. The featured artists include Ana Bianchi, Joe Bologna, Kevin Byall, Larry Colvin, Henriette Cons Ponte, Tam Doan, Jake Edwards, Douglas Heine, Roger Heitzman, Stan Huncilman, and Karina Kudymova. For a full list of artists, and to purchase general admission tickets, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ sculpture-show-2022/. The garden is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. Phone (925) 944-9352. ”Galaxy Sunburst” by Holly Wallace, is one of the pieces of sculptural art for sale.
articles.title: Sculpture in the Garden at Bancroft Garden open to Aug. 27

articles.text: Review by Anastasia Edel Pandemic has made us hermits. Our worlds have shrunk to our families and our phone screens. What was first perceived as a calamity – our home confinements – has become a norm and now, with pandemic easing and medications available, a choice. We spend our weekdays inside our homes on Zoom calls, for which only the upper halves of our bodies need to look presentable, and our weekends roaming the same rooms, backyards, and town blocks, this time without any attempts at presentability. We’ve watched every TV show and hiked every trail. Pandemic is amplifying the affliction of our post-modern world: boredom. Luckily, there are remedies. Going to a live show and watching people perform for other people is one of them. This weekend, San Francisco’s Ballet and Stanford Live teamed up to present “Under the Starry Skies,” a celebration of dance, music, and nature at the Frost Amphitheatre at Stanford University. Judging by the amount of sharply dressed people streaming into the amphitheater – some with their picnic blankets, to sit on the lawn, wine glasses in hand – plenty of us are finally ready to break out of our pandemic shells. That the show was outside made the decision easier. It was good to see the faces of strangers without worrying too much about catching Covid, again. The program’s late start of 8 p.m. gave us ample time to explore Palo Alto’s lively restaurant scene. We had dinner and cocktails at an Indian restaurant so contemporary there was no rice or curries on the menu. Parking at a prepaid Stanford lot was much easier than at the War Memorial Theatre, SF Ballet’s home base – and safer. We didn’t have to worry about our car being vandalized, and no random person screamed at us on our way to the performance. Arriving at our chairs on the Lower Bowl of the grassy amphitheater, a lit-up stage straight ahead, I felt a forgotten sense of excitement. The afternoon breeze had died down. The clouds were gone and a pale half-moon hung above the stage, lantern-style. “Starry nights” offered an eclectic program. It started with Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight, an artistically expressive and technically striking ballet set to four concertos by Johann Sebastian Bach. The precise movements of eight dancers (principal dancer WanTing Zhao was a particular pleasure to watch), Photo by Erik Tomasson Wona Park and Joseph Walsh perform with San Francisco Ballet in William Forsythe’s Blake Works. their strict black costumes, and Bach’s timeless music (occasionally augmented by cicadas in nearby trees), transported the audience. Not a single phone rang or flashed. Without the usual confines of the theatre walls, the stage looked smaller, less formal. When the dancers took their bows to enthusiastic applause, I realized that the daylight was almost entirely gone, and a few pale stars appeared above. Life imitated art. Jerome Robbins’ In the Night moved us some two hundred years forward, from Bach’s baroque and to the romantism of Fredrik Chopin, whose piano etudes provided a musical backdrop for the exploration of relationship stages as portrayed by three different couples. In that piece, passion alternated with reserve, longing with calm, struggle with submission. The dancers were precise and often charming, yet there was less energy, and the narrative drive between the three cameos seemed weak. At times, the couples’ oneby-one performances to a lonely piano score (the orchestra had packed up for the night) had a feel of a high-end recital. But the costumes were marvelous, as was the age-defying Yuan Yuan Tan, a Shanghai-San Francisco miracle, who danced in the final part of the ballet. Because there was no additional rehearsal space, the dancers did their warmups on stage during intermissions. Without shedding one bit of their allure, they looked more approachable during those moments, a bunch of youths in leg warmers, vests, and funny Ugg-style boots you might run into in a school gym. The picture-taking that occurred on stage during intermissions gave another window into the ballet’s enigmatic world, where hours of strenuous practice are alleviated by a sense of camaraderie, and by the plain old fun one must get from effortlessly striking a pose that most of us wouldn’t be able to do even after months of training. The evening concluded with William Forsythe’s Blake Works I, a ballet that, according to San Francisco Chronicle, “explodes your ballet prejudices.” Set to the seven songs of award-winning English musician James Blake’s album The Colour in Anything, the ballet was an innovative exploration of intersections between classical and contemporary. Familiar moves got broken to fit the electronic music (no easy task given that pointe technique requires adherence to certain cannons). Some 30 dancers interpreted songs with lyrics like “Put it Aside and Talk to Me.” Initially rehearsed in pandemic-safe pods, this innovative and vigorous ballet felt like an affirmation of the art – and of the human determination not to give up on it. As the dancers came for their final bows, one couldn’t help but marvel at their physical and mental form, and the effort required to maintain them throughout the long months of lockdowns, quarantines, and masked rehearsals. Those beautiful and talented men and women remain an inspiration, their commitment to the real and the physical piercing the ever-expanding digital bubble. Boredom is simply not in the cards once you put yourself into the genius hands of Helgi Tomassen and his posse. I look forward to the 2023 ballet season with the new artistic director Tamara Rojo. I hope you can join me. Anastasia Edel is a dance, music and art reviewer, and a regular contributor in the New York Times.
articles.title: A summer evening with San Francisco Ballet – at Stanford

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey The In the Tradition Piano Trio returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) on Sunday, August 14, to perform a concert in tribute to Richard Rodgers, widely regarded as the premier composer of the American musical. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram. With 43 Broadway musicals and over 900 songs to his credit, Rodgers is considered one of the most important American composers of the 20th century. His compositions have had a significant influence on popular and modern music. The concert is a benefit for the bob-profit Center and will showcase PCA’s Steinway grand piano. Tickets are $20 at the door, and are available online at https:// bpt.me/5316993. Seating will be limited to the first 70 people. The concert begins at 3 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday.

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco International Piano Festival returns on August 18 for its fifth season, with a centennial celebration of J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier. Festival concerts will continue through August 28. “In the midst of much turbulence and tragedy in our world, we continue to make music and celebrate the unstoppable force that is the creative spirit,” said festival founder and artistic director, Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist and one of the festival’s artists. “The 300th anniversary of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier provides a natural focus that the festival will explore in both conventional and unexpected performances.” The festival will be presented in five venues in San Francisco and Berkeley between August 18 and 28, and will feature 15 artists, including eight pianists, and 18 composers, ranging from Bach to contemporary. For information on concerts, repertoire, festival artists, ticketing links and COVID-related restrictions, visit sfpiano.org. With 43 Broadway musicals and over 900 songs to his credit, Rodgers was one of the most important American composers of the 20th century, and his compositions had a significant influence on popular music. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. articles.text: Oakland Symphony has seen some tough times in recent years. Two of their popular conductors died while in harness, and a third deserted the orchestra when they needed him the most. But I can assure you that things are looking up. The symphony is conducting a search for a new Music Director to replace the ever-popular Michael Morgan, who died suddenly one year ago in August. I attended a wonderful free concert in front of Oakland City Hall on Thursday evening. August 4. The setting was festive and so was the attitude of the large audience. Some tables were set ringside and the rest of the audience was seated inside, somewhat like the Hollywood Bowl. The audience expected something good and they received it. The music was directed by a young conductor, Kedrick Armstrong. Take note of his name and the spelling. He has all the qualifications to be the Symphony’s permanent conductor in my opinion. Conducting is not just waggling a stick in front of an orchestra. Yes, the conductor needs to have good technique, but there are many other things that come into play. Success is rather difficult. Psychology comes into play. Conducting is – in great part – psychology itself. Armstrong elicited some very beautiful playing from the musicians. He has a winning smile and his sincerity, both musically and personally, is obvious. The concert began with a very convincing performance of Mozart’s Symphony No. 29. These days, conductors like to race through the music faster than the musicians can play it. Not Armstrong. His musicality reminded me of some of the great conductors in the past, names like Sir Thomas Beecham and 14-year old violinist Amaryn Olmeda performed with Oakland Symphony at an outdoor concert on August 4 in front of Oakland City Hall. Kedrick Armstrong was the guest conductor with Oakland Symphony last week. Hans Knappertsbusch. Those great conductors knew how to get the best performance from their orchestras. I think that young Maestro Armstrong knows these things, too. There are other items which set Armstrong apart, but far too many to mention here. Many in high positions would prefer to have a young black conductor. Armstrong is that. As such, he acknowledges his role in the scheme of things, and said as much to me. Most importantly, the orchestra responds well under his direction. I watched everything very carefully. I would mention that the orchestra needs to pay more careful attention to dynamics. The conductor indicated many things, but the orchestra seemed to ignore them. Armstrong is also a very gracious accompanist. A 14-year old violin soloist named Amaryn Olmeda played impressively. Her vehicles last Thursday were Summerland by William Grant Still and the St-Saens perennial evergreen, Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso. Olmeda played stylishly and with just the right virtuoso ingredients. The audience loved it. In fact the audience loved everything about the concert. Here is something to consider: even in the best of times, great musical art needs the support of the politicians. Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf was there, but she was very discreet. I think that the former mayor Jean Quan was there also. These are good things. and let’s hope the support will continue. About Kedrick Armstrong In addition to having sterling qualities as a musician and as a person, he tells me that he is a gourmet as well. His specialty is shrimp and grits. If that doesn’t whet your appetite… nothing will. The future looks bright.
articles.title: Things are looking up

articles.text: Robben Ford grew up in Ukiah, California. He first played sax, then began guitar when he was 14. He and his brothers Patrick and Mark formed the Charles Ford Blues Band named after their father. Robben has played with a great diversity of artists, a list that inclides blues legends Charlie Musselwhite and Jimmy Witherspoon, followed by George Harrison, Tom Scott and the L.A. Express (on Joni Mitchell’s Miles of Aisles; also with Michael McDonald, Miles Davis and Larry Carlton. Tone has always been important to Robben. His electric guitar tone is similar to a blues harmonica. In the Charles Ford Blues Band, his single note lines were often hard to distinguish from those of his blues harpist brother, Mark. Robben has mainly used the revered Dumble blues guitar amp, Telecaster guitars and Les Paul guitars. Blues scales are the tonal basis of Robben’s improvisation but he also uses diminished half-whole scale and Lydian dominant. Robben refers to the diminished half-whole scale as “double diminished”, since is a combination of two diminished seventh arpeggios. Bars 24 and 30 of Misdirected Blues Bebop Improv linked near the end of this article use diminished halfwhole scale. “I learned chords out of Mickey Baker’s Complete Course in Jazz Guitar,” he explained. Guitarist Robben Ford :They’re all on page one and two. I applied those chords directly to Chicago blues music, which is what I was playing at the time with Charlie Musselwhite. Instead of just the straight-up nine or seven chords, I started using altered chords. Charlie liked jazz and didn’t mind hearing these behind him.” Starting in 1999, Robben listened to a lot of music by Jimi Hendrix. “My influence up to that point had been straight-up blues or jazz, but I started really getting into that more fluid, strumming, Hendrix-style of rhythm playing.” Playing with mentor Tom Scott (sax player, composer, arranger and bandleader) while in the L.A. Express, Robben learned to think like an arranger and composer. I tell my students to think like a composer/arranger and like a sound engineer. Robben teaches online on TrueFire and at his Robben Ford Guitar Dojo. In the 1990’s Robben started

Robben Ford Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com By Jim Gleason Robben Ford grew up in Ukiah, California. He first played sax, then began guitar when he was 14. He and his brothers Patrick and Mark formed the Charles Ford Blues Band named after their father. Robben has played with a great diversity of artists, a list that inclides blues legends Charlie Musselwhite and Jimmy Witherspoon, followed by George Harrison, Tom Scott and the L.A. Express (on Joni Mitchell’s Miles of Aisles; also with Michael McDonald, Miles Davis and Larry Carlton. Tone has always been important to Robben. His electric guitar tone is similar to a blues harmonica. In the Charles Ford Blues Band, his single note lines were often hard to distinguish from those of his blues harpist brother, Mark. Robben has mainly used the revered Dumble blues guitar amp, Telecaster guitars and Les Paul guitars. Blues scales are the tonal basis of Robben’s improvisation but he also uses diminished half-whole scale and Lydian dominant. Robben refers to the diminished half-whole scale as “double diminished”, since is a combination of two diminished seventh arpeggios. Bars 24 and 30 of Misdirected Blues Bebop Improv linked near the end of this article use diminished halfwhole scale. “I learned chords out of Mickey Baker’s Complete Course in Jazz Guitar,” he explained. Guitarist Robben Ford :They’re all on page one and two. I applied those chords directly to Chicago blues music, which is what I was playing at the time with Charlie Musselwhite. Instead of just the straight-up nine or seven chords, I started using altered chords. Charlie liked jazz and didn’t mind hearing these behind him.” Starting in 1999, Robben listened to a lot of music by Jimi Hendrix. “My influence up to that point had been straight-up blues or jazz, but I started really getting into that more fluid, strumming, Hendrix-style of rhythm playing.” Playing with mentor Tom Scott (sax player, composer, arranger and bandleader) while in the L.A. Express, Robben learned to think like an arranger and composer. I tell my students to think like a composer/arranger and like a sound engineer. Robben teaches online on TrueFire and at his Robben Ford Guitar Dojo. In the 1990’s Robben started using turnarounds and other jazz elements in his playing. Since then, he has gone back to more blues and rock roots. My students who were Robben Ford enthusiasts were sorry to see his jazz elements decline. Misdirected Blues Bebop Improv, linked below is an example of his improvisational style with jazz elements. I’ve added more jazz than he usually would. Robben has lived in Nashville since 2018 and is planning to move to France. Listen to and read my improvised example for this Robben Ford column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is a guitar instructor and author. articles.text: Paul Walter Hauser protrays the title character, Richard Jewell, in the movie directed by Clint Eastwood. Richard Jewell, a Clint Eastwood film, is based on events that took place during and after the 1996 Atlanta Summer Olympics when a bomb exploded, killing two people and wounding some 100. Working as a security guard that night was Richard Jewell (Paul Walter Hauser), a wannabe police officer, driven by his law and order enthusiasm and his deference to authority. This zealousness has led to the loss of various jobs in law enforcement, from a campus security position to a stint with a local sheriff’s department. Sadly, he seems unable to see himself as others see him, and is puzzled by the ridicule that comes his way – a 33-year-old man, living with his mother, Bobi (Kathy Bates). His core values are pure, and he wishes only to be part of a uniformed cohort that is committed to keeping order. His quest is to find that niche that rewards his sincerity. For him, clearly, police work is more than an identity; it’s a religion and he is its dedicated disciple. The contradiction is that for all of his immersion in policing, he remains an innocent, unable to see the dark side of a world he longs to serve and protect. And so, when the full weight of the F.B.I. and the press/media bear down on him with an unequivocal rush to judgment, he is at best puzzled and is unwilling to believe that he stands accused. He is convinced that no matter the deviousness of the government (they’ve profiled him as a “false hero”) or the rapacious pursuit of headlines by the Atlanta Journal Constitution (AJC), he is insulated by his membership in what he believes to be a fraternity of kindred spirits. His obliviousness is total, despite being interviewed by the Feds and being shown the Journal’s dramatic, accusatory stories. Finally, into this fast moving avalanche of guilt vs. innocence steps a small-time Atlanta attorney, Watson Bryant (Sam Rockwell), who is far from naïve regarding the rights of his new and serendipitously found client. From the get go, Watson attempts, initially without much success, to jolt Richard out of his “cop to cop” compliance, pushing back when he sees his reflexive desire to assist in his own conviction. Slowly, he schools Richard in the facts of the investigation, carried out by a duplicitous agent, Tom Shaw (Jon Hamm), as well as a “whatever it takes” AJC reporter, Kathy Scruggs (Olivia Wilde). And so, Watson steps forward and gives Richard the fierce representation he needs if he has any hope of extracting himself from a profile being etched not only in institutional stone but in public opinion. From the beginning to the end this is a harrowing tale of a man who is the antithesis of anyone remotely close to a “hero bomber,” yet he is just quirky enough and porky enough to make such an identification seem plausible. Having said all that, it should be pointed out that Eastwood has, to a disappointing degree, turned two institutions (the F.B.I. and the press) into caricatures. Both in today’s world are perpetually denigrated by this administration. It gives this film an added chilling relevance. But in the end, this tightly told story is a character study. It is also an example of exceptional actors doing some of their best work. Kathy Bates and Paul Hauser Walker both step fulsomely into their roles and give this fact-based story an abiding verisimilitude. A final note: In the film’s last scene, that takes place some years later, Watson walks into a police station where Richard, in uniform, is standing behind a wide desk, and gives him his long awaited moment of complete redemption. The bomber has been identified. Both nod and smile widely. Finally, at that moment, Richard Jewell’s ordeal has ended. Richard Jewell. Directed by Clint Eastwood. Starring Paul Walter Hauser, Sam Rockwell, Olivia Wilde. Released in 2019 . Now streaming on VUDU/Prime? Apple tv. 2hrs 9min. Rated R.

The story opens with a bevy of critters emerging one early morning from hibernation to find to their surprise that most of the woodlands have been razed to make room for a stretching housing tract. articles.text: Horton Hears a Who! is an animated feature based on the popular Dr. Seuss children’s book. It was released into theaters in 2008 and is now streaming. The story begins with a wisp of dust, a mere speck, floating through the jungle of Nool. This dot on a clover is actually a self-contained planet that exits in its own cosmos. Along comes Horton (Jim Carrey), a gentle pachyderm who believes that an elephant is “faithful one hundred percent.” Of course, with his large ears, to his surprise, he hears a voice coming from the tiny dust moat. Following the tiny alarmed voice, Horton discovers that it’s coming from a microcosmic city called Who-ville, and the call for help is coming from Who-ville’s daffy mayor Ned McDodd (Steve Carrell). The call for help by the mayor is caused by his belief that Whoville is in serious danger. Horton agrees to help, believing that a “person is a person, no matter how small,” and agrees to move Who-ville to a safer sanctuary. When Horton tells some of the denizens of the jungle of Nool about the existence of Who-ville, they laugh and ridicule him, as does the Kangaroo (Carol Channing), who is snootily derisive. Even Horton’s best friend, Morton the mouse (Seth Rogen), doesn’t believe that there could be such a place as Who-ville. And the citizens of Who-ville doubt the mayor. “What peril?” they ask, even when it begins to snow during the summer. But one person believes Ned, and that’s Dr. Larue, a purple-haired nerdette (Isla Fisher) with thick safety glasses, who supports the mayor and believes that the city should be moved to the top of Mt. Nool where they will not be in peril. It’s a given that Horton Hears a Who! will connect with younger kids and plays to their curiosity. And not to forget that there’s a bevy of creatures that will appeal, such as a goofy vulture named Vlad (Will Arnett), and Tommy, a fat orange bear (Jonar Nila). And not to forget that there are, of course, some gentle life lessons about friendship that never come off as lectures. It’s all lots of fun, quirky, and good natured. Horton Hears a Who! Animated adventure- comedy. Directed by Jimmy Hayward and Steve Marino. With voices of Jim Carrey, Steve Carrell, Amy Poehler, and Isla Fisher. 1 hr., 28 min. Rated G. Released in 2008. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv. A scene from Horton Hears a Who! based on the children’s book by Dr. Seuss.

articles.text: On July 18, seven Scouts from Troop 15 and three adults set out on the Troop’s annual Sierra trek for four days and three nights of backpacking near beautiful South Lake Tahoe. The trip followed 25 miles on the Pacific Crest Trail and Tahoe Rim Trail. We had lots of fun on both trails, and we all composed and sang a lot of songs and made up lots of trail nicknames: Davey “the Deuce” Ackerman, Ben “Tenderfoot” Gitter, Gabriel “Daniel-son” Barbosa Topete, Alex “A-Rod” Chin, Thomas “Daddy” Moision, Sammy “The Barrister” Ragones, and Nate “M&M” Scher. The leaders’ nicknames were Fred “The Salesman” Ackerman, Vanessa “the Wolf” Oklejas, and Dave “Blood of Spanish Dragons” Ragones. We camped at three lakes on the trip. They were stunning but the first two lakes, Round Lake and Showers Lake, had mosquitoes. The third lake, Dardanelle Lake, was mosquito-free. On the Mission accomplished. Troop 15 Sierra Trekkers return to the Big Meadows Trailhead: Vanessa “The Wolf” Oklejas (front), Ben “Tenderfoot” Gitter, Gabrial “Daniel-san” Barbosa Totepe, Alex “Arod” Chin, Davey “The Deuce” Ackerman, Sammy “The Barrister” Ragones, Thomas “Daddy” Moision, Nate “M&M” Scher, Dave “Blood of Spanish Dragons” Ragones. first day we trekked four miles to Round Lake. The next day was a 7-mile hike to Showers Lake, We passed different hikers and backpackers including some who had been hiking for weeks and looked cheerfully seasoned. Each time we arrived at our lake, we would drop our 30-pound packs and split up to find a suitable campsite. After finding the perfect campsite, we would bring our packs over and have lunch. We would then unpack our heavy loads, assemble the water filter equipment and decide who should be on water duty as we started pitching our tents. Then it was time to unwind and swim in the Sunset on Lake Dardanelle on the Tahoe Rim Trail. Scouts enjoy the sun on the banks of Lake Dardanelle after a long day. Thomas Moison and Gabriel Barbosa Topete fish at Round Lake on the Tahoe Rim Trail. Trip co-leaders Fred “The Salesman” Ackerman and Vanessa “The Wolf” Oklejas enjoy the vista overlooking Lake Tahoe.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 10, 2022 21 Troup 15 Continued from page 20 lakes. Our hike on the second day took us to 9,000 feet. Around 6:00 pm, we started helping with dinner. After a great dinner (sometimes a burrito) and a delicious dessert of cherry crisp, we played a little and then we turned in for the night. The mornings were always a bit of a hustle to pack up and get on the trail so we could get to the next lake before lunch. The trail on the third day was better because one was uphill and the other was downhill. When we arrived at the third lake we understood how lucky we are to live in California because of the great nature. Dardanelle Lake was the most amazing of the three. We camped on a cool island and had to balance on a log to get there. The best thing about it was that it was mosquito-free. The last day we all had mixed feelings – sad because we had to go, but happy to take our packs off, and excited for next year’s trip. When we caught a glimpse of a road everyone went crazy to see cars. We unclipped our packs from our waist and chest and climbed into the van. We drove a little bit until we arrived at In & Out Burger. After a delicious lunch we headed home to Piedmont. The trip was awesome. Special thanks to our adult volunteer leaders, Fred, Dave, and Vanessa, for all their planning, guidance and support on the trip. Sammy Ragones prepares a dessert of berry cobbler. articles.text: Perhaps more than any room, homeowners either love or hate their bathrooms. Luxurious en suite primary baths are desired by many. What can you do if you don’t have the budget, time or space to build the bathroom of your dreams? The main thing to keep in mind when the budget is tight is to limit the scope of work to something you can afford to have done properly. It is better to take on less work and do it with high quality than to tackle a major bath remodel with substandard workmanship and materials. First, evaluate what is “wrong” with your existing bathroom. Do you have leaks or rot? Cracked or ugly tile? Outdated lighting? Are your plumbing fixtures failing? Do you have enough storage? If you want to change all the plumbing fixtures, rip out the tub/ shower, install new electrical and Updating shower tile and fixtures, while keeping the tub and rough plumbing. venting systems, replace a window, move the door, add a skylight, or other more complicated changes, you have entered the world of the “full bath remodel”. Work of this kind by a licensed qualified contractor can easily exceed $75k and may cost twice that. You can keep the cost down if you can retain not only the layout of the walls but also the locations of the plumbing fixtures, presuming your pipes are good. You may find all you need is a refresh, rather than a full remodel. By replacing fixtures and finishes only, you can reduce both the expense and time you are required to be without use of your bathroom. For example, you could select a standard shower door, rather than an all-glass, frameless shower door. There are inexpensive tile options with a handmade look and feel to add style. Consider a pre-made vanity, rather than custom cabinets. A good general contractor can help value engineer your project. In the end, limiting scope of work is the best way to control costs. Be realistic about your standards and years you plan to spend in your home. If you need a full bath remodel and can’t or don’t want to spend what it takes, it might be better to just do a couple of repairs and wait until you can do the bathroom the right way. Otherwise, you could end up with permanent mediocrity, which may not be the best investment of your time and money. “Relying On Experience” is a new feature by McCutcheon Construction, Inc., an employee-owned company, highlighting A freestanding, prefabricated vanity and countertop Colorful tile, fresh paint and a new light fixture with the richness of custom cabinetry. livens up this classic bathroom. the latest innovations and best practices of home remodeling. articles.text: • Farmers markets have practically been screaming this combination for a quintessential summertime frittata. There are so many interesting squashes from which to choose, but using zucchini brings a bright color contrast to the eggs and corn. Use this recipe as a guide and make substitutions according to your preferences and what’s available. Red bell peppers are a natural here. Likewise, you can switch up the cheeses. I used Pecorino Romano, but any other gratable Italian cheese such as Parmesan, Grana Padano, or a firm asiago will be delicious. (Watch for the varying levels of saltiness of the cheese you use and adjust additional salt to taste. Similarly, feel free to scale the recipe for a smaller frittata, or a deeper one if making in a 12-inch skillet. Just remember to adjust the oven baking time accordingly. Baking on a convection setting minimizes an overcooked bottom of the frittata, which has already been cooked on the stovetop. The circulating air of the convection fan also speeds the baking and helps set the top of the frittata. • • • 2 tablespoons fresh basil, minced, plus more for garnish A few slices of fresh mozzarella cheese, for garnish, optional 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Summertime Fresh Corn and Zucchini Frittata Makes a 12-inch frittata, about 1/ 2-inch thick INGREDIENTS • • • • • • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra virgin 10 extra-large eggs, 1 large cob of corn, kernels removed, about 1-1/2 cups of kernels 3 small zucchinis, about 10 ounces, sliced crosswise into 1/8̋ rounds (coins) 1/2 cup white or yellow onion, diced 1/4 cup Pecorino Romano cheese, finely grated, lightly packed Place an oven rack to the center position, preheat the oven to 325° F, ideally on a convection setting. Break the eggs into a medium bowl and lightly scramble. Add the grated Pecorino Romano cheese, minced basil, salt, and pepper. Stir to combine and set aside. In a 12-inch non-stick skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat for a minute, then add the diced onion and sliced zucchini. Stir occasionally until the onions become translucent and the zucchini are just beginning to brown on one side. Add the corn and stir to evenly distribute the vegetables in the skillet. Pour the egg mixture over it, making sure the liquid flows to the edges of the skillet and is level. Cook over medium heat for about 5 minutes until the edges just begin to set. Transfer the skillet to the preheated oven and continue cooking for about 15 minutes. The frittata will puff slightly, and will be done when a clean butter knife is inserted in the center and comes out clean. Take care to not overbake it, it’s better to err to the soft and jiggly side than dry. Carefully remove the skillet to a heat-safe surface and let set for about 5 minutes before slicing to serve. Remember to place a potholder or cloth over the skillet’s handle to let everyone know the handle is H.O.T. pages.text: Wednesday, August 10, 2022 23 Defining creativity My family, in all their creative individuality. By Laura Martin Bovard As a parent, I have to frequently check that I am not labeling our children. I’ve noticed it only serves to make them question their uniqueness. What seemed like a harmless way of acknowledging what is special about them I realize can devolve into labels and comparisons that unintentionally make them feel bad about themselves. Once Scott and I saw the error of our ways, we really tried to put the kibosh on that behavior. Still, we aren’t perfect. Every once in a while, I’ll catch myself comparing them, and have to remember not to. I have often said that growing my business has taught me to be a more self-aware, conscious person, and that is even more true when it comes to raising children. Like my business, I don’t think I grew them as much as they grew me. I imagine that most of us bear the wounds of being labeled when we were children either by our parents, our teachers, or other well-meaning elders. One of the labels my own father frequently repeated was that my brother Steve was “the creative one.” It didn’t occur to me to be offended or disagree with that statement at the time. He was my father – the boss, and the holder of all knowledge. It made sense to me at the age of 8 to believe him, so I did. What he meant was that Steve could draw well, which was true. Because he had an interest in it, he drew and drew and got better and better. One could surmise that yes, in fact, Steve was a creative one. But it turns out he wasn’t the creative one. He was simply creative. Meanwhile, during the era Steve received his honorary title, I was the one making leis, selling lemonade, cooking up a storm in the kitchen, and decorating and redecorating every room in the house. I also loved to tutor my younger siblings so they could get a leg up in school and be well prepared. I adored my English classes and wrote regularly in my journal. I was constantly curious. Being the patriarchal guy that he was, my father characterized my kind of creativity as “women’s work,” which was expected rather than celebrated. Women’s work came second to that of boys and men, and so I did not reap the same status for my efforts as my brother did. It may seem blatantly obvious to anyone who knows me that I am a creative person. I design, I write, I am an entrepreneur, and I curate life in general. But because of the labels that were placed on me that I accepted hook, line, and sinker, it’s taken me a long time to actually own the fact that I am creative. I used the output of my creative energy to serve others. Now that I’ve shifted my thinking and allowed that truth to be my own, I am enjoying my life infinitely more. I invite anyone who rejects the idea that they are creative to challenge that thought. We are creating our lives in every moment of every day. Creativity isn’t just painting, drawing, or playing the piano. It’s also how we put ourselves together, how we present ourselves to the world. We create every time we choose our words, get dressed, and make a meal. If we slow down and approach these daily practices as an art form instead of rushing through to the finish line, all these things can be considered creative. It’s in the how. So next time, before you utter the words “I’m not creative,” slow down and ask yourself if that’s really true. It’s all in how you define it. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. articles.text: Piedmont Boy Scouts visited the Northern Tier High Adventure Base for Piedmont´s annual high adventure trip, June 21-29. Two crews totaling 11 Scouts and 4 adult leaders from troops 1, 4, and 11 participated. The Charles L. Sommers canoe base, known as Northern Tier, is located in Ely in Northern Minnesota in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. It has more than one million acres of protected wilderness with the north section in Canada. Northern Tier offers trips to boys and girls aged 14 and older who are in Scouting. Scouts must be in good physical shape, strong swimmers, and able to carry at least 75 lbs. Over 4,000 youth each year visit Northern Tier to experience the beauty of the wilderness area. The trip was led by Troy AlerEvan Dickason and George Stein relax in a hammock. Troy and Ethan Alering with a double hook up of a smallmouth bass. Tommy Ashton holds up a Lake trout he caught. Ethan Alering with a smallmouth bass. Using a fly rod, Henry Smith caught the largest smallmouth bass during the week. Kevlar canoes were used on the Scouts’ trip to Northern Tier. Miguel Long sits in a waterfall. ing, Jason Stein, Javier Jerez, and Jason Lambert, with Ethan Alering of Troop 11 and Kai Lambert of Troop 1 as Scout Leaders. Traveling together, the Scouts stayed at the Northern Star Council Base in Minneapolis before taking a 5-hour bus trip to the Northern Tier Canoe Base in Ely. Upon arrival, the Scouts broke into their separate crews, did a shakedown to eliminate any unnecessary personal gear, then headed to a depot to check out their crew gear and choose their routes. Each crew had an interpreter Members of Crew #1 (right) and #2 (left) on the weeklong trip to Northern Tier on the Minnesota-Canadian border.

Merkel and her husband, Joachim Sauer, keep their lives very private. Marton was not allowed to interview Merkel for this book. So, Marton’s extensive research relates Merkel’s youth, her moving away from a scientific career into politics, her government’s policies, and her interactions with other world leaders. articles.text: A road rage altercation over a traffic maneuver early morning on August 2 on Oakland Avenue turned violent when six shots were fired and two struck the victim’s car. The victim, an Oakland resident in an Acura LX, was driving on Oakland Avenue near Monte Vista at around 6:30 a.m. when suspects behind him in a newer white Alfa-Romeo took offense to a traffic maneuver and honked their horn. The driver of the Acura honked back and some words were exchanged. “It got a little crazy after that,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. Six shots were fired from the Alfa-Romeo near Oakland Avenue and Olive Avenue in Piedmont, hence the jurisdiction fell to Piedmont Police. Two of the bullets struck the Acura. One went through the trunk, and then through the backseat, before stopping in the headrest on the driver side. The other bullet entered the victim’s Acura above the taillight and ricocheted around in the frame. Four other shots were fired but have not been located. No bullet shell casings were found. Crime lab analysis is being done on the bullet found lodged in the back of the headrest. The driver was not injured. “We’ve got some video from a homeowner where you can hear the shots and see the victim vehicle, but we never see the suspect vehicle in the video,” said Monahan. No images of the suspect vehicle have yet to be collected, but based on the victim’s descriptions, police estimate it to be a 2015-2020 white fourdoor Alfa-Romeo with paper plates and “dark rims.” The model is rare in the United States. The victim said there were at least three people in the Alfa-Romeo, and one of them fired a handgun. The car was going approximately 45 miles per hour when the shots were fired. Once the victim saw the suspects were no longer behind him, he pulled onto Sunnyside Avenue to collect himself. He then continued to drive to work and called 911 later from his office in Oakland. The Piedmont Police Department is actively investigating this crime, in conjunction with other local agencies. “Our detectives have been inspecting matching vehicles stopped by other law enforcement agencies. That will continue until we find the suspect vehicle,” Monahan said. Anyone with information associated to this event, including surveillance images from the area, are asked to contact Det, George Tucker at (510) 420-3013 or Det. John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015. If this vehicle is seen, call 911 immediately and reference the event. on other outdoor skills, including fishing, pioneering, first aid, wilderness survival, and orienteering. Other activities included leatherwork, basketry, art, photography, sculpture, and wood carving. Several STEM-based adventures were offered also, including sustainability, composite materials, and chemistry. These were offered alongside camp classics such as astronomy, weather, and mammal study. Oceanography was a great one for Scouts to tackle at this camp, as they saw garibaldis and jellyfish while snorkeling at the waterfront. One evening, Scouts even got to help make homemade ice cream faster than usual, using liquid nitrogen as the freezing agent for the sweet cream base. Time spent with friends at the campsite is a special part of the experience. Some Scouts worked on a chess merit badge during down time, while others enjoyed card games and a chance to relax. Eric Venner checks his regulator before going on a SCUBA dive. After a long and busy week, the Scouts were ready for the travel home, complete with having pizza delivered while waiting at the airport for the flight home. Plenty of future activities are being planned by Troop 11, to include campouts at Kings Canyon and Point Reyes, and an archery-focused overnighter at Camp Tamarancho in Fairfax in Marin County. For more information, contact the Scout Council office at 510-547-4493 (contact@piedmontbsa.org, or contact Troop 11 Scoutmaster Rob Kobal at rjkobal@earthlink.net.

The first morning the Scouts picked up their food, checked out their canoes and learned how to lift their canoe onto their shoulders. By 10 a.m. each crew was launched and heading out. Scouts rotated camp duties during the trip, including cooking, cleaning, setting up the rain fly, and hanging a bear bag with a food box. The Scouts also performed conservation projects, cleaning at each campsite they visited, picking up any trash left over from prior visitors. Crew Leaders Ethan and Kai chose adventurous routes with a goal of paddling a total of 50 miles. Both crews met their paddling goals. Both crews went east due to routes in the west being flooded, with water levels up nearly 5 feet making it difficult to find and navigate portages. articles.text: Editor: I have been a resident of Piedmont a good part of my life. My family moved here in 1953. I attended Piedmont schools and left after I graduated from Piedmont High in 1969 to pursue my education and life and did not return until 1994. However, my parents remained, and so I witnessed the demolition of the high school, which was architecturally beautiful with spacious and light-filled classrooms. It was razed because of what turned out to be an unfounded concern that the structure was not earthquake sound. It was replaced by a structure that has since been replaced because it was seismically unsound. I saw the loss of Hamby’s, the drug store, and the Sweet Shoppe (in the middle of town) when the site was “improved” in the early 1970s and is now occupied by Wells Fargo and offices. I saw Safeway, which had a butcher, exit to be replaced by a bank and Convenient, now fortunately Mulberry’s. The latest plan to address the state’s housing mandate, to raze the Veterans Hall, relocate the police and fire department and additionally build on the tennis courts and the grassy strip on Highland, is even more poorly conceived and is distressing. The proposed changes to the city’s core would be a travesty and would forever change the character of Piedmont. While understanding the need to respond to the legislature’s mandate, the community would be ill-served by these proposals. Moving the fire department to the outskirts of the city would be a detriment to public safety. Has anyone considered the impact of rush hour gridlock on Moraga Avenue would have on the ability of emergency responders to get into the heart of the city when there is an urgent need? Objections to the proposal to build in Blair Park and the complaint that the residents of this housing would be “isolated” ignore the even more remote locations of residences on Maxwelton Road, Abbott Way, Echo Lane, and Nellie Avenue. Rezoning on Grand Avenue to accommodate multi-family housing is logical. The infrastructure already exists, and it would be situated on the only existing street in the city that could accommodate the additional traffic if restored to four lanes. The proposal to alter the city center, which has the endorsement of individuals who are not city residents, specifically staff and the outside consultants, is insensitive and out of touch with the community. Moving the tennis courts away from [proximity to] the high school would be a detriment to the school and raise its own safety issues. We are not Woodside, whose residents are seeking to avoid the construction of housing by prioritizing the needs of mountain lions. Our 1.7 square miles of land is already developed. The legislature’s mandate of 587 new housing units amounts to a 15% increase in households. 460 Boulevard Way, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS

When looking at Jesus in the temple, we don’t have much reference about him since his birth. This is inaugural in which he proclaims his personal mission. This is before he goes out to do all the good works. He selects a passage from a scroll. He could have chosen any number of passages, but he selected a passage from the prophet Isaiah. Before I go down that road, I want to discuss what you think of your personal mission statement. A mission statement is something that describes who you are and what you will achieve in the world. At St. John’s we say to manifest the love of God through the Holy Spirit with each other, our community and the world through worship, spiritual growth and Christian service. My question is, do you feel you manifest God’s love through the Holy Spirit? Do you do this with each other here in community, do you do this in the world? Do you do this through worship? Do you dedicate yourself to spiritual growth? What acts of Christian service do you perform? This is what we say at St. John’s, and I am curious if this aligns with your personal mission? I am going to use another passage and see if this aligns. Are you a person embodied in justice for all people and for God’s creation, and you believe in church vitality? Are you rooted in spirituality or transparent and accountable as a leader as you build Inclusive community? I just quoted the Diocese of California. Carrying out a mission is not easy. We all have a variety of gifts, and they are not all the same. articles.text: Editor: The time has come for Piedmont residents concerned about locating 215 or so low-income housing units to propose, rather than reject, sites. Proposals should, I believe, avoid assigning all, or nearly all, the units to one location. Fifty years of research tells us that day-to-day problems encountered by all communities, regardless of income distribution or history, become more divisive and difficult to solve in cities that create, by policy, low-income, stigmatized enclaves. And although the architectural community may believe otherwise, experience tells us that design alone will not overcome the stigma problem. The stig ma associated with concentrated, low-income enclaves has led to other approaches including “voucher” programs that enable low-income families to participate in the rental market. This approach will not work in the Bay Area because the supply of affordable housing remains so limited that vouchers simply lead to inflated rents. The “next-best” alternative has been “scattered site housing” or affordable units broadly distributed, in small groupings, in a community. Research finds that this approach creates less stigma and leads to better integration of families into the schools and social life of a community than do larger, concentrated enclaves. I suggest that Piedmont pursue, consistent with adopted city policy, the scattered site strategy. I propose a “5 by 40” approach meaning we should find 5 sites where 40 units can be reasonably integrated into the city. I recommend 40 units because research suggests that the relationship between project size and stigma is not linear. After about 40 units, the stigma accelerates quickly. I nominate 5 sites: • the corporation yard (yes, my “backyard”) • the skateboard park near the corporation yard • the Sylvan Learning Center and Ace Hardware sites on Grand Avenue • the land occupied by Highland Way • the last 15 units could go on the site city staff has identified on Park Boulevard The only “new” site here is Highland Way. The city owns the land. Using it for housing would not require replacing an existing city facility. All utilities and infrastructure are on site. Adjacent uses are commercial and institutional with height and mass consistent with multi-unit housing. Keeping 20 yards or so at the western terminus as a street would, moreover, preserve access for the gas station and pedestrian steps to the church. I look forward to seeing other schemes for a 5 by 40 solution.
articles.title: It’s time for citizens to propose housing sites

Proposals should, I believe, avoid assigning all, or nearly all, the units to one location. Fifty years of research tells us that day-to-day problems encountered by all communities, regardless of income distribution or history, become more divisive and difficult to solve in cities that create, by policy, low-income, stigmatized enclaves. And although the architectural community may believe otherwise, experience tells us that design alone will not overcome the stigma problem. The stig ma associated with concentrated, low-income enclaves has led to other approaches including “voucher” programs that enable low-income families to participate in the rental market. This approach will not work in the Bay Area because the supply of affordable housing remains so limited that vouchers simply lead to inflated rents. The “next-best” alternative has been “scattered site housing” or affordable units broadly distributed, in small groupings, in a community. Research finds that this approach creates less stigma and leads to better integration of families into the schools and social life of a community than do larger, concentrated enclaves. I suggest that Piedmont pursue, consistent with adopted city policy, the scattered site strategy. I propose a “5 by 40” approach meaning we should find 5 sites where 40 units can be reasonably integrated into the city. I recommend 40 units because research suggests that the relationship between project size and stigma is not linear. After about 40 units, the stigma accelerates quickly. I nominate 5 sites: • the corporation yard (yes, my “backyard”) • the skateboard park near the corporation yard • the Sylvan Learning Center and Ace Hardware sites on Grand Avenue • the land occupied by Highland Way • the last 15 units could go on the site city staff has identified on Park Boulevard The only “new” site here is Highland Way. The city owns the land. Using it for housing would not require replacing an existing city facility. All utilities and infrastructure are on site. Adjacent uses are commercial and institutional with height and mass consistent with multi-unit housing. Keeping 20 yards or so at the western terminus as a street would, moreover, preserve access for the gas station and pedestrian steps to the church. I look forward to seeing other schemes for a 5 by 40 solution. Piedmont Post at your door and online The Piedmont Post remains available online to all subscribers, no matter where they live. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702- 9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: On July 28, the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) reported over 750 confirmed monkeypox cases in California, 58 of which are Alameda County residents. Monkeypox is a disease belonging to the Orthpoxvirus genus, which includes smallpox, and is caused by a pathogen or infectious agent that has jumped from an animal host to human. Monkeypox occurs naturally in Africa, and is described by the County Health office as “a disease… that has been rarely exported to other regions beyond Central and West Africa.” Symptoms of monkeypox include flu-like illness, fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes, chills and fatigue. These symptoms are followed by a rash that typically begins on the face or hands. Lesions are well-rounded and resemble pimples; scabs are described by patients as painful until the healing phase when they become itchy and crust. “Any rash-like illness consistent with the clinical descriptions above during travel or upon return should be immediately reported to a health care professional, including information about all recent travel, sexual history, and smallpox immunization history,” said Dr. Nicolas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Officer. Monkeypox can spread through touching materials used by an infected person that haven’t been cleaned, such as clothing, towels and bedding. It can also spread by respiratory secretions during prolonged, close, faceto-face contact, according to the Center for Disease Control (CDC). The County has created a screening worksheet and urges all individuals with symptoms of Monkeypox to complete the worksheet, which requires the patient to send photos of rashes and collect specimens. The form is available at https://acphd-web-media.s3-uswest-2.amazonaws.com/media/ communicable-disease/monkeypox/docs/monkeypox-screening-form-2022.07.10.pdf. Questions may be directed to the County Health office by e-mail at monkeypox@acgov.org, or by calling 510-267-3250. Individuals experiencing symptoms may also call an on-call ACPHD Public Health Duty Officer at (925) 422-7595. State response The California Department of Public Health is monitoring monkeypox transmission in the state and throughout the U.S. “The risk of monkeypox to the public is currently very low based on the information available. While monkeypox can infect anyone, many of the recent cases in 2022 have occurred among persons self-identifying as men who have sex with men,” said CDPH Director Dr. Tomas Aragon. “Vaccination helps to protect against monkeypox when given before or shortly after an exposure. JYNNEOS and ACAM2000 are two monkeypox vaccines currently available in the United States via the Strategic National Stockpile.” As of August 1, the federal government has allocated a limited number of JYNNEOS vaccine doses to Californians. “CDPH is working with local health departments to make these doses available to protect against monkeypox,” Dr. Aragon confirmed. The state department recommends avoiding close physical contact with people who have symptoms, wear personal protective equipment including masks, and to practice good hand hygiene. The CDPH stated that monkeypox is “much less contagious than COVID-19, is not a new virus and does not spread in the same way as COVID-19.” two weeks before the RHNA for Piedmont was finalized. “We had an opportunity to appeal [the RHNA] and we did not appeal because it would be a losing battle, and in hindsight, that was correct,” said Council Member Betsy Andersen. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will discuss Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper at its upcoming book meeting on August 16. Pepper’s Laboratories shows the “high profile antics of national politics,” and spotlights what can often be corruption in statehouses across the nation, which the author asserts pose the greatest threat to American democracy. The book outlines 30 steps that need to be taken, from federal action to individual steps, that help every citizen fight back against corruption in their own communities. Pepper is a writer, lawyer, former elected official, and served as the Chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party between 2015 and 2021. He earned his B.A. from Yale University and his J.D. from Yale Law School. The discussion will begin via Zoom at 5 p.m. on August Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper 16. You do not need to be a LWV member to join the book club discussion. articles.text: As the calendar inches its way through the summer into fall, today marks one week before Piedmont students return to school, August 10. Whether summer has entered the dog days or flown by, starting a creative project is rewarding for everyone. Creating a zine can be that be end-of-summer fun project. A zine is a homemade production of a magazine on a small scale. A zine may be nothing more than a flip book, or a single sheet of paper that is folded into a small 8-page pamphlet. Zines have grown in popularity and possess a counter-culture of “rebellion” as media in a physical form with anonymity. However, the creation of a zine can quietly work the brain and improve scholastic skills while having fun. Potential topics are endless for your kid’s’ creative project. It can be a how-to booklet, a joke book, a superhero comic book, or just a collection of photos. Simply folding and cutting the paper and mapping out the page numbers can be enough of a spark to have kids feeling like the next renegade anonymous artist with the fame of Banksy awaiting them. As digital media dominates the life of kids (and adults) via online school and work, parents The one page mini-zine is created with a couple of folds, a cut in the middle of the paper pages numbered as shown. may be looking for anything in the physical realm to ease the strain on their kids’ eyes. Even if your child does not have the gift of writing or drawing, they can have fun making a zine which can expand their horizons beyond a screen. Consider diving into multi-media by cutting out pictures from old magazines or newspaper; that can be done by anyone with or without any artistic ability. One doesn’t need a story to tell to create a zine; it doesn’t have to make any sense. Once the work of art is completed, the process of distribution can be the most fun of all. After making photocopies, your kids can give them out to friends, patrons at Mulberry’s Market, or neighbors. They can be anonymously inside books at a bookstore or library. Leaving one’s creation in public, even at the tiny free libraries, means there’s no limit to the places they will end up. The sand of summer’s hourglass may be dwindling, but there is still time for one last fun amazine project.

articles.text: School is coming. Having the kids out of the house will be nice, but we need to make sure they are ready to go when they get back to school. So, the questions are, “Should we prep for school or just rest? When do we start? How hard do we push? Where do we go for help? Do we review or learn new material?” Let’s address each one individually. To Prep or Not to Prep To answer this question, we need to assess the students’ circumstances and the students themselves. If your student is going to enter their freshman year, they will most likely spend a good portion of the beginning of the year with preparatory instruction since none of the freshman will know what high school is like. If your student is going into the junior year or is in middle school, and their grades are on the fence, you probably don’t have the leeway of a slow start and should get your student ready to hit the ground running. When Should You Start? Once you have decided that you need to get your student ready for school ahead of time, the next question is when should you start. Some parents decide not to take a break at all. For students who struggle or tend to lose a lot of ground during the summer, this makes sense. For other students who want to be ready for a solid start, a few weeks or just a week of prep is generally enough since most students will have some review at the start of the year and just need to make sure their school brain is in gear. What to Study? You can review the material from last year or front load the new material. If you are studyIt is a good idea to do some academic preparation before school begins. ing math or foreign languages, it makes the most sense to review the material from last year since the classes are likely cumulative. If you are getting ready for any other class that is not cumulative, review the material that the class will cover at the start of the year. If you hire a tutoring service or an ex-teacher, a lot of the leg work on finding what to learn will be done for you. Otherwise, you can get a lot of information and help at the California standards website (www.cde.ca.gov/ be/st/ss/), or contact us for more information. Who Should Teach the Material? For motivated students, all you will need to do is point them in the right direction and let them go. Other students will need a parent or tutor to set up their prep work and gather their materials for them. It can be really hard for students to be motivated as summer comes to an end, so if you only have a few weeks to get ready, it probably makes sense not to rely solely on students without some supervision. What if It’s Too Late? It’s never too late, but it may be too late to get ready ahead of time in the summer. If you find the school year is upon you and your student isn’t ready, doing an extra review and studying at the start of the year can be almost as effective as summer pre-studying. Use the first few weeks to make sure any required knowledge is fresh and that students are familiar with the material that is coming. If you have any questions about prepping for the school year or any other education-related questions, please do not hesitate to contact Paul Osborne (DBA Paul the Tutor) at 4235 Piedmont Avenue. Tel. (510) 730-0390. Free 30-minute consultations are available, and we’re happy to answer any questions you have. info@ paulthetutors.com.
articles.title: Prepping before the start of school

articles.text: Photos courtesy of International Fencing Federation Rafaella Gomes of Piedmont competed at the Fencing World Championship in Cairo, Egypt, reaching the Round of 64. Representing Brazil, Piedmont High School Class of 2021 graduate Rafaella Gomes recently competed on the world stage in the Fencing World Championship in Cairo, Egypt the week of July 15. Given the No. 46 overall seed in the preliminary round, she upset No. 19 Kim Kirschen of Germany 15-7. She attained the No. 61 seed in the Round of 64 and battled against the eventual runner up in the finals, No. 4 Arianna Errigo of Italy, losing 15-8. Her results improved Gomes’ world ranking from No. 100 to No. 77. “To make it to the second day is to compete with the greats. And I did just that, facing Arianna Errigo right off the bat. She is an amazing fencer, who I greatly respect and admire. I fenced the match with all I had, fueled partly by a newcomer’s burning desire to prove myself. Though I lost, I am proud of the way I fenced,” said Gomes. Facing Errigo is no easy task; the Italian eventually reached the Finals, where she lost to Ysoara Thibus of France 15-10. To take eight points from a finalist says a lot about Gomes’ potential. “The experience added fuel to my passion and to my ambition. I want to reach higher, and I am not afraid of the work it will take to make that happen,” she added. Prior to the tournament, Gomes had just two weeks to train for the tournament after recovering from COVID-19. She trains at the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, a pre-Olympic program that Gomes trained with Rafaella Gomes (right) improved her world ranking in fencing to No. 77. Rafaella Gomes (right) represents Brazil on the international circuit.
articles.title: Rafaella Gomes competes in Fencing World Championship in Cairo

articles.text: In its first time starting in Denmark, this year’s Tour de France winner was a Dane. Jonas Vingegaard, 25, officially dethroned Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar for the Yellow Jersey on July 24, holding the lead in General Classification over the last 10 stages of Le Grand Boucle and finishing with a 2-minute, 43-second advantage. Vingegaard stunned the world on Stage 11 when overtaking Pogačar and building a staggering advantage when attacking on the Col du Granon with 3.5 kilometers to go. The Dane’s triumphant performance is a testament to the strength of his teammates on Jumbo-Visma, while Pogačar had little help from UAE Team Emirates. Jumbo-Visma continually attacked on Stage 11 to string Pogačar thin without necessary teammates to maintain a manageable pace. By the time the course reached Col du Granon, Vingegaard turned on the after-burners and cranked his way up the mountain, leaving Pogačar in the dust. Jumbo-Visma cyclist Wout Van Aert won the Green Jersey for the lead in Points Classification. Following Stage 11, Vingegaard prevented numerous attacks by Pogačar, including continuous sprints by the Slovenian on the mountains of stages 17 and 18. Pogačar was able to win Stage 17, but did so without picking up any time advantage on Vingegaard. The Jumbo-Visma rider, meanwhile won Stage 18 with a mighty 1 minute, 4 second advantage over Pogačar, solidifying his place as the next Tour de France champion. Some of the pundits successfully predicted Pogačar’s fall from the top spot early on after pushing to win Stage 7’s mounPhoto courtesy of LeTour.fr Two-time winner Tadej Pogačar relinquished the Yellow Jersey after Stage 11 and couldn’t pick up any ground on Vingegaard. tain course. Questions loomed about whether the Slovenian used too much energy in the early portion of the tour, which seemed to be the case once Pogačar cracked on Stage 11. It prevented Pogačar from becoming the first three-time champion since Chris Froome in 2015-2017. Pogačar did win his third consecutive Best Young Rider classification. Vingegaard, meanwhile, was also crowned Best Climber. The 2023 Tour de France starting location has already been announced. It will start outside of France for the second consecutive tour, this time in Bilbao, Spain— which will be the first time Le Grand Tour will begin in Spain since 1992. Photo courtesy of BBC

articles.text: TRINITY ZAMORA Basketball Trinity Zamora was named honorable mention for the Post’s Athlete of the Year award after being named the WACC’s Player of the Year last season and a firstteam All-League recipient. She was named Sophomore of the Year in 2021 and Freshman of the Year in 2020 by the Post. Zamora helped lead the basketball team last winter to a 24-7 overall record. The team was runner-up in the North Coast Section, and advanced to the second round of the CIF State tournament as the No. 1 seed. It was the team’s first appearance in the NCS finals in 11 years. Zamora was the team’s leading rebounder, defender, and always a premier scoring presence. Some of Zamora’s highest outputs included 29 points in the NCS Finals, 23 points and 19 rebounds against Oakland Tech, and 28 points and 16 rebounds against Alameda. In two games with O’Dowd, she had 18 points and 22 rebounds and 17 points and 10 boards. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Michael Aikawa emerged as a leader of the baseball team as a sophomore in 2021 and earned the Post’s Sophomore of the Year award this year. Staff Photos Michael Aikawa was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year. He enters his senior year as a key member of the baseball team. He’s competing this summer on a travel and participating in highlevel tournaments prior to the start of school this fall. He helped the Highlanders post a 19-9 record and a league title in the Shoreline Division. He earned a first-team All-League selection in the process. articles.text: Oak Fire nearing 20,000 acres, 72 percent contained Photo courtesy of The Weather Channel The McKinney Fire is raging in the Klamath National Forest with no containment at the moment.. The McKinney Fire in Klamath National Forest near the Oregon border has exploded in less than a week and has increased to nearly 60,000 acres. It is the largest fire this year in California, and claimed two lives in Siskiyou County. Gov. Newsom has declared a state of emergency in the area. Siskiyou County was designated as being in extreme drought conditions. The blaze began on Friday, July 29 and has rapidly grown due to strong winds and lightning strikes in the area, spreading to 80 square miles in two days. U.S. Forest Service spokesperson Adrienne Freeman describes that the dry lightning causes erratic winds which moves the fire in unpredictable directions. “The fuel beds are so dry and they can just erupt from that lightning,” Freeman said. “These thunder cells come with gusty erratic winds that can blow fire in every direction.” The fire is believed to have begun prior to the weekend’s lightning strikes. Brad Schaaf of the National Weather Service reiterated that the thunderstorm exponentially increased fire activity. “We had 100 lightning strikes in western Siskiyou County last night. It looks like the fire definitely came first, before the thunderstorms,” Schaaf said. “It looks like there was a wind gust from the fire that aided the thunderstorm development. The first lightning strikes happened after 7 p.m.” Around 2,500 residents have been evacuated from Siskiyou County, in addition to several hikers on the Pacific Crest Trail. Oak Fire The Oak Fire in Mariposa County began on Friday, July 22 and has increased to 19,244 acres as of Monday. This blaze, however, is nearing containment at 72 percent after being at just 45 percent as of Friday, July 29. Photo courtesy of Ftp.wildfire.gov A map of the McKinney Fire near the Oregon border. Photo courtesy of Reuters.com The Oak Fire has consumed nearly 20,000 acres in Mariposa County, and is now 70 percent contained.

articles.text: Califor nia State Parks announced that as of this Friday, August 5, the campgrounds at Portola Redwoods State Park in San Mateo County will be closed temporarily due to a low amount of water in Peters Creek, the park’s primary water source. “As California’s current drought situation worsens, Californians must again focus on making the most out of its limited water supplies across the state. At State Parks, staff are conserving water by continually locating and repairing water leaks throughout their distribution systems, installing timers on irrigation systems, and implementing other water conservation efforts,” the park stated in a press release. The park is contacting impacted reservations to provide refunds. This comes with fire season waging in Northern California, predominantly with the ongoing McKinney Fire in the Klamath National Forest and Oak Fire waging in Mariposa County. Photo courtesy of CAStateParks.gov California State Parks declared that Peters Creek has a low amount of water flow, which requires them to shut down camping facilities. Portola Redwoods State Park is 2,800 acres large and offers 18 miles worth of hiking trails, 55 family campground sites, four group sites, a visitor center, and a trail camp for backpackers which is along the way to Peters Creek– which has an ancient grove of trees. Located in the South Bay, the park is frequently visited by Bay Area residents for a quick getaway to see some historic redwood trees and is usually fully booked long before the start of the summer months. We visited Portola Redwoods State Park in January of 2021 and visited the Old Tree Trail, which featured a 1,200-year-old redwood called “Old Tree.” Although camping is prohibited for the rest of the summer, day use areas and the backpacking trail camp will remain open. However, fires will obviously be not allowed during stark drought conditions. The park urges outdoor enthusiast to educate themselves in water conservation techniques at www.SaveOurWater.com. Staff Photo Portola Redwoods has some historic redwood trees and is usually fully booked well ahead of the camping season. Pictured here is Old Tree, a 1,200 year old redwood. Staff Photo
