pages.text: Wednesday, August 3, 2022 15 HIKING ABROAD WITH JON Walking through the center of Lisbon By Jonathan Comeaux Lisbon, Portugal is considered a great city for walking and hiking. The streets are tightly packed with rolling hills similar to San Francisco. And like San Francisco, it’s a city where you can find great food, culture, warm weather, and a lot of history. It’s easy walking through the heart of the city from Parque Eduardo VII, down Avenida da Liberdade and Rau Augusta to the historic Praça do Comércio and edge of the Tagus River. All that in just 2.1 miles of walking. The route from Praça do Comércio, or Commerce Square, goes slightly uphill on its way to Park Eduardo VII, so we start our venture at the top at the park for an easy point A-B-C walk. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. The park is named after King Edward VII of Great Britain after he visited Portugal in 1903 to strengthen the relationship between the two countries The trail goes down Avenida da Liberdad, which has several monuments like this one to Antonio Feliciano De Castillo, a famous writer from the 1800s. After Avenida da Liberdad is Monumento aos Restauradores. The path leads to Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV. One of the most visited locations in Lisbon is Commerce Square with its large monument to King Jose I. We go abroad to Lisbon, Portugal, starting at Parque Eduardo VII. and reaffirm their alliance. The park has a central strip of grass and an intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you can see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. Praça do Marquês de Pombal is a roundabout and square dedicated to the Portuguese statesman and diplomat who effectively ruled the Portuguese Empire from 1750 to 1777 as chief minister to King Joseph I. From there, you venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon that could draw comparisons to the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. The largest monument is dedicated to the fallen soldiers in World War I. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores (Monument to the Restorers), to memorialize Portugal’s victory in the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640-1668 and erected in 1886. The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. The monument is dedicated after Pedro I, who was the first ruler of the Empire of Brazil. Before you reach the column, take a tasty detour after the Monumento aos Restauradores by turning left to A Ginjinha for a further dive into Portuguese culture. It is an historic openfront bar that opened in 1840, and where you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry liquor. The location was helped publicized by travel journalists like Anthony Staff Photos Bordain and Rick Steves. From the Column of Pedro, head down R. Augusta avenue, where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on its way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. The location has been used as a welcoming point to several prominent figures, like Queen Elizabeth II in 1957. From there you can see Ponte 25 de April, a bridge with a striking similarity to the Golden Gate, with Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left. Take off your shoes and dip your weary feet in the water after a day of walking around Lisbon. Take a detour to A Ginjinha, a historic watering hole dating to 1840 to drink Portugal’s famous ginjinha—a cherry infused liquor. The path is nearing its end down R. Augusta avenue to the Arco da Rau Augusta. Our trail ends at Cais das Colunas, where you can take in a view of Ponte 25 de April and Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left.

articles.text: Festival. The very word connotes joy. And that’s as it should be. In the good old days, the concert season went from autumn through spring. The summer months were reserved for rest, reflection and preparing for the following concert season. As a side note, you might be interested to know that the great violinist Jascha Heifetz was afraid of the fast pace. He urged a retard in musical activities, but that did not happen. In fact, the concert season intensified. Some music festivals are famous throughout the world. The Hollywood Bowl hosts “Concerts Under the Stars.” The summer home of the New York Philharmonic was Lewisohn stadium in the heart of Harlem. During the summer of 1964 I heard some of the most illustrious musicians in the world perform there, including Marian Anderson. The festival of Two Worlds united the continents of America and Europe. It takes a tremendous backing to produce a successful festival, requiring lots of money and great organization. Remarkably, Piedmont, as small as it is, can boast a world-class music festival. Two weeks ago the non-profit Center for the Arts hosted its Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only one of its kind in the East Bay. Modeled loosely after the Carmel Bach Festival, the visiting musicians are housed for one week by Piedmont families. The founders of the Piedmont festival are well-known to Piedmont music lovers, Piedmont native, violinist Wayne Lee and his pianist wife Juliana Han. Their organizational skills are truly awe inspiring. The programming for the festival’s three concerts was interesting in every aspect. Musicians were selected with great care and the performances proceeded like clockwork. There was an ideal balance of musical styles with every piece complementing the others. Some pieces stood out in a way which made them special. In the third concert there were three spicy Rags for string quartet written by the William Bolcom. These works were just as good as those by the more famous ragtime composer Scott Joplin. Another impressive performance was the String Quintet No. 2 by Felix Mendelsohn. The ensemble featured Francisco Fullana and Jasmine Lin on violins, Teng Li and Paul Laraia on viola, and Clancy Newman on cello. Their playing was totally resplendent and truly virtuoso. In the adagio movement, in particular, emotion welled up from the very soul of the composer. It was the very essence of the Mendelssohn ethos. The ensemble showed every evidence of marvelous technical ability. But sometimes the musicians strayed from pure musical intent and tried to show the audience they were having fun. The enthusiastic audience loved this foolishness and applauded wildly. The important thing to know is that the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival has been and continues to be a fabulous success. I remember dress rehearsals open to the public at the Hollywood Bowl. Hundreds of people came to watch early during the day and then attended the evening concerts. The concerts were every Tuesday and Thursday for the entire summer. The experience was memorable. Keep up your good work Wayne and Juliana, and if possible, add more concerts in the future. Joseph Gold is a violinist and a weekly contributor in the Post with his column, The Musical Gourmet. Musicians celebrate at the conclusion of the weeklong Piedmont Chamber Music Festival on July 24: Wayne Lee (left), Paul Laraia, Clancy Newman, Francisco Fullana, Juliana Han, Ting Li, Jasmine Lin, and Deborah Pae.
articles.title: Piedmont celebrates 5th annual Chamber Music Festival

articles.text: Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist, is founder and artistic director of the San Francisco Piano Festival. The San Francisco International Piano Festival returns on August 18 for its fifth season, with a with a celebration of J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier. The festival continues with concerts through August 28. “In the midst of much turbulence and tragedy in our world, we continue to make music and celebrate the unstoppable force that is the creative spirit,” said festival founder and artistic director, Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist and one of the festival’s artists. “The 300th anniversary of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier provides a natural focus that the festival will explore in both conventional and unexpected performances.” Festival concerts will take place in five San Francisco and Berkeley venues and will feature eight pianists and 18 composers, ranging from Bach to contemporary. For a full list of dates, locations, program notes and ticket information, see sfpiano.org. articles.text: American blues singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Taj Mahal will headline a free concert this Sunday at Stern Grove, following performances by Monophonics and DJ Shortkut. Henry St. Claire Fredericks Jr., better known by his stage name Taj Mahal, plays a plethora of instruments including the guitar, piano, banjo, and harmonica. His 50-year career spans a variety of musical genres, including Caribbean, Africa, India, Hawaii and the South Pacific. Originally from Harlem, New York, Fredericks began his music career in Los Angeles in 1964 when he formed the band Rising Sons. His performance at Stern Grove will follow a set by Monoinstruments, including a Mellotron, lap steel guitar, harp, and Moog. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization that presents free music festivals in the city since its inception in 1938. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The concert begins at 2 p.m. Reservations are required to attend. Attendees may bring food and drinks to the festivals. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet returns with two days of performances this weekend, Friday and Saturday, August 5-6, with a program of three short ballets under the stars at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheater. The program includes Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight, Jerome Robbins’ In the Night, and William Forsythe’s Blake Works I. The short ballets range greatly in theme and choreography, with music by Bach, Chopin and James Blake. Both performances begin at 8 p.m. The Frost Amphitheater is located at 351 Lasuen Street on the Stanford University campus in Palo Alto. To purchase tickets visit https://www.sfballet.org/calendar/ starry-nights-at-stanford-live/. Photo by Erik Tomasson Jennifer Stahl and Tiit Helimets perform with San Francisco Ballet in Jerome Robbins’ In the Night.

articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, August 14, to perform a 3 p.m. concert in tribute to Richard Rodgers, widely regarded as the premier composer of American musicals. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram. With 43 Broadway musicals and over 900 songs to his credit, Rodgers is considered one of the most important American composers of the 20th century. His compositions have had a significant influence on popular and modern music. The concert is a benefit for the Center and will showcase PCA’s Steinway grand piano. Tickets are $20 at the door and online at https://bpt. me/5316993. Seating will be limited to the first 70 people.
articles.title: In the Tradition Piano Trio at PCA Aug. 14

articles.text: American Conser vator y Theatre presents the UK-based production of Passengers at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll is the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area,” said Carroll, whose career started years ago at Club Fugazi in North Beach. “The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved Shana Carroll, director and choreographer of Passengers, returns to San Francisco where her career began. The UK production of Passengers will be performed by ACT in San Francisco opening on September 15. San Francisco. The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” Carroll is the co-founding artistic director of Montreal’s Les 7 Doigts de la Main (7 Fingers circus company), where she has directed and choreographed the company’s major touring shows, including Traces (Drama Desk nomination), Sequence 8, Loft, La Vie, Le Murmure du Coquelicot, Cuisine & Confessions, and Psy. Tickets for the Geary Theater production are available by calling the box office at (415) 749- 2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/passengers/.
articles.title: ACT’s Passengers opens at Geary Theater September 15

articles.text: The beautiful Pardee Historic Home Museum located in downtown Oakland is looking for volunteers to help with their highly rated teas. Since being acclaimed the number one best tea in the Bay Area, and the lifting of stringent COVID protocols, the demand for teas has increased. These successful teas have been an East Bay tradition for decades. The Museum and gardens are supported entirely by teas, tours and donations, and by our wonderful group of volunteers. Additional volunteers are needed to work the teas served mostly in the beautiful garden. Volunteers might make tea, sandwiches, and lovely deserts, serve the tea or help with setup and clean up. A wonderful group of volunteers await your company. Please consider volunteering and help to maintain this elegant 1868 home of Governor George Pardee, with all its original furnishings intact. Please go to our website at pardeehome.org for further information on the house and its programs. There are also opportunities for docents to lead our popular tours including full training. For more information, please contact Michael Henn at 510-834-7128, or mhennfam@aol.com.

articles.text: Tom Cruise and Cameron Diaz star in Knight and Day. Review by Chris Honoré Tom Cruise is, indisputably, a top-tier movie star and has been since he slid across the hardwood floor of his parents’ two-story colonial wearing white briefs, playing air guitar, in the memorable and breakthrough film, Risky Business. He lives a life that can only be imagined, one that has generated a cottage industry of fans, paparazzi and tabloid media, all desperate for information about him, professionally and most certainly personally. Cruise has always been intelligent about his career and discrete about his personal life, that is until his ill-fated interview with Oprah Winfrey. Filled with raw, adolescent emotion, in the throes of a new romance with Katie Holmes, a Hollywood ingénue with a short resume, Tom approached Oprah’s faux living room ready to levitate. He was (not to get too SoCal about it) “stoked.” So much so that Oprah barely had time enough to ask him even a preliminary question when Tom, in a moment of startling and unexpected exuberance, in front of the studio audience and millions of viewers, “jumped the couch.” It was a move that would have made any gymnast proud. As quickly as one can say Internet, “jumping the couch” dropped into the daily lexicon of common language, linked forever to that one moment when Cruise took flight and got all jiggy with it. This is all to say that Cruise has spent the ensuing post-couch years trying to dispel that YouTube, viral video moment – compounded before and after by endless displays of PDA – hoping folks would refocus on his career as an actor of seriousness and heft. The film Valkyrie, however, didn’t help. Somehow, Cruise in Nazi costume and eye patch and Sieg Heil, knee-high, heel-clicking leather boots with jodhpurs required more suspension of disbelief than most audiences were capable of. The suspicion began to take hold that Cruise was content to do Cruise, no matter the role. Which brings us to Cruise’s romantic comedy, Knight and Day, made in 2010 in which he portrays a rogue government agent, Roy Miller, in concert with Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting, hapless traveler on her way from Wichita to Boston. Strangely, interestingly, she’s carrying a suitcase filled with retro parts for a muscle car restoration. Accidentally she bumps into Roy in the Wichita Airport, or so she assumes. And suddenly she finds herself ensnared and in some serious jeopardy. Bad people are trying to kill Roy. Even good people are trying to kill Roy. And June is trying to keep her head down when she’s not rendered unconscious, a recurring event that’s actually charming. So, is the film good entertainment? Surprisingly, it is. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter turns out to be an enjoyable, breezy, sincere film. And, as a bonus, it has a wonderful MacGuffin. A MacGuffin is an object (papers, brief case, necklace) that soon catches the audience’s attention and helps drive the plot as a recurring theme throughout the movie. In the Maltese Falcon it was, well, the Maltese Falcon. In Knight and Day it’s the Zephyr, a selfcharging battery that provides an endless source of energy. The good guys and the bad guys are not only after the MacGuffin, but the scientist who invented it, one Simon Fleck, played geekily to the max by Paul Dano. And so the romantic thriller unfolds with Roy and June slipping into and out of improbable but nicely executed scrapes, pumping up the volume and the bullets and generally having a good time. As does the audience. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold, Starring Tom Cruise, Cameron Diaz, Peter Sarsgaard, and Viola Davis. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on Prime/Paramont+/Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Knight and Day an enjoyable romp with Cruise

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Don’t worry kids, if you watched the first Ice Age and thought Scrat (Chris Wedge), the squirrel-rat, was one of the most delightful characters, you’ll be happy to know that he is back in Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. And joining him are Manfred the wooly mammoth (Ray Romano) and Sid the sloth (John Leguizamo). Soon after their journey north begins, the two are joined by Diego, the saber-toothed tiger (Denis Leary), creating a dynamic trio. The two amigos, Sid and Many, live in a valley surrounded by massive high ice walls on all sides. To their surprise, they discover that the walls are holding back a huge reservoir of water that could flood the valley. To their horror, they observe a huge chunk of the ice wall break off (climate warming), causing them to decide it’s time to leave. While all of the denizens of the valley agree that it’s time to get out of Dodge, they head south. Manny and Sid, however, go north. And thus begins their adventure. On their journey they encounter a bevy of different animals to include Ellie (Queen Latifah), a large female wooly mammoth who Manny finds attractive. They also meet up with two annoying opossums, Crash and Eddie (Sean William Scott and Jonathan Peck). Meanwhile, Sid is kidnapped by a tribe of minisloths who believe he is god-like and plan on throwing him into the mouth of a volcano. Of course, Sid manages to escape. The northern most part of the valley is flooded as the ice walls collapse, lots of close calls ensue, but in the nick of time the gang finds a large boat and make their way out of the valley to safety. Kids will enjoy the intermittent appearances of Scrat, the big-eyed rodent who is still chasing that acorn. Plus the group is in a race to escape the flooding waters from the reservoir. Can they make it? The dialogue is often hilarious, the animation top notch, and the characters fun to spend time with. Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. Animated comedy-adventure. Directed by Carlos Saldanha. With voices of Carlos Saldanha, Chris Wedge, Ray Romano, John Leguizamo. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2006. Now streaming on Disney+/ VUDU/Hulu.
articles.title: Ice Age 2: The Meltdown, with the return of Scrat

articles.text: Who could have guessed where Arthur ended up? You have to love those medieval movies where everyone has a membership to 24 Hour Fitness and superb dental care. Nevertheless, King Arthur: Legend of the Sword, is an origin story regarding the Arthurian legend, that durable British myth where Arthur pulls a sword, the Excalibur, from the stone, thereby establishing his identity as the heir to the throne. That would be the throne stolen by Vortigen (Jude Law), thuggish brother of the king, Uther Pendragon (Eric Bana). Pendragon’s small son, Arthur (Charlie Hunnan), is rescued from the dark castle. pages.text: Wednesday, August 3, 2022 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Knight and Day an enjoyable romp with Cruise Tom Cruise and Cameron Diaz star in Knight and Day. Review by Chris Honoré Tom Cruise is, indisputably, a top-tier movie star and has been since he slid across the hardwood floor of his parents’ two-story colonial wearing white briefs, playing air guitar, in the memorable and breakthrough film, Risky Business. He lives a life that can only be imagined, one that has generated a cottage industry of fans, paparazzi and tabloid media, all desperate for information about him, professionally and most certainly personally. Cruise has always been intelligent about his career and discrete about his personal life, that is until his ill-fated interview with Oprah Winfrey. Filled with raw, adolescent emotion, in the throes of a new romance with Katie Holmes, a Hollywood ingénue with a short resume, Tom approached Oprah’s faux living room ready to levitate. He was (not to get too SoCal about it) “stoked.” So much so that Oprah barely had time enough to ask him even a preliminary question when Tom, in a moment of startling and unexpected exuberance, in front of the studio audience and millions of viewers, “jumped the couch.” It was a move that would have made any gymnast proud. As quickly as one can say Internet, “jumping the couch” dropped into the daily lexicon of common language, linked forever to that one moment when Cruise took flight and got all jiggy with it. This is all to say that Cruise has spent the ensuing post-couch years trying to dispel that YouTube, viral video moment – compounded before and after by endless displays of PDA – hoping folks would refocus on his career as an actor of seriousness and heft. The film Valkyrie, however, didn’t help. Somehow, Cruise in Nazi costume and eye patch and Sieg Heil, knee-high, heel-clicking leather boots with jodhpurs required more suspension of disbelief than most audiences were capable of. The suspicion began to take hold that Cruise was content to do Cruise, no matter the role. Which brings us to Cruise’s romantic comedy, Knight and Day, made in 2010 in which he portrays a rogue government agent, Roy Miller, in concert with Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting, hapless traveler on her way from Wichita to Boston. Strangely, interestingly, she’s carrying a suitcase filled with retro parts for a muscle car restoration. Accidentally she bumps into Roy in the Wichita Airport, or so she assumes. And suddenly she finds herself ensnared and in some serious jeopardy. Bad people are trying to kill Roy. Even good people are trying to kill Roy. And June is trying to keep her head down when she’s not rendered unconscious, a recurring event that’s actually charming. So, is the film good entertainment? Surprisingly, it is. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter turns out to be an enjoyable, breezy, sincere film. And, as a bonus, it has a wonderful MacGuffin. A MacGuffin is an object (papers, brief case, necklace) that soon catches the audience’s attention and helps drive the plot as a recurring theme throughout the movie. In the Maltese Falcon it was, well, the Maltese Falcon. In Knight and Day it’s the Zephyr, a selfcharging battery that provides an endless source of energy. The good guys and the bad guys are not only after the MacGuffin, but the scientist who invented it, one Simon Fleck, played geekily to the max by Paul Dano. And so the romantic thriller unfolds with Roy and June slipping into and out of improbable but nicely executed scrapes, pumping up the volume and the bullets and generally having a good time. As does the audience. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold, Starring Tom Cruise, Cameron Diaz, Peter Sarsgaard, and Viola Davis. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Ice Age 2: The Meltdown, with the return of Scrat Review by Chris Honoré Don’t worry kids, if you watched the first Ice Age and thought Scrat (Chris Wedge), the squirrel-rat, was one of the most delightful characters, you’ll be happy to know that he is back in Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. And joining him are Manfred the wooly mammoth (Ray Romano) and Sid the sloth (John Leguizamo). Soon after their journey north begins, the two are joined by Diego, the saber-toothed tiger (Denis Leary), creating a dynamic trio. The two amigos, Sid and Many, live in a valley surrounded by massive high ice walls on all sides. To their surprise, they discover that the walls are holding back a huge reservoir of water that could flood the valley. To their horror, they observe a huge chunk of the ice wall break off (climate warming), causing them to decide it’s time to leave. While all of the denizens of the valley agree that it’s time to get out of Dodge, they head south. Manny and Sid, however, go north. And thus begins their adventure. On their journey they encounter a bevy of different animals to include Ellie (Queen Latifah), a large female wooly mammoth who Manny finds attractive. They also meet up with two annoying opossums, Crash and Eddie (Sean William Scott and Jonathan Peck). Meanwhile, Sid is kidnapped by a tribe of minisloths who believe he is god-like and plan on throwing him into the mouth of a volcano. Of course, Sid manages to escape. The northern most part of the valley is flooded as the ice walls collapse, lots of close calls ensue, but in the nick of time the gang finds a large boat and make their way out of the valley to safety. Kids will enjoy the intermittent appearances of Scrat, the big-eyed rodent who is still chasing that acorn. Plus the group is in a race to escape the flooding waters from the reservoir. Can they make it? The dialogue is often hilarious, the animation top notch, and the characters fun to spend time with. Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. Animated comedy-adventure. Directed by Carlos Saldanha. articles.text: Just the Way I Like It A bus took us from Herning, Denmark, to Hamburg, Germany for the second leg of our international choir tour this summer. The AC worked this time, so the temperature was much more amenable for exchanging our Danish homestay experiences, singing, and other choir tomfoolery. After checking into our hotel in the center of Hamburg and changing into our uniform, we immediately went to rehearsal for a concert. Our rehearsals consisted of two hours to get used to the space and run through all of our pieces and make sure we sounded our best. Our first concert in Germany was in the heart of Hamburg in a small but echoey church. The concert started with a performance by the Hamburg Girls Choir, and then us, the Ensemble group in Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. We sang No Time, a farewell song; Every Time I Feel the Spirit, a poem that enslaved people would sing; and Salut Printemps, by Claude Debussy about welcoming spring. At the end we joined the Hamburg Girls Choir to sing Hymn to Freedom and Guten Abend, Gut’ Nacht. During our three days in Hamburg we went on many adventures. We took a city boat tour (fun fact: there are 2,496 bridges in Hamburg because of all the canals. Because of that it is nicknamed “Venice of the North”). We visited the last Baroque style church in Germany, St. Michael’s, and listened to a beautiful organ concert. We went to a square with different food vendors for lunch. Hamburg has an abundance of great restaurants. For dinner the first night we split off into groups with our tour chaperones and were given the liberty to choose a restaurant and wear whatever regular clothes we had packed. After doing some light shopping and sightseeing, two friends and I popped into a grocery store and bought fresh strawberries – the best strawberries I have ever tasted. One morning my hotel roomies and I got up early and went to explore the city center. We walked to the lake and sat on a deck on the water where we could dangle our feet over the edge. We kept reminding ourselves how we were in awe of the fact that we were on tour. We made friends with ducks and picked flowers by the side of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir singers in Ensemble performed their final concert of the tour in the main church in Mosbach near Hochhausen, Germany. lake and handed them to random people we saw on the street. Seeing the smiles on their faces made it all worth it. After our short stop in Hamburg, it was back on the road heading south. Our bus driver was a Czech named Vladimir. He studied Russian for 30 years, so I was glad to talk with him in the language I speak with my family. It was a long ride – nine hours – in what we expected to be a six-hour trip to Hochhausen. It’s safe to say that we all went crazy on the bus. When we took our lunch break, I saw two friends almost end their friendship over cheese, salami, and hummus. Everyone was hungry and food was scarce, so it was decided to share all the food. When we finally made it to Hochhausen, we stumbled out of the bus, happy to be at the final destination of our tour. The houses were multi-colored with brown trim all around to create that iconic German look. There was only one road which branched off into a couple of small ones leading to the further parts of the town. You could see it was a very small town, and our arrival possibly added another ten percent to the town’s population. We were greeted by the oneand-only Sue Malick, a longtime board member of the choir, a Piedmont resident, and my neighbor. Her husband’s family owns a rustic farm in Hochhausen, and the entire choir was invited to use their farm house as our headquarters. Sue is an amazing person. She accompanied us to every location we visited and told us the history and of the town and surrounding area. She and her husband John hosted a farewell potluck for us the day before we left. After we arrived, we dragged ourselves up multiple hills with our luggage to get to Sue’s house and meet our homestay families. The people of Hochhausen who came to take choir members to their homes, were as excited to welcome us as we were to be in their town. Our host, Karren, apparently got lost, so we were the last group to be picked up. How she managed to get lost in the tiny town that is Hochhausen is anyone’s guess. But she did arrive and took us to a house with a common room, a bathroom, and a 7x7-foot white box designated as our bedroom. We slept on air mattresses and had to share a pillow. But we didn’t complain; can you really complain to a person who lives with a fridge filled with condiments and beer? Plus, two stray kittens found their way into the backyard and into our room. We loved having so many choir members on our street so we could easily meet with friends and roam around town. One afternoon as a large group of us decided to explore the town, it started raining and raining hard. We marveled at the fat drops of warm water sliding down our faces, hitting the ground. We started dancing and singing in the rain until our legs almost gave out. We met up with another group of choir kids and made our way to a small playground as I filmed everything, including the moment when a friend fell off the see-saw. We eventually gathered in a circle and someone started singing “Rasputin” by Boney M. and everyone was trying to do the Slavic dance when you kick your legs out from underneath you while in a crouched position. After filming those iffy attempts, I summoned my Slavic ancestry, stepped in and showed how it was supposed to be done. It was certainly a night to remember. While in Hochhausen we visited the Mosbach farmers market, a big open market with stalls where farmers sell their own products. Typical German buildings surrounded the square. We hiked up many hills to find the town pool and cool off and then have an amazing dinner at a farm-to-table restaurant where I tried a Wienerschnitzel and my world was rocked. Hochhausen is the home of Count Dider who lives in a castle and owns the forest surrounding the town. His family has lived there for centuries, and he and his wife are friends of the Malicks. We were given a tour of his schloss and sang for him and his wife. One of the nights we also had a dinner hosted by the hunting club where we were served wild boar from the Count’s forest. We gave plenty of concerts, and the concerts in Hochhausen had a magic energy around them. Everyone who listened to our music left the church with an Chaperones Kay Sibal (left) and Clare Weiss at the top of the Hornberg Castle in Mosbach, Germany. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org Members of the Ensemble group gathered in the rain in Hochhausen for a group photo.

articles.text: Part 49 in a biweekly series All good designs have at their source a strong, clear vision, or concept. This can be defined as the overall main idea – a view into the future of what the project should look like, feel like and how it will function. The built environment around us – the places we work, live, play and interact with each other – is in reality an ongoing design process that has an important effect on all of our lives, often much more than we realize. As we must continually upgrade, accommodate, and adapt to the new, this process especially requires a strong vision. Walking around Piedmont and looking at the various finished buildings, landscapes, urban designs and planning decisions at various different scales, it is instructive to judge how clear the initial visions were, and how well they were adhered to during the often lengthy design and construction processes. It makes us ask how strong will be our evolving city vision(s) going forward in the next months, years and decades? articles.text: Photos by Mitch Shenker and Ed Kaplan. This project involved creating a great room space with a new kitchen and living room area combined. We added large openings in the rear wall with new large windows and doors to a newly landscaped rear yard. I grew up on the East Coast and moved to the Bay Area to start high school and then go on to earn my BA and MA in architecture. As a recent transplant, I remember my wonder and enjoyment of the beauty of the outdoors which is enhanced by the temperate climate we have. I noticed immediately how some ranch style homes took advantage of the indoor and outdoor connections in a minor way with large sliding patio doors. The Eichler home designs in many ways embodied that effort for the home to bring in natural light and create a easy flow to the outdoors, although they were an outlier in production home design. Most housing stock that exists today was built by developers who used stock plans from plan books, or they hired production design firms to develop generic designs to plop down (not a technical term) on any given site. Little effort was made to design the house to take advantage of the specific site’s characteristics and features. Additionally, if the house was designed many years These original three rooms at the back of this 1920’s house were combined with an addition to make one large space for a new kitchen and family room. ago, the layout and flow of the house may not suit the needs of today’s lifestyle. As I started architectural practice 40 years ago, one common lost opportunity I noticed was that most houses were not designed to open up to the outdoors, especially the rear garden space. Oddly, the back wall of many homes facing the rear garden is composed of more wall area than window area. In many homes, the utility spaces such as laundries and bathrooms take up too much of the rear walls of the house blocking off the house’s This project combined three spaces and adding about 5 feet to the rear of the house to create one large kitchen and family room. The laundry room was relocated, and the kitchen and family room were arranged to maximize on the window area out to the rear garden.
articles.title: Orientation to views, sun, and rear garden

articles.text: • 2017 Domaine Saint Gayan Rasteau The Saint Gayan Rasteau is a beauty. Offering great ripeness in its kirsch, pepper and spring flower-like aromas and flavor, it is medium-bodied, silky, supple with fine tannin and good freshness. Drink over the next 5-7 years. Would partner well with roast chicken. Last month I had the opportunity to attend a seminar and tasting focused on the wines of Rasteau. The village of Rasteau is situated in the Cotes du Rhone region in the southern Rhone River area of France. It was founded by the Romans over 2000 years ago and has been continuously occupied. Still, today’s population is only 803 people. The Rasteau wine area was established in 2010 as a recognized AOC by the French government. It consists of 19,000 hectares, roughly half the size of Berkeley. In that area there are 60 small wineries and one large Cave Cooperative. Vines were probably growing in Rasteau as early as 30 B.C., but the vineyards remained largely forgotten until the Middle Ages. Orientation to views, sun, and rear garden Photos by Mitch Shenker and Ed Kaplan. This project involved creating a great room space with a new kitchen and living room area combined. We added large openings in the rear wall with new large windows and doors to a newly landscaped rear yard. By Ed Kaplan, AIA I grew up on the East Coast and moved to the Bay Area to start high school and then go on to earn my BA and MA in architecture. As a recent transplant, I remember my wonder and enjoyment of the beauty of the outdoors which is enhanced by the temperate climate we have. I noticed immediately how some ranch style homes took advantage of the indoor and outdoor connections in a minor way with large sliding patio doors. The Eichler home designs in many ways embodied that effort for the home to bring in natural light and create a easy flow to the outdoors, although they were an outlier in production home design. Most housing stock that exists today was built by developers who used stock plans from plan books, or they hired production design firms to develop generic designs to plop down (not a technical term) on any given site. Little effort was made to design the house to take advantage of the specific site’s characteristics and features. Additionally, if the house was designed many years These original three rooms at the back of this 1920’s house were combined with an addition to make one large space for a new kitchen and family room. ago, the layout and flow of the house may not suit the needs of today’s lifestyle. As I started architectural practice 40 years ago, one common lost opportunity I noticed was that most houses were not designed to open up to the outdoors, especially the rear garden space. Oddly, the back wall of many homes facing the rear garden is composed of more wall area than window area. In many homes, the utility spaces such as laundries and bathrooms take up too much of the rear walls of the house blocking off the house’s See An Architect’s Eye on page 32 This project combined three spaces and adding about 5 feet to the rear of the house to create one large kitchen and family room. The laundry room was relocated, and the kitchen and family room were arranged to maximize on the window area out to the rear garden.

articles.text: With wind in his face, and a little ocean spray, he’s sailing away. Born in 1928, Herman Anton Trutner – Tony to all who knew him – died on July 22, 2022. He was 94. Born in 1928, Tony moved to Piedmont from Oakland at the age of 10 with his father Herman Trutner III, his mother Evelyn, and his brother and sister Tom and Fritzi. He remained a resident of Piedmont (except for a short time at the Delta Tau Delta house at UC Berkeley and in the U.S. Army) until his death. Tony delighted in sailing, Tahoe time, friends, cycling, family gatherings at Sun River, raviolis, the annual Big Game (go Cal!), probate law, colleagues, camping, music, a good book, backpacking, whiskey sours, traveling abroad, and Fenton’s hot fudge sundaes. He could not, however, abide his young children stirring their ice cream or putting their elbows on the dinner table. He mellowed over the years; his grandchildren could get away with anything. Classical music coursed through his blood (his father and grandfather were both professional musicians who played French horn for the San Francisco Symphony), but he was also a huge fan of the Beatles. Tony adopted his unique approach to carpe diem at an early age. During the summer of ‘49, he and three UC Berkeley fraternity brothers pooled $100 to purchase an Oldsmobile convertible with no top, in which they spent two months on the road traveling to New York and back to Berkeley. The four buddies, who remained lifelong friends, limped along on used oil and retread tires, taking turns sitting in lawn chairs in the dilapidated rumble seat. Tony proclaimed himself the “transportation leader,” having bought and sold more than 16 cars before his 18th birthday, beginning with a Model A Ford convertible. He earned the seed money working at the Cole honey factory on Piedmont Avenue. Tony’s ambition and sense of adventure led to his decision to enroll in night law school while working as a trust officer with three young daughters at home. Ann gave birth to their twin sons before he graduated. Tony’s career as a trust and estates lawyer spanned six decades. It began at Tony Trutner, a resident of Piedmont for more than 80 years, passed away on July 22 at age 94. the firm then known as Burnhill, Rhode, Moffitt and Moore, which over the years morphed into Larson, Burnham and Trutner. At the age of 63, Tony became a sole practitioner, and did not fully retire until age 88. Tony was known for problem solving and often served as a neutral administrator or trustee. His daughter, daughter in law, and grandson, all attorneys, are grateful for his mentoring. Through the years, Tony cycled the Pacific coast with his wife and teenage sons, sailed a chartered yacht in the Aegean Sea, and captained his sailboat in the Transpac race from Los Angeles to Hawaii. Tony’s membership in the Single Handed Sailing Society as captain and owner of the 41-foot Regardless was a source of great pride and sensational stories. Tony and Ann traveled the world until well into their 80s, often with friends known since college and earlier. Cruising in Antarctica, traveling by train across Russia, and riding tuk tuks in Bangkok were beloved memories. Tony loved being the patriarch of a sizable clan and presiding over “August” family occasions. He cherished his wife Ann (nee Bakken) and their 69-year marriage, his three daughters, Kathleen (husband Mark), Barbara (husband John) and Elizabeth (husband Jim), his twin sons Erik (wife Leslie) and Kurt (wife Cynthia), his 11 grandchildren, their partners, and his great-grandchildren. They will forever hold Tony in their hearts. His sails were always full. The wind is behind you, Tony. Time to set the spinnaker.

articles.text: As members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled on July 27, they talked about how fortunate they are to live in this area with its wonderful climate. Dallas had had 31 days of over 100-degree weather with at least ten more 100+ days forecast, and St. Louis had nine inches of rain in 24 hours. There was a solid, summer turnout of 26 walkers and one K-9 on hand. The group welcomed Recreation Department supervisor Eva Phalen and Karina Epperlein, who will be teaching Tai Chi and who gave the walkers a Tai Chi demonstration. With their sights set on seeing Beach School, the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, on the 300 block of El Cerrito Avenue and down Oakland Avenue to the crosswalk at Latham Street. On Greenbank, they passed t he home of former State Assembly member Audie Bock and its signature white picket fence. The home, built in 1896, is now owned by the Medhekar family and has a children’s swing in the front yard. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and continued up Greenbank to Lake Avenue. Laura Goldman, who lives nearby, pointed out a home that has recently been transformed from a small bungalow into a much larger home. Only the front door area is the same. This section of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days. The streets Nace, Howard, and Lake, were built around 1908. The oldest houses on Nace are the 1910 “Gibson House” at 46 Nace and the 1911 “Govan House” at 18 Nace. The giant tree in front was planted by the Gibsons in the 1920s. Walking down Howard, the walkers came to Beach School’s entrance on Lake Avenue. Drawing on research from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society and Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, the history of the school was shared. The history of Egbert Beach Elementary School dates to the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. On that April 18 morning, thousands of people fled the city to the East Bay. Many decided not to return, and Piedmont grew 19 times over the course of the next year. Piedmont was incorporated as a city the following year, in September 1907. City leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The city’s first school, Bonita Avenue School, opened in 1911, and was later renamed Havens School after the land donor, Frank C. Havens. Bonita Avenue School quickly filled to capacity, and Lake School across town on Lake Avenue, was built in 1913. Four teachers taught 100 students in six grades. In 1918, the school was renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in honor of Egbert William Beach, who was the first Piedmonter killed in World War I. The rapid growth of the city from 1920 to 1930 created school housing needs that could not be met with school funds. The entire enrollment at Beach was housed then in portables. At Wildwood and Havens, approximately onethird of the students were taught in cramped, wooden school rooms that the locals called “shacks.” In 1933 Beach School was condemned as a fire trap and an earthquake menace and torn down in 1934. Beach School was replaced by two separate Works Progress Administration (WPA) projects. The main wing was built in 1936, and the auditorium/classroom wing was added in 1940. It was an entire new building of eight classrooms, kindergarten, administrative unit, library, health room and auditorium. This reconstruction was part of the FDR New Deal program’s larger effort to upgrade almost 300 schools in California. In Piedmont, the WPA built a total of 28 new earthquake-ready classrooms at Beach, Havens, Wildwood, and Piedmont High School. In the early 2000s, as part of city-wide seismic facility upgrades, Beach hosted some of the Havens students for the 2009- 10 school year while Havens was entirely rebuilt. During the following year (2010-11), Wildwood students s hared the Beach campus when their school underwent construction. In 2011-12, when Beach had its turn for renovations, the school temporarily relocated to Emeryville with school buses shuttling Piedmont students back and forth each day. In the fall of 2012, Beach School re-opened its campus. The updated facilities included two new classrooms, new playground facilities, an edible garden, and seismic upgrades. Walker Pat Keller was able to find an unlocked gate on Linda Avenue and the walkers saw the old entrance to the school, a perfect location for a group photo. The group walked through the playground past the Schoolmates building and the Linda-Beach Playfield. Then it was down Linda to Grand Avenue, and a walk up Fairview Avenue. The walkers took its lower section to a very hidden pathway that took them down to Nova and Magnolia Avenues for their climb back up the hill to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers on July 27 included Alicia Rivera, Lisa Euphrat, Kat Lang, Elizabeth Richter, Adrienne Hamlin, Lois Price, Pat Keller, Nadine Guffanti, Marion Lin Yankowitz, Martin Levy, Melba Yee, Susan Callen, Mark Davis, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kellogg, Jeff Callen, Jim Kuo, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Sarah Johnson, Charlene Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Mike Henn, Priscilla Wanerus, Peggy Rourke, Mary Carter, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band mobilized the morning of July 4 for its annual appearance in the city’s 4th of July Parade. It was the first time in two years due to COVID. The band is comprised of musicians, primarily residents, ranging from amateur to professional. Some come from as far away as Minnesota. The group was founded by Jane Reed in 1984, who has organized and managed the band throughout much of its history. Mobilizing musicians was no easy feat this year and required a lot of phone calls by Reed. The band is unique for its overqualified musicians. One year a symphony musician heard there was no one who had signed up to play the triangle for the John Phillip Sousa marches, so he volunteered to play it, marching proudly down the street with the diminutive triangular metal instrument. Piedmont resident Ken Kawaichi has served as leader of the band for 36 years dressed as “Emperor Norton” - a nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, a resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Norton I., Emperor of the United States” in 1859. Resident Elaine Lindenmayer is the band’s solo majorette – who, at age 70, led the band twirling and tossing her baton in the air for her 35th year. Lindenmayer said it is a tribute to the leadership of Reed and Kawaichi and the camaraderie of the band members that so many showed up this year to play. Next week: an interview with founder Jane Reed, band leader Ken Kawaichi, and majorette Elaine Lindenmayer The Piedmont Community Band, led by majorette Elaine Lindenmayer, marches on Highland Avenue during the 55th annual Piedmont 4th of July Parade.

articles.text: City on track to meeting Climate Action Plan goals A report on the 2020 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions inventory prepared by Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman found that there was a slight reduction in emissions compared to the previous year. Piedmont City Council received and reviewed the informational report at its most recent meeting on Monday, July 18. The report provides information on the 2020 GHG emissions inventory, which includes estimates for both community and municipal emissions. Piedmont’s GHG emissions were 33,402 metric tons of CO2e, of which 722 metric tons of CO2e are attributed to municipal activities, explained Dykman. pages.text: Wednesday, August 3, 2022 25 Piedmont Community Band, an original By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Community Band mobilized the morning of July 4 for its annual appearance in the city’s 4th of July Parade. It was the first time in two years due to COVID. The band is comprised of musicians, primarily residents, ranging from amateur to professional. Some come from as far away as Minnesota. The group was founded by Jane Reed in 1984, who has organized and managed the band throughout much of its history. Mobilizing musicians was no easy feat this year and required a lot of phone calls by Reed. The band is unique for its overqualified musicians. One year a symphony musician heard there was no one who had signed up to play the triangle for the John Phillip Sousa marches, so he volunteered to play it, marching proudly down the street with the diminutive triangular metal instrument. Piedmont resident Ken Kawaichi has served as leader of the band for 36 years dressed as “Emperor Norton” - a nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, a resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Norton I., Emperor of the United States” in 1859. Resident Elaine Lindenmayer is the band’s solo majorette – who, at age 70, led the band twirling and tossing her baton in the air for her 35th year. Lindenmayer said it is a tribute to the leadership of Reed and Kawaichi and the camaraderie of the band members that so many showed up this year to play. Next week: an interview with founder Jane Reed, band leader Ken Kawaichi, and majorette Elaine Lindenmayer The Piedmont Community Band, led by majorette Elaine Lindenmayer, marches on Highland Avenue during the 55th annual Piedmont 4th of July Parade. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, August 3, 2022 By Jen Ferguson Piedmont Council’s Troop 11 Scouts encountered great weather, breathtaking views and lots of wildlife during their 4-day backpacking trip along Northern California’s remote Lost Coast Trail the week of July 17. They hiked 25 miles along the rocky coastline, each Scout carrying 35-40 pound backpacks with food and gear for the trek. The Lost Coast is a famously beautiful yet isolated and challenging stretch of coastline, inaccessible by car. The trail includes several sections of coastline that are impassable twice daily during high tide, which required the troop to study tide charts and plan the timing of their traverse carefully. High Troop 11 Scouts hike the Lost Coast Trail winds and unpredictable weather all year can bring big wave swells and occasional “sneaker” waves, increasing the challenge. The Troop set out southbound from Mattole Beach, the trail’s northern terminus near the small community of Petrolia in Humboldt County. We were all crying because the tour was over and 20 of us would be moving to the next choir level. One of the special moments was meeting a family that had fled from Ukraine and sharing a moment of heartbreak and hope with them. It’s these moments that made me realize that life moves pretty fast, and if you don’t stop to look around every once in a while you might miss it. Thank you, Ensemble, and everyone who worked hard to make the trip possible, especially Heather Saulnier and Eric Tuan who made the tour live up to our motto: “Just the way I like it.” I will never forget these two magical weeks in Germany and Denmark. articles.text: Editor: The Post’s coverage in narrative and photographs of this year’s 4th of July Parade was quite extensive! Descriptions of the holiday’s events appeared on 8 pages, and I counted 60 photos. Imagine my surprise and disappointment, therefore, not to find any reference in all of this parade coverage to the participation of the Piedmont Community Band, which has played in the parade for 38 years. The only reference at all (that I almost missed) was to those who may “join the Piedmont marching band” on page 20 in the article about American music. The Post’s articles about the parade mentioned over 25 entries, including music provided by the Barrelhouse Jazz Band (1 photo), the Zenith Parade Band (2 photos), and the California Percussionists (3 photos), and there was 1 photo of the Cub Scout Kazoo Band. I don’t begrudge any of those entries the coverage they got; I think it’s great. But there was nothing about the homegrown Piedmont Community Band; Jane Reed, its Founder and Coordinator of 38 years; Ken Kawaichi, it’s band leader of 36 years; Elaine Lindenmayer, its majorette who at age 70 twirled for her 35th time; or its dedicated musicians, many of whom dust off their instruments annually just to delight parade-goers with their perky drum cadences and marching music. I admit my bias, since the band’s majorette is my mom, but I know that much of our Piedmont community looks forward annually to our local band’s appearance. Indeed, the Piedmont Community Band is a Piedmont treasure. The Post no doubt played a part in the band’s performance this year by dedicating space to calls for musicians, and in the past, the Post has duly recognized the Piedmont Community Band. Perhaps this year was an aberration. I hope the Post will give it due recognition in the future. Thank you for considering my thoughts. Evan Lindenmayer
articles.title: Piedmont Community Band

articles.text: As I write it is Wednesday of Vacation Bible Camp week at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. I am sure that those most directly involved in the camp are very tired, wondering if they can summon the energy for two more days while the campers are wishing that there were two more weeks of camp instead of two more days. VBC is a most impressive effort, one that shapes all those involved. For the adults it is an opportunity to connect directly with the kids. For the youth leaders it is a valuable opportunity to grow as teacher, mentor, organizer and leader. For the campers it is an invitation to learn the stories of the Bible and learn to think theologically about their lives and the world around them. In this year’s camp the Bible stories on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday focused on Joseph of Egypt. On Thursday, Jesus of Nazareth, particularly his passion, was the focus. There are important parallels between Joseph and Jesus. These have long been noted by Christian theologians, leachers and leaders. Their names are similar. Joseph means “God gives increase.” Jesus means “God saves.” Both experienced family conflict. Both “went down” to Egypt. Both knew rejection. Both knew suffering, Joseph was imprisoned in a cistern. Jesus was buried in a tomb. Joseph saved his people from famine. Jesus saved his people for a ministry of love. The five Bible points from this year’s camp pertain to both Joseph and Jesus and provide the basis for a healthy theology as well as healthy theological reflection. • God loves you no matter what. (In the midst of family tension, it was important for Jesus and Joseph to remember this.) • God is with you everywhere. (This was true for Joseph when he was in prison and for Jesus when he was being tempted in the wilderness.) • God is in charge. (Even when, like Joseph, you are entrusted with helping a country survive a famine and, like Jesus, you need to feed 5,000 with five loaves and two fish.) • God is stronger than anything. (The cold cistern and the quiet tomb included.)
articles.title: Good Theology

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will discuss Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper at its upcoming book meeting on August 16. Pepper’s Laboratories shows the “high profile antics of national politics,” and spotlights what can often be corruption in statehouses across the nation, which the author asserts pose the greatest threat to American democracy. The book outlines 30 steps that need to be taken, from federal action to individual steps, that help every citizen fight back against corruption in their own communities. Pepper is a writer, lawyer, former elected official, and served as the Chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party between 2015 and 2021. He earned his B.A. from Yale University and his J.D. from Yale Law School. The discussion will begin via Zoom at 5 p.m. on August Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper 16. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved on July 18 an agreement with ELS Architecture and Design (ELS) for frontage and right-of-way improvements for the proposed municipal pool. “Our project management team, led by George Sanen [of Griffin Architecture] has been keenly aware of grabbing opportunities to save time and money, as well as to mitigate risk, all three of which are in play here,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. ELS was awarded an agreement to provide design services for the new Community Pool in October 2021. The original agreement did not include rightof-way or pedestrian improvements, or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility access ramps. Tree removal and replacement, sidewalk and curb improvements were also omitted. The improvements are necessary, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The right-of-way is defined as the area that is behind private property – usually the sidewalk, the parking strip and/or the roadway on both sides of the street – all of which will be impacted as construction begins on the pool. “Once you have left the poolside itself, that area needs i m p r ove me nt ,” G on z a le s explained. “In the case of our project, the pool stops at the fence line. The area [beyond that] was not included in the original agreement [with ELS]. Those areas were not included, but will be impacted by this project. Looking at that, Public Works has identified this as the most beneficial time to look and contemplate how we can go about these improvements.” There are several benefits to begin improvements as soon as possible, Gonzales added, the primary benefit being cost savings. Improvements would start on Bonita Avenue at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, go down past the existing pool, past the Recreation Building and wrap around to Hillside Avenue. Gonzales noted that not all elements may need improvements, but that there is urgency is beginning an analysis now. “The last thing we want to do is finish site improvements, and then say we can’t open yet because we will have to work on the front [entry] itself,” he said. “It would be a shame to have this gorgeous, new facility, and have to tell [visitors] that they may need to park elsewhere or not use the sidewalks,” agreed Council member Betsy Andersen. The trees that surround the pool are “less than ideal for this setting,” Gonzales said, and added that this is a good time to look at replacing them with more suitable trees. Drainage improvements from fixing curb and gutter areas will also be assessed. The total cost of the improvements are not to exceed $75,140, according to the agreement between ELS and the City. business hours.

Right-of-way improvements for new pool to begin By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont City Council approved on July 18 an agreement with ELS Architecture and Design (ELS) for frontage and right-of-way improvements for the proposed municipal pool. “Our project management team, led by George Sanen [of Griffin Architecture] has been keenly aware of grabbing opportunities to save time and money, as well as to mitigate risk, all three of which are in play here,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. ELS was awarded an agreement to provide design services for the new Community Pool in October 2021. The original agreement did not include rightof-way or pedestrian improvements, or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility access ramps. Tree removal and replacement, sidewalk and curb improvements were also omitted. The improvements are necessary, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The right-of-way is defined as the area that is behind private property – usually the sidewalk, the parking strip and/or the roadway on both sides of the street – all of which will be impacted as construction begins on the pool. “Once you have left the poolside itself, that area needs i m p r ove me nt ,” G on z a le s explained. “In the case of our project, the pool stops at the fence line. The area [beyond that] was not included in the original agreement [with ELS]. Those areas were not included, but will be impacted by this project. Looking at that, Public Works has identified this as the most beneficial time to look and contemplate how we can go about these improvements.” There are several benefits to begin improvements as soon as possible, Gonzales added, the primary benefit being cost savings. Improvements would start on Bonita Avenue at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, go down past the existing pool, past the Recreation Building and wrap around to Hillside Avenue. Gonzales noted that not all elements may need improvements, but that there is urgency is beginning an analysis now. “The last thing we want to do is finish site improvements, and then say we can’t open yet because we will have to work on the front [entry] itself,” he said. “It would be a shame to have this gorgeous, new facility, and have to tell [visitors] that they may need to park elsewhere or not use the sidewalks,” agreed Council member Betsy Andersen. The trees that surround the pool are “less than ideal for this setting,” Gonzales said, and added that this is a good time to look at replacing them with more suitable trees. Drainage improvements from fixing curb and gutter areas will also be assessed. The total cost of the improvements are not to exceed $75,140, according to the agreement between ELS and the City. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) released health guidance for public schools in the next academic year, which does not include a mandated mask policy. State guidance was updated in a June 30 press release to recommend face masks rather than require them. Last year, the agency mandated stricter policies than the Center for Disease Control (CDC) and required that all students and faculty wear a face mask while on public school campuses. Now, CDPH is aligning with the CDC, which recommends masking indoors and in areas of poor ventilation. The guidance became effective on July 1. “ M a s k s , p a r t i c u l a r l y high-quality and well-fitting masks, remain highly effective, inexpensive, and dynamic tools to protect oneself and mitigate transmission of COVID-19 and other respiratory pathogens,” said State Public Health Director Tomas Aragon. “COVID-19 is here to stay, but we have learned methods and gained tools to decrease its impact on our health and well-being. California’s schools can manage this disease in sustainable and adaptive manners.” School districts may elect to impose their own mask mandates, however. pages.text: Wednesday, July 20, 2022 5 Just The Way I Like It Piedmont Choir’s Ensemble goes to Europe By Larissa Edel Part 1: Denmark The weeks of June 14 through 28 this summer were some of the best weeks of my life. After two-and-a-half years of the global pandemic, the Ensemble level of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir finally embarked on its long-awaited international tour to Denmark and Germany. The flight to Frankfurt was smooth and, overflowing with excitement, few of us slept. The food on our flight wasn’t that great, but we reminded ourselves of our tour motto, No matter what we eat, we have learned to say, “It’s just the way I like it.” That motto certainly came in handy on the bus ride from Frankurt to Denmark, where it was 90 degrees (F), and the bus AC broke down. Luckily, the stunning Danish countryside gave us a nice distraction. I have never seen such pristine fields of wheat, and forests so lush, or even seen so many animals just roaming free – deer, elk, even two rabbits and a fox running in a field. Denmark struck me as extremely flat: not a single mountain or even hill was spotted the entire time we were there. As it got hotter on our four-hour bus ride, our sense of reality and time started to crumble, so we decided to start singing, because after all we were a choir. The singing was out of tune, too slow, and not sung with conviction, just delirium. But we made it through to Herning, a city in central Denmark. In Herning we stayed with families of the MidtVest Children’s Choir. When time came to be given our rooming assignments, we all had our fingers crossed hoping that we would be placed with our friends. I was with one of my good friends, so I was all set. Our homestay’s name was Julie, but her name was pronounced Ulia. We were nervous because we wanted to make a good impression and had not experienced homestays before, but we all hit it off with our host families right away. Homestaying was one of the best parts of the tour. Our hosts were the kindest, most caring, and funny people that I have met. We even learned some Danish phrases: “god morgen” is “good morning,”, “tak,” is “thank you,” and “sov godt” is “sleep tight.” Even though we had a slight language barrier, it never got in the way; we always found a way to understand each other. Leaving Julie and her family when we left for Germany was one of the harder parts of the tour. While in Denmark we visited Skovsnogen (Deep Forest Art Land), a museum but an unconventional one. It was completely outside, and all the artwork was either a sculpture or some sort of Tour chaperone group, The Delta Nu’s are pictured in Deep Forest Art Land while looking out into the field in front of them: Kailamae Sands (left), Juliane Crossland, Olive Zager, Miranda Couch, Veda Pao Ziegler, and Larissa Edel. 3D object. Our choir split up into two groups, by tour chaperone groups, and we each had a guide. My group got a lovely woman named Henrietta and the other group got one of the owners of Skovsnogen, René Schmidt, an artist who created the museum in 2009. Both groups took different paths and saw different art pieces with some overlap. The art installations were each creative See Piedmont Choir on page 30 Veda Pao Ziegler and Larissa Edel in front of an art exhibit in Skovsnogen (Deep Forest Art Land). Miranda Couch and Larissa Edel enjoying lunch after a long day of singing and exploring in Denmark. Friends Larissa Edel and Sophia Meisel pose in rehearsal in Herning, Denmark.

articles.text: Sukanya Goswami began her tenure as the new principal of Piedmont High School, on July 1, coming most recently from Miramonte High School in Orinda, where she was Assistant Principal. Goswami sat down with the Post to talk about her career and the tasks that lie ahead in her first year as the high school’s top administrator. She takes over for Adam Littlefield, who retired after five years as PHS Principal. Goswami has 20 years of experience in secondary education. She taught for 14 years as an English teacher at Newark Memorial High School, including five years as the Department Chair. Her foundation as a teacher should serve her well in the new role. “As a high school teacher, it was more than just content, it was mentoring them, guiding them, and working with their families. And I really enjoy that whole-child approach, giving and guiding them towards the future,” she explained. In 2018 she moved into an administrative role as Vice Principal at Westmoor High School in Daly City, a position she held for three years until moving to Miramonte last school year. She is no stranger to different cultures; Goswami was born and raised in Calcutta, India, and started her career teaching students and families from different backgrounds,” she said. Goswami said her goal is to always keep in mind what is best for the students. “Whenever I am having a conversation (with students, parents, staff or administrators), I want to bring the discussion back to the goal: Is this really helpful for the student? That is where it starts and that’s where it ends,” she explained. Goswami’s first task is to assemble a full roster of teachers before the school year starts. In recent years, Piedmont High has started the year lacking staff in Spanish, Science and Music. “Hiring is a big focus now at this time in all school districts. We are reaching out to the community; we are reaching out to the local colleges. California is going through a big teacher shortage; all districts are struggling to fill positions and that is very real,” she said. Goswami wants to hit the ground running and knows that outreach and transparency are key. “I would like the community to know that I am a collaborative leader, and I’m a very authentic person,” Goswami said. “So, anybody should feel free to reach out to me with their comments, concerns, and feedback. If they want to drop by and talk to me, I’m always open to that.” Staff photo Sukanya Goswami took over as the new Piedmont High School Principal on July 1 in preparation for the 2022-2023 school year. articles.text: Looking for something new to do this summer? Do you enjoy gardening and want to support the community around you? Look no further than the Piedmont Community Service Crew’s (PCSC) upcoming event on Thursday, August 4th from 9:00-11:00 a.m.. PCSC will team up with Clausen House to build two large planter boxes in the backyard of their Perkins Street residential home in Oakland. The planter boxes can hold four cubic yards of soil and will be used for growing tomatoes, basil, and cilantro. To increase engagement in the project, the Clausen House residents did their own research and compiled a list of possible plants and vegetables. Clausen House is a non-profit dedicated to providing support and services to adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Founded in 1967, it has provided housing, an employment program, education support, independent living, and recreation and health services to low income and elderly residents for over 55 years. The planter boxes will provide food and increase accessibility to gardening for residents. The project also aims to improve communal teamwork, and provide a fun, engaging activity for residents right in their own backyard. Piedmont Community Service Crew is under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council and encourages teens to lead and create events and projects oriented on providing service for the community. The non-profit teen group strives to develop projects that fit the interests and talents of crew members who express the desire to take on increased ownership in what they do by actively building, repairing, and interacting with the larger community. pages.text: Wednesday, July 20, 2022 7 PCSC to build planter boxes at Clausen House on August 4 By Ella Puckett Looking for something new to do this summer? Do you enjoy gardening and want to support the community around you? Look no further than the Piedmont Community Service Crew’s (PCSC) upcoming event on Thursday, August 4th from 9:00-11:00 a.m.. PCSC will team up with Clausen House to build two large planter boxes in the backyard of their Perkins Street residential home in Oakland. The planter boxes can hold four cubic yards of soil and will be used for growing tomatoes, basil, and cilantro. To increase engagement in the project, the Clausen House residents did their own research and compiled a list of possible plants and vegetables. Clausen House is a non-profit dedicated to providing support and services to adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Founded in 1967, it has provided housing, an employment program, education support, independent living, and recreation and health services to low income and elderly residents for over 55 years. The planter boxes will provide food and increase accessibility to gardening for residents. The project also aims to improve communal teamwork, and provide a fun, engaging activity for residents right in their own backyard. Piedmont Community Service Crew is under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council and encourages teens to lead and create events and projects oriented on providing service for the community. The non-profit teen group strives to develop projects that fit the interests and talents of crew members who express the desire to take on increased ownership in what they do by actively building, repairing, and interacting with the larger community.
