articles.text: Jody Weverka retired from Piedmont High School’s English Department and as the yearbook advisor after 19 years, and a 36-year career which began at age 24 in 1986. Weverka attended high school in Hayward, before attending UC Santa Barbara where she met her future husband Phil. She earned her Master’s degree and teaching credential at Stanford and then took her first teaching job at Monte Vista High School in Danville. She then taught at San Ramon Valley High for 16 years before coming to Piedmont. At Piedmont she primarily taught American Literature to juniors. When asked how her job remained fresh over the 36 years of teaching, she said, “I promise, to the last week I was learning, it was never the same. The world gives you so much curriculum. There’s plenty going on to continuously have a fresh lens on American Literature.” “This is all I’ve done in my adult life, and was what I wanted to do. I think I’ve always loved the power of story; it’s the way people make meaning of their lives and think about other experiences in the world,” said Weverka. Weverka poured herself into her class, from start to finish, sometimes working 70-hour weeks. As the advisor to the yearbook class from 2011-2020 she found an additional dimension to her career in education, beyond academics. Inspired by Department chair Jody with Phil Weverka three months into her teaching career in 1986 at her apartment on Park Boulevard. Jody Weverka (front right) and the 2017 PHS English Department show their skill of being able to read upside down. Jody Weverka with son Jacob at the Piedmont graduation ceremony in 2011.
articles.title: Jody Weverka retires from Piedmont High School after 36-year career

articles.text: Walk for Wellness, Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s largest annual fundraiser, will take place August 21 through 27 this year. The event is a series of walks around town open to all. The event focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. The Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Center also helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including but not limited to stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. According to Wellness Center staff, approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. Martha Joerger and Lindsay Thomasson are this year’s co-chairs. To learn more, and to sign up or sponsor the event, visit https:// pef.schoolauction.net/wfw22/ homepages/show.

pages.text: Wednesday, July 13, 2022 7 By Eric Behrens Have you ever wondered what goes into building a float for the annual Piedmont Fourth of July parade? For answers, I spoke with Brian Kelleher, a veteran builder of 9 or 10 floats, most constructed during a friendly multi-year competition between the Monte-Mesa and Nova neighborhoods. Don Ashburn, Piedmont Community Church’s Associate Pastor, along with Brian’s wife Kathy, asked him if he would spearhead building a float for the church this year, and he readily agreed. Brian [Kelleher] was right: building a float is a great community builder. – Eric Behrens Piedmont Community Church At the outset, Brian stated that float building is a great community builder, is fun and is easier to do than one might think because “the float only needs to last about 25 minutes rolling down Piedmont’s main street”. articles.text: Nº 57 in a biweekly series France celebrates National France Day on July 14, and Paris is the pinnacle of some magnificent pomp. The nation’s republic is deeply rooted in self-governing principles when the Paris mobs showed their grit and stormed Versailles and kidnapped the king, their outrage erupting over heavy taxes and a population dying of starvation. Paris mobs had terrified the crown for a century. Versailles was built for the king to get far away from the madding crowds, and plenty grand to house the nobles at close range. When an armed crowd sacked the medieval fortress, the commoners cheered, and the symbol of tyranny was taken down, stone by stone. A century later, the National Assembly chose a national date, and the Fête happened to share the Bastille Day remembrance date without being about the Bastille. Salut, heureux quatorze juillet, rather than a happy Bastille Day. The Paris extravaganza boasts the most lavish parade in the world, and speeches by dignitaries are broadcast to the nation. The Fête is joyous and starts with a traditional military ceremony and full-dress parade down the Boulevard Champs Elysée. Jet propelled planes flying at low altitudes and trailing the tri-color streams thrill the audience. Picnickers vie for the prime spots on the grassy knolls at Champ de Mars, with their blankets and food baskets, though wine and champagne and all alcohol is banned from the park. A formal A concert of classical music with full orchestra performs at Champs-deMars. Full military parade to the Arc de Triomphe la Fête Nationale Française. classical concert begins shortly after 9 pm. Earlier, the music sets are by popular deejays. Fireworks fire off around 11 pm over the Eiffel Tower and Trocadéro Garden. And around midnight from 700,000 to as many as a million people begin to find their way home. They proceed largely on foot, at least to reach an open Metro station and queue for the regional commuter trains. The Paris Insider Guide suggests where to situate in Paris for the best views of the fireworks. Cross the Seine to the Trocadéro esplanade, but one must arrive early for this popular perch. Sacre Coeur church in Montmartre is at a high point, and the Parc de Belleville in the 20th district. The top floor of the Tour Montparnasse has a 360º nighttime view at the price of a four-star dinner. The bridges of Paris offer a mostly unobstructed view, especially Pont des Arts, Pont de la Concorde, and Pont Alexandre III. Two years ago in 2020, for the first time since the end of World War II, a restricted military marched in parade dress and reduced by half in respect to the year of Covid-19. One year ago, 2021, the vigorous full program was restored, but the crowds were curtailed while mask requirements were still in effect. In midMarch, France suspended the requirements for vaccine passes, and the nation celebrated. Eiffel Tower opening (engraving) on July 14, 1889. The coronavirus is not defeated, only weakened, yet commerce is back in full swing. Tourism has returned in full force to France, and café society is back in swing. Possibly, travelers have taken note that the U.S. dollar is at $1.02 per euro and has rapidly spiked to near parity, a dramatic climb for the U.S. dollar since just February when a Euro transacted at $1.14. Parity hasn’t occurred since 2002. In the 2008 global financial crisis, according to Bloomberg, a euro was transacting at $1.60. articles.text: Jasper Schuetz, who will be a freshman at Piedmont High this fall, has big plans as a member of the school’s Mountain Bike team. On June 4, Schuetz competed in the Lost and Found Gravel Festival in Downieville, a grueling 60-mile event which he won at the junior level with a time of 5:08:07.1. Schuetz, who was 111th overall out of 337 riders, beat his competitor by 27 minutes. Riding elevation is no easy task. His route started at 4,829 feet in Portola, and ascending to 6,673 feet. “I split it into three different climbs,” he explained. “There was one climb that started at 4,900 feet and ended at about 6,500 feet, and that was the starting climb, which was probably the hardest part of the race. The way I really approached this long race was keeping my head in it and staying comfortable with the pace I was doing. I didn’t want to blow myself out in the middle of the race. The first idea was surviving and then winning,” said Schuetz. To prepare for racing at high elevation, Schuetz camped the night to get his body acclimated to the thin air and made sure to start strong on the initial climb. “I camped the night before to get acclimated to the elevation. At the start, I really just warmed my body up to it. Because it was such a tough climb at the start, I wanted to start with a high cadence and get the lactic acid out of my muscles, and really just clear my body before going up the hill. That ended up working, I rode at a comfortable pace most of the time,” said Schuetz. Prior to the race he trained with Piedmont Mt. Bike Team, the high school team. “To prepare for this race, I was practicing with the mountain bike high school team. I was an 8th Jasper Schuetz describes his preparation and mindset for the grueling 60-mile event at high elevation. grader last school year and I got the privilege to train with the high school team. We would do spin classes, strength and conditioning, rides around Joaquin Miller, and I would compete for the middle school. I was doing some training on my own after the season ended,” explained Schuetz. Another caveat in long races is making sure your hydration and conditioning is on point in order to avoid cramps. Schuetz explains that he trained his body to have water-tolerance in order to go long distances without needing an exorbitant amount of hydration. “I trained for water-tolerance. I would do long rides and not bring water; that sounds like a bad idea, but I was training myself to just be tolerant and limit my intake of water,” said Schuetz. The Lost & Found Gravel Festival event was a combination of gravel, dirt roads, and paved surfaces. Schuetz elected to ride a mountain bike to take advantage of the off-road and mountainous terrain but admits that he lost some time to those on faster pace road bikes once the course hit the flat and paved portions. “The course was a little bit of road at the start and at the end, but it was mostly dirt fire roads. I used a mountain bike even though it was a gravel race and a lot of riders had gravel bikes. It was pretty tough at the end because a lot of people on road bikes were passing me and I lost all the time I gained on the dirt,” said Schuetz. The course itself started in Portola and went around Crocker Mountain, Lake Davis, and Smith Peak. “The scenery made you almost forget that you were in a cycling race,” described Schuetz. Schuetz looks toward the school year to ride for Piedmont MTB high school team. Their races schedule typically are held from February through May, including year-round training. Jasper Schuetz, an incoming freshman at PHS, won the junior category at the Lost and Found 60-mile event in Downieville. Jasper Schuetz finished his race in 5:08:01.1, beating the next junior rider by over 27 minutes.
articles.title: Jasper Schuetz wins 60-mile mountain bike race

articles.text: Photos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Tadej Pogačar, last year’s s back in the Yellow Jersey, taking the lead after Stage 6. Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar,a sSlovenian rider with UAE Team Emirates, is back in the Yellow Jersey in the 109th Tour de France, regaining the lead in general classification following Stage 6. Pogačar won the stage’s hill course on July 7 and Stage 7 in the mountains the following day, charging to the lead in the last tenth of a mile up the La Super Planche Des Belles FIlles. He also finished third in the Stage 8 hills and fifth in the Stage 9 mountains. Tuesday’s Stage 10 had to be halted briefly after climate activists shut down a portion of the course. The stage resulted in some changes in the top 10, including American Nielson Powless who placed 11th overall, 1 minute, 55 seconds back of the lead. Powless, 25, rides for EF Education–EasyPost and is embarking on his third Grand Tour appearances after competing in in 2020 and 2021. He jumped to second place in general classification from Stage 5 and 6 before falling to eighth over the next two stages and ninth after Stage 9. “I’m really happy with how the first week went. I had a really smooth ride, I just seemed to always be at the right place in the right time,” said Powless, via Velonews.com. “I had a lot of fun just moving through the peloton, trying to find the right moves to go in. It was exciting, it’s exciting to be racing at the front. I’m really happy to be there.” Le Tour moves to back-toback mountain courses on Stage 11-12 today and tomorrow. Stage 11 rides 152 kilometers from Albertville to Col du Granon containing an 11.9 kilometer at a 7.1 percent gradient climb up Col du Telegraphe, another 17.7 kilometer climb at 6.9 percent up Col du Galibier, and a final summit finish up Col du Granon Serre Chevalier for 11.3 kilometers at a steep 9.2 percent grade. Stage 12 will be the final mountain ride until Stage 17 on July 20. It will be an exhaustive course with another three steep ascents; the first climb is 23 kilometers at a 5.1 percent grade, there will be another 29 kilometer climb up Col de la Croix de Fer at 5.2 percent, and a second consecutive summit finish with 13.8 kilometers and a grueling 8.1 percent grade up Alpe D’Huez.
articles.title: Defending champ Tadej Pogacˇar takes over lead in Tour de France

pages.text: Wednesday, July 13, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. RAFAELLA GOMES Fencing Piedmont High Class of 2021 UC San Diego Class of 2025 Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, is a fencer competing with UC San Diego and the Brazil National Team. In last week’s Post, we covered Gomes placing 16th of 44 in the 2022 Pan American Fencing Championships’ Foil Women’s Senior Individual bracket in Asunción, Paraguay. She also helped Brazil finish fourth among 10 teams. She was the youngest competitor on the Brazilian team. In the 2021 Junior South American Championships, Gomes won a bronze medal (3rd place) in the junior foil individual bracket. Gomes is currently ranked No. 49 in the world’s junior category after taking bronze at the Junior Pan American Championship. She’s currently No. 100 globally in the senior category and has the Photo courtesy of cbesgrima.org.br Rafaella Gomes stands proudly with her bronze medal at the 2021 Junior Pan American Championship. third-highest senior ranking for the Brazil National Team. As a freshman at UC San Diego, Gomes reached the NCAA National Championship on March 27 and qualified for the prestigious tournament after taking silver at the NCAA West Regional Championship out of 11 competitors on March 12. She also finished second in the Mountain Pacific Sports Federation Fencing Championships’ Women’s Foil on March 13, earning her the MPSF Newcomer of the Year award. Gomes is now training for the 2022 Senior World Championships in Cairo, Egypt, which takes place July 15-23. She is working with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco and U.S. Men’s Foil Fencing Team’s coach Greg Massialas, which has churned out Olympic talent over the years. Below is her training regimen ahead of the World Championships. What is your workout program this summer? Fencing goes year-round. When I am not competing for UC San Diego in the NCAA circuit, I am competing in the Brazilian national circuit. Because I do not have an off season, my training program changes all the time at the mercy of my competition schedule. No matter where I am though, I stretch every morning and night, and I run every morning I am able. If I have access to a gym, I follow the training program I learned from UC San Diego coach Patrick McLeroy, who works with the entire UCSD fencing team. What are your fitness goals for this summer? First, recovery. I am working to get back to where I was athletically before I caught COVID19. Once there, I will be focusing on increasing my explosive strength and decreasing my reaction time. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by comparing it to where I was before I caught COVID. Quantitatively, I can compare how heavy I lift or how fast I run now as opposed to then. I can compare how easily I tire or how effectively I execute technical skills. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I have practice at the Massialas Foundation every week day and Saturdays for two hours. Practice includes 30 minutes of intense, fencing-specific footwork drills, an hour of fencing, and 30 minutes of one-on-one work with a coach. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I ended my first season in the Brazilian national circuit as a new member of the Brazilian national junior and senior teams. My results include two silver and two bronze medals, one of each for the junior and senior categories. articles.text: 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree & prehistoric Tafoni Rock Formation El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve in San Mateo County has some easily accessible features that many more acclaimed destinations in the Bay Area don’t come close to offering. Located near Highway 35 (Skyline Boulevard) is a tree that predates the Europeans settling of America, the estimated 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree. It is the only old growth redwood tree in the Santa Cruz Mountains outside of Big Basin State Park and is known as the “Big Old Tree on Skyline.” The Peninsula Open Space Preserve describes the Methuselah Tree as having sprouted in 217 AD, experiencing Ohlone natives bark cultivation in 1,000 AD, and witnessing European settlers and Mexico’s independence from Spain in 1821. Lumber mills in the 1870s’ California Gold Rush likely determined that its massive burl made Methuselah impossible to harvest. In our visit in December 2020, the entrance to the tree was closed due to dry conditions, but it has since re-opened to the public. It’s an excellent place for a photo-op and starting point for a day of hiking. You can walk up to the Big Old Tree and sit on its stump. Across from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark—the Tafoni Rock Formation. The nearly 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone is an estimated 30 million years old. A platform sits at its base with informative panels and a close view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name that describes the sandstone’s cavernous result of weathering. coast, as wind and waves eat away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating back to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. A half-mile away from the rock formation, continuing on the Fir Trail, is Vista Point, another place of note. The overlook has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and a bench for resting and viewing. An interesting memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the point’s entrance. It was erected in 2006 to commemorate a British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines commercial airplane that was bound for Sydney, Australia, but crashed during a storm in October 1953. One can still find pieces of the wreckage on the park’s Resolution Trail. From there, continuing back to the car rounds out your day at a mellow 3.6 miles. But continuing past the Tafoni Rock formation on the Tafoni Trail – turning right when exiting the pathway from the giant chunk of stone – will provide a 5.15 mile day and slightly under 1,000 feet in elevation gain—while surrounding you with redwood trees and stumps from old giants. When considering that 49 of the hikers we saw were in the first 2.1 miles from the trailhead to Vista Point and the Tafoni formation, this loop is certainly in the “hidden treasure” category. The trails are a common place for mountain bikers zooming downhill and off berms, meaning no dogs are allowed in El Corte de Madera Creek. Punch in “Methuselah Tree, Redwood City” to your GPS device to access the area. articles.text: You may have noticed an alert on your phone or email this week about king tides impacting the Bay Area. It is an event that results in higher tides typically in evening hours, which is expected to cause flooding in several lowland locations in the coming days. The predicted king tides are expected to last longer than usual and could continue this week through Friday, July 15. This natural phenomenon typically occurs during the winter months when the sun and moon reach their closest points to Earth. However, king tides return around the summer solstice two weeks ago. “King Tides happen around the solstices, when the alignment of the sun, moon, and Earth creates a stronger pull on the tides, resulting in higher high tides and lower low tides,” said Annie Kohut Frankel of the California Coastal Commission. The National Weather Services announced it expected the first high tide to arrive in San Francisco last night, Tuesday, July 12, with tides of up to 7-1/2 feet near the Embarcadero around midnight. On Thursday, July 14, a tide of 7.51 feet is expected. Flooding in Sausalito occurred on Monday, July 11 with the northbound Highway 101 offramp to Stinson Beach closed. Mill Valley’s Tamalpais junction is susceptible to flooding. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA)’s exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, is on display now through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist who founded Heath Ceramics. The exhibit includes over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo by Christina Cueto The newest collection at Oakland Museum of California showcases Edith Heath’s ceramics.
articles.title: Edith Heath exhibit continues through October at Oakland Museum

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora [MoAD] in San Francisco presents its newest exhibition, entitled Still Lives in Contemporary Art, now through August 12. The group exhibition brings together an international group of artists who have unique takes on contemporary art and still life. The artists have created works within a framework of Black diasporic identities, histories, and collective experiences. Featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. articles.text: The Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates returning to live concerts this summer with three public performances at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening on Wednesday, July 20. Festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind one that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jasmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Paul Laraia (viola), and Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), back by popular demand. This Week’s Featured Artists: WAYNE LEE, Piano, JULIANA HAN, Piano American violinist Wayne Lee has enjoyed a prolific career worldwide as a member of two internationally-acclaimed chamber ensembles. Since 2012, he has been a member of the Formosa Quartet, a string quartet that performs extensively in North America, Europe and Asia, with recent engagements at London’s Wigmore Hall, the Berlin Philharmonie, Taipei’s National Concert Hall, and the Chan Centre for the Performing Arts in Vancouver. For over a decade he was a member of the Manhattan Piano Trio, an ensemble acclaimed as “outstanding” by the Washington Post and lauded as “a grand departure from the usual” by the News Herald. A dedicated teacher and arts advocate, Wayne has previously taught at the University of Illinois at Champaign-Urbana and the Juilliard School in New York. Pianist Juliana Han is an active collaborator, chamber musician, and soloist, lauded not only for her inspired performances but also for her musical lectures, which illuminate classical works for diverse audiences. She has performed in notable venues across North America and Asia, including Carnegie Hall, Alice Tully Hall, and the National Taichung Theater. Her other festival appearances include Music Academy of the West, Norfolk Chamber Music Festival, and Kneisel Hall Chamber Music Festival. Violinist Wayne Lee and pianist Juliana Han will lead the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival next week in its fifth summer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey Festival Napa Valley, now in its 16th season, opens this Friday night, July 15 with conductor Carlo Ponti leading the Festival Orchestra Napa in Dvorak’s New World Symphony. The 9-day summer arts festival will take place in iconic Napa Valley locations. “The performances at Festival Napa Valley this summer illuminate the importance of the arts in today’s world,” said Festival President & CEO Richard Walker. “Our mission is more vital than ever.” “We are dedicating the 2022 season to the sounds of America. From Copland and Bernstein to jazz, swing, Broadway, bluegrass and country, this is the music that celebrates our common heritage,” added Robin Baggett, Chairman of the Festival’s Board of Directors. Noteworthy artists performing this year include Trisha Yearwood, Nia Imani Franklin and the Young People’s Chorus of New York City, soprano Mikayla Sager, tenor Mario Chang, baritone Lester Lynch, violinist Tessa Lark, and soprano Alexandra Armantrading. Performances will be held outdoors on the Festival Napa Valley Conductor Carlo Ponti will lead Festival Orchestra Napa in Dvorak’s New World Symphony this Friday, July 15, opening night of Festival Napa Valley. Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, at the Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at the Culinary Institute of America at Copia in Napa, and at wineries, estates and other venues throughout Napa Valley. For the full festival schedule and program and to order tickets, visit: https://festivalnapavalley. org.

articles.text: The panorama of music in America is like no other. Every culture who came to our shores has fructified our scene. How lucky we are. Strangely, the indigenous peoples had to wait a long time to be recognized. America’s first composers were rather conservative. They were both rooted and indebted to the European origin, as such they were no different from the mainstream European composers. This can be said about the entire American culture from colonial days until the Civil War. One composer should be singled out for his uniqueness. He was Benjamin Franklin. Yes, Franklin did compose music. He also invented a popular musical instrument known as the glass armonica… Not the glass harmonica. Composers in America continued their conservative ways. Two notable exceptions were the immensely popular song composer Stephen Foster and the sensational New Orleans born pianist Louis Moreau Gottschalk. They towered above their countrymen like a colossus in a sea of mediocrity. Despite their immense popularity, neither had an immediate effect on the musical scene in the United States. The American dollar was a huge inducement to foreign virtuosos. They came here in droves and humored the rustic American audiences with pop-style ditties. The few who remained in America did not have any real influence on American musical culture. We didn’t have much music education, as Americans always went to the music conservatories in Europe. All that changed when the Czech composer Antonin Dvorak came to America in 1892. He realized that America must recognize its indigenous music. He became This program from 1843 is typical. Sensational publicity was the order of the day. “The world’s greatest pianist and the world’s greatest violinist will play the world’s greatest music in a brilliant concert.” Meredith Willson was the epitome of an American composer and one of the great raconteurs I ever knew. America’s greatest musical advocate. Everywhere Dvorak went, he instructed American composers to incorporate indigenous music and African inspired music. No one in the history of American music was as influential. Because of Dvorak the entire course of American music was changed. At about the same time Scott Joplin made ragtime music fashionable. There were white ragtime composers as well as black ragtime composers. The popularity of ragtime was the catalyst for the beginnings of jazz and all that came afterwards. In Europe, operetta was popular. In America, musicals were our version of operettas. Fortunately, the musical was easily adaptable to all manner of ethnic music. Jewish musical theater thrived and so did Chinese opera. Jewish musical theater stars made an easy transition to mainstream American music. Curiously, many people thought that George M. Cohan was Jewish. My father knew George M. Cohan and thought his name was Cohen. When I told my father that he was an Irishman, my father said: “Cohan always spoke in Yiddish to me.” You may be interested to know that Chinese opera influenced the great violinist Fritz Kreisler. On a night out in San Francisco, Kreisler went to one of the Chinese theaters in Chinatown and was inspired to write his famous piece Tambourin Chinoise. Tremendous immigration to our shores enlivened our musical scene. Virtually every musician embraced the American spirit… the results of their compositions showed it. Irish- born Victor Herbert even formed ASCAP. First-generation composers like the Gershwins, Leonard Bernstein and Ferde Grofe made significant contributions. Every ethnic group inf luenced the others. The most interesting thing to remember is that American music always sounds American. From our conservative European past until the riotous cacophony of today, American music is always readily identifiable.

articles.text: Django Reinhardt was born January 23, 1910 in Liberchies, Pont-à-Celles, Belgium into a family of Manouche Romani descent. Romani is an IndoAryan ethnic group that originated in Northern India (Rajasthan and Punjab). Manouche is the French group of Romani people. His legal name-was Jean Reinhardt, but he was known as “Django”, a Gypsy name meaning “I awake.” Django married at 17. A year later, he accidentally knocked over a candle in the wagon he shared with his wife and started a fire with the celluloid his wife used for making artificial flowers. They escaped the fire, but over half of Django’s body was burned. He was told he would never play guitar again. Though he only had full use of his fretting hand index and middle fingers (his ring and little fingers could only fret chords), he went on to become one of the greatest jazz guitarists of all time! I know what that’s like. When I was 22, I cut my fretting hand middle finger to the bone with a circular saw and the surgeon said I would never play guitar again. Unacceptable! I worked hard for six months and recovered. Twenty years later, the finger recovered nerve sensation. Django and violinist Stéphane Grappelli separately made a living in the 1920’s busking (playing for donations) on the streets of Paris. In 1928, Grappelli was a member of the orchestra at the Ambassador Hotel while bandleader Paul Whiteman and jazz violinist Joe Venuti were performing there. Grappelli modeled his playing after Venuti. From 1934-1939, Django and Grappelli played together in the Quintette du Hot Club de France, originally Legendary “gypsy guitarist” Django Reinhardt. at the club in the Hotel Claridge, but the Quintette name was used in performances across Europe. Django was an “ear player”, building his phrases from a creative aural perspective in the vocal context (thinking like an improvising vocalist). In transcribing his solos, I suspected he was listening to his imagination, rather than his logical-mathematical left brain. Charlie Christian played with the same perspective, based on “feel” and modeled much of his style after Django. Topsy, the example of Django’s improvisational style linked below, is based on the Andalusian cadence, a middle-eastern chord progression brought into Spain during the Arabic civilization in Spain (1711-1492). In the key of C minor, the Andalusian cadence is Cm-Bb-Ab-G. The second chord in the main progression of Topsy, C minor with Bb bass, functions much like Bb major. The Ab7 darkens the key, including the “Gb” note (the dark flat five of C minor). Listen to and read my improvised example for this Django Reinhardt column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is a Piedmont author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com.

Jewish musical theater thrived and so did Chinese opera. Jewish musical theater stars made an easy transition to mainstream American music. Curiously, many people thought that George M. Cohan was Jewish. My father knew George M. Cohan and thought his name was Cohen. When I told my father that he was an Irishman, my father said: “Cohan always spoke in Yiddish to me.” You may be interested to know that Chinese opera influenced the great violinist Fritz Kreisler. On a night out in San Francisco, Kreisler went to one of the Chinese theaters in Chinatown and was inspired to write his famous piece Tambourin Chinoise. Tremendous immigration to our shores enlivened our musical scene. Virtually every musician embraced the American spirit… the results of their compositions showed it. Irish- born Victor Herbert even formed ASCAP. First-generation composers like the Gershwins, Leonard Bernstein and Ferde Grofe made significant contributions. Every ethnic group inf luenced the others. The most interesting thing to remember is that American music always sounds American. From our conservative European past until the riotous cacophony of today, American music is always readily identifiable. READ IT IN THE POST

Starring Review by Chris Honoré If you’re a fan of the adrenaline-producing, jump ball, game clock is ticking, pedal-to-themetal, flat out thriller, well, don’t miss Taken. It’s an unpretentious rush. Forget any minor plot holes. Just sit back and enjoy. It was co-written by Luc Beeson (Transporter series and Tell No One), whose films define slickness and are meant to be visceral rather than cerebral. The cinematography and the script in Taken conspire to create a sense of motion that accelerates until act III gives the audience whiplash. It’s always a pleasure to watch Liam Neeson, no matter the role. He’s a fine, versatile actor. In Taken he portrays Bryan Mills, a retired black ops CIA agent who has left the agency to be closer to his 17-year-old daughter, Kim (Maggie Grace), who lives with her mother (Famke Janssen) and very rich stepfather (Xander Berkeley) in Los Angeles. The setup of the film is straightforward while steeped in foreboding. Kim begs her mother and father to let her go to Paris for the summer with her best girlfriend. They’re going to live in a swank penthouse of some friends and tour the City of Lights. Bryan is not pleased, knowing that there are dangers in the world that his ex-wife and daughter are simply unaware of. Finally, he relents and gives Kim an international phone while insisting she call him twice daily. Within one hour of landing in Paris and arriving at the apartment, the girls are kidnapped. And so begins a classic hunt film, predictable to be sure, but also entertaining. Bryan is lethal and refuses to collaborate with the French police. Alone, he searches for what turns out to be a ruthless ring of Albanian white slavers that auction off women to international buyers like sports cars. He has 96 hours, he’s told, to find Kim and her friend before they are sold and swept away into a brutal world from which they will never return. What happens next, well, if you’re a fan of the kidnap genre, Liam Neeson stars in Taken. nothing will surprise. But this isn’t a film about surprises; rather, it’s a hard case revenge/ vigilante tale that appeals to all of our baser instincts – in a good way. It features one very angry father willing to do whatever it takes to find his daughter. And who wouldn’t? It helps, of course, if you happen to be a highly trained covert agent with some very cool skill sets. Let the games begin. Taken. Directed by Pierre Morel. Starring Liam Neeson, Famke Janssen and Maggie Grace. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Now streaming on Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Taken.

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Ratatouille. As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who along with his large family plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, to “eat his garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his new-found friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy becomes the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. But there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/ Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. Not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time gives the restaurant a glowing review. Indeed, the story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios: its colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille. Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. With the voices of Patton Oswalt, Ian Holm, Lou Romano. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G. Released to theaters in the 2007. Now streaming on Wudu/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Released in 1993, Free Willy is a family-friendly drama that will undoubtedly appeal to a new generation of kids. At the center of this most engaging film are a 7,000-pound Orca whale named Willy, and a 12-year-old boy, Jessie (Jason James Richter), who are both struggling to adjust to their situations. For Willy, captured while swimming with his pod (think family), it’s the confines of the Northwest Adventure theme park. Jesse, an orphan who was abandoned by his mother at a very early age, grew up in various foster homes, but prefers to hustle on the streets with his urchin buds, scrounging for spare change, and begging for food from the back door of local restaurants. Both Willy and Jesse have an attitude. Willy refuses to work with his trainer, Rae (Lori Petty), and Jesse is surly and filled with resentment at life in general. It’s obvious that if something doesn’t happen to turn Jesse around, he will slip through the cracks and be lost for good. One night, Jesse sneaks into a theme park with a can of spray paint, intent on leaving behind his signature graffiti. He begins with a window overlooking one of the large water tanks where the Orcas perform. He is interrupted by the police who give him three mandatory options: return the next day and clean the window, move in with a foster family, Glen and Annie Greenwood (Jane Atkinson and Michel Madsen), who have agreed to give him a home, or take a hard pass and go to juvi. Not eager to go to jail, Jesse agrees to live with the Greenwoods, and returns to the park to scrub the observation window. Walking by the tank, Jesse is warned by Rae to be careful, there’s an Orca just below the surface. Ignoring Rae, of course, he slips and falls in. But to the surprise of Rae and other park employees, to include the owners of Northwest, Willy gently lifts Jesse out of the water and places him gently onto the side of the pool. Now living with the Greenwoods, Jesse sneaks out at night, and returns to the tank and sits on the side, playing his harmonica. Willy hears him and swims over. And so the two begin to bond. Jesse, surprisingly, is hired by the owners, who have all but given up on Willy (he’s more valuable if sold or even euthanized). They give him a job of assisting Rae as a neophyte trainer. With Jesse in the water, Willy becomes compliant and starts performing. Meanwhile, Jesse comes to realize that the Greenwoods are the family he has been hoping for, and they patiently make it clear that he is more than welcome. And so gradually Jesse, Willy, and the Greenwoods cohere. What is unresolved is the intent of the greedy, villainous owners. They are still considering Willy’s fate. Jesse gets wind of their indecision, and so begins acts three and a plan, which will delight the kids in the audience. Free Willy finds the sweet spot in the end. Free Willy. Directed by Simon Wincer. Starring Jason James Richter, Lori Petty, Michael Madsen, Jane Atkinson, and Keiko as Willy. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG. Released in 1993 and now streaming on Netflix Jason James Richter stars in Free Willy.

articles.text: Part 48 in a bi-weekly series The quality of our built environment is always a primary concern for pretty much everyone. High quality reflects positively on people’s lives adding aesthetic and social amenity as well as economic value for everyone in the community. This applies to all aspects of landscaping, urban design and of course buildings. There are multiple interrelated factors and interests related to quality. Things like beauty, function, safety, comfort, environmental friendliness, and community enhancement all enter into the equation. As a result, quality is a somewhat subjective concept and sometimes difficult to define. If for example we design and build a beautiful building with artistically proportioned facades but the plumbing leaks, or, after two years the materials start corroding, how do we measure or evaluate the overall quality? It seems to me that for a proposed improvement to have a Amenities that are provided for the public to enjoy, such as public esplanades, parks, civic monuments and artwork, are measures of the quality of a community. Interestingly, the costs of these items usually pay dividends by dramatically increasing the value of everything around them— just look at Central Park in New York or Coit tower in San Francisco. high degree of quality, to have true value, it must be considered from three basic scales: the scale of the general surrounding area or neighborhood, the scale of the immediate site or building, and the scale of the details. Unless there is a direct, intelligent and informed response to all of these, a high degree of quality cannot really be achieved. If any are lacking, quality will certainly be compromised and the results will, at a minimum, be higher maintenance costs. At worst, it results in a poorly functioning plan or even blight and reduced property values as (for example) a building that quickly is deteriorating. While everyone certainly wants the highest quality in their cities, communities and homes, Quality begins in programming and design, continues through construction, and relies on continuous maintenance for the life of any project. stand out as examples of high quality.

This applies to all aspects of landscaping, urban design and of course buildings. There are multiple interrelated factors and interests related to quality. Things like beauty, function, safety, comfort, environmental friendliness, and community enhancement all enter into the equation. As a result, quality is a somewhat subjective concept and sometimes difficult to define. If for example we design and build a beautiful building with artistically proportioned facades but the plumbing leaks, or, after two years the materials start corroding, how do we measure or evaluate the overall quality? It seems to me that for a proposed improvement to have a A responsive, rational, and imaginative urban design response is one component of quality in new improvements. Piedmont’s Havens School entry courtyard is a fine example. Amenities that are provided for the public to enjoy, such as public esplanades, parks, civic monuments and artwork, are measures of the quality of a community. Interestingly, the costs of these items usually pay dividends by dramatically increasing the value of everything around them— just look at Central Park in New York or Coit tower in San Francisco. high degree of quality, to have true value, it must be considered from three basic scales: the scale of the general surrounding area or neighborhood, the scale of the immediate site or building, and the scale of the details. Unless there is a direct, intelligent and informed response to all of these, a high degree of quality cannot really be achieved. If any are lacking, quality will certainly be compromised and the results will, at a minimum, be higher maintenance costs. At worst, it results in a poorly functioning plan or even blight and reduced property values as (for example) a building that quickly is deteriorating. While everyone certainly wants the highest quality in their cities, communities and homes, This older, quality craftsman home in Piedmont is certainly the beneficiary of not only special design and careful construction, but surely diligent maintenance over the years. there are barriers to achieving it. First among them is often cost. This does not mean the most expensive buildings with the most exotic materials are required. It does mean, however, employing the most reasonable, most site responsive and well thought-out comprehensive designs. The real economic solution lies by starting with balancing the scope of projects with what can realistically be paid for. It also means that management of what the industry calls quality assurance (specified standards) and quality control (compliance to specified standards) must be employed throughout any project of any size. This pursuit of the appropriate level of quality must be continuous through all phases of development, It must begin with programing and design, be carried out during construction, and then followed through with the oft neglected but imperative of ongoing maintenance. Quality of design and construction are really best measured over time. It has been my experience that the municipalities, developers and owners who follow through on these concepts have ended up contributing the most to their communities, have had the most satisfaction and, more often than not, the highest level of economic return on their projects. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through will@MakingDesignSense.com Quality begins in programming and design, continues through construction, and relies on continuous maintenance for the life of any project. The degree of quality in buildings is reflected in the details. The custom designed heavy gauge copper gutters and downspouts on this hotel in Carmel, as well as the sensitively designed signage/fencing on Havens School stand out as examples of high quality.

To consciously choose beauty can be a gateway to living a healthier, happier life. Choosing beauty makes a life with meaning, a life with intention and purpose. When we consciously choose to see beauty, we tend to access a higher vibration in general. I know this because I have lived it, and I see its impact on relationships when people make the shift. As a person who grew up in a family with little means, I can attest that those with limited resources can sometimes misinterpret that beauty is associated with luxury and wealth… that it’s a pretension, a frivolity. Nothing could be further from the truth. It’s what happens when we stop to meditate on a flower, a poem, or a meal. It can bring us closer to our hearts. It can bring us closer to each other. Beauty is not limited to well-designed spaces or quality, handmade objects as I often point toward. As one of my favorite writers on beauty, Shakti Maira, says, “when an environment is healthy, it tends to be beautiful… When a flower or animal is vital and well-formed, it is invariably beautiful. When people are mentally and emotionally in balance, harmony and good rhythm, they feel beautiful within. Likewise, families with harmony, balance and proportion are beautiful, and this can be extended to all systems. Beauty is a sign or a signal of health and well-being in every system and network.” This is at the heart of our business. I recall when I took a class in ancient Greek mythology while at UC Berkeley. I was captivated by the elegance and beauty of the words, and how they formed visions that were so full of light and intentional creation. I wished I could have lived during that time. The downside of what might have been happening in terms of the treatment of humans was not in my consciousness. I was swept away by my imaginings, which were replacing the images implanted in me through my religious upbringing. In the books I was reading, it seemed that beauty represented the ideal expression and ultimate ambition for what humanity could be. A good life was a beautiful life, and I enjoyed my shifting perspective about beauty. For me, beauty became not just a thing for wealthy people with access. It turned into something anyone could seed and grow. As I turned my attention to this thought, life began to look and feel brighter. It became a daily prayer to seek what was beautiful. I began to attract people who showed me how to be a beauty maker. Something began to grow within me that would ultimately become my life’s work… though I didn’t realize that at the time. I realize now that my upbringing had me fooled into thinking beauty was frivolous. I was not shown the value of beauty. Its meaning was stripped of its spiritual core. In my father’s view, beauty was a symbol of the upper classes, of unattainable luxury, of ostentatiousness. Connection to the divine was a forced energy: “do this, or you will go to hell.” He failed to see how beauty is at the root of spirituality. My father missed what I have found, which is that through beauty, we learn our own truth. We land in our hearts. We find deep and meaningful connection. The journey is in recognizing not just what looks beautiful, but more importantly, recognizing when beauty invites us to pause and access our higher selves. articles.text: Frank Anderson, a life-long Piedmont resident and a former Piedmont Vice Mayor, passed away peacefully at his longtime home in Piedmont on May 24, 2022. Born Frank Stoakes Anderson in Oakland in 1928, he was the son of David L. Anderson and Marguerite Stoakes Anderson. He started as a kindergartener at Havens Elementary School and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1946. He regaled his family with stories of working at Buzz’s gas station in Piedmont and his time as a yell-leader for PHS. He graduated from University of California Berkeley in 1950 with a Bachelor’s degree in Business Administration, followed by Army service at Fort Leonard Wood, Mo. Frank went to work for Fred J. Early Construction Company in San Francisco as a project manager and estimator. He then launched his own company, Anderson Constructors, Inc., which had offices in San Francisco and Oakland, specializing in commercial tenant improvements and insurance restoration work. Through his work, Frank got to know many great restauranteurs in San Francisco and was a member of the city’s Merchants Exchange Club. Frank was dedicated to Piedmont and for a stint was the city’s Vice Mayor. Frank Anderson, a lifelong Piedmont resident and former Vice Mayor, died on May 24. He was 94. Frank skied throughout Europe and was a season ticket holder at Squaw Valley in California for more than 40 years. He enjoyed many sailing adventures with his friends, loved biking with the Piedmont Pedal Pushers, and was an avid duck and upland game bird hunter. Frank is predeceased by his wife Lill, who passed the same day in 2016. He is survived by his brother David; his children Jeff, Richard, Kelly, Fredrik and Kristen, and his six grandchildren Michael and Tyler, Ben and Evan, and Andreas and Markus. A true bon vivant, Frank will be missed by many, near and far. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests a memorial donation be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation or Planned Parenthood.

articles.text: Participants of the Walking on Wednesdays group on July 6 included Jim Kellogg (left), Peter Persoff, Nancy Henn, Matt Gerhardt, Bob Wong, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Swee Ling Chen, Mike Henn, Martin Levy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sarah Johnson, Harriette Louie, Edith Lee, Nadine Guffanti, Lois Price, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Claudia Lopez, Stella Houston, Melba Yee, Albert Chen, Priscila Wanerus, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Charlene Louie, Mary Carter, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays group had another great day for walking on July 6 and had a strong turnout of 32 walkers and two K-9 best friends. The group was pleased to welcome back 8-year-old Charles Katzel and father Aaron for a second summer walk. It also welcomed first-time walkers Martha Swartz and Meghan Bennett with them. Meghan grew up in Piedmont, and has created the “History of Piedmont” website (https://www. historyofpiedmont.com) with information that the group has used on its walks. Two weeks earlier the walkers had gone to Piedmont streets that were on the early 20th Century Key System streetcar Numbers 10 and 12 lines. The 10 line went from Piedmont Avenue in Oakland to Crocker Park, and the 12 line went down Fairview Avenue to Grand Avenue and downtown Oakland. There were two other Key System lines in Piedmont, and the walkers thought it would be good to complete their Key System exploration with a walk to where the C and 11 lines also once ran. A quick Key System refresher was provided. In the 1890s land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate” that acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay for homes. The Key System was conceived by Smith as a way to sell the syndicate’s land. The Key System began service in 1903 in Berkeley and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. On her website Bennett provides lots of information on Piedmont and the Key System. She reports that shortly after Piedmont was incorporated in 1907, the B electric car line from Trestle Glen and the C line from 41st Street and Piedmont Avenue, provided connections to the ferry terminal in West Oakland. In 1924, the C line was extended to its terminus at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street in Piedmont. Following completion of the Bay Bridge, the Key System provided direct rail service on both lines to San Francisco. The No. 11 Oakland Avenue line ran from Rio Vista Avenue near the Kaiser Hospital up Piedmont Avenue to Linda Avenue, and then down Oakland Avenue and Broadway to 7th Street. The line was started as a part of Consolidated Piedmont Cable in 1892 and was later electrified. As a cable line, this route ascended the steep Oakland Avenue hill using a long gravity loop. This was not practical as an electric line, so the route was divided with the steep hill line abandoned, and the lower end diverted via a private rightof-way to Piedmont and Linda Avenues, thus avoiding the heavy grades. At the about time the Bay Bridge was opening in 1936, National City Lines, a small bus fleet in Minnesota, was organized into a holding company with equity funding from General Motors, Firestone Rubber, Phillips Petroleum, Standard Oil of California, and Mack Trucks. It began purchasing local transportation systems across the United States. It was a corporate conspiracy to monopolize the sale of buses across the United States, The buses were made by Mack and GM, that were exclusively fueled by Phillips and Standard gasoline, and driven on Firestone tires. By 1946, it controlled 46 transportation companies in 45 cities across 16 states. National City Lines tore up the tracks and the overhead wires and burned the trolley and train cars. In 1946, it acquired a majority stake of Key System stock and slowly began dismantling the system. The local streetcar lines were replaced by buses after World War II, with the right-of-ways converted to other uses, including parks and private homes. On June 26, 1948, the Key System rail service on Oakland Avenue was replaced by buses. The Transbay trains to Piedmont stopped running and the Key System was dismantled in 1958. In 1960, the Key System was sold to the newly formed public agency, AC Transit. In 1949, a Federal Court convicted National City Lines, General Motors, Standard Oil of California, Firestone Tire, and others of criminally conspiring to monopolize the sale of buses and related products to their subsidiary transit companies throughout the U.S. and violating the Sherman Anti-Trust Act. However, they were only fined $5,000. Some corporate executives were found criminally guilty, but only fined $1. With all this Key System information and understanding from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, the group was ready to walk. They started off going up Highland Avenue to Oakland Avenue which was part of the Number 10 line. The walkers turned down Oakland to Latham Street, the only Piedmont roadway named “street.” This was where the C line ended. Some of the houses that were built along Latham were noted for their long, narrow footprints that allowed them to fit on the strip of Key System right-of-way land after the trains stopped running. The walkers turned on Blair Avenue and went up York Drive. At Holly Place it was noted that this was once a stop on the C line, and that a pathway in the middle of the block on York goes up to Ricardo Avenue. This made it easier for riders to get to the trains. Charlene Louie shared old photos of the trains with still recognizable homes in the background. The group came to Arroyo Avenue, where the C line merged with the 10 line, and went down Pleasant Valley Avenue to Piedmont Avenue. The walkers went up Arroyo, crossed Pleasant Valley, and started up Rose Avenue. Rose is on the Piedmont/Oakland border with homes on its north side in Oakland and on the south side in Piedmont. The street also has some of Piedmont’s oldest homes. The group admired two Victorians, one of which was

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) will discuss Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper at its upcoming book meeting on August 16. Pepper’s Laboratories shows the “high profile antics of national politics,” and spotlights what can often be corruption in statehouses across the nation, which the author asserts pose the greatest threat to American democracy. The book outlines 30 steps that need to be taken, from federal action to individual steps, to help fight corruption in their own communities. Pepper is a writer, lawyer, former elected official, and served as the Chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party between 2015 and 2021. He earned his B.A. from Yale University and his J.D. from Yale Law School. The discussion will begin via Zoom at 5 p.m. on Tuesday, Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper August 16. You do not need to be a LWV member to join the book club discussion. Registration is required at: https:// lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx? page_id=4002&club_id=601389 &item_id=1749470&event_date_ id=255/.

articles.text: MB Jessee offers to paint the iconic gate at Lakeside Park Torii Gate at Lakeside Park in Oakland. The Oakland-Fukuoka Sister City Association (OFSCA) recently received a gift from Matt Jessee and his team of painters with MB Jessee Painting. The company generously donated their time and expertise to enhance the Torii Gate at Lakeside Park by Lake Merritt in Oakland. It is especially timely, since there will be an unveiling of a custom mosaic project by the sister cities of Oakland and Fukuoka, Japan on August 28. The Torii Gate is dedicated to the memory of Frank H. Ogawa, an Oakland City Council member who fostered a strong working relationship with the city of Fukuoka. The gate was erected on September 4, 2002 on the 40th anniversary of the Oakland-Fukuoka Sister City Relationship. The Oakland-Fukuoka Sister City Association is celebrating its 60th anniversary in August and will be hosting a delegation from Japan then in festivities honoring personal and business friendships. The sister city program between Oakland and Fukuoka began with U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower’s “people-to-people” program, which made the pairing of American communities with those abroad a national priority. OFSCA helps to promote cultural awareness, understanding, and friendships between the people and cities of Oakland and Fukuoka. “It is the belief that this collaboration will strengthen us as Matt Jessee, owner of MB Jessee Painting, in front of the Torii Gate. individuals, strengthen our cities, our regional communities and our Sister City organizations which will ultimately enhance international understanding and harmony between cities and nations,” said Valerie Lee Ow, OFSCA Board President. For further information, visit www.oakland-fukuoka.org. President of OFSCA Gary Tominaga, OFSCA Treasurer Liane Scott, Owner of MB Jessee Painting Matt Jessee, and OFSCA Board Member Valerie Lee. articles.text: ing, let us be cautious about what we are thankful for. I suppose it’s only human practice what I call “comparative gratitude”, that is, being thankful for things we have that others do not. But Jesus actually defined blessings as challenges. In his most famous sermon on the mount, he said, “Blessed are the hungry, blessed are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something that draws us toward a new and larger vision, maybe we should be thankful, not only for what we have now, but also for the opportunity to create and build something more inclusive, more peaceful, more beautiful, that might be described as one nation under God. Perhaps this understanding of what a real blessing is will help us not be discouraged by chaos, but rather, inspire us to pick up our shovels, hammers and levels and begin to build a better future for all. articles.text: Every home remodeling project is driven by budget and schedule. A reputable General Contractor will give you a detailed written scope of both. No doubt, you expect your contractor to stick to the deal. Every project will have surprises, what we call “unforeseen circumstances”. An old pipe in a wall, dry rot around a window, electrical wiring not up to code. These types of issues will increase the cost of your project, typically done by a written change order. More than two years into the pandemic, most of us have experienced some frustration with global supply chain issues. As remodelers, we are not immune. Some kitchen appliances have a 12-month lead time. Bathroom fixtures – even a simple towel bar - can take six months to arrive. Recessed lights are delayed by months because of computer chip shortages. Window production lead times can exceed six months. Orders of locally made tile, which relies on raw materials from abroad, are outstanding for up to eight months. Promised delivery dates are not being met. Does this impact your project’s budget and schedule? Yes! Using the example of tile, for a bathroom, if the product doesn’t arrive on time, a domino effect of delays occurs. Cabinetry, countertops, plumbing, electrical/lighting, finish carpentry and painting can all be pushed out. Add to this the overall high demand for qualified contractors and you have a scheduling disaster. No surprise – in remodeling, time equals money. So, what can you do? The first thing is, select a General Contractor who communicates with you from the beginning on potential issues. Be prepared that with any project delay you are likely to incur additional costs for materials, shipping and labor. Some homeowners expect their remodeler to pay for these extras since they contracted at a fixed price. With the small profit margins in construction, contractors are simply unable to absorb the additional costs. Even for the most experienced remodeler, the past couple of years have been a painful education. The good news is we have learned to not delay in decision-making. We order desired items immediately – even without a fully designed project. Homeowners are putting aside extra funds for unanticipated costs. The keys to maintaining a good contractor-client relationship are communication, transparency, patience and kindness. By looking for solutions, rather than faults, you’ll achieve your project goals and forge a lasting partnership. articles.text: Today, we’ll turn our attention to some of Piedmont’s more recent history. Readers of a certain age may remember fire alarm boxes. Before telephones were considered reliable, and before every house had a telephone, the fire alarm box was the main way to summon the fire department. Piedmont maintained more than 50 fire alarm boxes on street corners. To report a fire, you ran to the nearest fire alarm box, lifted the cover and pulled the handle. A blue light on top of the alarm box lit up when the alarm was activated. You were to stay at the alarm box to direct the firefighters to the fire. The boxes were connected directly to the Piedmont Fire Department through a low voltage wire which allowed them to work even in a power failure. The alarm box sent out a coded signal A photo of an early fire alarm box in Piedmont is in the Piedmont Historical Society collection. It originally had a blue light bulb on top that lit up when the alarm was activated. A ticker tape machine in the Piedmont Fire Station would receive the coded location of an activated fire alarm box. The ticker tape machine now is part of the collection of the Piedmont Historical Society – and still has ticker tape.

articles.text: Evans quickly moved into administration as Vice Principal, Principal, Associate Superintendent and Superintendent in several schools in San Diego, East Palo Alto, Oakland, Compton, and Hayward. He most recently was the Superintendent of Berkeley Unified School District from 2013-2019 before retiring. In retirement Evans has kept busy as mentor, consultant, and coach of several superintendents throughout the time of Covid. “I actually felt like I was going through it with them. I was there doing a lot of coaching,” he said. With teacher shortages across California, rising inflation, low retention rates faculty and teachers demanding raises, Evans views his fresh perspective as a resource. “I am hoping to do a lot of listening to the community to really know what they want. That’s really the great thing about being an outsider,” said Evans. Evans has experience with the similar levels of parent involvement for which Piedmont is well known. When teaching in Point Loma he said it was not unusual to see five or six parents in his classroom. “I really liked it. That type of involvement is something I actually appreciate,” said Evans. His time in Berkeley also provides him valuable familiarity in working with parents that demand the most out of their school district. “Berkeley parents are very involved and they’re very, very vocal. I think it’s a great thing,” said Evans “I see my role as: how do I facilitate the needs of our kids, along with the concerns parents might have, but also looking at what our teachers are providing. I just want to make sure our kids are competing at the highest level.” Evans is not the only newcomer for the 2022-2023 school year. McConathy cited the Park and Playground Act of 1909, codified in Government Code 3800. He explained to commissioners that a two-thirds city council majority vote and a ballot measure are “statutorily required before the city can abandon this dedicated park for housing.” He also pointed to the Park Preservation Act of 1971, which says a park cannot be sold, donated, or transferred to another governmental agency without “swap for comparative park space.” “If the city wants to use Blair Park for housing, it will need to create another park with comparable characteristics in town. articles.text: A Piedmont pedestrian was robbed at gunpoint by two young males who were arrested less than 24 hours later. The Rolex watch that had been stolen was returned to him (see photo). The male resident was walking near the intersection of Sea View and La Salle Avenues in Piedmont at 3:40 p.m. on Wednesday, July 6, when the two youth approached him. One suspect pointed a firearm at the victim while the other took the victim’s Rolex watch from his wrist. Automatic License Plate Readers captured images of the license plate numbers on the suspects’ red, four door, Nissan Altima with tinted windows. The suspects were described as Black males in their early 20’s, 5’5’’, 150 lbs. and wearing dark clothing. Within 24 hours, deputies from the Alameda County Sheriff’s office located the suspect vehicle in a parking lot at 151st Street and East 14th Street in San Leandro. Resident Mike McConathy cited numerous government codes that could hinder development in Blair Park. “Contrary to what [Lisa Wise] consulters are telling us, Piedmont is going to have serious problems with selling, donating, or transferring city park land for low income housing as proposed,” he said. McConathy cited the Park and Playground Act of 1909, codified in Government Code 3800. He explained to commissioners that a two-thirds city council majority vote and a ballot measure are “statutorily required before the city can abandon this dedicated park for housing.” He also pointed to the Park Preservation Act of 1971, which says a park cannot be sold, donated, or transferred to another governmental agency without “swap for comparative park space.” “If the city wants to use Blair Park for housing, it will need to create another park with comparable characteristics in town. This seems difficult with no other city-owned space,” he said. “The consultants and City Attorney [Michele Kenyon] have been suggesting that we can creatively skirt state law and public opinion by designating Blair Park as surplus land, but this is not as easy as they claim.” Jackson said that he was not prepared to respond to McConathy’s claim at that time. Planning Commission Chair Rani Batra added that the sites inventory is not a “plan to build,” but a plan to allow exploration by developers and the city. “The process that you look at a specific project - including cost [to build], impact on neighbors, and the community-at-large, is a public process that will continue when there is better and more specific information brought by a developer,” she said. “We’re making a commitment to the state of California that we will allow consideration for those sites.” Batra pointed to the sites inventory from the last 5th cycle draft housing element. “Not all of those sites have been built-out. Because, as you can imagine, the low-hanging fruit has already been built. We expect this next cycle will generate more housing, but I want to caution that we are not talking about every single site being maxed out within eight years. That’s not realistic with the pace of development or with the very real financial and physical constraints of these sites,” she said. articles.text: NASA describes this photo as follows: “What looks much like craggy mountains on a moonlit evening is actually the edge of a nearby, young, star-forming region NGC 3324 in the Carina Nebula.” NASA released the first high resolution photographs from the James Webb Space Telescope, on July 11. This striking image of star birth dubbed “‘Cosmic Cliffs” is 7,600 light years away and shows the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity in the Carina Nebula. The Webb telescope is a joint partnership of NASA, the European Space Agency and Canadian Space Agency. President Biden was given the honor of unveiling the first of the greatly awaited images on Monday, and four more were released yesterday. The James Webb telescope uses infrared light by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam). NIRCam was built by a team at the University of Arizona and Lockheed Martin’s Advanced Technology Center. This image reveals previously obscured areas of star birth. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, not seen, but above the image. The high-energy radiation from these stars sculps the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. NIRCam – with its crisp resolution and unparalleled sensitivity – unveils hundreds of previously hidden stars, and even numerous background galaxies. NASA explains the features in the image. The “steam” that appears to rise from the celestial “mountains” is actually hot, ionized gas and hot dust streaming away from the nebula due to intense, ultraviolet radiation. Dramatic pillars rise above the glowing wall of gas, resisting the blistering ultraviolet radiation from the young stars. Bubbles and cavities are being blown by the intense radiation and stellar winds of newborn stars. Protostellar jets and outflows, which appear in gold, shoot from dust-enshrouded, nascent stars. A “blow-out” erupts at the top-center of the ridge, spewing gas and dust into the interstellar medium. An unusual “arch” appears, looking like a bent-over cylinder. This period of very early star formation is difficult to capture since it lasts only about 50,000 to 100,000 years. The full set of the telescope’s first full-color images and spectroscopic data, which uncover a collection of cosmic features elusive until now, were released on July 12 and are available nu NASA at: Nasa.gov/webbfirstimages.
