This striking image of star birth dubbed “‘Cosmic Cliffs” is 7,600 light years away and shows the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity in the Carina Nebula. The Webb telescope is a joint partnership of NASA, the European Space Agency and Canadian Space Agency. President Biden was given the honor of unveiling the first of the greatly awaited images on Monday, and four more were released yesterday. The James Webb telescope uses infrared light by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam). NIRCam was built by a team at the University of Arizona and Lockheed Martin’s Advanced Technology Center. This image reveals previously obscured areas of star birth. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, not seen, but above the image. The high-energy radiation from these stars sculps the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. NIRCam – with its crisp resolution and unparalleled sensitivity – unveils hundreds of previously hidden stars, and even numerous background galaxies. NASA explains the features in the image. The “steam” that appears to rise from the celestial “mountains” is actually hot, ionized gas and hot dust streaming away from the nebula due to intense, ultraviolet radiation. Dramatic pillars rise above the glowing wall of gas, resisting Wednesday Walkers Continued from page 24 the blistering ultraviolet radiation from the young stars. Bubbles and cavities are being blown by the intense radiation and stellar winds of newborn stars. Protostellar jets and outflows, which appear in gold, shoot from dust-enshrouded, nascent stars. A “blow-out” erupts at the top-center of the ridge, spewing gas and dust into the interstellar medium. An unusual “arch” appears, looking like a bent-over cylinder. This period of very early star formation is difficult to capture since it lasts only about 50,000 to 100,000 years. The full set of the telescope’s first full-color images and spectroscopic data, which uncover a collection of cosmic features elusive until now, were released on July 12 and are available nu NASA at: Nasa.gov/webbfirstimages. built in 1895. The walkers went down Linda Avenue, where the 11 line once ran to Oakland Avenue and then downtown Oakland. Construction work being done on the path in the Linda Avenue Dog Park and the park was closed, but the walkers recognized that this area around Linda Avenue was once part of the 11 line. The group emerged on Grand Avenue and walked to Fairview Avenue. Again, Fairview was the top portion of the 12 line, so the group walked on the lower portion of the street where it becomes divided. The walkers found another pathway on this lower street that made it easier for residents to access the trains. This path connected Fairview with Nova Drive, and the walkers quickly got to Magnolia Avenue for their return climb up the hill to the Exedra. On their morning walk the group walked portions of all the Key System’s Piedmont lines in an hour and a half – with no transfers necessary. articles.text: Piedmont’s 55th annual July 4 parade was back in full swing Monday morning after a twoyear hiatus due to COVID. An estimated 2500 parade goers flooded Highland Avenue to see the parade, some sitting in chairs that were placed on the sidewalk as early as June 26. Piedmont’s own Uncle Sam, the celebrated artist Bruce Wolfe. Patti Edmonds’ bubble machine on the reviewing stand provided magic for paradegoers. Morning festivities began at 8 a.m. with the pre-parade pancake breakfast at Veterans Hall orchestrated by Piedmont Community Service Crew youth (see story on page 6). Diners enjoyed an al-fresco breakfast of sausages, fruit, pancakes, and coffee while being serenaded by the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band outside on the plaza. Floats and classic cars assembled at Highland and Park Way beginning at 10 a.m. City Council and school board members and other dignitaries climbed into their designated cars as the Zenith Parade Band practiced their first line tunes. Family photo opportunities were plentiful - the rainbow unicorn display at the Exedra, designed by the Piedmont Recreation Department, was a huge attraction, as was Smokey the Bear on one of the city’s fire engines. Piedmont Paramedic/Firefighter Matt Ziebarth went undercover as Smokey this year and took photos with many starstruck kids, who were then given tot-sized fire helmets by Fire Department staff. Piedmont Police officers were at each intersection along the route on Highland Avenue, greeting passersby and ensuring a safe event. The parade officially began at 11 a.m., with tuxedo-clad Roland Lazzarotto guiding all parade Cars in Piedmont’s parade move slowly down Highland Avenue. entries to their designated starting locations. Uncle Sam (Bruce Wolfe) and the Zenith band in the lead, Grand Marshal Dr. George Rutherford, Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration at UCSF, was driven in a 1960 Oldsmobile convertible. Rutherford was followed by Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, City Council members Jennifer Long, Conna McCarthy and Betsy Andersen, School Board members Veronica Thigpen, Megan Pillsbury, and Amal Smith, and new Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami. Making their first official appearance in the parade were Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales and family and Fire Chief Dave Brannigan with his wife and son. Youth Candy Ambassadors passed out sweet treats to kids and adults along the route. Also included in the parade was the TuTu School of Montclair, Oakland Zoo’s Zoomobile, League of Women Voters, Oakland brewery Line 51, Daughters of the American Revolution, Children’s Fairyland, Piedmont FoodFest volunteers, the Art Deco Society and Deco Belles, Skyline Lacrosse Club, and Oakland A’s Mascot “Stomper.” The Barrelhouse Jazz Band play Dixieland music on the W.A. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

When looking at Jesus in the temple, we don’t have much reference about him since his birth. This is inaugural in which he proclaims his personal mission. This is before he goes out to do all the good works. He selects a passage from a scroll. He could have chosen any number of passages, but he selected a passage from the prophet Isaiah. Before I go down that road, I want to discuss what you think of your personal mission statement. A mission statement is something that describes who you are and what you will achieve in the world. At St. John’s we say to manifest the love of God through the Holy Spirit with each other, our community and the world through worship, spiritual growth and Christian service. My question is, do you feel you manifest God’s love through the Holy Spirit? Do you do this with each other here in community, do you do this in the world? Do you do this through worship? Do you dedicate yourself to spiritual growth? What acts of Christian service do you perform? This is what we say at St. John’s, and I am curious if this aligns with your personal mission? articles.text: The Linda Beach off-leash dog park will be closed now through Friday, July 15. The city is replacing the concrete pathway in the park. Construction on the pedestrian pathway began yesterday and will be completed today, July 6. The pedestrian pathway that runs between Lake and Oakland Avenues was closed for two days to allow for construction trucks to haul out concrete debris. The park will remain closed for 10 days. For more information, contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050. Construction at Linda Dog Park began on July 5.

articles.text: The Piedmont-Montclair Rotary club’s annual pancake breakfast at the Veterans Hall feeds the masses before the 4th of July Parade. Alan Carr and his famous colorful parasol led the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band down Highland Avenue to open the Piedmont Fourth of July Parade. articles.text: On July 1 Angela Barrett began her tenure as Piedmont Middle School’s new Assistant Principal. She is filling the roll vacated by Karyn Shipp who was named principal with the move out of state by Ryan Fletcher. In an exclusive interview with the Post, Barrett discussed her aspirations in her new capacity. – Angela Barrett Piedmont Middle School Asst. Principal Q: What initially drew you to work with young people? How did you choose education? Was it to be an English teacher? A: When I was younger, I wanted to be an FBI agent. I really don’t know why. I grew up in Southern California and went to a comprehensive high school. I remember while going through high school I felt like I was lost in the cracks. That kind of changed me, and it got me passionate about young people in education. I saw so many of my peers who needed able to really build some deep relationships with kids. Then I started to notice things that needed attention in education in general. I realized that to really make the changes that I wanted to make, I couldn’t do it in the classroom. I needed a different role, and for me, that is administration. Q: What are your initial thoughts on what you’d like to do in your first year at Piedmont Middle School? A: I think first years are always years of learning. I really take the stance of being a learner. Every school, every district, has their own ways. In order for me to really understand where I can best provide support, I have to take that first step of observing and be a learner. My first year is really about learning the culture. Q: What did you see in terms of education loss due to COVID? What was going on at Envision and Nea during the pandemic? A: As an administrator, it was finding ways to support students and staff. The things our kids and our staff were experiencing were things we hadn’t encountered. I focused on being creative and trying to figure out how to give support and also push for the things that are important. I asked myself how can I balance both of those things and ensure that everybody feels supported? That was tough – very, very tough. articles.text: Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. Honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic home/office/gym/classroom/ playground space where we do separate things next to one another – enhances learning and creativity benefits for both. According to Richard Louv, author of The Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. Since March, I have had the Dragon fun at Children’s Fairyland. benefit of looking out of my magical window to see this notion unfolding each day; children and adults reestablishing their connection to play, the outdoors, and one another after 15 months of keeping too much of their energy and toxic stress inside, both literally and figuratively. I watch children become swashbuckling mates on a pirate ship, play peekaboo with a donkey, climb on the back of the happy dragon, or catch bubbles blown by an elf. I also see their adults running behind them full of glee, smiles, relief, and a cup of coffee. Ever yone deser ves this moment to explore, imagine, create, play, scream, and run. Invest in restorative self-care for the whole family—get outside and play. Kymberly Miller is Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, located on the shores of Lake Merritt in the heart of Oakland, California. Since 1950.

articles.text: There will always be a need for people who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, the Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers and provide credit to students. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute is a community-based non-profit with over 120 members. Founded in 1992 by Dr. Richard Bailey, teams of volunteers remove 5,000 pounds of trash from Lake Merritt. Clean ups are held five times a week during the school year and three to four times a week in the summer. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue, next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help/ for more information and scheduling. Piedmont Community Service Crew Did you have pancakes at the pre-parade breakfast on Monday? Those flapjacks were prepared entirely by Piedmont Community Service Crew students. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a youth-led organization that accepts students age 14 through 21. Members are mostly from Piedmont High School, but all are welcome to join. Students get hands-on experience in many facets and work closely with Rebuilding Together Oakland and take the complete responsibility for the renovation of a low-income elderly person’s home. The group also does meal preparation and cooking at St. Mary’s Senior Center, Alameda County Community Food Bank, Dream Catcher Diner, and more. The crew was founded in 2004 by Piedmont resident Ken Li. Visit https://www.pcservicecrew. org/new-member to sign up. Running for a Better Oakland Running for a Better Oakland (RBO) strives to build a tolerant, healthy, and prosperous community - through running. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute is a community-based non-profit with over 120 members. Founded in 1992 by Dr. Richard Bailey, teams of volunteers remove 5,000 pounds of trash from Lake Merritt. Clean ups are held five times a week during the school year and three to four times a week in the summer. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue, next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. Students get hands-on experience in many facets and work closely with Rebuilding Together Oakland and take the complete responsibility for the renovation of a low-income elderly person’s home. articles.text: Rafaella Gomes graduated from Piedmont High in 2021 and competes year-round on UC San Diego’s fencing program and with the Brazilian National Team. She recently competed with Brazil at the 2022 Pan American Fencing Championships from June 2-8 in Asunción, Paraguay, finishing 16th of 44 in the Foil Women’s Senior Individual category. She helped Brazil finish fourth of 10 teams and was the youngest competitor in her group, the result helped qualify her country for the 2023 event. She is now in the midst of training for the prestigious 2022 Senior World Championships in Cairo, Egypt on July 15-23. “When I am not competing for UC San Diego in the NCAA circuit, I am competing in the Brazilian national circuit, representing Brazil at international tournaments throughout the year. I tested positive for COVID following the event but was lucky enough to avoid the most serious condition. Now, I am back at practice with the Senior World Championships right around the corner,” said Gomes. Gomes continues to train with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, which is run by the Photos courtesy of cbesgrima.org.br Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, competes internationally with the Brazil National Team. She’s pictured here after winning Bronze at the 2022 Junior Pan American Championship. U.S. Men’s Foil Fencing Team coach Greg Massialas and routinely produces Olympic talent. She trained with the foundation for eight years prior to starting her collegiate fencing career. Rafaella Gomes reached the NCAA Championships with UC San Diego and is currently the world’s No. 100 ranked fencer in the senior category. Rafaella lets out an exuberant yell at the Senior Pan American Championship. She placed 16th overall and helped Brazil finish fourth. “I am far from where I want to be with my fencing, so I am in an intensive training program. I have practice at the Massialas Foundation every weekday and Saturdays for two hours. Practices includes 30 minutes of intense, fencing-specific footwork drills, an hour of fencing, and 30 minutes of one-on-one work with a coach,” described Gomes. As for her collegiate career at UC San Diego, Gomes had a remarkable freshman year. She reached the NCAA National Championship on March 27, and qualified for the prestigious tournament after taking silver at the NCAA West Regional Championship on March 12. She also finished second in the Mountain Pacific Sports Federation Fencing Championships’ Women’s Foil on March 13 and earned the MPSF Newcomer of the Year award. She said that her results at the NCAA Championship only fuels her fire after competing on short-rest from the Junior Pan American Championships shortly before. “I loved my first year in the NCAA. Next year, my goal is to qualify for NCAA Nationals again and place in the top 16. I arrived at the competition at 1 a.m. the morning of the tournament directly from the Junior Pan American Championships and was unable to perform my best. One of the biggest challenges I have faced is juggling a rigorous academic workload along with three independent competition circuits,” explained Gomes. Gomes is currently ranked No. 49 in the world’s junior category after taking bronze at the Junior Pan American Championship last March. She’s currently No. 100 globally in the senior category and has the third-highest senior ranking for the Brazil National Team. Look for more coverage of Rafaella following the 2022 Senior World Championship tournament in Cairo.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of TeamJumboVisa.com Wout van Aert currently holds the Yellow Jersey by leading the General Classification standings at the Tour de France through four stages. Nearing the completing of the first week of the 2022 Tour de France, the peloton is ascending into hills and mountains for the next eight stages. Belgium’s Wout van Aert of Jumbo-Visma currently leads the General Classification standings after placing second in the first three stages and an impressive win on Tuesday’s hill ride. It has been a strong first week for the Jumbo-Visma team with three of its riders in the top seven. Van Aert is considered one of the strongest sprinters in cycling but is usually slotted in as the team’s third rider behind Primož Roglič and Jonas Vingegaard, who are currently in sixth and seventh. Back-to-back defending champion Tadej Pogačar is in third, 32 seconds back of van Aert and seven back of second-place Yves Lampart, who is also from Belgium. The next week of riding could provide dramatic changes to the general classification standing. Photo courtesy of LeTour.fr Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar is in third, 32 seconds back of the lead. Photo courtesy of LeTour.fr Stage 7 this Friday is the first mountain stage of this year’s Tour de France.

Wednesday, July 6, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. KAI JOHNSON Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Weber State Class of 2025 Kai Johnson was a four-year starter at Piedmont High and recently completed her freshman year at Weber State. She appeared in 26 games last season, with 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one block. At Piedmont, she burst on the scene in 2017 and was the team captain for her final two years at the school. She was named nu the Post as 2021 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. She earned first-team All-League honors as a junior and senior a PHS. Johnson was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball program, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. What is your workout program this summer? On Mondays, I lift from 7:45- 8:30 a.m. followed by practice from 9-11:30 a.m. and individual training workout. Tuesdays, I have practices from 9-11:30 a.m. On Wednesdays I work in the gym and shoot during the day. Thursday, I lift from 7:45-8:30 a.m., practice, and then have a group workout. Friday includes practice from 9:30-11 a.m., lift from 11:30-12:45 p.m. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My one and only goal for my fitness is to get to a point where I can consistently keep running without getting tired, which is both physical and mental. How are you measuring your development? My development is measured through how I’m producing in practice. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m training by myself, with teammates, and coaches at school. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? A milestone is being able communicate effectively on the court while being tired. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? I would say work for what you want, because nothing is handed to you in sports at the collegiate level. You have to not only compete with yourself, but also with your teammates because you want a spot on the court. You have to work for the things you want, no matter if you’re a freshman, because that spot isn’t guaranteed. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Photo courtesy of WeberStateSports.com Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, just finished her freshman year at Weber State. Piedmont High Class of 2024 Natalia Martinez is entering her junior year at Piedmont High and was recently named the 2022 Sophomore of the Year by the Post. Her team went 24-7 last season and made the North Coast Section finals, where they were seeded #2. They lost to No. 1 Marin Catholic in the finals but qualified for their first CIF State Tournament in 11 years. Martinez scored 31 points in the second round of the State tourney in a game Piedmont lost by 7 points to No. 8 Lincoln. She earned first-team AllLeague honors and scored 19 points in the NCS Finals, while scoring 14 points in the second half. Martinez also exploded for 33 points in the NCS quarterfinals against St. Mary’s and 27 in the opening round with Swett. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program is to get my shots up when I wake up, usually about 5 am. Later on, I go to my team practice/workouts, whether it is high school or AAU. In the evening, I do some individual cardio, strength training, and stretching. What are your fitness goals for the summer? One of my fitness goals is to gain strength in my upper and lower body. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by setting deadlines and by tracking milestones. For example, one of my deadlines was to squat 120 before June 20th, and as of right now, I’m squatting 120 clean with no struggle. Staff Photo Natalia Martinez was the Post’s 2022 Sophomore of the Year and Freshman of the Year one year earlier. She enters a big junior season this winter. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I do workouts by myself all the time. I still work with my coaches in the offseason to get sharper, and I also work my trainer from Fit Evolution for lifting and conditioning. I would advise younger athletes to practice good fundamentals all the time in whatever sport you play, and don’t cut corners. Everyone has the same 24 hours and every day that passes is a chance for you to get better. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A milestone I recently achieved was receiving my first college scholarship offer. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? articles.text: With summer here, the Class of 2023 looks to next school year as a time that could be a defining year of their sports careers. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons ahead. WILSON WONG Volleyball Wilson Wong has been the volleyball team captain since his sophomore year, when the program began after an absence of 20 years. Last spring, Wong helped lead the team to qualify for the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs for the first time since 1999. Staff Photo Wilson Wong will be entering his third year as captain of the volleyball team. In the playoffs, Piedmont received the No. 11 seed and upset No. 6 Analy High School on the road in Sebastopol 3-2 on May 3. Wong was instrumental in Piedmont’s first-round win over Analy with five kills and six aces. Their trip in the playoffs ended with a 3-1 loss to Archie Williams in San Anselmo on May 5. The bulk of the Highlanders’ lineup from last season will be returning next spring, including Wong, John Champion, Kai Lambert, Owen Kelly, Brayden Day, Eric Olaru-Hagen, James MaNguyen, and Shunji Higashi. MOLLY ASHTON Lacrosse Photo by Todd Marshburn Molly Ashton earned an All-League selection last spring and will be a key player on the lacrosse team next spring. articles.text: Photos courtesy of McDonald’s official Instagram Mackie McDonald improved his world ranking five spots to No. 50 on the ATP ladder. Former Piedmont tennis star Mackie McDonald saw his trip to Wimbledon come to an end in the second round on Thursday, June 30, losing to Richard Gasquet of France in four sets, 6-3, 3-6, 6-4, 6-3. Despite the result, he improved his ATP World Ranking five positions to No. 50, one shy of his career high. Against Gasquet, who entered with the No. 69 world rank, McDonald was inconsistent while serving with 10 aces but committed eight double faults. He hit more winners than Gasquet (66), but committed 52 unforced errors compared to the Frenchman’s 27 – the clear difference in the match. McDonald had several opportunities in break points against Gasquet as the returner on serves but was only able to convert three of 16 attempts. He missed three break points in the last set, which he lost 6-3. Gasquet took his fifth and sixth-game match winner after McDonald held a break point opportunity in both games. Mackie opened the first set well but missed a break point with the set tied 2-2 to fall behind 3-2. He could have gone ahead 4-3 as the returner but missed break points while ahead 40-15 and 40-30. Gasquet eventually won 6-3. McDonald won the second set 6-3, but it was the only set he was able to claim. He took the third game as the returner and thwarted off Gasquet to win set-point while the Franchman was up 40-0, powering back to deuce and eventually take the set. But Gasquet won the third set cleanly 6-4, including set-point as the returner, charging ahead to 40-30, but McDonald couldn’t battle his way to deuce. The next Grand Slam tournament on the ATP Tour schedule is the U.S. Open from August 29 through September 11 as the schedule progresses into the Outdoor Hard-court phase. McDonald has historically competed in the Atlanta Open following Wimbledon, which is the first hard-court tournament on the ATP calendar. McDonald will look ahead to the hardcourt portion of the ATP schedule, and will likely compete in the Atlanta Open later this month.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald loses in second round at Wimbledon

pages.text: Wednesday, July 6, 2022 15 HIKING WITH JON Tilden Park’s Lake Anza and Jewel Lake By Jonathan Comeaux In Berkeley’s Tilden Park is an easy 4.9-mile loop that will take you by Lake Anza and Jewel Lake, some of its shining features without exerting much leg work with just 500 feet in elevation gain. It’s a perfect spot for hikers of all skill levels, including children and seniors. Lake Anza is formerly a popular swimming hole at Tilden, but it is currently closed due to harmful bacteria. It still provides a good starting point for your day of hiking. The lake was created by the construction of the Tilden Park Dam in 1938 and was named after Spanish explorer Juan Bautista de Anza. Jewel Lake is another manmade pond and a former reservoir along Wildcat Creek. Although the spillway has been dry for several years, it is still a great location to spot ducks and turtles resting on a plank in the middle of its water. With current construction at the Lake Anza parking lot, my day started on the northern end of the lake to venture along the Wildcat Gorge Trail – which Walking along the Wildcat Gorge Trail goes along Wildcat Creek. The pathway to Jewel Lake is shaded and surrounded with lush greenery. Take the Lower Packrat Trail on your right after venturing around Jewel Lake. The Selby Trail provides a great look at the Berkeley Hills. Staff Photos Lake Anza is the start of our day. The former recreational swimming hole was created in 1938. Jewel Lake is another quant location where you can spot ducks and turtles. travels adjacent to Wildcat Creek. The trail is a gorgeous walk under a canopy of Redwood trees, California Bay Laurel and Oak trees. The creek is mostly dry, but still has some good resting points. Walking for 1.2 miles, the path intersects with Central Park Drive, which leads to a bustling parking lot for Tilden’s Little Farm – a popular location for kids. After 0.4 of a mile, the parking lot becomes the Wildcat Creek trail. You’ll only be spending a brief time on the path, turning left after 0.2 of a mile towards the walkway leading to Jewel Lake. On the pathway, you’ll be surrounded by luscious green plants in all directions, making it a great spot to snap some photos with the sun reflecting off the leaves. The walking around Jewel Lake intersects with the Lower Packrat Trail, which you will walk along for 1.1 miles before traveling along the Selby Trail back to your car. The Selby Trail will remind you that it is goat season in the Bay Area, where much of the path will be fenced off on your right side as hundreds of goats graze in the hills to remove underbrush to eliminate fuel for potential wildfires. In addition to some close exposures to your barnyard friends, the path gives some great views of the Berkeley hills. Walking 1.6 miles on the Selby Trail takes you back to your car at the Lake Anza parking lot. Regarding foot traffic, we passed a total of 43 people on a Saturday around noon. The majority on the Wildcat Gorge and Wildcat Creek trails. I passed just five people on the Packrat trail and only two on the Selby Trail, so if you’re craving some solitude, you can stick to the Selby and Packrat trails to bypass other hikers and still reach the same locations. You’ll pass by grazing goats along the Selby Trail. The tail end of the Selby Trail has a beautiful grove of Redwood trees.

articles.text: Museum to celebrate opening of Diego Rivera’s America San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is celebrating the opening of an exhibit titled Diego Rivera’s America with a free day of community activities and art on Sunday, July 17 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Diego Rivera’s America is an in-depth examination of the artist’s work and brings together more than 150 of Rivera’s paintings and drawings. The exhibition focuses on the artist’s work from the 1920’s to the mid-1940’s. In partnership with City College of San Francisco, Diego Rivera’s Pan American Unity mural has been made free-to-the-public in the Roberts Family Gallery on the first floor of the museum. Visitors will gain admission to the museum for free that day, Howard Street Entrance, Floor 1 Theater, Floor 1 Peterson White Box, Floor 4 Koret Education Center, Floor 2 Floor 2 Charles Schwab Hall, Floor 2 Charles Schwab Hall, Floor 2 Schwab Hall, Floor 2 Peterson White Box, Floor 4 San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and will see a display of lowrider vehicles outside on Third Street and a mercado featuring arts and crafts by local artisans. A digital mural installation by Lauren Rose D’Amato and Derek Holguin will be accompanied with a performance by local musician and activist La Doña. Dance performances will be curated by SFMOMA’s community partner-in-residence Accíon Latina, including Grupo Jaranero Yucatán, Inti Batey, Carlos Aguirre, Edna Mira Raia and more. Admission for Diego Rivera’s America requires timed tickets and has limited capacity. Reserve your slot in advance by visiting tickets.sfmoma.org. A schedule of the day’s events is listed below.

articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Bejing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei?utm_medium=email&utm_source=famsfmktg&utm_campaign=guopei&utm_content=consideration_20220408&mc_cid=e- 25a62443e&mc_eid=573801a180 to obtain tickets. Photo by Drew Altizer The magnificent gold gown from the “Samsara (Lifecycle)” collection is currently on view in the “Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy” exhibit at the Legion of Honor museum in San Francisco.

articles.text: The 18th annual “Sculpture in the Garden” continues at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek through the summer. Sculpture in the Garden is the annual art show and sale that combines sculptural art with the natural sculptural beauty of the Garden. All sculptures in the Garden are for sale. Admission to the event is free with regular garden admission. Featured artists include Ana Bianchi, Joe Bologna, Kevin Byall, Larry Colvin, Henriette Cons Ponte, Tam Doan, Jake Edwards, Douglas Heine, Roger Heitzman, Stan Huncilman, and Karina Kudymova. For a full list of artists, and to purchase general admission tickets, visit https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/sculpture-show-2022/. The gardens are located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. Phone (925) 944- 9352. “Neural Anemone” by Kevin Byall is located at Sculpture in the Garden at Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek.

Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli, and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Ever y T hu rsd ay n ig ht throughout the summer, Bluebird Bar is serving margaritas and a selection of wine and beers in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. Cochinita Food Truck serves tacos, burritos, fried plantains and more from 5 to 7:30 p.m. And, a live, traditional Irish Session Band will play at the pool pavilion from 5:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. each evening. articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert celebrating composer Harry Warren this Sunday, July 10. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of the most successful film composers; Warren has composed music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and piaIn the Tradition Piano Trio nist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at https://bpt.me/5316993 or at the door. San Francisco Symphony shown performing at Stern Grove in 2013. The Symphony is a regular headliner of the summer music festival.
articles.title: In the Tradition Piano Trio concert at PCA this Sunday

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet goes dark for the majority of the summer but will have two days of performances August 5 and 6. The company will perform a program of three short ballets under the stars at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheater. The program includes Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight, Jerome Robbin’s In the Night, and William Forsythe’s Blake Works I. The short ballets range greatly in theme and choreography set to the music of Bach, Chopin and James Blake. Both performances will begin at 8 p.m. Frost Amphitheater is located at 351 Lasuen Street on the Stanford University campus in Palo Alto. Visit https://www. sf ballet.org/calendar/starrynights-at-stanford-live/ to purchase tickets. Photo by Erik Tomasson Hansuke Yamamoto and Daniel Deivison-Oliveira in Tomasson’s 7 For Eight

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony will close out this month’s performances at Stern Grove Festival, a series of free music festivals at an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. Conductor Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser and violinist Benjamin Beilman join San Francisco Symphony for this special outdoor performance. The program includes music by Nicolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Sergei Prokofiev, Dinuk Wijeratne, Johannes Brahms, and Igor Stravinsky. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization that presents free music festivals in the city since its inception in 1938. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The concert begins at 2 p.m. Reservations are required to attend. Attendees may bring food and drinks to the festivals. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2021-22/SUMMER-22-Stern-Grove to reserve tickets.

articles.text: The 5th annual San Francisco International Piano Festival, a range of concerts spanning 10 days, opens August 18 with a celebration of J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier. “In the midst of much turbulence and tragedy in our world, we continue to make music and celebrate the unstoppable force that is the creative spirit,” said festival founder and artistic director Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist and one of the festival’s artists. “The 300th anniversary of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier provides a natural focus that the festival will explore in both conventional and unexpected performances.” The festival will be presented in five venues between August 18 and 28 in San Francisco and Berkeley. It will feature 15 artists, including eight pianists, and 18 composers, ranging from Bach to contemporary. For information on concerts, repertoire, festival artists, ticketing links and COVID-related restrictions, visit sfpiano.org. pages.text: Wednesday, July 6, 2022 19 In the Tradition Piano Trio concert at PCA this Sunday By Allyson Aleksey In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert celebrating composer Harry Warren this Sunday, July 10. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of the most successful film composers; Warren has composed music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and piaIn the Tradition Piano Trio nist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at https://bpt.me/5316993 or at the door. San Francisco Symphony shown performing at Stern Grove in 2013. articles.text: The Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates returning to live concerts this summer with three public performances at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening July 20. Festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist: Deborah Pae. Cello A member of the Formosa Quartet with Festival founder Wayne Lee, Deborah Pae returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for the fifth year. Praised by critics for her “focused intensity…superb tone” and “high level of interpretative intelligence,” Korean-American cellist Deborah Pae has received international acclaim for her powerful performances and devotion to the arts. She has appeared as soloist, recitalist, and chamber musician throughout the United States, Europe, Canada, and Asia, at venues including Carnegie Hall, Auditorium du Louvre in Paris, London’s Wigmore Hall, Taipei’s National Concert Hall, and the 45th GRAMMY Awards at Madison Square Garden. Cellist of the award-winning Formosa Quartet and founding member of Namirovsky-Lark-Pae Trio, she has been a featured artist at Marlboro and Ravinia festivals, and has recorded numerous solo and chamber music works for radio and television broadcast as well as for labels including New World, TYXarts, Bridge, and Outhere Records. Committed to mentoring the next generation of young artists, Ms. Pae is Professor of Cello at Eastern Michigan University in Ypsilanti. Tickets are $45, with a savings on season passes for all three concerts for $120. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in Piedmont.

articles.text: The Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, now in its fifth year with performances the week of July 18 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is seeking a few families who would like to host one or two guest musicians. The festival in Piedmont is the only residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, and a source of great pride to the community, modeled on the annual Bach Festival in Carmel, where guest musicians and families make lifelong connections and friendships. Host responsibilities are to provide a private room and bath and light breakfast, and if possible, transportation to morning rehearsals at PCA. All other meals and transportation are taken care of. articles.text: A scene from the Coen brother’s movie, A Serious Man. Review by Chris Honoré Known for their original sometimes off-center films, the prolific Coen Brothers have been at work refining and expanding their craft since 1991. During that time, they’ve garnered eight Academy Award nominations, and won three Oscars for No Country for Old Men. Their films are wide ranging, from comedies to thrillers, some unflinchingly violent while others meld various genres. They’re also known for boxing the compass regarding settings: O Brother Where Art Thou? was set in the South during the Great Depression; Fargo in the Dakotas; No Country for Old Men in the Southwest; The Big Lebowski on the West Coast; and Burn After Reading in D.C. Of all their films, A Serious Man, released in 2009, may be their most contemplative if not their most personal. It focuses on Larry Gopnik (Michael Stuhlberg), a physics professor, married, two children and a man about to experience a major existential crisis. Like dominos falling, he is suddenly faced with a series of unexpected developments: his wife, Judith (Sari Lennick), announces she has fallen in love with Sy Ableman (Fred Melamed) and wants a divorce; his neighbor, an anti-Semite, is encroaching on his yard; his much anticipated tenure seems in jeopardy; his son, on the cusp of his bar mitzvah, is a pothead; his daughter wants a nose-job; and his brother, Arthur (Richard Kind), is sleeping on the sofa and prone to crying jags when he’s not up late at night, lancing a boil on his neck. Though the cultural context is a Midwestern Jewish community in 1967, Larry’s abiding angst is strikingly universal. His life is out of control. Perpetually perplexed, Larry tries to cope and keep up, but he can’t summon the will to strongly react. He is drowning in reasonableness as his life slips into a grim comedy of errors, as if the universe is conspiring against him. And though he never laughs, or even smiles, clearly the Coens believe that humor may be, at least for the audience, the only refuge. A Serious Man is a character study that frustrates and infuriates and happily entertains. Life sorts itself out and that pervasive sense of perplexed despair eventually morphs into something more positive, more manageable. It just requires a bit of tenacity – being tenaciously reasonable. A Serious Man. Written and Directed by Joel and Ethan Coen. Starring Michael Stuhlbarg, Fred Melamed, Jessica McManos, Richard Kind, Adam Arkin, Sari Lennick and Aaron Wolff. 1 hr. 45 min. Rated R. Released in theaters in 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS A Serious Man a contemplative story

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The iconic fantasy adventure Peter Pan, a timeless allegory, was co-written by director P.J. Hogan. It’s a live-action film based on J.M. Barrie’s 1911 novel, and, when fully titled, is referred to as The Boy Who Wouldn’t Grow Up. It was released into theaters in 2003 and is now streaming. This incarnation, with a darker, edgier tone stars Jeremy Sumpter as cocky, self-confident Peter, who is not only an American actor but also male, as opposed to the fact that the character Peter Pan of the past has always been played by pixie-like women (think Mary Martin). The story begins in an Edwardian London nursery where teen Wendy Darling (Rachel Hurd Wood) is telling a riveting story to her younger brothers John (Harry Newell) and Michael (Freddie Poppelwell). Meanwhile, Peter Pan is listening to Wendy’s tale just outside the nursery window, intrigued by her narrative and ability to create a mesmerizing tale. The adventure begins when Peter, with the help of the magical fairy dust of the astonishing Tinker Bell (Ludville Sagnier), invites the children to fly with him to Neverland where Wendy can meet the Lost Boys and tell them her stories. She soon becomes a surrogate mother to the remarkable clan. This version of Peter Pan makes a valiant attempt to remain true to Barrie’s original story. There is, naturally, the often nefarious, scary, flying Captain Hook (John Isaac) who has the ability to change his missing arm (bitten off by an alligator) as he pleases. Meanwhile Wendy’s mother, Mrs. Darling (Olivia Williams) is at home worried about her missing children. The Lost Boys are continually intriguing, and Hook’s pirate ship is wonderful. As is Tinker Bell, nicknamed Tink by Peter. And let’s not forget the confrontation between Wendy, on the verge of womanhood, and Peter who makes it clear to her that he wishes never to grow up. Their budding romance, however, is ever present. The film is filled with scary moments, lots of action, sword fights, amazing flights across the sky, and the remarkable Asiatic mermaids who emerge from the Neverland lagoon. This version of Peter Pan is a magical adventure that will capture tweens and teens, as if pixie dust had been sprinkled on every scene. Peter Pan. Directed by P.J. Hogan. Live-action adventure, fantasy. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released into theaters in 2003. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Jeremy Sumpter as Peter Pan.
articles.title: 2003 remake of Peter Pan a lovely film

It focuses on Larry Gopnik (Michael Stuhlberg), a physics professor, married, two children and a man about to experience a major existential crisis. Like dominos falling, he is suddenly faced with a series of unexpected developments: his wife, Judith (Sari Lennick), announces she has fallen in love with Sy Ableman (Fred Melamed) and wants a divorce; his neighbor, an anti-Semite, is encroaching on his yard; his much anticipated tenure seems in jeopardy; his son, on the cusp of his bar mitzvah, is a pothead; his daughter wants a nose-job; and his brother, Arthur (Richard Kind), is sleeping on the sofa and prone to crying jags when he’s not up late at night, lancing a boil on his neck. Though the cultural context is a Midwestern Jewish community in 1967, Larry’s abiding angst is strikingly universal. His life is out of control. Perpetually perplexed, Larry tries to cope and keep up, but he can’t summon the will to strongly react. He is drowning in reasonableness as his life slips into a grim comedy of errors, as if the universe is conspiring against him. And though he never laughs, or even smiles, clearly the Coens believe that humor may be, at least for the audience, the only refuge. A Serious Man is a character study that frustrates and infuriates and happily entertains. Life sorts itself out and that pervasive sense of perplexed despair eventually morphs into something more positive, more manageable. It just requires a bit of tenacity – being tenaciously reasonable. A Serious Man. Written and Directed by Joel and Ethan Coen. Starring Michael Stuhlbarg, Fred Melamed, Jessica McManos, Richard Kind, Adam Arkin, Sari Lennick and Aaron Wolff. 1 hr. 45 min. Rated R. Released in theaters in 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Peter Pan. 2003 remake of Peter Pan a lovely film Review by Chris Honoré The iconic fantasy adventure Peter Pan, a timeless allegory, was co-written by director P.J. Hogan. It’s a live-action film based on J.M. Barrie’s 1911 novel, and, when fully titled, is referred to as The Boy Who Wouldn’t Grow Up. It was released into theaters in 2003 and is now streaming. This incarnation, with a darker, edgier tone stars Jeremy Sumpter as cocky, self-confident Peter, who is not only an American actor but also male, as opposed to the fact that the character Peter Pan of the past has always been played by pixie-like women (think Mary Martin). The story begins in an Edwardian London nursery where teen Wendy Darling (Rachel Hurd Wood) is telling a riveting story to her younger brothers John (Harry Newell) and Michael (Freddie Poppelwell). Meanwhile, Peter Pan is listening to Wendy’s tale just outside the nursery window, intrigued by her narrative and ability to create a mesmerizing tale. The adventure begins when Peter, with the help of the magical fairy dust of the astonishing Tinker Bell (Ludville Sagnier), invites the children to fly with him to Neverland where Wendy can meet the Lost Boys and tell them her stories. She soon becomes a surrogate mother to the remarkable clan. This version of Peter Pan makes a valiant attempt to remain true to Barrie’s original story. There is, naturally, the often nefarious, scary, flying Captain Hook (John Isaac) who has the ability to change his missing arm (bitten off by an alligator) as he pleases. Meanwhile Wendy’s mother, Mrs. Darling (Olivia Williams) is at home worried about her missing children. The Lost Boys are continually intriguing, and Hook’s pirate ship is wonderful. As is Tinker Bell, nicknamed Tink by Peter. And let’s not forget the confrontation between Wendy, on the verge of womanhood, and Peter who makes it clear to her that he wishes never to grow up. Their budding romance, however, is ever present. The film is filled with scary moments, lots of action, sword fights, amazing flights across the sky, and the remarkable Asiatic mermaids who emerge from the Neverland lagoon. This version of Peter Pan is a magical adventure that will capture tweens and teens, as if pixie dust had been sprinkled on every scene. Peter Pan. Directed by P.J. Hogan. Live-action adventure, fantasy. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released into theaters in 2003. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Jeremy Sumpter as Peter Pan. articles.text: There were three other Key System lines in Piedmont, and the walkers thought it would be interesting to see where they ran. The route of the No. 12 line in Piedmont was selected as the morning’s destination on June 29. Before starting off, a short review of the Key System was provided as a refresher for those on the previous walk, and an introduction for those who hadn’t been on it. In the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay population grew in the late 1800’s, developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established The Realty Syndicate. This company acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay for homes. Potential buyers needed transportation to get from their new homes to work in the area and in San Francisco. The Key System was conceived by Borax Smith as a way to sell The Realty Syndicate’s land. The Key System began service in 1903 in Berkeley, and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. Some background information on the No. 12 Line was also shared before the group started off. It was originally called the “Grand Avenue & Hollis Street Line.” At its fullest, this line went along Oakland, Fairview, Grand, Webster, 14th, Market, 24th, Adeline, 32nd, Hollis, to Yerba Buena. The Grand Avenue & Hollis Street line began as a shuttle on Grand Avenue from Wildwood Avenue, at the city limits, to Perry Street near where Oakland Avenue and the MacArthur Freeway are today. The line connected there with cars of the Lakeshore Avenue line. In 1915 the end of the line was extended from Grand Avenue up Fairview Avenue. The route had a few name changes over the years, but in 1928 its name was finalized as the “No. 12” line.” However, on June 27, 1948 the No. 12 Grand Avenue streetcar service was abandoned, and buses replaced the service. The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, then down Jerome Avenue on their way to Fairview. They couldn’t pass up the opportunity to walk up the charming, short Keefer Court cul-de-sac. This street has a home at its end with a marvelous, cactus garden front yard that is a delight to see. Other homes have a similar look. Long-time walkers remembered stories of how the homeowner transformed his garden to the marvel that it is today from what was an ordinary yard. After enjoying Keefer, it was on to Fairview. It was noted that the Key System C Line, which ran to San Francisco, ended across the now visible Oakland Avenue at Latham Street, the only Piedmont street with the name “street.” The group made their way down Fairview and then up to its high point at the intersection of Arbor Drive, where there is a Thirty-one members of the Walking on Wednesdays group gathered in front of the house at Fairview Avenue and Arbor Drive for a group photo on June 29. Pictured are Noemi Alvarado (left), Harriette Louie, Jim Kellogg, Priscilla Wanerus, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Swee Ling Chen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Quincy Dong, Mike Henn, Sherry Jacobs, Brenda Ferrero, Albert Chen, Bob Wong, Jim Kuo, Alicia Rivera, Alan Goldhammer, Martin Levy, Edith Lee, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Helen Dong, Cheryl Stanton, Judy Wong, Mary Carter, Renee Goldhammer, Charlene Louie, Melba Yee, Stella Houston, and Dick Carter. The group welcomed first time walker Tracy Lee and veteran walker Matt Gerhardt, who last year created a map and narrative of a self-guided walking tour of the perimeter of Piedmont.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost-making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials then can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. More information can be found at the City’s news and notifications page. Contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov or (510) 420-3058 if you have any questions. Staff photo Visit the Corp. Yard to pick up free compost. Bring your own gloves, shovel, and bag.

articles.text: The popular Dress Best for Less bag sale continues at the same location on the last Saturday of the month. From 10 a.m. to noon residents can fill a paper grocery bag with items like clothing, toys, and books for $10 at the Marking Room, 799 Magnolia Avenue. Founded in 1982 by Piedmont resident Wendy Willrich and a group of Havens School moms, Dress Best is a way to collect unneeded household items and clothing to sell to the community to raise money for the school district. They were given an unused room at Havens School, but quickly outgrew the space and rented a storefront on Piedmont Avenue, their original retail location. DBFL donates most of its profits to the Piedmont Education Foundation, a non-profit that raises money for Piedmont schools. DBFL has donated more than $1 million since its inception. Donations that cannot be sold in the store are donated to other non-profits. The store gives back to the broader community by donating to St. Vincent de Paul, Children’s Hospital, and animal rescue organizations in the East Bay. More than half of clothing donations received by DBFL are donated to St. Vincent de Paul, helping families in need in Alameda County through gifts made directly to them or through proceeds made from the store. These proceeds allow the organization to provide food, rent, job training and other services to those in need. DBFL also donates children’s items to Love Twice, a non-profit organization that provides newborns in need with quality baby clothing for the first year of life. Donations of gently used, high Dress Best Marking room is located at 799 Magnolia Avenue. quality clothing and home goods are welcome, and all donations are tax deductible. The retail store is at 4020 Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. Store hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. DBFL’s marking room for sales and donations is by appointment only. Visit http://dressbestforless.org/donate/ to make an appointment. The group continued on down Fairview to Grand Avenue where they saw the long stretch of land that separates the upper and lower portions of the street. This was once right of way Key System land where the trains ran. The group went to Grand and noted a rare city limits sign that said they were now in Oakland, went past Grand Piedmont Liquors and turned up Boulevard Way, where they passed the Piedmont Post’s office. Before continuing on Boulevard, they walked up the short portion of Crofton Avenue that is in Piedmont; so they could include it in the Piedmont streets they had walked. The walkers turned up Warfield Avenue, and on their way to Wildwood Avenue, they noticed two places where broken pieces of ceramics had been cemented into holes in the sideway. Not only were they unique and attractive, but they also filled the holes. The group passed Wildwood School, entered Piedmont Park, and made their way back to the Community Hall and town center. It had been a beautiful morning with old and new friends, seeing another part of the historic Key System, and other interesting parts of Piedmont and Oakland. There will be three ascents, first 13.3 kilometers up Cole des Mosses, followed by a steep 7.6 percent grade up Col de la Croix for 8.8 kilometers and long descent. The final climb is a long 15.4 kilometers at a 6.1 percent grade up Pas de Morgins. The tour has only visited Châtel once, which was in 1975 when another Belgian, Lucien van Impe, won a time trial from France’s Morzine to Châtel, notably defeating legendary cycling legend Eddy Merckx. I’ve attended four college camps, including Cal Poly, UC Davis, San Jose State, and the University of California. I’ve also gained weight, height, and got faster, in addition to learning more offensive and defensive techniques. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My advice is to enjoy every minute of your sport; the time goes by quickly and can be taken away at any time. Workout on your off time by yourself or with friends. Finish what you start, show up early and stay late. Follow your dreams and give 100 percent every time you step on the field. Always have a good attitude and be grateful to all the coaches and your parents who support you.
